puzzles.title: The Rain Rule
puzzles.question: If it rains, the match is cancelled. It rained this morning. What necessarily follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. This is modus ponens: the rule guarantees cancellation whenever rain happens, and rain happened.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the match is off. The conditional 'if rain then cancelled' plus the fact of rain forces the conclusion by modus ponens. Any other option quietly denies a premise.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Modus ponens is the simplest guaranteed-valid argument form: if P then Q; P; therefore Q.
Logicians call it affirming the antecedent — the rule's trigger fires, so the consequence must follow.
Its power is unconditional: once both premises hold, the conclusion cannot fail.
Refund policies, warranties and cancellation rules are all written as conditionals, and applying them is pure modus ponens.
Share this: next time a policy says 'if X then Y' and X happens, ask a friend whether Y is now guaranteed.

puzzles.title: The Alarm Test
puzzles.question: If the alarm works, it beeps when tested. It did not beep when tested. What can you conclude?
choices: The alarm never beeps at all
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — modus tollens. A working alarm would have beeped; the silence rules out the working alarm.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the alarm is not working. Since a functional alarm must beep on test, the missing beep eliminates that possibility — modus tollens in action. A dead battery is a possible cause, but it is an extra guess the premises never mention.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Modus tollens runs a conditional backwards by negation: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
It is the logical engine of debugging — a missing expected effect eliminates the assumed cause.
Scientists use it constantly: a failed prediction kills the hypothesis that predicted it.
The only trap is confirming that Q truly failed — silence only counts when silence is impossible.
Share this: when something expected doesn't happen, trace which if-then rule just got falsified.

puzzles.title: Wet Ground Logic
puzzles.question: If it rained, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Is the conclusion 'it rained' logically valid?
choices: Yes — wet ground proves rain fell
Yes — rain is the only source of moisture
No — something else could have wet it
No — the ground must be dry
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — something else could have wet it
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — this is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. The rule runs from rain to wet, not backwards.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: something else could have wet it. A sprinkler, a hose, or a spilled bucket all produce wet ground without rain. Affirming the consequent treats 'if P then Q' as if it were 'if Q then P', which is exactly the trap here.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Affirming the consequent is the classic broken inference: if P then Q; Q; therefore P.
The rule points one way, but the effect usually has many possible makers.
Doctors and detectives live inside this gap daily: a symptom fits a cause without proving it.
The repair is asking what else produces the same effect before committing to one explanation.
Share this: catch one headline today that assumes a single cause and ask aloud what else fits.

puzzles.title: Missed the Train
puzzles.question: If you catch the 8:00 train, you arrive by noon. You missed the 8:00 train. Does it follow that you cannot arrive by noon?
choices: Yes — she cannot arrive by noon
Yes — noon arrival requires that exact train
No — another route could still arrive by noon
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — another route could still arrive by noon
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — denying the antecedent. The rule only promises the noon arrival for that train; it says nothing about other ways to arrive.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: another route could still arrive by noon. The premise guarantees that the 8:00 train suffices, never that it is necessary — denying the antecedent treats sufficiency as if it were exclusivity.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Denying the antecedent mistakes a sufficient condition for a necessary one: if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q.
The rule never said P was the only route to Q — other doors may stand open.
'Guaranteed by' and 'only achievable through' are different claims entirely.
Schedule logic, guarantees and eligibility rules all run on this distinction.
Share this: reread one guarantee today and ask whether it promises sufficiency or exclusivity.

puzzles.title: The Chain Rule
puzzles.question: Every emerald is harder than every opal. Every opal is harder than every pearl. If E is an emerald and P is a pearl, what follows?
choices: E and P are equally hard
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — hardness chains by transitivity: emerald over opal, opal over pearl, so emerald over pearl.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: E is harder than P. 'Harder than' is transitive — if E outranks the opal and the opal outranks the pearl, E outranks the pearl. Any other ranking reverses or ignores the chain.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Transitivity lets relations chain: if A outranks B and B outranks C, then A outranks C.
Not every relation obeys it — 'beats' in rock-paper-scissors famously loops instead of chaining.
Orderings like taller than, earlier than and heavier than chain safely; preferences and pairwise votes can cycle.
Spotting which relations transfer is a quiet superpower in rankings and comparisons.
Share this: next time you see a ranking, ask whether the relation actually chains or just loops.

puzzles.title: The Shared Label
puzzles.question: All chess players are strategists. All generals are strategists. Does it follow that all chess players are generals?
choices: Yes — both groups use strategy daily
Yes — one strategist group contains the other
No — the middle term is undistributed
No — chess players are not strategists
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — the middle term is undistributed
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Both groups merely sit inside 'strategists' — nothing says they overlap each other.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the middle term is undistributed. Sharing a category with something does not put you inside it — that is the fallacy of the undistributed middle. The premises place chess players and generals inside 'strategists' but never connect the two groups directly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The undistributed middle is the shared-category trap: all A are C; all B are C; therefore all A are B.
Both groups live inside the same tent, but the tent's floor plan never connects them.
Venn-diagram thinking defuses it instantly — draw the big circle and watch the two groups drift apart inside it.
The same trap powers stereotypes: sharing one label with a group says nothing about overlapping further.
Share this: catch one 'they're all the same' claim today and name the shared tent doing the work.

puzzles.title: Mutual Exclusion
puzzles.question: 'No ghosts are physicists.' Which statement follows with certainty?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — E-propositions convert cleanly: mutual exclusion runs both directions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: no physicists are ghosts. 'No A are B' converts to 'No B are A' because exclusion is symmetric. The other options sneak in existence or overlap that the premise never grants.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'No A are B' converts cleanly to 'No B are A' — exclusion is symmetric, so the flip costs nothing.
Conversion is safe for exclusions and for 'some' statements, the two shapes logic can flip without loss.
Universals of the 'all' type do not convert — flipping those is the illicit move.
Knowing which statements flip is half of traditional syllogistic craft.
Share this: take one 'no X are Y' claim you hear and enjoy that it reverses for free.

puzzles.title: Overlap Proof
puzzles.question: 'Some poets are engineers.' What follows necessarily?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — partial overlap is symmetric: the same people counted from either side.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: some engineers are poets. If at least one person is both, then reading the overlap from the engineering side gives the same result — I-propositions convert. Widening 'some' to 'all' or denying the overlap both overstate the premise.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Some A are B' converts as well: the overlap is the very same people counted from either side.
This is why partial-overlap statements feel reversible — one direction hands you the other.
The conversion preserves quantity: 'some' never inflates to 'all' or collapses to 'none' by flipping.
Careful reading of surveys and statistics is mostly careful tracking of which direction was claimed.
Share this: find one 'some' claim today and state its converse — notice it costs you nothing.

puzzles.title: The Reverse Trap
puzzles.question: 'All drones are machines.' Which statement is NOT guaranteed by this alone?
choices: Every drone counts as a machine
Drones belong to the machine family
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — reversing a universal is illicit. The premise puts drones inside machines, not the other way around.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 'all machines are drones' is not guaranteed. 'All A are B' never implies 'All B are A' — that is illicit conversion. The other options merely restate or weaken the original claim, which is always safe.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'All A are B' cannot be flipped: B is usually the larger set, and A merely sits inside it.
Logicians call the flip illicit conversion — swapping subject and predicate of a universal breaks it.
The classic instance: all roses are flowers, yet not all flowers are roses.
Subset-to-superset is a one-way street; remember it and half of category errors vanish.
Share this: catch one category flip in conversation today and gently reverse it back.

puzzles.title: The Age Chain
puzzles.question: All kids are learners. All learners are curious. All curious minds ask questions. If Mia is a kid, what follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — the chain links kid to learner to curious to questioner, so membership travels all the way down.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mia asks questions. This is a sorites — three universal links chained together — and each one carries Mia's membership forward. The other options break a link the premises never break.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A sorites chains several universals into one conveyor: A to B to C to D carries membership the whole way.
The name is Greek for heap — the original puzzle asked when grains become a heap.
Each link must be universal; a single 'some' or 'most' anywhere breaks the chain's guarantee.
Long eligibility rules and cascading requirements are sorites in the wild.
Share this: pick one multi-step requirement you know and check whether every link truly says 'all'.

puzzles.title: Two Doors
puzzles.question: Either the butler or the gardener opened the door last night. The gardener was locked outside all evening. Who did it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a disjunctive syllogism. With one option eliminated, the other must hold.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the butler opened it. The premise offers exactly two candidates; eliminating the gardener leaves the butler by pure elimination. 'Cannot be determined' ignores that the disjunction named the only possible openers.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A disjunctive syllogism eliminates: either P or Q; not P; therefore Q.
It is the logic of process-of-elimination — the surviving option wins by default, not by direct evidence.
The move only works if the either-or genuinely exhausts the possibilities.
Sherlock Holmes called the exhaustive version his method: remove the impossible and whatever remains must be the truth.
Share this: next time you eliminate options, ask whether the list was ever complete to begin with.

puzzles.title: The Negative Pair
puzzles.question: No cats are dogs. No dogs are felines. Does 'no cats are felines' follow?
choices: Yes — the chain of negatives transfers downward
No — this pattern is structurally invalid
Yes — exclusion spreads to overlapping groups
No — one premise must mention felines twice
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — this pattern is structurally invalid
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — two negative premises connect nothing. Cats and felines stay unlinked by these premises.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no — this pattern is structurally invalid. Two negative premises cannot yield any conclusion about how cats and felines relate; in fact cats are felines, which shows how wrong the chain of negatives is. Classical logicians flagged this as the exclusive-premises rule.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Two negative premises prove nothing about connection — they only state what excludes what.
Classical logicians banned pairs of 'no' statements from yielding any conclusion: the exclusive-premises rule.
The reason is structural: nothing bridges the two terms that need relating.
The cat-and-feline counterexample shows why — nature had already settled what the logic forbids concluding.
Share this: when you meet two 'no' statements in a row, pause before trusting whatever follows.

puzzles.title: Ticket to Enter
puzzles.question: Having a ticket is necessary to board. Riya has a ticket. Can she definitely board?
choices: No — some tickets can be fake at the gate
No — the ticket permits boarding but doesn't guarantee it
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — the ticket permits boarding but doesn't guarantee it
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — necessary is not sufficient. A ticket removes one barrier; other conditions can still block boarding.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the ticket permits boarding but doesn't guarantee it. 'Necessary' means 'without it, no boarding' — not 'with it, boarding'. Gate closures, lost seats, or a second requirement can all still stop her. Confusing necessary with sufficient is one of the most common reasoning errors.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Necessary means without it, impossible; sufficient means with it, guaranteed.
The two are mirror images, and most real requirements are necessary but not sufficient.
Degrees for jobs, keys for engines and tickets for entry all follow the same asymmetry.
Asking 'is this a must-have or a game-ender?' sorts requirements instantly.
Share this: list one thing you treat as sufficient today and check whether it is merely necessary.

puzzles.title: The Contrapositive
puzzles.question: 'All metals conduct electricity.' Which statement is logically equivalent?
choices: Nothing that fails to conduct electricity is a metal
All conductors of electricity are metals
Some metals do not conduct electricity
puzzles.correctAnswer: Nothing that fails to conduct electricity is a metal
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — contraposition. 'All A are B' and 'All non-B are non-A' say the same thing from opposite ends.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: nothing that fails to conduct electricity is a metal. Flipping and negating both sides preserves the meaning exactly — contraposition. Reversing without negating (option two) is illicit conversion, and option three contradicts the premise outright.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Contraposition is the one transformation that preserves a universal exactly: all A are B equals all non-B are non-A.
It flips and negates both sides — doing only one of those breaks the equivalence.
Contrapositives power indirect proof: to show something belongs, show it cannot belong to the complement.
Insurance clauses and eligibility rules often hide their contrapositive form in plain sight.
Share this: take one 'only members may enter' sign and state its contrapositive aloud.

puzzles.title: Only Members
puzzles.question: Only members can enter the vault. Ravi just entered the vault. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 'only members enter' reverses the direction: entering forces membership.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Ravi is a member. 'Only A can B' means 'whoever B's is an A' — so entering the vault certifies Ravi as a member. The 'only' flips the conditional's direction, and missing that flip is the classic trap.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Only A are B' translates to 'all B are A' — the 'only' reverses the direction of containment.
'Only members may enter' means every enterer is a member; it never means every member enters.
Mistranslating 'only' is among the most common logic slips in exams and contracts alike.
The fix is mechanical: rewrite the sentence as 'all ... are ...' before reasoning about it.
Share this: find one 'only' sentence today and rewrite it the all-way before deciding what it promises.

puzzles.title: The Bell Condition
puzzles.question: You may leave only if the bell rings. The bell did not ring. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 'only if' makes the bell a requirement, and a failed requirement blocks the permission.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: you may not leave. 'Leave only if bell' means leaving requires the bell — with no bell, leaving is off the table. This is modus tollens applied to the 'only if' translation, which many readers misread as 'if bell then may leave'.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'P only if Q' means Q is a requirement for P: without Q, no P.
It translates as 'if P then Q' — pointing forward from the action to its requirement.
Contrast 'if Q then P', which makes the requirement itself sufficient — the exact reversal.
Contracts and permissions are full of only-if clauses doing quiet work.
Share this: find one 'only if' in a rule you follow and translate it the if-then way.

puzzles.title: The Unicorn Count
puzzles.question: 'All dragons are fire-breathers.' Which inference commits the existential fallacy?
choices: Dragons that exist would breathe fire
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — 'all dragons are X' is vacuously true if no dragons exist, so it cannot promise that any fire-breathing dragon actually exists.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 'some fire-breathers are dragons'. A universal claim about dragons says nothing about dragons existing — 'some' assertions demand existence. Assuming existence from a universal is the existential fallacy, the exact gap between traditional and modern logic.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Universals carry no existence promise: 'all dragons breathe fire' is vacuously true if dragons don't exist.
The existential fallacy squeezes a 'some' out of an 'all' — inventing members the premise never delivered.
Modern logic keeps universals existence-free, which is why 'some' claims need their own evidence.
The gap matters in law and data alike: a rule about all cases says nothing about any case existing.
Share this: catch one 'so there must be some' inference today and ask who proved the 'some'.

puzzles.title: Perfect Form, False Fact
puzzles.question: All planets are stars. Mars is a planet. Therefore Mars is a star. How is this argument best described?
choices: Valid and sound — Mars is a star
Valid but unsound — form holds, premise false
Invalid — the conclusion contradicts the premises
puzzles.correctAnswer: Valid but unsound — form holds, premise false
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Validity is about form; soundness adds true premises. The form is perfect — the astronomy is not.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: valid but unsound — form holds, premise false. The conclusion follows the premises flawlessly, which makes it valid; but 'all planets are stars' is false, which breaks soundness. Validity and truth are separate judgements — an argument can be impeccably built on rubbish.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Validity is about shape: if the premises were true, the conclusion could not fail.
Soundness stacks truth on top: a sound argument is valid and actually has true premises.
A valid argument can therefore conclude nonsense — built perfectly on a false floor.
The two axes are independent, and judging them separately is the first discipline of logic.
Share this: take one argument you admire and grade it twice — once for form, once for facts.

puzzles.title: The Broken Link
puzzles.question: If A then B. If B then C. If C then D. We know A. An intern claims: 'So D.' Is the intern right?
choices: Yes — each link carries A to D
Yes — but only if D causes A
puzzles.correctAnswer: Yes — each link carries A to D
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — hypothetical syllogism. Conditionals chain forward: A reaches B, B reaches C, C reaches D.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is yes: each link carries A to D. Chained conditionals transmit truth forward — that is the hypothetical syllogism, the conditional cousin of the sorites. The intern deserves the credit; the skepticism misreads how forward-chaining works.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Chained conditionals transmit forward: if A then B, if B then C, if C then D lets A reach D.
This is the hypothetical syllogism — the conditional conveyor belt.
The chain is only as strong as its weakest link: one false conditional severs the whole path.
Cascading consequences in code, law and dominoes all follow this exact structure.
Share this: trace one if-then chain in your own plans and find its weakest link.

puzzles.title: The Majority Rule
puzzles.question: Most runners are early risers. Most early risers drink tea. Does it follow that most runners drink tea?
choices: No — the overlaps may barely intersect
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — the overlaps may barely intersect
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — 'most' does not chain. Two 60% overlaps can share as little as 20% of the group.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the overlaps may barely intersect. Two majorities can cross in a small zone — if 60% of runners rise early and 60% of those risers drink tea, as few as 36% of runners might be tea drinkers. Only universals ('all') chain safely; 'most' leaks.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'All' chains safely; 'most' leaks. Two majorities can cross in a minority of the group.
If most of a club cycles and most of the cyclists also swim, the overlap can still be a small corner of the club.
This quantifier slippage powers many a misleading statistic.
The safe rule: only universals compose; qualified claims need explicit overlap math.
Share this: next time two 'most' claims stack in an argument, do the overlap arithmetic aloud.

puzzles.title: The Border Check
puzzles.question: Every swan in this park is white. A black swan arrives and it is a swan. What must be true?
choices: This swan is white despite appearances
This swan came from somewhere else
puzzles.correctAnswer: This swan came from somewhere else
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — the premise scopes whiteness to this park only, so a black swan simply originates beyond it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: this swan came from somewhere else. The premise is a scoped universal — 'in this park' — and the black swan's existence contradicts nothing outside that scope. Denying the bird's existence or colour fights the very premise the question grants.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Universals often arrive scoped — 'every X in this park', 'all X before Friday' — and the scope is doing real work.
A scoped rule says nothing about the world outside its fence; exceptions outside survive unharmed.
Black swans famously lived outside Europe's 'all swans are white' scope until Australia was explored.
Reading the fence carefully is most of the game in rules and generalizations.
Share this: find one generalization today and ask where its fence actually ends.

puzzles.title: The Broad Brush
puzzles.question: All dogs are animals. Some animals are wild. Does 'some dogs are wild' follow?
choices: Yes — wildness spreads through all animals
No — no dog has ever gone wild
No — the wild animals need not include dogs
Yes — dogs descend from wolves anyway
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — the wild animals need not include dogs
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — the 'some animals' may be entirely non-dogs. The conclusion's subject overreaches its premise.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the wild animals need not include dogs. The premises never say which animals are wild — the wild ones could all be bears. Concluding about dogs from an unspecified 'some animals' is the illicit major fallacy in action.
puzzles.lessonContent:
When a conclusion's subject reaches beyond what its premise ever pinned down, the argument overreaches.
Logicians call the worst case illicit process: a term gets used in the conclusion beyond how the premise used it.
The repair is scope-matching: conclusions may only talk about what premises actually fixed.
Headlines generalize from narrow studies through exactly this gap.
Share this: catch one story that generalizes beyond its study and name what the scope excluded.

puzzles.title: The Step Down
puzzles.question: 'All tasks here are urgent.' Assuming tasks here exist, which weaker claim must also hold?
choices: All urgent things are tasks here
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — subalternation: a universal about existing things drops down to its 'some' version.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: some tasks here are urgent. If every task is urgent and at least one task exists, then at least one urgent task exists — the universal implies its particular. The reversal option commits illicit conversion again, and the negative options contradict the premise.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Subalternation is the safe weakening: 'all' implies 'some', provided members actually exist.
'Every card in this deck is red' hands you 'some cards in this deck are red' for free.
It never reverses — 'some' climbs to nothing, and existence is the quiet assumption doing the work.
Downgrade-from-all is always available; upgrade-from-some never is.
Share this: take one 'all' claim you trust and freely weaken it to 'some' — then notice how rarely the reverse is allowed.

puzzles.title: One Truth Only
puzzles.question: Exactly one of the two switches is on. Switch A is off. What do we know?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — an exclusive disjunction with one side settled forces the other side.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: switch B is on. 'Exactly one is on' means one and only one; with A off, B must carry the 'on'. Treating the disjunction as inclusive (option three) or as undecided (option four) misreads 'exactly'.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Either P or Q' comes in two flavours: inclusive (maybe both) and exclusive (exactly one).
The word 'exactly' upgrades to exclusive — and an exclusive pair with one side settled forces the other.
Logic puzzles lean on this constantly: one truth among candidates, eliminate the rest.
Contracts use it too: 'sole discretion', 'one winner' — exclusivity doing logical work.
Share this: find one 'either-or' today and ask whether it secretly allows both.

puzzles.title: The Silent Shipment
puzzles.question: If the shipment made it onto the truck, it left on time. The shipment did not leave on time. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — modus tollens. No on-time departure means the truck condition never happened.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the shipment missed the truck. A loaded truck forces an on-time departure; the departure failed, so by modus tollens the loading never occurred. 'Nothing follows' ignores that conditionals run backwards when negated correctly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Failed expectations are information: the effect that never arrived falsifies the cause that promised it.
This backwards elimination is how checklists catch silent failures and how tests kill bugs.
One caveat: the conditional must be airtight — other paths to the same effect break the elimination.
Engineering culture is built on cherishing exactly these silent negatives.
Share this: when something quietly fails to appear, write down which promise just got falsified.

puzzles.title: Millions Agree
puzzles.question: An advert claims: 'Millions of people use this shampoo, so it must be good.' This appeals to popularity rather than evidence.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — that is argumentum ad populum: a head-count is offered where evidence belongs.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The argument swaps user numbers for actual proof of quality — the textbook appeal to popularity. Millions of people can be wrong, misled, or simply copying each other.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Argumentum ad populum swaps a head-count for evidence: many believe it, therefore it is true.
Popularity tracks spread, not truth — rumours and fashions are popular by design.
The tell is structural: look for numbers of believers standing where reasons should be.
History's scoreboard is humbling — majorities once backed geocentrism and bloodletting.
Share this: next time an advert counts its fans, ask what evidence besides the count is on offer.

puzzles.title: The Dropout Defence
puzzles.question: Dismissing a colleague's budget argument because she failed maths in school commits an ad hominem.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — her school maths marks have no bearing on whether this budget argument holds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The response targets the person making the argument instead of the argument itself, which is the defining move of an ad hominem. A bad grade decades ago cannot make a valid budget case invalid.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Ad hominem answers an argument by attacking its author — credentials, history, habits.
Its flaw is relevance: the arguer's traits cannot flip a premise from false to true.
The two-part test: is the point about the person, and is it doing the argument's work?
Debate judges watch for exactly this substitution.
Share this: when a debate turns personal, note whose claim is suddenly not being discussed.

puzzles.title: The Scarecrow Tactic
puzzles.question: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack is called a straw man.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — you build a weaker scarecrow version of their view, then knock it down and claim victory.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The straw man fallacy is precisely this: replace the real position with a distorted, weaker one, then attack that instead. The name comes from fighting a dummy rather than the actual opponent.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A straw man works in two steps: quietly replace the real position with a weaker caricature, then defeat the caricature loudly.
Victory over the copy is presented as victory over the original.
The defence is the steel man habit: restate your opponent's view until they would endorse it themselves.
Only then attack — and watch how often the urge to attack evaporates.
Share this: restate one opinion you reject until its holder would say 'yes, that's it'.

puzzles.title: Herd Mathematics
puzzles.question: 'Everyone in my class is buying this phone, so I should too' is a deductively valid argument.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — popularity drives no logical conclusion. The class could all be making the same mistake together.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. What the class buys has no logical power over what one should buy — that is the bandwagon fallacy wearing a school uniform. A valid argument needs premises that force the conclusion, not peer pressure.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Bandwagon pressure exploits belonging: agreeing with the group feels safe and social.
Asch's conformity experiments showed people denying their own eyes to match a group.
Knowing the mechanism is half the defence; the other half is asking 'but is it true?'
First dissenters pay a social price — which is why they deserve attention, not mockery.
Share this: in your next group decision, be the one who asks what the group hasn't considered.

puzzles.title: Name-Dropping Rule
puzzles.question: Mentioning a person at any point during an argument automatically commits an ad hominem.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — the fallacy is replacing argument with attack, not merely naming a human.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. An ad hominem occurs only when personal traits are used as the reason to dismiss a claim. Quoting someone, praising them, or discussing their actions is not automatically an attack.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Not every mention of a person is an attack on one — the fallacy needs the personal point to replace engagement.
Quoting, crediting and criticising conduct are all legitimate; substitution is the crime.
Crying 'ad hominem!' at every name is itself a conversation-stopper.
The category boundary matters: about the argument, or instead of it?
Share this: collect one example today of a name used as evidence and one used innocently.

puzzles.title: The Weakened Clone
puzzles.question: Refuting a weaker version of an opponent's claim counts as refuting their actual claim.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — defeating a distorted copy defeats only the copy. The original claim walks away untouched.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Knocking down a weakened version of a position leaves the real position standing — that is exactly why the straw man is a fallacy. Refutation must engage what the opponent actually asserted.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Refutation is target-locked: it defeats exactly what it engages, nothing more.
Defeating a distortion is a no-op against the original claim.
That is why honest debaters quote opponents verbatim before attacking.
Quote-then-attack is not politeness — it is accuracy.
Share this: next time you see a quote attacked, check the quote against the original source.

puzzles.title: The Petrol Car
puzzles.question: 'How can you trust Dr. Mehta's climate research? She drives a petrol car.' This attacks the arguer instead of the research.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — her driving habits are irrelevant to the data. The tactic shifts focus from the science to the scientist.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The reply ignores the research entirely and aims at the researcher's lifestyle — a textbook ad hominem. Her car choices cannot alter the measurements or the analysis.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The hypocrisy jab feels devastating because hypocrisy is genuinely annoying — but annoyance is not logic.
A claim's truth is independent of its speaker's consistency.
Tu quoque — 'you too' — is the formal name when the attack is the accuser's own behaviour.
The real question survives the gotcha untouched.
Share this: enjoy one gotcha moment today, then ask what claim it actually disproved.

puzzles.title: Bandwagon Twins
puzzles.question: The bandwagon fallacy and the appeal to popularity are essentially the same error.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — both treat 'many people believe it' as if it were 'therefore it is true'.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The bandwagon image (jump on because everyone did) is just the folksy name for argumentum ad populum. The error is identical: crowd size substituting for evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The fallacy family has many names for cousin-moves: ad populum, bandwagon, appeal to the masses.
They share one core: crowd size offered as proof.
Learning the aliases sharpens spotting — the same trick wears different name-tags in ads, politics and group chats.
Once you see the skeleton, the costumes stop mattering.
Share this: name the fallacy family next time an ad counts its believers.

puzzles.title: The Harsh Test
puzzles.question: A straw man fallacy strengthens the original argument by stress-testing a harsher version of it.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the fallacy replaces the argument rather than testing it. Nothing about the original gets stronger.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A straw man does not test anything — it swaps the real claim for a caricature and attacks that. The original argument is simply never engaged, which is the whole deception.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A stress-test strengthens an argument by surviving the strongest attack; a straw man dodges by attacking the weakest version.
The difference is direction of distortion — one goes harder than reality, the other softer and sillier.
Real critical thinking seeks the strongest form of an opponent's case.
Steel-manning is the discipline; straw-manning is the reflex.
Share this: take one view you reject and ask what its strongest version would say.

puzzles.title: Nine Out of Ten
puzzles.question: 'Nine out of ten dentists recommend this brand' is, all by itself, conclusive proof that the brand is best.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — an endorsement count is not proof. Which dentists, chosen how, compared to what?
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A recommendation tally is weak testimony at best, never conclusive proof — the survey could be cherry-picked, sponsored, or vague. Notice the claim never says best among what alternatives.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Endorsement statistics are testimony, and testimony's value depends on who, how many, and chosen how.
Sponsored surveys, cherry-picked panels and vague baselines all hollow the number out.
The question 'compared with what?' restores the missing baseline.
Dentist endorsements began as advertising's most successful formula — and remain its most parodied.
Share this: ask 'nine out of ten of whom?' about the next statistic you see.

puzzles.title: Evidence versus Insults
puzzles.question: Criticising the quality of someone's evidence is itself an ad hominem attack.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — attacking the evidence is exactly what good argument is supposed to do.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. An ad hominem attacks the person; scrutinising their evidence targets the argument itself. 'Your sample was too small' is legitimate criticism, not a personal attack.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Legitimate criticism targets premises, inferences and evidence — the three parts of any argument.
Personal attacks target a fourth thing that is not part of the argument at all.
Keeping the map straight is what separates scrutiny from smearing.
Reviewers and referees practise this separation professionally.
Share this: grade one argument today premise by premise and notice how little the author matters.

puzzles.title: Centuries of Belief
puzzles.question: The ad populum fallacy says that a claim's widespread acceptance, on its own, never proves the claim true.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — popularity is not truth-tracking. Nearly everyone once believed the sun circled the earth.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The fallacy exists precisely because mass belief and truth are different things — continents of people have been confidently wrong for centuries. Acceptance needs evidence behind it to count as proof.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Acceptance and truth vary independently: some true claims were long rejected, some falsehoods were long believed.
Continental drift was ridiculed for decades; geocentrism ruled for millennia.
The lesson is not cynicism — it is that belief needs evidence, not duration.
Long-standing consensus among informed experts earns trust; mere longevity does not.
Share this: find one thing 'everyone has always known' and check when it was last tested.

puzzles.title: The Factory Phantom
puzzles.question: Responding to 'we should recycle more' with 'so you want to shut down every factory' builds a straw man.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — the reply inflates a modest proposal into an absurd extreme, then attacks the extreme.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. 'Recycle more' never implied shutting down industry — the response invents a ridiculous version of the position and fights that instead. Inflating to an absurd extreme is the most common straw-manning move.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The commonest straw-manning move is inflation: stretch 'some' into 'all', 'prefer' into 'obsess', 'regulate' into 'ban'.
The inflated version is always easier to mock, which is exactly the point.
Inflation-spotting is a learnable reflex: listen for 'so what you're saying is' and check the stretch.
The counter-move is restating the original scale before responding.
Share this: count the 'so you want to' inflations in one conversation this week.

puzzles.title: The Truth Condition
puzzles.question: An ad hominem fallacy only occurs when the personal attack is factually false.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — even a true personal fact is irrelevant if it is used to dismiss the argument.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The fallacy is in the irrelevance, not the falsity: 'he really did fail maths' still says nothing about his budget argument. A true fact deployed as a substitute for engagement is still an ad hominem.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The ad hominem's flaw is relevance, not accuracy — even a true personal fact proves nothing about the argument.
A genuine failure decades ago still leaves today's reasoning untouched.
Fallacies are about connections: a true statement in the wrong place is still a wrong move.
Relevance is the master concept — most informal fallacies are relevance failures in costume.
Share this: when a true fact is dropped into a debate, ask what it is supposed to prove.

puzzles.title: Unpleasant but Right
puzzles.question: An argument can be rejected on solid logical grounds even when its proponent is thoroughly unpleasant.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — validity depends on the argument's structure, not the arguer's personality.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A rude person can present a flawless argument, and a saint can present a broken one. Judging the reasoning is separate from judging the person — that separation is what the ad hominem fallacy violates.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Two independent judgements: the person (kind, consistent, pleasant?) and the argument (valid, sound?).
Conflating them is how bad arguments from good people slide by, and good arguments from bad people get dismissed.
Courts understood this long ago: even a criminal's testimony is weighed, not automatically discarded.
The separation feels cold and is actually fairness.
Share this: separate the messenger from the message in one judgement you make today.

puzzles.title: The Friendship Motive
puzzles.question: 'You only support this policy because your friends do' addresses the actual reasoning behind the policy.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — it speculates about motives while saying nothing about the policy's merits.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The reply is about why the person might hold the view, not whether the view is sound — a motive-focused sidestep. Even if the motive were true, the policy's arguments would stand or fall on their own.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Explaining why someone holds a view is psychology; evaluating the view is logic.
Both can be done — but only one of them settles the argument.
Motive-talk is a spotlight shift: engaging, vivid, and silent about the actual claim.
Even a correct motive report leaves the claim's evidence exactly where it was.
Share this: catch one motive explanation today and re-ask the original question.

puzzles.title: When Crowds Know
puzzles.question: Appealing to what a crowd believes is always fallacious, even when the crowd consists of relevant experts.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — expert consensus earned through evidence is testimony with weight, not head-counting.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. When specialists converge after examining evidence, citing that consensus is citing informed testimony — categorically different from 'everyone believes it, so true'. The ad populum fallacy targets popularity as proof, not expertise as evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Citing expert consensus differs from crowd-counting: the experts' numbers carry the weight of evidence behind them.
Astronomers agreeing the universe expands is testimony to data, not to popularity.
The carve-out has limits: it assumes genuine, independent convergence.
Asking why the experts agree upgrades the shortcut into understanding.
Share this: next time you cite a consensus, be ready to name one piece of evidence behind it.

puzzles.title: Who Builds It
puzzles.question: The straw man fallacy is committed by the person whose position gets misrepresented.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — the fallacy belongs to the misrepresenter, the one who builds and attacks the scarecrow.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The victim's position is the raw material — the fallacy is committed by whoever distorts it. Being misrepresented makes you the target, not the culprit.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fallacies are committed, not suffered: the misrepresenter owns the straw man, not the misrepresented.
Keeping the arrow of blame straight matters when both sides accuse each other of the same move.
Ask 'who changed the claim?' and the culprit reveals itself.
Quotation is the currency of accountability in argument.
Share this: in the next dispute you witness, track who quoted and who paraphrased.

puzzles.title: Empty but Loud
puzzles.question: An ad populum argument can be emotionally persuasive while remaining logically empty.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — that gap between persuasive power and logical content is what makes the fallacy dangerous.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. 'Everyone knows this' feels reassuring and requires no thinking, which is exactly why it persuades. Emotional pull and logical emptiness happily coexist — the fallacy works because it feels like belonging.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Persuasion has many engines — emotion, belonging, repetition, confidence — and logic is only one of them.
A fallacy can be perfectly engineered persuasion while proving nothing.
Feeling convinced is data about you, not about the claim.
Advertisers and demagogues alike optimize for the feeling, not the proof.
Share this: notice one moment today when confidence, not evidence, moved you.

puzzles.title: The Decay Gambit
puzzles.question: 'My opponent wants less spending; clearly he wants this city to decay' is closest to a straw man.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — 'less spending' is quietly rewritten as 'wants decay', a much easier target to attack.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Wanting less spending does not mean wanting decay — the speaker substitutes a sinister motive for the actual position. That substitution-and-attack pattern is the straw man signature.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Slipping a sinister motive into an opponent's position is straw-manning with a mask.
The fake motive is always more attackable than the real policy.
Watch for motive verbs — wants, hopes, plans — that the opponent never used.
The counter is asking them to state their own goal in their own words.
Share this: replace one assigned motive today with a direct question about intent.

puzzles.title: Insult plus Proof
puzzles.question: Calling an argument stupid is technically an ad hominem even when you also completely refute it.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the fallacy is abuse standing in for argument. Here the refutation does the actual work.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Rude packaging around a genuine refutation is bad manners, not a fallacy — the reasoning is still fully engaged. Ad hominem means the personal jab replaces engagement with the argument, not accompanies it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rudeness alongside a full refutation is a manners problem, not a logic problem.
The fallacy label applies only when the jab substitutes for engagement.
This is why 'that's ad hominem!' sometimes loses arguments it should win — the refutation stands regardless.
Judging packaging and content separately is the mature skill.
Share this: separate one speaker's tone from their reasoning today and grade each on its own.

puzzles.title: The Latin Label
puzzles.question: The formal Latin name for the appeal-to-popularity fallacy is argumentum ad populum.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 'argument to the people', the scholarly name for crowd-as-proof.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Argumentum ad populum literally means 'argument to the people' — appealing to the crowd's beliefs as if numbers were evidence. Spotting the Latin label helps you notice the move in polished writing.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Latin tags like argumentum ad populum are compression: a whole failure-pattern packed into a name.
Named patterns get spotted faster — the label primes the recognition.
The same holds for ad hominem ('to the person') and its many cousins.
Taxonomy is not pedantry; it is a spotting toolkit.
Share this: teach one fallacy name to someone today and watch them start seeing it everywhere.

puzzles.title: Why It Works
puzzles.question: Straw-manning often succeeds because the audience never heard the original position.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — with no original for comparison, the caricature becomes the position in the audience's mind.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The distortion only fools listeners who lack the original for comparison — once you have heard both, the fake collapses. That is why checking primary sources defuses straw men so reliably.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Straw men thrive on audiences that never heard the original — with nothing to compare, the caricature becomes the claim.
That is why secondhand summaries are the fallacy's natural habitat.
The antidote is primary sources: read the speech, not the tweet about the speech.
Verification beats eloquence in any serious disagreement.
Share this: read one primary source behind a summary you consumed today.

puzzles.title: The Spotlight Shift
puzzles.question: An ad hominem turns the spotlight from the claim onto the claimant.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — that redirect is the entire mechanics of the fallacy: judge the person, forget the point.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The move works by changing the subject of the sentence — from 'is this claim true?' to 'what is wrong with this person?' Once the spotlight moves, the original question quietly disappears.
puzzles.lessonContent:
An ad hominem changes the sentence's subject: from 'is the claim true?' to 'what is wrong with the claimer?'
Once the spotlight moves, the original question quietly exits the stage.
Noticing the redirect half-defuses it — drag the light back to the claim.
Interviewers and moderators earn their keep by exactly this move.
Share this: in one debate today, name the moment the subject changed from claim to person.

puzzles.title: Experts versus Crowds
puzzles.question: Believing a claim because most qualified experts accept it after reviewing evidence is the ad populum fallacy.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — that is deferring to informed consensus, which is evidence-based testimony, not head-counting.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Ad populum counts noses regardless of knowledge; expert consensus carries the weight of training and evidence behind it. Trusting qualified consensus is reasonable shorthand, not a fallacy — though checking why experts agree is even better.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One question separates healthy deference from the bandwagon: what generated the agreement?
Evidence-examined convergence earns trust; fashion, fear and follower counts do not.
It is also fine to ask both: what do the experts say, and why do they say it?
The 'why' is where your own judgment gets trained.
Share this: next time you defer to consensus, spend thirty seconds on the why.

puzzles.title: The Missing Frame
puzzles.question: A film cuts from a man waking to him brushing teeth, then to him at work. Audiences never feel the gap — even though hours of his life vanished between shots. What is the storyteller really relying on?
choices: The audience's laziness in checking details
The mind's automatic stitching of events into cause and flow
Special effects hidden inside the cut
The audience never noticing anything at all
puzzles.correctAnswer: The mind's automatic stitching of events into cause and flow
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the cut works because the brain supplies the missing hours. The filmmaker edits; the viewer builds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the mind's automatic stitching of events into cause and flow. Film editors call it the Kuleshov insight — meaning is assembled in the spectator's head, not on the screen. The same stitching runs your own life: you experience 'a day', not ten thousand disconnected moments. Memory is your personal editor, and it takes the same liberties.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The Kuleshov effect showed that audiences supply meaning between two unrelated shots.
Your memory performs the same edit nightly — sleep consolidates fragments into continuous narratives.
Confabulation is the clinical name for confidently filling gaps with invented detail.
The storytelling brain explains why eyewitness testimony is shakier than it feels.
Share this: recall this morning in one sentence and count how many gaps your mind silently bridged.

puzzles.title: The Third Act
puzzles.question: A magician shows you an ordinary bird. A moment later, the bird is gone — and finally it returns, transformed, somewhere impossible. Which act of the classic trick structure is doing the real work?
choices: None; the work happens before the show
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the pledge and the turn only set the table. The prestige is where astonishment lives, because it retroactively makes the ordinary seem impossible.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the third — the impossible return. Magicians name the acts the pledge, the turn and the prestige; the third act is the payoff that reframes the first two. Every great reveal story works this way — the ending reaches back and changes what the beginning meant. The first two acts are interest; the third collects.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stage magic formalizes the reveal: the pledge establishes the ordinary, the turn breaks it, the prestige restores it transformed.
The structure reappears in jokes (setup, twist, punchline) and in proofs (premise, surprise, resolution).
What the third act really sells is retroactive meaning — the audience re-reads what they saw.
Any explanation you ever give inherits its power from where the reveal lands.
Share this: retell your favourite film ending and notice how it recolours its opening scene.

puzzles.title: The Unreliable Camera
puzzles.question: A narrator describes a generous benefactor funding a village school. At the end we learn the narrator owns the land the school occupies. The story never lied once. What happened?
choices: The story deceived by selection, not statement
The narrator technically lied by omission of feeling
The school was secretly harmful to villagers
Nothing; the narrator's stake is irrelevant
puzzles.correctAnswer: The story deceived by selection, not statement
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — every sentence was true; the frame was the falsehood. What was left out did the misleading.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the story deceived by selection, not statement. Unreliable narration at its most elegant never utters a falsehood — it curates truths until the picture lies. News feeds, reviews and résumés work the same way: honest sentences, dishonest frame. The defence is asking what a truthful teller would have included that this one didn't.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unreliable narrators mislead by emphasis and omission while every stated fact stays true.
Frame control is the technique: what you show first becomes the reference point for everything after.
Studies of selective disclosure show people judge honesty by what was said, rarely by what was absent.
Asking 'what would the other side include?' is the reader's counter-move.
Share this: read one news story today and list two facts a different editor would have led with.

puzzles.title: Nested Rules
puzzles.question: In a dream inside a dream, falling in the deeper level wakes you one level up — never two. A character wants to escape from the deepest level. What must the plot guarantee before that escape is possible?
choices: Enough time passing in the deepest level
A wake event in every level above it
Strong emotion to power the climb
A rule that deep levels ignore waking
puzzles.correctAnswer: A wake event in every level above it
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — nested systems need their escape conditions satisfied at each layer, or the chain stalls.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a wake event in every level above it. Layered fictions earn their complexity by obeying their own rules per level — the escape cascades. Nested systems in reality behave identically: quitting an app inside a virtual machine still needs the host to cooperate. Rules kept faithfully are what make impossible structures feel real.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Layered realities obey their own physics per level — that discipline is what makes them believable.
Nested systems cascade: an exit condition must trigger at every enclosing layer.
Computer science lives this daily — processes inside virtual machines inside hosts.
A story's rules are a promise; breaking them cheaply costs more than never making them.
Share this: next time a plot 'breaks its own rules', name exactly which level's rule got violated.

puzzles.title: The Wall Rifle
puzzles.question: A playwright introduces a rifle hanging on a wall in scene one. It never fires again for the whole play. What has the writer broken?
choices: The audience's trust in meaningful detail
The rule that weapons must be staged safely
The requirement that scene one be short
puzzles.correctAnswer: The audience's trust in meaningful detail
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — Chekhov's principle: introduce a rifle and it must matter. The audience's attention is a contract.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the audience's trust in meaningful detail. Chekhov's gun is the dramatist's economy — whatever you place on stage, the audience will invest meaning in, so it must pay off. Detail that never matters teaches readers to stop attending. The inverse holds too: what's absent from a story can be load-bearing silence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Chekhov's gun: any element placed on stage earns meaning and must eventually matter.
Audiences treat every highlighted detail as a promise — wasted promises train inattention.
The inverse power: deliberate absences can carry more weight than presences.
Good non-fiction and good design obey the same economy — every element earns its place.
Share this: scan a webpage or document today and find three details that never pay off.

puzzles.title: The Honest Liar Scene
puzzles.question: In a classic mystery, the narrator describes every scene truthfully — yet the solution shocks every reader, and rereading reveals the clues were always in plain sight. What craft made this possible?
choices: Hiding clues in the final chapter only
Fair-play clue placement with misdirected attention
Making the clues physically tiny in print
Using a solution nobody could deduce
puzzles.correctAnswer: Fair-play clue placement with misdirected attention
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the golden-age discipline: every clue on the table, attention pointed elsewhere. The reread is the proof of fairness.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: fair-play clue placement with misdirected attention. The locked-room tradition treats the reader as a collaborator: solvable in principle, deceived only by emphasis. Misdirection borrows from stage magic — the eye follows motion, so the writer supplies motion. A puzzle that hides information breaks the contract; one that hides it in view honours it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The fair-play tradition: all clues visible before the reveal, deception only via attention.
Misdirection works because attention is a spotlight — motion and emotion steer it.
The reread test: a good mystery improves when you know the answer.
Puzzle designers grade themselves by whether the solver says 'it was in front of me'.
Share this: reread one thing you were fooled by and trace where your attention was steered.

puzzles.title: Two Clocks
puzzles.question: A soldier's one week on land and a civilian boat's single day are cut together, and each hour of the sea story weighs as much as the soldier's whole week. What is the editing really doing?
choices: Making the sea story seem longer by accident
Weighing time by emotional meaning, not minutes
Signalling the sea story is fiction
puzzles.correctAnswer: Weighing time by emotional meaning, not minutes
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — braided timelines can run at different clock speeds because the currency is meaning, not duration.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: weighing time by emotional meaning, not minutes. Braid-structure storytelling interlaces timelines whose lengths differ wildly, letting each carry equal narrative weight. Your memory edits the same way — an afternoon of crisis outlives a year of routine. The craft move simply makes the mind's native bias visible.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Braided narratives run multiple timelines whose clock speeds differ by design.
The unit of story time is meaning, not minutes — crisis dilates, routine compresses.
Memory performs the same trick: emotional salience decides what a 'long' year is.
Time perception experiments confirm duration judgments track attention and novelty.
Share this: ask someone which single hour of their last month felt longest, and why.

puzzles.title: The Turning Word
puzzles.question: A poet ends a piece with 'success in failure' — a phrase that seems to cancel itself. What device is in play, and why does it land?
choices: A typo that readers forgive in context
Paradox pairing two half-truths into one whole truth
Rhythm covering the lack of sense
puzzles.correctAnswer: Paradox pairing two half-truths into one whole truth
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — each word is a half-truth; the tension between them is where the full meaning lives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: paradox pairing two half-truths into one whole truth. Oxymorons and paradoxes work by forcing two valid partial readings into one phrase — the spark is in the collision. 'Cruel kindness' and 'hurry up and wait' both point at real experiences no single word covers. Minds hold the tension, and that holding is the thought.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Paradox compression: two partial truths forced into one phrase, each exposing the other's limit.
Oxymorons are its smallest unit — 'sound of silence' names a real experience no plain phrase reaches.
The reader's moment of holding both is the meaning; resolve it too fast and it dies.
Great aphorisms from Heraclitus to Dickinson run on this engine.
Share this: coin one oxymoron about your own week and test if it lands on a friend.

puzzles.title: In Medias Res
puzzles.question: The oldest epic in the West begins not with the war's start but years in, a man weeping on a beach, already mid-story. What does starting in the middle buy the teller?
choices: Immediate stakes plus a past the audience must reconstruct
puzzles.correctAnswer: Immediate stakes plus a past the audience must reconstruct
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — in medias res opens at maximum pressure and lets the backstory arrive as earned discovery.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: immediate stakes plus a past the audience must reconstruct. The Odyssey drops you into year ten of a ten-year homecoming — curiosity about the missing decade powers the whole poem. Beginning mid-crisis converts exposition into mystery. The audience assembles the past themselves, which makes it theirs.
puzzles.lessonContent:
In medias res: begin inside the storm and let the calm be discovered backwards.
Exposition delivered late becomes revelation; delivered early, it becomes homework.
The device converts backstory from cost into currency.
Homer's audiences knew the war's end — the poem's mystery was always the man, not the war.
Share this: next conversation, start with the most interesting moment and fill in history only when asked.

puzzles.title: Dramatic Irony
puzzles.question: An audience watches a character toast their trusted friend — knowing what the character doesn't: the friend has already betrayed them. Where is the story's tension actually located?
choices: In the audience, holding knowledge the character lacks
In the wine, which is poisoned too
puzzles.correctAnswer: In the audience, holding knowledge the character lacks
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — dramatic irony relocates suspense from 'what happens?' to 'when will they find out?'.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: in the audience, holding knowledge the character lacks. Dramatic irony splits the room: the audience knows, the character acts blind, and the gap between those two knowledge states is the tension. Tragedy has used it since ancient Greece — the horror is in the waiting, not the event. Everyday life runs small versions whenever you watch someone walk into a known mistake.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dramatic irony: the audience knows what the character doesn't, and the gap generates suspense.
It shifts the question from 'what happens?' to 'how long until they see it?'.
Greek tragedy built its deepest effects on the audience's helpless foreknowledge.
The same gap powers cringe comedy and every 'don't open the door' moment.
Share this: notice today when you watch someone act on outdated information and feel the gap.

puzzles.title: The Rule of Three
puzzles.question: A comedian says: 'I have three hobbies — chess, hiking, and emotional damage.' The joke's engine is best described as what?
choices: The list being exactly three items long
Two expected patterns establishing, the third subverting
Chess being an inherently funny word
The audience mishearing the first two items
puzzles.correctAnswer: Two expected patterns establishing, the third subverting
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — two setups buy the pattern, and the third spends it. The laugh is the pivot.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: two expected patterns establishing, the third subverting. The rule of three is rhythm plus betrayal: the first item introduces, the second confirms a pattern, the third breaks it with a switch of frame — from hobbies to self-diagnosis. Humour researchers call the mechanism incongruity resolution. Three is the smallest number that can build a pattern and break it in one breath.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The rule of three: establish, confirm, subvert — the smallest complete pattern-break.
Incongruity resolution is the lab name for the 'aha' inside a joke's pivot.
The third item works by switching frames — outer activities to inner states.
Lists, jokes, mottos and fairy tales all default to three because two is a pair, four is a crowd.
Share this: build one rule-of-three joke about your own week and test it on a friend.

puzzles.title: The Palindrome Plot
puzzles.question: A film is structured so its second half plays the first half's events in reverse order, meeting its own beginning at the middle. What must the writer plan before writing a single scene?
choices: The ending alone; the middle is free
Every scene's mirror twin in advance
That audiences will watch it twice
puzzles.correctAnswer: Every scene's mirror twin in advance
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — a palindrome forecloses improvisation: each half is the other's reflection, so neither can be written alone.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: every scene's mirror twin in advance. Mirror structures are rigid by nature — the second half's existence is fully determined by the first, so architecture precedes drafting. Poets have written palindromic verse for centuries under the same constraint. Formal constraints don't kill creativity; they concentrate it where it still has room to move.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Palindrome structures make the second half a reflection of the first — determined, not free.
Formal constraints concentrate creativity instead of killing it — poets have used mirror verse for centuries.
Sestinas, sonnets and palindromes all trade freedom elsewhere for intensity here.
Knowing where your structure is fixed tells you where your invention must live.
Share this: impose one constraint on a task today and notice where your creativity moves.

puzzles.title: Disguise and Home
puzzles.question: A hero returns home after twenty years but enters his own house disguised as a stranger. The story's real question is no longer 'will he survive the journey?' What has it become?
choices: Whether the house still deserves the name home
Whether his disguise will fool the dog
Whether he can defeat the disguised villain
puzzles.correctAnswer: Whether the house still deserves the name home
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the survival plot ends at the shore; the identity plot begins at the door. Coming home is the harder test.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: whether the house still deserves the name home. The Odyssey's deep subject is not travel but return — the man who arrives is no longer the man who left, and only the dog recognizes him instantly. Disguise in such stories tests the world: who sees the person beneath the years? The homecoming question is whether continuity survives change.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The homecoming story shifts the stakes from survival to identity — the harder test begins at the door.
Disguise at home is a probe: it measures what recognizes you when nothing obvious does.
The Odyssey gives the instant recognition to the dog — loyalty bypasses appearance.
Your own return to old places runs the same test every time.
Share this: revisit one place from your past and note what recognizes you and what doesn't.

puzzles.title: Chekhov's Absence
puzzles.question: In one play, a character talks constantly about going to a city the audience never sees; the city never appears. What is the unseen city doing to the audience?
choices: Failing the story by breaking the gun rule
Becoming larger than any staged city could be
Proving the playwright forgot the plot
Signalling the story is a dream
puzzles.correctAnswer: Becoming larger than any staged city could be
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — the never-seen destination grows in the imagination precisely because it is never staged.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: becoming larger than any staged city could be. A stage is a budget; the unseen city is unlimited, and it grows in each viewer's imagination. Horror runs the same law — the glimpse outscares the reveal.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Negative space: the never-shown element grows beyond what any production could stage.
Horror's law — the glimpse beats the reveal — is the same economy pointed at fear.
Longing stories aim the device at places: the city unseen carries each viewer's own hope.
Restraint is a budget choice as much as an aesthetic one.
Share this: name one thing a story left unseen that lives larger in you than any shown thing.

puzzles.title: Deadpan Delivery
puzzles.question: A comedian reports absurd events in a completely flat, serious tone, never signalling that anything is funny. Why does the straight face amplify the joke?
choices: The audience must do the noticing themselves
The joke only works in a courtroom
Flat delivery hides the punchline from microphones
puzzles.correctAnswer: The audience must do the noticing themselves
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the comic refuses to flag the absurdity, so the audience performs the double-take themselves. Discovery beats announcement.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the audience must do the noticing themselves. Deadpan works by withholding the laugh cue — no wink, no giggle, total commitment to the bit. The viewer then does the frame-switching internally, and self-generated humour lands harder than signalled humour. Dry delivery is a gift wrapped as indifference.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Deadpan withholds the laugh cue, forcing the audience to notice the absurdity unassisted.
Self-discovered humour lands harder than announced humour — the frame-switch is your own work.
The technique demands total commitment: any wink collapses it.
Understatement and dry tone borrow the same engine in everyday speech.
Share this: deliver one absurd true story today with a perfectly straight face and watch the room.

puzzles.title: The Scale Mismatch
puzzles.question: A novel spends two full chapters on a family argument, then dispatches a world war in one sentence. The absurd proportion is the point. What effect does this inversion create?
choices: It accidentally reveals the author's politics
It recasts the war as background to private life
It proves the family argument caused the war
It hides the war from careless readers
puzzles.correctAnswer: It recasts the war as background to private life
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — proportion is meaning. By spending words against convention, the author declares what the story is actually about.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: it recasts the war as background to private life. Narrative scale is an argument: whatever gets the word-count gets the importance. Inverting expected proportions makes history the backdrop of a household — a deliberate reweighting of the world. Readers feel the strangeness before they can name it, and the name is the lesson.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Proportion is meaning: what a story spends its words on is what it claims matters.
Inverting expected scale — epic in a sentence, quarrel in chapters — is a silent argument.
Readers feel scale mismatches before they can articulate them.
The same lens reads news: check what got column inches versus what got a line.
Share this: compare two headlines' lengths today and ask what the scale is arguing.

puzzles.title: The Long Take
puzzles.question: A director refuses to cut for five full minutes, following one character through a building in real time. No hidden edits, no tricks. What does the audience gain that cutting would remove?
choices: Proof the actors memorized more lines
Knowledge that the space and time are continuous
Freedom to imagine the other rooms
puzzles.correctAnswer: Knowledge that the space and time are continuous
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the unbroken shot is a promise: nothing was stitched, this happened, once, in this order.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: knowledge that the space and time are continuous. A long take functions as an integrity proof — the cut, which normally lets fiction cheat time and space, is removed from the toolbox. The audience's trust shifts from 'trust me' to 'verify for yourself'. Continuous performance is why the trick can't hide: everything must actually work, all at once.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The long take removes editing — the storytelling cheat — and stakes everything on continuous performance.
Uncut presentation functions as a proof of work: what you see happened, in this order.
Live theatre sells the same integrity every night.
Demos, live streams and unedited records borrow the credibility of the unbroken take.
Share this: watch one uninterrupted five-minute performance and notice your trust rising.

puzzles.title: Suspension Standards
puzzles.question: An audience accepts dragons in a story, then complains when a dragon survives a fall 'unrealistically'. What rule did the storyteller actually break?
choices: The story's own established rules were contradicted
Audiences dislike surviving falls in any story
The dragon should have been the hero
puzzles.correctAnswer: The story's own established rules were contradicted
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — disbelief suspends for the premise, not for everything. Internal consistency is the contract; realism never was.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the story's own established rules were contradicted. Audiences grant impossible premises but audit everything after against the story's established physics. If dragons elsewhere in that world respect falls, this one must too — the violation reads as cheating, not fantasy. World-building is promise-keeping, world-rule by world-rule.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Disbelief suspends at the door for premises, not for contradictions — the audit shifts inside.
Internal consistency is the real contract; realism was never on the table.
Fantasy worlds are legal systems: their physics binds their authors first.
Audiences forgive impossible, not inconsistent.
Share this: catch one inconsistency in a show you love and name which established rule it broke.

puzzles.title: The Cold Open
puzzles.question: A series begins with a stranger's funeral — a character the audience has never met — before the title card, then jumps back years. Why open on grief for an unknown?
choices: To trick viewers into thinking they missed an episode
To make every later scene with that person a countdown
To establish the town's cemetery budget
To hide the character's true importance
puzzles.correctAnswer: To make every later scene with that person a countdown
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — the funeral is a promise of ending; from then on, every scene with that person runs on borrowed time.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: to make every later scene with that person a countdown. The cold open buys dramatic irony wholesale: knowledge of the ending installed before the story begins. Every warm moment with that character now carries a shadow the audience holds alone. It's the oldest trick in tragedy, reloaded as a structural flash-forward.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The cold open can install the ending first — every subsequent scene inherits its gravity.
Flash-forwards convert ordinary scenes into countdowns the audience alone can see.
It's dramatic irony at structural scale, not just scene scale.
The technique trades surprise (spent in minute one) for dread (earned for hours).
Share this: think of one thing you know will end and notice how it colours the present.

puzzles.title: The Unreliable Room
puzzles.question: A locked-room mystery: the door bolted from inside, the only window painted shut, no chimney, no secret passages — yet the detective proves no crime occurred at all. What was the actual trick?
choices: A hidden tunnel the detective forgot to mention
The room was never locked during the events
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the cleanest solution dissolves the puzzle by showing it was staged: the impossible situation was the trick, not a barrier to it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the impossibility itself was manufactured. The elegant locked-room solutions rarely fight the constraints — they reveal the constraints were built to mislead: bolts thrown from outside, scenes arranged after the fact. The puzzle was never an obstacle; it was the criminal's performance. Real-world analogues are staged impossibilities in fraud and propaganda — the frame was the crime.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The finest locked-room solutions reframe the impossibility as the criminal's construction, not a wall.
The constraints were authored by someone — ask who benefits from the framing.
Fraud and propaganda run the same play: manufacture an impossible situation, then sell its explanation.
'Who built this box?' outperforms 'how did they escape the box?'.
Share this: next time a situation looks impossible, ask who authored the impossibility.

puzzles.title: Echo Endings
puzzles.question: A novel's final sentence repeats its opening sentence word for word, but every reader swears the second one means something different. What changed between them?
choices: The words were secretly redefined mid-book
The reader did — three hundred pages of experience now sit inside the line
