puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the case mix differs wildly between them. If one hospital treats mostly hard cases, its overall rate sinks even while winning each fair comparison. Lumped averages hide cocktail recipes; subgroup tables tell the truth.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Simpson's paradox: pooled numbers can reverse every subgroup trend when group mixes differ.
Always ask what mixture produced the average before trusting it.
The same reversal haunted kidney-stone tables and admissions data.
Compare like-sized mixtures, or weight by subgroup properly.
Share this: next time two averages are compared, ask what went into each pot.

puzzles.title: The Selective Ward
puzzles.question: Among hospital patients, two unrelated conditions appear negatively linked — patients rarely carry both. Yet the conditions are independent in the public. What happened?
choices: One disease must block the other
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — admission itself selects people carrying at least one condition, so inside the ward the two trade off artificially.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: only selected admissions were studied. Conditioning on a shared filter manufactures links the open population never had — Berkson's paradox. The ward is a filtered sample, not a mirror of the world.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Berkson's paradox: studying a selected slice can invent correlations whole.
Any admission rule shared by two traits welds them together in the sample.
Elite colleges and hospital wards both manufacture 'trade-offs' this way.
Ask who is missing from any dataset before believing its links.
Share this: find one correlation tonight built on a filtered crowd.

puzzles.title: The Thirty-Seven
puzzles.question: You must hire the single best of 100 candidates seen once each in a row, deciding on the spot. What is the classic optimal strategy?
choices: Reject the first 37, then take the next best
puzzles.correctAnswer: Reject the first 37, then take the next best
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — observe roughly the first 37%, then hire the first candidate beating everything seen so far.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: reject the first 37, then take the next best. A calibration sample teaches your eye what 'best' looks like; committing to the first record-breaker after it maximizes your odds near 37%. Intuition either leaps too early or dithers forever.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Optimal stopping: in one-pass decisions, spend a fixed calibration phase observing, then commit on a threshold.
The 1/e ≈ 37% split balances information against dwindling options.
House-hunting and hiring both fit the one-pass frame.
Decide your stopping rule before you start, not mid-panic.
Share this: set a 37% observe-window before your next big one-way search.

puzzles.title: The Dozen Plus One
puzzles.question: How many people are needed to guarantee that two share a birth month?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — twelve people can cover twelve distinct months, but the thirteenth has no fresh month left.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: thirteen at minimum. Twelve slots, thirteen occupants — the thirteenth must repeat a month. The pigeonhole principle turns pure counting into an iron guarantee.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The pigeonhole principle: more items than slots forces a repeat — no probability, pure guarantee.
Its power is turning 'must happen' conclusions from arithmetic alone.
Hash collisions and birthday guarantees both live here.
Ask 'how many holes?' whenever a repeat is suspected.
Share this: bet a friend that among 13 people, two share a birth month — you cannot lose.

puzzles.title: The Handshake Count
puzzles.question: 8 colleagues each shake hands once with everyone else. How many handshakes happen in total?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — each of 8 people shakes 7 hands, giving 56 endpoints; every handshake owns exactly 2, so 56 ÷ 2.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: twenty-eight. Count endpoints (8 × 7 = 56) and halve for double-counted pairs, or simply add 7 + 6 + 5 + … + 1. Answering 56 forgets that every shake was tallied twice.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Pair-counting: n objects create n(n−1)/2 unordered pairs — halve the endpoint count.
Double counting is both the trap and the tool: count twice, divide once.
The same arithmetic prices tournaments and network links.
Whenever relations are mutual, suspect the halving step.
Share this: compute the handshake total for your own dinner party before it meets.

puzzles.title: The Sock Drawer
puzzles.question: A drawer holds two red and two blue socks in the dark. You pull two at random. What is the chance they match?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — after the first sock, three remain and only one matches it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: one third. Fix the first sock pulled; among the three left behind, exactly one shares its colour. The 'half' instinct treats the second draw as a fresh coin flip — but the drawer changed when the first sock left it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Without-replacement draws shrink the pool: recompute after every pull.
Sequential conditioning beats formulas: fix the first outcome, price the second.
Card hands, lotteries and quality sampling all run this way.
The first draw silently edits the second's odds.
Share this: try the drawer trick with four real socks and count the matches.

puzzles.title: The Prosecutor's Error
puzzles.question: One person in a million carries a rare trait; the suspect matches it. The prosecutor says this makes him 'a million to one' guilty. What is the flaw?
choices: The trait might be planted evidence
It swaps 'trait if innocent' with 'innocent if trait'
puzzles.correctAnswer: It swaps 'trait if innocent' with 'innocent if trait'
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the million scales how often innocents match; it says nothing directly about this suspect without the base rate of suspects.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: it swaps 'trait if innocent' with 'innocent if trait'. The one-in-a-million prices the match among innocents; the courtroom needs the reverse conditional. With enough suspects tested, matching innocents abound — the transposed-conditional trap.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Conditionals do not commute: P(E|I) and P(I|E) are different quantities.
The prosecutor's fallacy reads the first as the second.
Base rates decide how far apart the two sit.
Screening tests and DNA dragnets stumble here most.
Share this: next 'one in a million' court headline, ask which direction the conditional runs.

puzzles.title: The Instructor's Curse
puzzles.question: Flight instructors praised great landings and got worse ones next; scolded poor ones and got better ones. They concluded feedback backfires. What did they miss?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — spectacular and terrible landings both drift toward the pilot's average next time; feedback merely rode the wave.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: extreme performances simply regress. An unusually great landing sits high partly by luck, so the next falls back — and punishment after bad ones 'works' the same illusory way. Kahneman told the instructors this and they refused to believe it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Regression to the mean: extremes contain luck, and luck evaporates — the next reading drifts inward.
Any feedback given at extremes inherits this illusion of causation.
Sports slumps, sick-day recoveries and fund years all regress.
Control groups exist precisely to separate drift from treatment.
Share this: before crediting a turnaround plan, ask what baseline drift predicted.

puzzles.title: The Hot Streak
puzzles.question: A fair coin flipped five times can land HHTHT or HHHHH. Which outcome is more likely?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — each ordered sequence of five flips carries probability 1/32; order has no favourites.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: they are exactly equal. Every named five-flip sequence has probability (1/2)⁵ — 'random-looking' orders are just as rare individually as streaks. Representativeness makes streakless runs feel likely, but equality is numerical, not aesthetic.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Equiprobable sequences: any exact ordered run carries the same tiny probability.
Randomness clumps — streaks and patterns are its texture, not its violation.
The representativeness bias judges sequences by looks instead of counts.
Named outcomes are individuals; frequency classes are the crowd.
Share this: ask someone to invent twenty 'random' flips and count the missing streaks.

puzzles.title: The Waiting Wheel
puzzles.question: On average, how many rolls of a fair die pass before the first six appears?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — a 1-in-6 event averages six trials; probability reciprocals set waiting times.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: six rolls. For a repeatable event with chance p, the expected wait is 1/p — here 1/(1/6). Feeling 'three, because it's half of six' has no arithmetic behind it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Waiting times: a repeatable event with chance p averages 1/p trials before first success.
Half the time you'll wait longer than the average — expectation hides skew.
Rare events (p small) mean long waits: 1/p explodes.
The rule prices everything from bus arrivals to radioactive decay.
Share this: predict how many cards until an ace, then check against 1/(4/52).

puzzles.title: Small Schools
puzzles.question: Both the best and the worst test scores in a district cluster among its smallest schools. What explains this?
choices: Small classes personalize both success and failure
Big schools quietly inflate their middling scores
Small schools attract both extremes of families
Small samples produce wilder averages by chance
puzzles.correctAnswer: Small samples produce wilder averages by chance
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a 20-student school's average swings hugely with each pupil; a 2,000-student average barely moves. Both extremes are small-sample noise.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: small samples produce wilder averages by chance. Averaging few observations leaves enormous room for fluke — one brilliant or disastrous cohort can carry a whole tiny school's average. Education policy was genuinely distorted by celebrating the 'small-school excellence' that was pure noise.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Small samples fluctuate: averaging fewer observations means wilder swings in both directions.
Both tails of district score tables are over-populated by small schools — the Wainer effect.
Policy built on extreme small groups is policy built on noise.
Always check the sample size behind any celebrated extreme.
Share this: find one 'best small X' ranking today and ask how many customers it averages.

puzzles.title: Rocket Clusters
puzzles.question: Wartime Londoners saw clusters in where bombs fell and mapped German targeting theories onto them. Statistical analysis later showed what?
choices: Bomb locations were indistinguishable from random scatter
The clusters were real aiming patterns
The Germans avoided specific suburbs deliberately
Londoners had mapped the bombs accurately
puzzles.correctAnswer: Bomb locations were indistinguishable from random scatter
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — pure randomness clumps; the clusters needed no aiming system to exist.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: bomb locations were indistinguishable from random scatter. Poisson randomness naturally produces apparent clusters — the mind, a relentless pattern-finder, then reads intention into the grouping. Clustering illusion: randomness looks like design to a species built for spotting design.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Clustering illusion: random scatter clumps, and pattern-hungry minds read the clumps as intention.
Wartime London even evacuated districts over imagined targeting logic.
Classic experiment: humans consistently judge truly random sequences as 'too clumpy' and arranged ones as random.
Demand the statistical baseline before accepting any map of meaning.
Share this: drop 50 rice grains on a tray and hunt the 'deliberate' clusters.

puzzles.title: Affirming the Rain
puzzles.question: If the sprinklers ran, the lawn is damp. The lawn is damp. Can you conclude the sprinklers ran?
choices: No — rain or dew do it too
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — rain or dew do it too
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — affirming the consequent: the rule gives P→Q, but Q alone never proves P.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: no — rain or dew do it too. 'If P then Q' plus 'Q' leaves P undecided; other causes reach the same effect. The invalid twin of modus ponens fools even careful reasoners daily.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Affirming the consequent: from P→Q and Q, nothing about P follows.
The invalid twin of modus ponens — same shape, hollow center.
Diagnosis, debugging and detective work trip here constantly.
List rival causes before accepting the obvious one.
Share this: catch one 'symptom proves cause' claim today and name its rivals.

puzzles.title: The Green Lamp
puzzles.question: If the vault is sealed, the lamp glows red. The lamp glows green. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — modus tollens: the predicted glow's absence denies the sealing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the vault is disarmed. 'If P then Q' plus 'not Q' yields 'not P' — the only valid backward move in conditional logic. The manual-reread option adds machinery the puzzle never granted.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Modus tollens: from P→Q and the absence of Q, infer the absence of P — the valid backward inference.
Science runs on it: failed predictions falsify the hypothesis.
The invalid backward moves are affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.
Check direction before trusting any conditional conclusion.
Share this: falsify one small belief tonight with a missing predicted glow.

puzzles.title: Necessary Keys
puzzles.question: A vault opens only for key-holders. Priya opens the vault. What must be true of Priya?
choices: She forced it with a spare key
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 'only key-holders open it' makes holding a key necessary for opening, and Priya opened it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: she is definitely a key-holder. Necessary conditions run one way: opening requires the key, though the key alone might not suffice. Reversing to 'all key-holders have opened it' would overclaim.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Necessary versus sufficient: a requirement for X need not guarantee X.
'Only members may enter' makes membership necessary, not sufficient, for entry.
Sufficiency runs the other direction: a sufficient badge always opens the door.
Test-makers and contracts live and die on this distinction.
Share this: find one 'only' sentence today and state exactly which direction it points.

puzzles.title: All That Glitters
puzzles.question: 'All drones are machines.' Which conclusion is guaranteed?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — if every drone sits inside the machine set, then some machine must be a drone.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: some machines are drones. 'All A are B' guarantees 'some B are A' (given drones exist), but never the flipped universal — illicit conversion. The tempting 'all machines are drones' reverses container and contained.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Universal statements convert only weakly: 'All A are B' yields 'some B are A', never 'all B are A'.
Illicit conversion — flipping container into contained — is the classic quantifier trap.
'All roses are flowers' never promised all flowers are roses.
Existential import quietly assumes the subject class is non-empty.
Share this: flip one 'all' sentence you hear today and check whether it survives.

puzzles.title: De Morgan Doors
puzzles.question: It is false that it is both raining and cold. What must be true?
choices: It is neither raining nor cold
It is not raining or not cold
puzzles.correctAnswer: It is not raining or not cold
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — denying a conjunction yields a disjunction of denials: not raining, or not cold, or both.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: it is not raining or not cold. De Morgan's law: NOT(A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B). Denying half a conjunction leaves the other half live — which is why 'neither' overclaims.
puzzles.lessonContent:
De Morgan's laws: 'not both' means 'at least one not'; 'not either' means 'both not'.
Negation distributes by flipping AND to OR and vice versa.
Code conditions, contracts and alibis all turn on these flips.
Mis-negation is the bug behind countless 'all exceptions' clauses.
Share this: negate one 'both' claim tonight using the OR-flip.

puzzles.title: The Valid Swap
puzzles.question: 'Some athletes are students.' What follows with certainty?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 'some A are B' converts cleanly to 'some B are A'; the overlap reads both ways.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: some students are athletes. Particular statements convert symmetrically — the overlap of the two groups is the same crowd either way round. Only the universals resist flipping.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Particular statements swap safely: 'some A are B' always gives 'some B are A'.
The overlap is one crowd viewed from either side.
Universals ('all') convert only to particulars, never to universals.
Syllogism checkers live on exactly these conversion tables.
Share this: convert one 'some' sentence you read today and verify the overlap.

puzzles.title: Denying the Antecedent
puzzles.question: If the power fails, the freezer thaws. The power is fine. Can you conclude the freezer is frozen?
choices: No — the door may hang open
It might still thaw for other reasons
puzzles.correctAnswer: It might still thaw for other reasons
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — steady power doesn't prove frozen contents; an open door thaws regardless.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: it might still thaw for other reasons. 'If P then Q' plus 'not P' leaves Q open — the invalid mirror of modus tollens. Power suffices for freezing; it was never necessary.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Denying the antecedent: from P→Q and not-P, nothing about Q follows.
The invalid mirror of modus tollens — same shape, hollow center.
Sufficiency is not necessity: rain could cancel the match without being its only canceller.
Check direction before trusting any conditional conclusion.
Share this: catch one 'no cause, so no effect' claim today and name its rivals.

puzzles.title: The Sunk Ticket
puzzles.question: You paid for a concert ticket but now feel ill and would rather rest. A friend offers an identical spare ticket free. Should the money already spent affect your choice?
choices: Yes — waste nothing you paid for
Only if the ticket was expensive
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the money is gone either way; only tonight's comfort versus tonight's concert should decide.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: no — ignore the sunk costs. Spent money is identical in every future, so it cancels out of rational choice. Honouring it anyway is how bad evenings, bad projects and bad wars continue.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sunk costs are unrecoverable and identical in every future — so they deserve zero weight.
The feeling of waste is real but points backwards, where decisions cannot go.
The Concorde fallacy names the plane nobody could stop funding.
Ask 'starting fresh today, would I choose this?' to cut the anchor.
Share this: audit one ongoing commitment tonight with the fresh-start question.

puzzles.title: The Breathing Gas
puzzles.question: Which gas do green plants absorb from the air to make their food?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — carbon dioxide goes in, and oxygen comes out as the by-product.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: carbon dioxide. Plants pull it from the air and, with sunlight and water, turn it into sugar — releasing the oxygen we breathe as the leftover. Forests are net absorbers of exactly this gas.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Photosynthesis runs on three inputs: light, water, and one airborne gas.
That gas has risen about fifty percent since industrialization began.
Plants return the favour as oxygen — the waste product we live on.
Oceans and forests split the absorbing work between them.
Share this: stand near one tree today and thank it for its half of your next breath.

puzzles.title: The Golden Code
puzzles.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — Au, from aurum, the Latin word for gold.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Au. Chemical symbols descend from Latin names — aurum for gold, argentum for silver, ferrum for iron. Memorizing the Latin dozen unlocks most of the periodic table's odd-looking codes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Many element symbols are Latin fossils: Au from aurum, Ag from argentum, Fe from ferrum.
Latin was the shared language of early chemistry across Europe.
The dozen Latin-derived symbols are the only ones that look surprising.
Once you know aurum, Au stops being arbitrary and starts being history.
Share this: decode Na, K and Pb tonight using the same Latin trick.

puzzles.title: The Heat Measurer
puzzles.question: Which instrument measures temperature?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a thermometer translates heat into a readable scale.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a thermometer. Whether mercury rising in glass or a digital probe changing resistance, the job is identical — convert molecular motion into a number. Galileo's air thermoscope was the great-grandparent of them all.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Temperature is average molecular motion, and instruments convert that motion into numbers.
Old glass thermometers read expanding liquid; digital ones read changing resistance.
The Celsius scale pins 0 and 100 to water's freezing and boiling.
Kelvin starts at absolute zero, where motion itself stops.
Share this: guess the room's temperature before checking, and calibrate your inner scale.

puzzles.title: The Frozen Form
puzzles.question: What do you call water in its solid state?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — ice: water's molecules locked into a crystal lattice.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: ice. Cool liquid water below zero degrees and its molecules settle into a hexagonal crystal — the solid form of H2O. That lattice takes slightly more room than the liquid, which is the whole reason the cubes float.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Freezing locks molecules into repeating crystal patterns instead of flowing freely.
Water's crystal is unusually spacious, so its solid floats on its liquid.
Snowflakes grow their six arms one water molecule at a time.
Glaciers are simply this crystal scaled to continents.
Share this: freeze water in a lidded bottle tonight and inspect the crystal bulge by morning.

puzzles.title: The Leap Total
puzzles.question: How many days are in a leap year?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a leap year packs 366 days, one more than usual.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 366. Earth needs about 365 and a quarter days per orbit, and the leftover quarters accumulate — every four years we bank one extra day to resync the calendar. Without it, seasons would drift through the months.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Earth's year is about 365.25 days, not a tidy integer — calendars must absorb the fraction.
Banking one day every four years keeps seasons pinned to their months.
Century years skip the leap unless divisible by 400 — 2000 qualified, 1900 did not.
The drift it prevents would otherwise move summer through winter over centuries.
Share this: ask someone born on February 29th how they count birthdays.

puzzles.title: The Closest Orbit
puzzles.question: Which planet orbits closest to the Sun?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — Mercury, sprinting around the Sun in just 88 days.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mercury. It hugs the Sun closer than any sibling world, racing through its year in 88 Earth days. Its sun-baked dayside and frozen nightside make it the solar system's most extreme commuter.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mercury orbits nearest the Sun, completing a year in 88 Earth days.
Proximity means extremes: scorching dayside, frozen nightside, almost no air to even things out.
Its oddly precessing orbit once puzzled Newton — only relativity explained the wobble.
A year there is shorter than a single one of its solar days.
Share this: look up Mercury's next evening appearance and catch the swift planet yourself.

puzzles.title: The Body Pump
puzzles.question: Which organ pumps blood around the human body?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the heart: a fist-sized muscle beating about 100,000 times a day.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the heart. This double pump pushes blood to the lungs and body in one loop, never resting between beats. It moves roughly 7,500 litres daily through 100,000 kilometres of vessels.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The heart is a double pump: right side to the lungs, left side to everything else.
It beats around 100,000 times a day without maintenance downtime.
Its vessels laid end to end would circle the planet twice.
Exercise remodels it like any muscle — athletes grow measurably larger ones.
Share this: find your pulse tonight and count the beats in a full resting minute.

puzzles.title: The Air Majority
puzzles.question: Which gas makes up most of the air you breathe?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — nitrogen: nearly four-fifths of every breath, inert and mostly along for the ride.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: nitrogen. About 78% of air is nitrogen, versus 21% oxygen — the famous one-fifth we actually use. Nitrogen's talent is stability: it dilutes oxygen to breathable strength without reacting with much.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Air is mostly nitrogen — 78% inert background gas, with oxygen second at 21%.
Nitrogen's laziness is a feature: it dilutes oxygen to safe, breathable strength.
Lightning fixes a little of it into soil food each storm.
Divers breathe doctored mixes precisely to dodge nitrogen's deep-water effects.
Share this: tell someone tonight that each breath is mostly one gas they never use.

puzzles.title: The Hardest Stone
puzzles.question: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance known?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — diamond: carbon locked in the tightest crystal lattice nature builds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: diamond. Every carbon atom grips four neighbours in a perfect tetrahedron, and that geometry defeats every other natural material. Only another one of its kind can cut it — which is why industrial drills wear it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Hardness is resistance to scratching, and carbon's tetrahedral lattice wins outright.
Graphite is the same atoms rearranged loosely — pencil lead versus jewel.
Structure, not just chemistry, decides a material's character.
Labs now grow gem-grade crystals that jewellers accept as genuine.
Share this: press a pencil tip and remember it shares atoms with the hardest thing known.

puzzles.title: The Positive Core
puzzles.question: What positively charged particles sit in an atom's nucleus?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — protons: the positive residents of the nucleus, and their count defines each element.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: protons. The number of protons in the nucleus is an element's atomic number — its entire identity. Neutrons add weight without charge; electrons, far lighter, orbit the whole assembly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Protons carry the atom's positive charge and define its element — change the count, change the substance.
Rutherford found the nucleus by firing particles at gold foil and watching them bounce.
Neutrons pad the mass; electrons, two thousand times lighter, do the chemistry.
Stars forge heavier nuclei by fusing lighter ones under crushing heat.
Share this: recite hydrogen, helium, lithium tonight — the first three proton counts.

puzzles.title: The Honey Source
puzzles.question: What sweet substance do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — nectar: the sugary bribe flowers offer in exchange for pollination.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: nectar. Bees haul this sugary liquid home, fan off its water, and seal the result as honey. Flowers evolved the bribe; bees evolved the collection service — pollination is the trade both sides signed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Nectar is a flower's payment to pollinators — sugar water offered for delivery services.
Bees evaporate most of its water and add enzymes to finish the honey.
Flowers advertise with colour and scent tuned to their couriers' senses.
The whole exchange is a contract written in chemistry.
Share this: watch one bee work a flowerbed and read the trade happening.

puzzles.title: The Red World
puzzles.question: Which planet is nicknamed the Red Planet?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — Mars, stained red by iron oxide dust across its deserts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mars. Its soil is rich in rusted iron, which dyes the whole world salmon-pink through telescopes. Ancient cultures named it for war on that colour alone, long before rovers confirmed the chemistry.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mars is red because it is rusty: iron oxide dust coats the surface and tints its sky.
Iron-rich rock plus ancient water chemistry plus wind equals a planet-wide patina.
The colour earned it war-god names across unrelated cultures.
Its sunsets reverse ours — blue halos around a dimmer Sun.
Share this: find a rusted bolt tonight and announce you are holding a piece of Mars's wardrobe.

puzzles.title: The Vast Ocean
puzzles.question: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the Pacific: wider than the Moon's diameter and deeper than Everest is tall.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Pacific. It sprawls across a third of Earth's surface — every continent could fit inside it with room to spare. Magellan named it for its calm, though typhoons would like a word.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The Pacific covers a third of Earth's surface — wider than the Moon is round.
Its trenches plunge past eleven kilometres, deeper than Everest stands tall.
The 'Ring of Fire' rims it with the planet's most violent geology.
Magellan's crew crossed it in 99 days without resupply — and named it peaceful.
Share this: spin a globe tonight and note how much of it is one blue expanse.

puzzles.title: Downward Always
puzzles.question: What invisible force pulls falling objects toward the ground?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — gravity: Earth's mass tugging everything toward its centre.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: gravity. Every mass attracts every other mass, and Earth's bulk wins every local contest — pulling apples, tides and satellites along their paths. Einstein later reframed it as spacetime itself curving around mass.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Gravity is mutual attraction between masses — Earth wins every nearby contest by sheer bulk.
It holds the Moon in orbit and the coffee in your cup.
Einstein's upgrade: mass dents spacetime, and falling is rolling downhill in four dimensions.
Weighing less on the Moon is the same force with a smaller planet behind it.
Share this: drop two different objects tonight and watch gravity refuse to discriminate.

puzzles.title: The Ringed Giant
puzzles.question: Which planet is famous for its spectacular system of rings?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — Saturn, girdled by rings of ice and rock hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Saturn. Its rings are billions of chunks of water ice, from dust grains to house-sized boulders — spanning a vast disc yet in places only ten metres thick. Other giants wear faint rings too; none wear them like this.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Saturn's rings are ice and rock in billions of pieces, from dust to boulders.
The span is planetary, the thickness in places just ten metres — a sheet of debris of absurd proportions.
Shepherd moons braid and gap the rings into structure.
The rings are likely young, and possibly temporary on cosmic timescales.
Share this: describe the rings tonight as 'a snowstorm a hundred thousand kilometres wide, thinner than a house'.

puzzles.title: The Solar Center
puzzles.question: What sits at the centre of our solar system, holding the planets in orbit?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the Sun: 99.8% of the system's mass, and gravity does the rest.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the Sun. It holds 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system, so its gravity dictates every orbit. Placing it at the centre took humanity until Copernicus — the sky looks geocentric until the mathematics is done.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The Sun owns 99.8% of the solar system's mass — the planets are crumbs by comparison.
Its gravity choreographs every orbit, from Mercury's sprint to Neptune's crawl.
Moving Earth from the centre took Copernicus, Kepler and Galileo combined.
A million Earths would fit inside it with room to spare.
Share this: hold a peppercorn at arm's length tonight and call it the scale of us to it.

puzzles.title: The Breath Gas
puzzles.question: Which gas do humans need to breathe in to survive?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — oxygen: the electron acceptor your cells use to unlock food's energy.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: oxygen. It is the terminal partner in your energy chemistry — without it, the mitochondrial assembly line stalls within minutes. Brain cells die fastest, which is why breathing outranks every other priority.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Oxygen is the acceptor that lets cells unlock food's stored energy — the fire that burns your fuel.
The brain consumes a fifth of it and tolerates minutes without it at most.
Plants exhale it as photosynthesis's waste — it is literally their exhaust.
Too much of it is also toxic; medicine doses it carefully.
Share this: take one deliberate slow breath and name the molecule doing the work.

puzzles.title: The Common Name
puzzles.question: What is H2O commonly called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — water: two hydrogens and one oxygen wearing the plainest name in science.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: water. The most common compound on Earth's surface hides behind a one-syllable everyday word instead of its formula. Chemists named thousands of substances systematically, then left the most important one with its childhood nickname.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Water's formula hides in plain sight: H2O, two hydrogens per oxygen.
Systematic naming would call it dihydrogen monoxide — nobody does.
The everyday name survived because the substance predates chemistry itself.
Ice, steam and liquid are one compound in three costumes.
Share this: say 'dihydrogen monoxide' with a straight face tonight and watch the room.

puzzles.title: The Faster Messenger
puzzles.question: Which travels faster: light or sound?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — light outruns sound by roughly a million to one.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: light. At 300,000 kilometres per second against sound's mere 343 metres, the race is not close — thunder always arrives as old news. The lightning-then-thunder delay is this gap made visible.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Light beats sound by about a million to one — the gap behind every flash-then-rumble.
Count seconds between lightning and thunder, divide by three: kilometres to the storm.
Concert-goers far from the stage hear the delayed truth of it.
The ratio is why the sky can be silent while still flashing.
Share this: time one storm's gap tonight and announce the storm's distance.

puzzles.title: The Web Spinners
puzzles.question: How many legs does a spider have?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — eight: the arachnid signature, two more than any insect.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: eight. Spiders are arachnids, not insects, and the leg count is the quickest field mark — six means insect, eight means spider. Harvestmen and ticks keep the same family number.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Eight legs mark the arachnids: spiders, scorpions, ticks and harvestmen.
Insects stop at six — the two extra legs are the field test.
Leg one on each side often works as a feeler, tasting and touching.
Spiders taste with their feet, which reframes every web they walk.
Share this: count the next spider's legs before deciding what it is.

puzzles.title: Martian Companions
puzzles.question: How many moons does Mars have?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — two lumpy captured asteroids: Phobos and Deimos, fear and panic.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: two. Phobos and Deimos are captured asteroids, too small to have rounded themselves — potatoes in orbit. Phobos is slowly spiralling inward and will one day shatter into a ring around Mars.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mars keeps two captured asteroids as moons — lumpy, cratered potatoes.
Phobos orbits so fast it rises twice per Martian day.
It is also doomed: spiralling inward, it will one day shatter into a ring.
Deimos, smaller and farther, drifts outward to safety.
Share this: tell someone Mars has two moons tonight and price their surprise.

puzzles.title: The Tallest Range
puzzles.question: Mount Everest sits in which mountain range?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the Himalayas: the planet's highest range, still growing a few millimetres a year.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the Himalayas. India is still ramming into Asia, and the collision keeps lifting the range — Everest grows taller while you read this. Fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres all stand in these mountains.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The Himalayas are a slow-motion collision: India driving into Asia, lifting rock skyward.
Everest grows a few millimetres yearly — the range is unfinished business.
Fourteen eight-thousanders stand in these mountains and nowhere else.
The same collision fuels the region's great earthquakes.
Share this: explain tonight why the world's tallest mountains are still under construction.

puzzles.title: The Water Formula
puzzles.question: What is the chemical formula of water?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — H2O: two hydrogens bonded to one oxygen.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: H2O. Two hydrogen atoms share electrons with one oxygen in a bent arrangement — and that bend gives water nearly all its strange talents, from surface tension to dissolving power. Three letters, one planet's whole chemistry set.
puzzles.lessonContent:
H2O's bent shape makes it polar — one end faintly positive, the other faintly negative.
That polarity dissolves salts, builds surface tension, and floats ice.
Water's strangeness is chemistry's most consequential accident.
Life may depend on no other molecule so completely.
Share this: draw the Mickey-Mouse head of H2O tonight — ears of hydrogen, face of oxygen.

puzzles.title: Boiling Point
puzzles.question: At sea level, water boils at how many degrees Celsius?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 100 degrees Celsius: the scale's upper anchor, defined at sea-level pressure.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 100. Celsius pinned its boiling point to water at sea level — zero at freezing, one hundred at boiling. Climb a mountain and the number drops, because thinner air lets bubbles form with less heat.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Celsius anchors 0 to freezing and 100 to boiling — at sea level, always add the pressure.
Higher altitudes boil cooler: climbers brew weak tea for physics reasons.
Pressure cookers reverse the trick, boiling hotter than 100.
Kelvin keeps the same degree size and simply starts at absolute zero.
Share this: guess your kettle's whistle temperature before checking — then climb to change it.

puzzles.title: The Hottest World
puzzles.question: Which planet has the hottest surface, even though it is not the closest to the Sun?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — Venus: a runaway greenhouse effect bakes it hotter than Mercury ever gets.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Venus. Its crushing carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat so completely that the surface melts lead — around 465 degrees. Proximity loses to atmosphere: Mercury, nearer the Sun, stays cooler for lack of a blanket.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Venus is the cautionary tale of runaway greenhouse warming — heat in, almost none out.
Its surface could melt lead, though it orbits farther than Mercury.
Soviet landers survived there for about an hour each — heroic engineering against hell.
Understanding Venus is partly how we model Earth's own climate levers.
Share this: tell someone the hottest planet isn't the nearest, and watch the blanket explanation land.

puzzles.title: Spine Without Bone
puzzles.question: I have leaves but I'm not a tree, a spine but no backbone, and I can take you anywhere without moving. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — a book. Leaves, spine and travel, all borrowed from other trades.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a book. Every clue borrows anatomy or travel vocabulary — leaves, spine, journeys — and applies it to paper. The riddle works because the metaphors are all perfectly literal in the new setting.
puzzles.hintText:
Stories live inside me.
I open flat on your lap.
Centuries fit between my covers.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stories compress whole lives into evenings — the oldest compression technology we own.
The novel's true unit is the voice, not the plot; voices linger for decades.
Reading trains one muscle above all: sustained attention in a skimming age.
Libraries are the only public buildings dedicated to borrowing minds.
Share this: reread the first page of a childhood favorite tonight.

puzzles.title: Arms That Never Hug
puzzles.question: I have arms but I cannot hug, a neck but I cannot swallow, buttons but no eyes. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a shirt. Anatomy words doing clothing duty.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a shirt. Arms, neck and buttons all belong to garments as much as to bodies, and the riddle leans on the shared vocabulary. Once you scan the wardrobe instead of the body, every clue lands.
puzzles.hintText:
You wear me every day without noticing.
I button up the front.
Laundry knows me well.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Clothes carry anatomy in their seams: collars, sleeves, waists live borrowed lives.
Fashion archaeology reads status and trade from cut and cloth.
The borrowed-body vocabulary makes dressing a daily act of metaphor.
Denim and linen each carry centuries of labor inside their weave.
Share this: count the body-words in your outfit tonight — neck, arm, waist, foot.

puzzles.title: The Noon Shrinker
puzzles.question: You see me in daylight but never at night; the taller you stand at noon, the smaller I become. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a shadow. High sun shortens it; low sun stretches it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a shadow. At noon the sun is nearly overhead, so your projected silhouette contracts to a stub — the taller the sun, the smaller the shade. Night removes the light source entirely, and with it, the whole phenomenon.
puzzles.hintText:
I shrink at noon and stretch at dusk.
Light makes me; darkness erases me.
Step into shade and I vanish.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Light defines form by what it withholds as much as by what it gives.
Chiaroscuro — the Renaissance play of bright against dark — is painting's grammar.
Photography is literally drawing with light, and half the skill is waiting for the dark.
Eclipses are the solar system staging the same drama at planetary scale.
Share this: at noon tomorrow, find the shortest version of yourself.

puzzles.title: The Honest Eye
puzzles.question: What lets you look straight through a solid wall without any hole in it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a window. The wall stays whole; only vision passes through.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a window. The trick plays on 'through': most senses are blocked by walls, but sight travels on light, and transparent solids let light pass. A wall you can see through breaks the assumption the verb smuggled in.
puzzles.hintText:
You are looking through one possibly right now.
Glass is my only material.
Curtains are my eyelids.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Glass architecture turned walls into weather you can watch — greenhouses first, skyscrapers after.
Transparency culture borrowed the metaphor: open books, open doors, open data.
Every view frames; every frame edits. The honest eye still chooses.
Museums place guards near what glass makes touchable-but-untouchable.
Share this: stare through any pane tonight and notice it, not the view.

puzzles.title: Eighty-Eight Keys
puzzles.question: What has 88 keys but cannot open a single door?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a piano. Eighty-eight sounding keys, zero locks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a piano. 'Key' does double duty: lock-openers and note-players share the word, and the question leans on the first meaning until the number 88 forces the second. The black-key grouping is the fingerprint that confirms it.
puzzles.hintText:
My black keys come in groups of two and three.
Composers fear and love me.
I weigh a quarter of a ton.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Equal temperament divided the octave into twelve fixed steps — the compromise all Western music rides.
Eighty-eight was chosen as the practical span of hearing's musical range.
Keyboard skill is really two-handed independence training.
The metronome, the tuner and the key are music's quiet infrastructure.
Share this: hum the lowest note you can reach and the highest, then measure the gap.

puzzles.title: Hands That Never Clap
puzzles.question: It has hands but cannot clap, a face that never smiles. What tells you the hour but never how much is left?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a clock. It shows the time while knowing nothing of anyone's remaining hours.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a clock. Hands and face belong to timepieces as much as to bodies, and the riddle's sting is in the second half: a device that displays every hour yet understands none of their weight. The melancholy is doing half the work.
puzzles.hintText:
Numbers ring my face.
I hang in classrooms everywhere.
Ticking is my voice.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Timekeeping began with shadows and water, graduated to gears, and ended in atoms.
The second is now defined by counting cesium oscillations — time's anchor is physical.
Every schedule you keep is a treaty with celestial mechanics.
Punctuality is a recent invention; most of history ran on tasks, not hours.
Share this: spend one morning without checking the time and feel the day widen.

puzzles.title: The Multiplied Self
puzzles.question: I show you everything and keep nothing. Break me and I multiply. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a mirror. It owns nothing it displays, and each shard reflects the whole.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a mirror. It stores no image — it borrows light moment to moment — and shattering it multiplies the reflections instead of destroying them. 'Keep nothing' rules out cameras and memories; 'multiply when broken' rules out everything else.
puzzles.hintText:
Vampires famously avoid me.
I reverse left and right.
Makeup happens in front of me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-recognition is rare in nature — a handful of species pass the mark test.
Vanity and vanitas share a root: reflections have preached mortality for millennia.
Reflection physics is simple angle-in-equals-angle-out; its meanings are not.
Camera selfies industrialized a face we once glimpsed only in water.
Share this: hold eye contact with yourself for sixty seconds and notice who blinks first.

puzzles.title: Locked Rooms of Sleep
puzzles.question: You enter me every night and leave without opening any door, and no thief can steal me. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a dream. Entered nightly, exited without doors, unstealable.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a dream. Every clue points at the architecture of sleep: entry without movement, exit without doors, property that cannot be taken. Sleep itself is too broad — the riddle wants the content of those hours.
puzzles.hintText:
REM sleep is my doorway.
I vanish within minutes of waking.
Falling visions are my most common trick.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sleep researchers divide the night into 90-minute cycles ending in vivid story-theater.
Lucid visitors can signal from inside the performance with agreed eye movements.
Memory consolidation runs its night shift during these hours.
Every culture keeps interpretation manuals because the material demands attention.
Share this: keep a notebook by the bed for one week and catch the fleeing plots.

puzzles.title: Three Minutes of Air
puzzles.question: I'm invisible, yet you cannot live three minutes without me; hold me and you lose. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — breath. Invisible, vital, and lost the moment you grip it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is breath. Air itself is everywhere and costs nothing, but the rhythmic taking of it is fragile — hold the taking and the body revolts within minutes. The twenty-thousand count is the fingerprint that confirms which invisible the riddle means.
puzzles.hintText:
Divers train to hold me longest.
Meditation counts me.
You take about twenty thousand of me daily.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Oxygen delivery runs on rhythm: inhale feeds, exhale clears — the exchange never pauses.
Free divers train the urge-to-inhale reflex the way musicians train scales.
Meditation traditions discovered controlled inhaling as a nervous-system lever centuries ago.
The average resting rate hovers near a dozen cycles per minute.
Share this: count tonight's cycles for one minute without changing them — harder than it sounds.

puzzles.title: The Corner Traveler
puzzles.question: I travel the whole world while never leaving one small corner. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a stamp. It rides every mile while staying glued to the envelope's corner.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a stamp. The corner is its permanent address; the travelling is done by the envelope it rides. Licking and collecting are the two human rituals that confirm the identity.
puzzles.hintText:
I cost a fraction of the envelope.
Lick me, says tradition.
Collectors trade me like treasure.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Postal systems were the first planet-spanning networks ordinary people could use.
Prepayment flipped the cost onto senders and funded daily delivery for a penny.
Philately turned the tiny squares into the world's most collected art.
Email killed the letter's urgency but not its ceremony.
Share this: mail one real letter this week and track how the waiting feels.

puzzles.title: The Monthly Trim
puzzles.question: Trim me and I return; ignore me and I curl into claws. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — fingernails. Cut them and they regrow; neglect them and they hook.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is fingernails. Only keratin appendages do all three: regrow after trimming, curl when ignored, and get bitten in anxiety. Hair neither claws nor gets manicured in quite this ritual way.
puzzles.hintText:
Manicures exist because of me.
I grow about three millimetres a month.
Biting me is the nervous habit.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Keratin also builds hair, horns and hooves — one protein wearing many uniforms.
Growth from the base means today's tip is months-old history.
Forensic science reads timelines in hair shafts and growth rings alike.
The body repairs constantly; visible growth is the evidence.
Share this: photograph one hand today and again in thirty days.

puzzles.title: Wind's Crying Pet
puzzles.question: I fly with no wings and I cry without eyes whenever the wind hurts me. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a kite. It flies tethered and 'weeps' its tail in gusty wind.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a kite. The crying is the tail's flutter and the string's hum in rough air — a kite 'weeps' audibly when the wind bullies it. Franklin's storm experiment is the historical anchor that confirms the whole picture.
puzzles.hintText:
String is my leash.
Franklin flew me into a storm.
I dance but never choose direction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stringed flight is humanity's oldest aviation — millennia before engines.
Lift needs only relative airflow; the tether replaces the engine.
Franklin's storm experiment is the famous (and genuinely dangerous) chapter.
Modern power wings haul ships and generate electricity.
Share this: on the next windy day, watch how a flag knows the wind's mind before you do.

puzzles.title: The One-Way Climb
puzzles.question: What climbs every single day but never, ever comes back down?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — age. It accumulates daily and retreats never.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is age. Birthdays and candles are the cultural odometers, but the phenomenon is plain accumulation: every lived day adds, and no mechanism subtracts. Clocks measure it; calendars merely announce it.
puzzles.hintText:
Birthdays mark my progress.
Candles count me yearly.
Nobody has ever reversed me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Birthdays count laps around the Sun, not the laps themselves.
Cellular wear accumulates in telomeres, joints and memory — the ledger never balances backward.
Longevity research chases the rate, not the direction.
Every culture marks the climb with candles and cake.
Share this: ask someone their proudest number from the climb so far.

puzzles.title: The Staring Contest
puzzles.question: I'm built of words that hide something in plain sight; the harder you stare at my surface, the faster the answer retreats. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a riddle. The description fits the very object you're holding.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a riddle. Self-description is the giveaway: fair clues, hidden answer, retreat under scrutiny — and you are mid-solve as you read. The meta-layer is the whole joke.
puzzles.hintText:
You are solving one right now.
I obey rules: every clue true, every path fair.
My own answer is my punchline.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-describing puzzles are the oldest form of play with language.
The form predates books: Exeter Book verses teased monks a thousand years ago.
A good one obeys its own rules — every clue true, every path fair.
Solving them exercises the muscle of shifting interpretation.
Share this: invent a two-line puzzle tonight and test it before breakfast.

puzzles.title: The Heavy Whisper
puzzles.question: Tell me and I'm gone; keep me and I grow heavy. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a secret. Speaking it ends it; holding it weights it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a secret. Telling destroys the defining property — exclusivity — while keeping accrues the burden of guarding. Gossip and spycraft are the two industries built on this asymmetry.
puzzles.hintText:
Gossip trades in me.
“Don't tell anyone” feeds me.
Spies are my professional keepers.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Information gains weight the fewer carry it — scarcity applies to knowledge too.
Cryptography turned keeping into mathematics.
Spycraft runs on the rule that telling halves the value.
Diaries and safes are the domestic version of the same instinct.
Share this: keep one small delightful thing unsaid for a full day and feel its weight.

puzzles.title: The Patient Turner
puzzles.question: Turn me and everything around me changes, yet I never move from where I stand. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a page. Turned, it swaps the whole world before your eyes while staying put.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a page. Everything 'around' it — the visible text — transforms with the turn, while the page itself stays exactly where bound. Chapters, dog-ears and numbering confirm: the medium of print, not a globe or a screen.
puzzles.hintText:
Chapters are fenced by me.
Dog-ears mark my favorites.
I number in the hundreds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Before chapters, scrolls unrolled stories in one long breath.
Pagination invented pausing — the reader's first control over narrative flow.
Dog-ears and bookmarks are the reader's votes for passages.
Digital reading removed the spatial memory of left-versus-right.
Share this: notice tonight whether you remember a passage by its side of the spread.

puzzles.title: The Slippery Catch
puzzles.question: The harder you chase me, the faster I run away; students dread losing me before exams. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a memory. Pursuit pressure scatters it; calm retrieval catches it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a memory. Exam dread, sleep-filing and photo-backups triangulate exactly one thing: the fragile, chaseable, losable content of recall. Tip-of-the-tongue states are this phenomenon mid-flight.
puzzles.hintText:
Exams test me under stress.
Sleep files me overnight.
Photographs are my external backup.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Recall strengthens with retrieval practice — testing beats rereading for keeping.
Sleep files the day's intake; cramming skips the archivist.
Forgetting curves are steepest in the first hours — review early.
The exam hall measures what's left after stress takes its cut.
Share this: test yourself on one fact tonight instead of rereading it.

puzzles.title: Five Into Six
puzzles.question: What five-letter English word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 'short' plus two letters is 'shorter', which names being shorter.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is short. Adding 'er' yields 'shorter' — the word performs exactly what it describes. Self-demonstrating words are rare in English, which is why the counting ritual misleads: you count up while meaning shrinks.
puzzles.hintText:
Count my letters: one, two, three, four, five.
Add two more letters and count again.
I name myself truthfully.
puzzles.lessonContent:
English delights in self-demonstrating words — the famous one grows longer by claiming the opposite.
Autological words describe themselves: 'English' is English, 'unhyphenated' is unhyphenated.
Logicians collect these as curiosities on the edge of paradox.
Crosswords and cryptics live on such double-dealings.
Share this: find one English word tonight that performs what it names.

puzzles.title: Armies Weep
puzzles.question: You cannot see me and you cannot hold me, yet I can move whole armies to tears. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a song. Invisible, intangible, and capable of moving multitudes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a song. Armies march to anthems and break to laments; radio and humming are the delivery systems. The variant answer 'music' is the same phenomenon in bulk — songs are its portable units.
puzzles.hintText:
Radio carries me everywhere.
Anthems and lullabies are my two uniforms.
Humming is my quiet form.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Armies have marched to drums, pipes and anthems for millennia.
Sound organizes bodies: tempo entrains footsteps without permission.
The physiology is honest — shared rhythm synchronizes heartbeats in choirs.
Lullabies weaponize the same channel for peace.
Share this: play one march and one lullaby back to back and feel the gears shift.

puzzles.title: Water's Colder Twin
puzzles.question: I am born when water gets cold, and I die when warmth returns. Great ships fear my drifting giants. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — ice. Cold-born, warmth-killed, and dangerous at scale.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ice. Born of cold water and killed by warmth, it carries the paradox of a solid that floats on its own liquid. The drifting giants that sank the Titanic are its large-scale form.
puzzles.hintText:
I crack loudly when dropped in warm drinks.
Titanic met my giants.
Skaters trust me only when I'm thick.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Water is nearly alone in shrinking when it melts — the solid floats on its own liquid.
That quirk keeps lakes liquid beneath winter's lid, sheltering life below.
The same expansion bursts pipes and splits rocks across freeze-thaw cycles.
Climate records sleep inside ancient cores drilled from deep sheets.
Share this: float one cube in a glass and watch the waterline refuse to move.

puzzles.title: Pressure's Jewel
puzzles.question: Born of crushing pressure, I live forever; cut me and I shine. Coal's famous cousin — what am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a diamond. Carbon under pressure, forever, and brilliant when faceted.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a diamond. Born deep under crushing pressure from the same element as coal, it is the hardest natural substance; cutting multiplies its shine instead of destroying it. Nothing else combines permanence, family resemblance to coal, and faceted brilliance.
puzzles.hintText:
Engagement rings display me proudly.
Only I can cut my own kind.
My hardness scores a perfect ten.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Carbon wears two famous costumes: soft dark graphite and the hardest natural substance known.
Kimberlite pipes carried their cargo up from hundreds of kilometres deep.
Hardness made them industrial before they were romantic.
Engagement-ring culture is younger than the light bulb.
Share this: press pencil lead and remember it shares atoms with the hardest thing known.

puzzles.title: The Faithful Pointer
puzzles.question: I always point the way but never travel; lose me in the wild and direction dies with me. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a compass. Direction without motion, guidance without travel.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a compass. It points by aligning with Earth's magnetic field — never moving itself — and wilderness navigation dies with its loss. Maps tell you where things are; this tells you which way you face.
puzzles.hintText:
Hikers carry me in a pocket.
I align with Earth's hidden field.
Sailors steered by me for centuries.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Earth's field is a planetary-scale magnet born of churning iron.
Navigators trusted lodestones before they trusted stars.
Declination — the gap between magnetic and true north — must be corrected on every serious map.
Birds, turtles and bacteria read the same field without instruments.
Share this: walk one straight bearing through a park using only a phone sensor.

puzzles.title: Ships' Night Nurse
puzzles.question: I stand still where the land ends, guiding ships home by never moving. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a lighthouse. Immobile by design, and guidance is precisely what stillness buys.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a lighthouse. It never moves, never travels, never leaves the rocks — and every clue (flashing, foghorns, Pharos) is lighthouse-exclusive. Beacons on buoys move; towers do not.
puzzles.hintText:
I flash a signature pattern all night.
Foghorns are my voice in whiteout.
Pharos of Alexandria was my famous ancestor.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rotating beams sweep the dark in timed patterns, each station with its own signature flash.
Before radio, these towers were the only long-range guidance shipping had.
Automation has emptied most towers; the lights still work uncrewed.
Pharos of Alexandria gave its name to the whole family.
Share this: learn your nearest tower's flash signature and watch for it once.

puzzles.title: Teeth That Never Bite
puzzles.question: I have teeth but cannot chew; twist me and locked doors obey. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a key. Teeth for tumblers, obedience from locks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a key. Its teeth lift lock pins to the shear line; the twist then turns the plug. Combs and zippers have teeth too, but neither opens locked doors — the obedience clause rules them out.
puzzles.hintText:
Pockets jingle because of me.
Locksmiths copy me daily.
Lose me and call for help.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Pin-and-tumbler mechanisms pair each lock to one exact silhouette.
Locksmithing is among the oldest trades — Egyptian locks used wooden pins.
Modern equivalents hide in fobs, cards and biometric templates.
Every lock advertises the paradox it sells: convenience against intrusion.
Share this: count how many different silhouettes you carried today and who guards the originals.

puzzles.title: The Nightly Changer
puzzles.question: I change my face every night but I'm always the same underneath. Sometimes I'm gone, yet I never leave. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the moon. Phases change the face; the body never moves away.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the moon. New moons, crescents and full discs are lighting geometry, not transformation — the far side never shows, the near side never leaves. Apollo's visit confirmed what the riddle's third clue all but names.
puzzles.hintText:
Tides follow my schedule.
I show the same face always.
Apollo 11 landed on me in 1969.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Phases are geometry, not change: sunlight, a sphere, and your viewpoint.
Tides follow the same geometry — the pull you feel is orbital bookkeeping.
Calendars worldwide counted the cycle before they counted much else.
The far side is not dark, only unseen from here.
Share this: track one full cycle nightly and predict the shape three days ahead.

puzzles.title: Achilles Waits
puzzles.question: Zeno argued that swift Achilles can never overtake a tortoise given a head start, because he must first reach each point the tortoise has already left: an infinite sequence of catch-ups.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — that is the genuine structure of the Achilles paradox: infinitely many sub-tasks before the overtake.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Zeno's Achilles must first reach the tortoise's starting point, then the point it has since reached, endlessly — infinitely many ever-shrinking tasks. Calculus later showed infinite series can sum to a finite total, so Achilles passes the tortoise where the series converges.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Zeno's paradoxes pit infinite divisibility against finite completion — and force mathematics to answer.
The convergent-series resolution took two millennia: infinite terms can sum finitely.
Philosophers still debate whether the mathematics dissolves the metaphysics.
Supertasks, Thomson's lamp and modern cosmology all descend from this starting gun.
Share this: halve the remaining distance to any door tonight and ask when you would arrive.

puzzles.title: The Set That Breaks
puzzles.question: Russell's paradox shows that the set of all sets that do not contain themselves both must and must not belong to itself.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the set belongs to itself if and only if it does not: a genuine contradiction at the foundations.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Ask whether R contains itself: yes implies no (it only holds non-self-containing sets), no implies yes (it qualifies). Frege's life's work collapsed on receiving Russell's letter; type theory and ZF axioms were built to fence the paradox out.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Naive set theory allowed any definable collection — until Russell's construction broke it.
The damage was foundational: it struck mathematics' attempt to ground itself.
ZF set theory survives by restricting which collections count as sets.
Type theory layers the universe so self-membership cannot even be stated.
Share this: ask a programmer tonight about the halting problem — same shape, new clothes.

puzzles.title: This Sentence Lies
puzzles.question: The sentence 'This statement is false' can be consistently classified as either true or false in classical logic.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — true implies false and false implies true; no consistent classical assignment exists.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. If the sentence is true, what it says holds, so it is false; if false, its denial holds, so it is true. Each assignment refutes itself. Tarski concluded that no language can contain its own truth predicate without such breakage.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The Liar paradox is self-reference weaponized: a sentence whose content is its own falsehood.
Classical bivalence (every statement true or false) cannot survive it.
Tarski's hierarchy separates object language from metalanguage to quarantine the damage.
Gödel's incompleteness theorems are the Liar dressed in arithmetic.
Share this: say 'everything I say is a lie' at dinner and watch the table divide.

puzzles.title: The Vanishing Heap
puzzles.question: Removing grains one by one from a heap yields a precise grain count where 'heap' objectively stops applying.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — vague predicates have borderline zones; logic expects a sharpness reality never supplies.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Each single removal is too small to flip heap-hood, yet the heap is eventually gone — so 'heap' has no sharp boundary. The sorites shows that some concepts are irreducibly vague, and demanding exactness is the error.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The sorites exposes vagueness: remove one grain at a time and no step crosses from heap to non-heap.
Sharp boundaries fail for heap, bald, tall and red — yet the concepts still work.
Fuzzy logic and supervaluationism are formal attempts to live with vagueness.
Law lives inside it: 'reasonable' has no grain count either.
Share this: ask at what sip a glass becomes 'empty' and enjoy the heaping trouble.

puzzles.title: The Perfect Predictor
puzzles.question: In Newcomb's problem, a near-perfect predictor has already placed a million dollars in the opaque box if and only if it foresaw you taking only that box.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the setup guarantees the correlation: one-boxers find the million, two-boxers find nothing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. That is the stated setup — the predictor's track record is the whole engine of the puzzle. The fight between one-boxers and two-boxers is entirely about what rationality means when your choice is already predicted.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Newcomb's problem stages the clash between evidential and causal decision theory.
One-boxers follow the correlation; two-boxers follow dominance — both reason impeccably from different principles.
Real analogues hide in commitment devices and reputation games.
The puzzle's fame comes from splitting expert opinion almost evenly.
Share this: pose both boxes to a friend and note which principle they reach for first.

puzzles.title: Rat Out First
puzzles.question: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma between rational players with no future rounds, defecting is each player's dominant strategy.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — whatever the other does, defection pays more; rationality traps both in mutual defection.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Dominance means defection beats cooperation against a cooperator and against a defector alike — so both rational players defect and land worse off than mutual cooperation would have made them. Individual rationality misfires collectively.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dominant strategies win regardless of the opponent's move — and can still produce mutual ruin.
Arms races, price wars and overfishing are prisoner's dilemmas wearing costumes.
Iteration (tit-for-tat) rescues cooperation; one-shots usually don't.
Institutions exist largely to rewrite such payoffs.
Share this: name one daily standoff tonight where both sides keep defecting.

puzzles.title: Stable Disappointment
puzzles.question: In a Nash equilibrium, at least one player could still do better by changing strategy while everyone else keeps theirs.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — a Nash equilibrium is defined precisely by no player having such a unilateral improvement.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Nash equilibrium means every strategy is a best reply to the rest — deviation alone cannot help anyone. Equilibria can still be miserable (see: mutual defection); stability is not the same as goodness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Nash equilibrium: a strategy profile where no single player gains by deviating alone.
It guarantees stability, not desirability — mutual defection qualifies.
Traffic jams are Nash equilibria: no single driver improves by rerouting alone.
Mechanism design reshapes payoffs so equilibria land somewhere decent.
Share this: spot one stable-but-miserable routine in your own week.

puzzles.title: Admitting Both Bars
puzzles.question: A bar is open exactly when it is not closed; a bar that is neither open nor closed on a given night violates the law of excluded middle.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the law covers propositions, not establishments; a half-open pub door is not a logical counterexample.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Excluded middle governs statements (each is true or false), not doors, which admit degrees and schedules. Conflating physical half-states with logical truth values is a category error, not a paradox.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Excluded middle: every proposition is true or false, with nothing between.
It governs statements, not doors, dimmers or half-open pubs.
Intuitionist logicians genuinely dispute the law for undecidable claims.
Category errors — applying logic's laws to non-propositions — power many pseudo-paradoxes.
Share this: catch one 'the law says' claim tonight that isn't about statements at all.

puzzles.title: The Honest Average
puzzles.question: If two subgroups each show treatment A beating treatment B, then A must also beat B when the subgroups are pooled.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — Simpson's paradox: unequal subgroup sizes let the pooled result reverse every subgroup trend.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. When one treatment handles far more of the easy cases, its pooled average is inflated by composition, not merit. The kidney-stone trials are the textbook instance: the 'worse' treatment won both subgroups and lost the total.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Simpson's paradox: subgroup truths can all reverse in the pooled total.
The culprit is composition — different mixtures, not different merits.
Berkeley admissions, batting averages and hospital tables have all hosted it.
Stratify before you conclude; pooled numbers are guilty until proven innocent.
Share this: find one league table tonight and demand its mixture breakdown.

puzzles.title: Ward Correlations
puzzles.question: Two diseases that are independent in the whole population can appear negatively correlated among hospital patients.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — Berkson's paradox: conditioning on hospitalization manufactures the link from thin air.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Patients reach the ward by having at least one condition, so within the ward each disease predicts the other's absence. The correlation is real inside the sample and false outside it — selection, not biology, wrote it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Berkson's paradox: conditioning on admission welds independent traits into false correlation.
Whenever entry requires A or B, the admitted pool shows A implying not-B.
Elite-university 'trade-offs' and dating-app patterns repeat the fallacy.
Always ask who is missing from a dataset before believing its links.
Share this: name one correlation tonight that might just be an entry requirement.

puzzles.title: The Silent Coin
puzzles.question: A coin flipped 1,000 times lands heads every single time; the most rational next prediction, absent other information, is tails.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — if fair, each flip stays fifty-fifty; but a thousand heads screams that fairness itself is the wrong assumption.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. 'Tails is due' is the gambler's fallacy; the sophisticated move is doubting the coin — a real thousand-head run is overwhelming evidence of bias. Strictly: if certainly fair, every flip is fifty-fifty; with any doubt, bet on the bias, not the balance.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Extreme runs do double duty: they test your model of the coin, not just your tally.
Bayesians update the coin itself — a thousand heads is overwhelming evidence of bias.
The rookie error is predicting tails; the expert error is ignoring what the run says about fairness.
Casinos calibrate equipment precisely because long runs invite exactly this audit.
Share this: decide in advance how long a streak must run before you suspect the coin.

puzzles.title: The Denying Detective
puzzles.question: From 'if the culprit fled by car, tire marks remain' and 'no tire marks remain', a valid reasoner may conclude the culprit did not flee by car.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — modus tollens: denying the consequent validly denies the antecedent.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. 'If P then Q' plus 'not Q' yields 'not P' — the only valid backward move in conditional logic. Detectives, debuggers and scientists all live on this inference; it is falsification in work clothes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Modus tollens is the valid backward inference: kill the consequent, kill the antecedent.
Science runs on it — failed predictions falsify the hypothesis that made them.
Its invalid twins (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent) share the shape but not the license.
Falsificationism is modus tollens promoted to a philosophy of knowledge.
Share this: falsify one small belief tonight with a missing predicted clue.

puzzles.title: The Wet Pavement Proof
puzzles.question: From 'if it rains, the pavement is wet' and 'the pavement is wet', a valid reasoner may conclude that it rained.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — affirming the consequent: sprinklers, cleaners and burst pipes reach the same wetness by other routes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. 'If P then Q' plus 'Q' leaves P undecided — the consequent has many parents. This is the invalid twin of modus tollens, wearing the same clothes. Medical diagnosis and debugging trip here constantly: symptoms suggest, they never entail.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Affirming the consequent treats a sufficient condition as a necessary one.
The consequent's many alternative parents are what the fallacy ignores.
Diagnosis, debugging and detective work all require ruling those rivals out.
Abduction — inference to the best explanation — is the disciplined cousin.
Share this: catch one 'symptom proves cause' claim today and name two rival causes.

puzzles.title: Conversion Caution
puzzles.question: From 'all roses are flowers' it validly follows that 'all flowers are roses'.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — illicit conversion: the container is larger than its famous member, so the flip fails.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. 'All A are B' places A inside B; the reverse needs B inside A, which was never granted. What does follow is the weaker 'some flowers are roses' — conversion licenses the particular, never the universal.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Quantifier conversion has strict licenses: universals flip only into particulars.
Illicit conversion treats a subset relation as symmetric — it never is.
Advertising leans on the slip: 'athletes drink it' quietly becomes 'drinkers are athletes'.
Venn diagrams expose the asymmetry in one glance.
Share this: flip one 'all' claim tonight and test whether the reverse survives.

puzzles.title: Straw's Twin
