puzzles.question: A trainee labels medical images and says she is 95% accurate. She has never seen expert labels and cannot describe common error patterns. What feedback would most improve both skill and self-assessment?
choices: Praise her confidence so difficult cases feel less intimidating
Let her repeat only the images she already labelled quickly
Compare each prediction with expert labels and explain near misses
Ask her to increase her confidence estimate after every completed set
puzzles.correctAnswer: Compare each prediction with expert labels and explain near misses
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Item-level correction teaches the distinctions required both to perform well and to recognize one's own mistakes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Compare each prediction with expert labels and explain near misses. Repetition without an answer key can automate errors; diagnostic feedback builds the knowledge that accurate self-grading requires.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Poor calibration persists when learners receive completion signals but no correctness signals.
Detailed feedback teaches both task rules and the boundaries of current skill.
Near misses are valuable because they reveal which distinctions remain blurred.
Confidence should be scored against outcomes, not rewarded for its own intensity.
Share this: seek item-level feedback on one task you currently judge only by feel.

puzzles.title: The Winning Metric
puzzles.question: A team expects its redesign to help. After launch, retention falls but time-on-page rises, so it declares time-on-page the real goal. What would have best protected the evaluation from this shift?
choices: Collecting many more metrics after seeing the initial results
Letting the design team explain why its preferred metric matters
Removing any measure that contradicts the redesign's intended story
Committing beforehand to primary measures and decision thresholds
puzzles.correctAnswer: Committing beforehand to primary measures and decision thresholds
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Advance commitments prevent the team from promoting whichever outcome happens to confirm its hope.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is committing beforehand to primary measures and decision thresholds. More metrics create more chances to find a flattering result; a preregistered rule separates prediction from post-hoc storytelling.
puzzles.lessonContent:
When many outcomes are available, almost any result can support a preferred story.
Choosing success criteria after results converts testing into rationalization.
Advance commitments preserve the difference between prediction and explanation.
Secondary measures remain useful when clearly labelled as exploratory.
Share this: define success and failure before starting your next personal experiment.

puzzles.title: Charisma at Scale
puzzles.question: Investors love a founder's confidence and compelling mission, then rate the startup's security, market demand, and financial controls highly without checking them. Which process offers the strongest defence?
choices: Score predefined evidence for each risk before meeting the founder
Invite the founder to give a longer and more detailed presentation
Average every investor's overall impression after the pitch
Treat confidence as evidence that hidden operational details are sound
puzzles.correctAnswer: Score predefined evidence for each risk before meeting the founder
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Independent, pre-pitch risk scoring prevents personal magnetism from becoming evidence about controls the investors have not examined.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, score predefined evidence for each risk before meeting the founder. Longer exposure and averaged impressions can spread the same halo across the group; predefined criteria make each risk answer to its own evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Charisma is vivid social information that can contaminate technical judgements.
Group discussion does not cancel a halo when everyone shares the same first impression.
Predefined criteria reduce the freedom to reinterpret missing evidence favourably.
Evaluating components before the whole protects analysis from global liking.
Share this: make a scorecard before the next persuasive pitch you hear.

puzzles.title: Calibration Class
puzzles.question: The weakest performers in a statistics course greatly overrate their scores. After training, their scores and self-estimates both improve. What is the most careful interpretation?
choices: Their original confidence must have caused their weak performance
Learning the subject also improved the tools needed to judge their work
Low performers always become less confident as soon as they practise
Accurate self-assessment develops independently of task knowledge
puzzles.correctAnswer: Learning the subject also improved the tools needed to judge their work
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The knowledge that improves performance can also reveal what counts as an error, so skill and calibration may rise together.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — learning the subject also improved the tools needed to judge their work. The result does not show that confidence caused low scores or that confidence must fall; it shows task knowledge can support metacognition.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-evaluation is not a separate magic faculty; it draws on domain knowledge.
Training can improve both answers and recognition of what a good answer requires.
Calibration means matching confidence to accuracy, not merely lowering confidence.
A learner may become more confident and better calibrated at the same time.
Share this: compare confidence and accuracy before and after your next study session.

puzzles.title: The Referral Note
puzzles.question: Before examining a patient, a doctor reads a referral strongly suggesting migraine. Every later symptom gets interpreted through that diagnosis. Which procedure best reduces the pull of the initial theory?
choices: Read the referral repeatedly until its reasoning is fully memorable
Ask the patient only questions that distinguish migraine subtypes
Record an independent differential from raw findings before viewing the referral
Search old migraine cases for symptoms resembling this patient's report
puzzles.correctAnswer: Record an independent differential from raw findings before viewing the referral
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. An independent assessment preserves alternatives before the referral hypothesis can organize attention and interpretation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is to record an independent differential from raw findings before viewing the referral. Repeated referral review and migraine-focused questions narrow the search further; temporal separation protects a second evidential path.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Diagnostic labels guide attention toward matching symptoms and away from alternatives.
Independent first-pass judgements preserve information that an anchor might suppress.
Differential reasoning keeps multiple causes alive until evidence separates them.
Order matters: evidence seen first can organize everything interpreted later.
Share this: form your own estimate before reading someone else's confident conclusion.

puzzles.title: Prestige on Paper
puzzles.question: Reviewers praise a candidate's writing, teamwork, and judgement after noticing she worked at a famous company. Which change most directly tests whether prestige is inflating unrelated ratings?
choices: Tell reviewers which famous teams the candidate collaborated with
Ask the candidate to describe why the company hired her
Have reviewers discuss the company's reputation before scoring
Remove employer identities and rescore the same evidence independently
puzzles.correctAnswer: Remove employer identities and rescore the same evidence independently
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. A blinded rescore changes the prestige cue while holding the underlying evidence constant.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: remove employer identities and rescore the same evidence independently. More discussion of the famous employer magnifies the halo; blinding creates a direct comparison of ratings with and without it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Institutional prestige can act as a halo around an individual's unmeasured qualities.
A clean test changes the identity cue while preserving the work being judged.
Independent rescoring prevents discussion from pressuring reviewers toward consensus.
Blind review cannot remove every bias, but it can isolate a specific source.
Share this: evaluate one piece of work before learning who made it.

puzzles.title: Confident but Vague
puzzles.question: In meetings, Arun confidently claims a project is 'certain to succeed' but gives no measurable forecast. Which request would make his self-assessment easiest to calibrate?
choices: Ask for a dated, testable prediction with a numerical confidence level
Ask him to repeat the claim after the team lists its concerns
Let him define success only after the project has finished
Count how many colleagues describe his delivery as convincing
puzzles.correctAnswer: Ask for a dated, testable prediction with a numerical confidence level
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. A specific forecast can be scored later, turning impressive certainty into evidence about actual calibration.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is to ask for a dated, testable prediction with a numerical confidence level. Vague certainty escapes correction because success can be redefined; scored forecasts reveal whether confidence frequencies match outcomes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Vague claims protect confidence from contact with failure.
Calibration compares stated probabilities with long-run outcome frequencies.
Dated forecasts prevent memory from polishing what was originally predicted.
Specificity turns confidence from a performance into a measurable claim.
Share this: attach a probability and deadline to one prediction you make today.

puzzles.title: The Beloved Stock
puzzles.question: An investor owns a company she admires. She reads every positive report and dismisses bad news as short-term noise. Which rule would best expose her thesis to genuine revision?
choices: Buy more whenever a favourable report confirms management's story
Write observable sell conditions now and review them on fixed dates
Follow additional commentators who already own the same company
Judge each negative report by how uncomfortable it makes her feel
puzzles.correctAnswer: Write observable sell conditions now and review them on fixed dates
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Advance exit criteria stop affection from moving the evidential goalposts whenever contrary information arrives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — write observable sell conditions now and review them on fixed dates. More like-minded commentary compounds selective exposure; predetermined conditions state what evidence must trigger revision before emotions negotiate exceptions.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Commitment makes disconfirming evidence easier to reinterpret as temporary noise.
A belief needs explicit revision conditions before contrary facts arrive.
Fixed review dates reduce reactions to daily emotional swings.
Decision rules are useful only when written clearly enough to resist later editing.
Share this: write one concrete condition that would make you abandon a current plan.

puzzles.title: Warmth and Trust
puzzles.question: A friendly contractor remembers everyone's names and apologizes charmingly for delays. The client therefore assumes his invoices are accurate. What evidence should carry the most weight?
choices: How sincerely he appears to regret each scheduling problem
How many clients describe him as pleasant to work with
Whether sampled charges match receipts, rates, and completed work
Whether his friendliness remains consistent during the audit
puzzles.correctAnswer: Whether sampled charges match receipts, rates, and completed work
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Warmth may matter for the relationship, but invoice accuracy is a separate claim requiring transactional evidence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, check whether sampled charges match receipts, rates, and completed work. Charm and sincere apologies can cast a halo over honesty; matching records directly tests the financial claim.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Warmth and integrity are distinct traits even when they often travel together.
Social ease can lower scrutiny precisely when verification still matters.
Sampling records tests a concrete claim without requiring global distrust.
Separating person-liking from process-checking protects both relationships and decisions.
Share this: verify one practical detail independently even when you like the person responsible.

puzzles.title: The Narrow Certificate
puzzles.question: After passing a short quiz on privacy rules, a manager claims she can design the company's entire data-governance system. What is the fairest way to assess that leap?
choices: Accept it because any formal certificate proves broad competence
Reject it because beginners can never assess their own progress
Repeat the same quiz until her score becomes nearly perfect
Test the additional skills with realistic, independently scored tasks
puzzles.correctAnswer: Test the additional skills with realistic, independently scored tasks
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The quiz supports only the skill it sampled; broader competence must be demonstrated on broader tasks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is to test the additional skills with realistic, independently scored tasks. A narrow credential can trigger overgeneralization, but automatic rejection is also unjustified; representative evidence should decide.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A test supports claims only about the knowledge and tasks it actually samples.
Beginners may overgeneralize a visible milestone into mastery of a wider system.
Representative tasks reveal planning, transfer, and error detection that quizzes can miss.
Fair calibration neither flatters nor dismisses; it measures the claimed scope.
Share this: state exactly what one of your credentials demonstrates and what it does not.

puzzles.title: The Silent Estimates
puzzles.question: A team lead predicts a two-week delivery and opens discussion by defending that estimate. Soon everyone finds reasons it is realistic. Which meeting change best preserves independent evidence?
choices: Collect private estimates and failure reasons before revealing anyone's view
Let the lead present more success stories before inviting objections
Ask only people who agree to explain their reasoning in detail
Take a public vote immediately after the lead's opening argument
puzzles.correctAnswer: Collect private estimates and failure reasons before revealing anyone's view
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Independent estimates prevent the leader's hypothesis from determining what everyone searches for and reports.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — collect private estimates and failure reasons before revealing anyone's view. Public discussion after an authoritative opening encourages supportive search and social alignment; simultaneous private input preserves diverse information.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A stated group preference becomes a search cue for reasons that support it.
Independent elicitation protects information held by quieter or lower-status members.
Failure prompts counter the natural tendency to plan from the success story alone.
Reveal order matters because early views shape later evidence production.
Share this: gather written opinions before discussion at your next group decision.

puzzles.title: The Small Payment
puzzles.question: Two employees privately dislike a dull task but must tell a new hire it was enjoyable. One receives $5, the other $500. If both comply freely, dissonance theory predicts the $5 employee is more likely to later report genuinely liking the task.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The small payment supplies weak external justification, leaving more pressure to align private attitude with the voluntary statement.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A large payment explains the lie without requiring inner change; a small payment leaves 'I chose to say it' in conflict with 'I disliked it,' making attitude revision a route to consistency.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Counter-attitudinal behaviour creates tension when it feels freely chosen.
Strong external rewards explain compliance and can reduce the need for internal change.
Weak external justification leaves the person to supply a reason from within.
The key comparison is not reward versus no reward, but sufficient versus insufficient explanation.
Share this: notice whether your reason for an unwanted action came from outside or was invented afterward.

puzzles.title: The Brutal Initiation
puzzles.question: A club randomly assigns equally committed applicants to an easy or humiliating initiation, then gives everyone the same mediocre club experience. If the hard-initiation group praises the club more, that result by itself proves the club experience was objectively better for them.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Greater praise can be effort justification: devaluing the club would make the voluntarily endured humiliation feel pointless.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Random assignment and an identical club experience remove objective quality as the likely cause; the extra effort creates pressure to elevate the outcome so the sacrifice feels warranted.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Effort justification can increase liking for outcomes that follow costly voluntary entry.
The mind protects a sacrifice by upgrading what the sacrifice supposedly purchased.
Random assignment helps separate prior enthusiasm from effects of the ordeal itself.
Praise after hardship is therefore not clean evidence of quality.
Share this: ask whether one thing you value is excellent or merely expensive in effort.

puzzles.title: The Forced Speech
puzzles.question: A student is threatened with expulsion unless she publicly defends a policy she opposes. Because her speech contradicts her belief, classic dissonance theory predicts more private attitude change than if she had delivered it voluntarily for a token reward.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The severe threat fully explains her behaviour; voluntary advocacy with little external justification creates the stronger need for internal reconciliation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Contradiction alone is not enough: perceived choice matters. Coercion lets the student say, accurately, 'I did it because I had to,' whereas lightly rewarded choice leaves more inconsistency attached to the self.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dissonance depends on personal responsibility, not merely observable inconsistency.
Coercion supplies an external account that protects the original attitude.
Freedom of choice makes behaviour more diagnostic of the self.
Minimal incentives can therefore produce more attitude change than overwhelming pressure.
Share this: separate what you chose from what circumstances made unavoidable today.

puzzles.title: After the Choice
puzzles.question: After choosing between two equally attractive jobs, Maya later emphasizes the chosen job's strengths and the rejected job's flaws. This pattern can reduce dissonance even if neither employer has changed since her decision.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Spreading the alternatives makes the completed choice feel less conflicted by increasing psychological distance between the options.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A difficult choice preserves attractive rejected features and unattractive chosen ones; re-evaluating both options after commitment reduces that residual conflict without any new external facts.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Difficult decisions leave behind the advantages of what was rejected and costs of what was chosen.
Post-decision revaluation can widen an initially narrow gap between options.
This protects confidence but can disguise how close the original choice really was.
Records made before choosing preserve preferences before consistency work begins.
Share this: compare your reasons before and after one recent irreversible choice.

puzzles.title: The Failed Forecast
puzzles.question: A tightly bonded group publicly predicts a dramatic event. It fails unmistakably, but members can reinterpret the failure together and recruit outsiders. Under Festinger's account, those social conditions can produce stronger commitment rather than straightforward abandonment.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Shared reinterpretation and successful recruitment can provide social validation for a belief threatened by public disconfirmation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Failed predictions do not always weaken commitment mechanically; when investment is high, failure is clear, and believers can support one another, proselytizing can recruit validation for the revised story.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Disconfirming evidence competes with commitment, identity, and social support.
A public, costly belief is harder to discard than a casual private guess.
Groups can manufacture validation by agreeing on an explanation together.
Recruitment turns new supporters into evidence that the movement still makes sense.
Share this: ask what social rewards would disappear if one of your group beliefs changed.

puzzles.title: The Easy Exit
puzzles.question: Two buyers choose the same laptop. One can exchange it tomorrow; the other's sale is final. Before receiving new information, dissonance theory predicts the final-sale buyer may become more certain that the laptop is excellent.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Irrevocability raises the cost of ambivalence, encouraging the committed buyer to consolidate the choice psychologically.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. An open option permits continued comparison, while a closed option leaves no behavioural escape; confidence and selective attention can rise to make the final choice easier to live with.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Irrevocable choices generate more pressure for psychological closure than reversible ones.
When action cannot change, interpretation remains available to change.
Certainty after commitment may therefore reflect adaptation rather than new evidence.
Cooling-off periods preserve behavioural options before rationalization hardens.
Share this: delay one irreversible decision until after a planned cooling-off period.

puzzles.title: The Public Promise
puzzles.question: If Ravi publicly champions a workplace policy and ties his reputation to it, later contrary data should be easier for him to accept than if he had only considered the policy privately, because public scrutiny always improves updating.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Public commitment can make revision threaten consistency and reputation, motivating defensive interpretation despite scrutiny.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Accountability can improve reasoning when it rewards accuracy, but commitment to a declared position can instead raise the cost of reversal and encourage selective defence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Public accountability and public commitment are not psychologically identical.
Accountability to accuracy can motivate care; accountability to a position can motivate defence.
Reputation makes changing a belief feel like changing the story of the self.
Institutions should reward visible correction, not only visible confidence.
Share this: praise someone openly for revising a public claim when the evidence changed.

puzzles.title: The Harmless Reminder
puzzles.question: Before confronting evidence that their environmental behaviour contradicts their values, participants write about an unrelated value they live by well. If they become less defensive, that can fit self-affirmation: the broader self no longer depends on winning this one dispute.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Affirming another valued part of the self can reduce identity threat and free people to process unwelcome evidence more openly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The reminder does not refute the evidence; it reduces the need to protect global self-worth through denial in this particular domain.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Threatened beliefs often defend a wider image of being competent or moral.
Self-affirmation broadens the identity resources available during criticism.
When global worth feels secure, a local mistake becomes easier to acknowledge.
The mechanism is reduced defensiveness, not proof that the criticism is correct.
Share this: name a stable value before reviewing feedback that threatens your self-image.

puzzles.title: The Smaller Issue
puzzles.question: Dana keeps behaving against a stated value but decides the value 'was never important anyway.' This is not dissonance reduction because neither her behaviour nor the factual evidence changed.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Trivializing the importance of the inconsistency is itself a way to reduce dissonance without changing action or facts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A person can reduce tension by changing behaviour, changing beliefs, adding justifications, or shrinking the importance of the conflict; factual revision is only one route.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Psychological inconsistency can be managed through several different strategies.
Trivialization lowers the stakes assigned to the clashing value or action.
Adding consonant reasons can also outnumber rather than remove the conflict.
Recognizing the strategy matters because relief does not guarantee truth.
Share this: notice when 'it doesn't matter' appears only after your actions become hard to defend.

puzzles.title: The Painful Course
puzzles.question: Students who complete a punishing course rate it highly. To conclude effort justification caused the praise, it is enough to compare them with students who voluntarily chose an easier course.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Self-selection leaves prior motivation, expectations, and preferences confounded with the amount of effort.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. People who choose the hard course may already value it more; a stronger test assigns comparable participants to different effort levels while holding the eventual experience constant.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Observed sacrifice and later liking can share a prior cause such as motivation.
Self-selection makes effort groups different before the effort begins.
Random assignment is powerful because it balances those hidden starting differences.
Causal claims need a credible account of what the comparison would otherwise have experienced.
Share this: identify one self-selection problem in a comparison you encounter today.

puzzles.title: Useful Training
puzzles.question: A demanding apprenticeship produces graduates who value it more and also perform much better because the hard exercises teach real skills. The higher valuation alone cannot tell us how much came from genuine benefit versus effort justification.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Productive effort can improve the outcome itself, so praise may mix real value with consistency-preserving revaluation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Effort justification is clearest when effort changes cost but not quality; when training improves skill, objective benefits and psychological rationalization are competing contributors.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Hard work can both create real value and create pressure to perceive value.
A clean test separates the burden of effort from the learning it produces.
Outcome measures help distinguish improved performance from improved storytelling.
Psychological explanations should not replace ordinary causal benefits without evidence.
Share this: separate what a difficult experience taught you from what its difficulty made you admire.

puzzles.title: One Contradictory Study
puzzles.question: A well-designed new study is less supportive of a treatment than earlier evidence. Rational belief updating requires abandoning the treatment immediately, regardless of the prior evidence's quantity and quality.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Updating should weight the new study by its diagnostic strength relative to the full prior evidence, not treat either old or new evidence as absolute.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Good updating changes confidence proportionally: one strong result may matter greatly, but it must be integrated with replication, precision, design, and the evidence already accumulated.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Belief updating is revision by evidential weight, not automatic reversal.
Prior confidence should reflect the amount and quality of evidence already available.
New evidence matters according to how likely it is under competing explanations.
Both stubbornness and whiplash can be failures of proportional updating.
Share this: revise one confidence estimate by degrees instead of switching from certain to impossible.

puzzles.title: Expected Surprise
puzzles.question: A diagnostic test is positive. The result should change your belief more when false positives are rare than when false positives are common, even if the word 'positive' is identical in both cases.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Evidence is informative to the extent that competing explanations differ in how likely they are to produce it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A result common both with and without the condition distinguishes little; the same label becomes stronger evidence when alternative causes rarely generate it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Evidence strength depends on likelihood under rival hypotheses.
A surprising observation under one explanation can sharply favour another.
Labels such as 'positive' hide false-positive rates and base rates.
Updating needs comparison, not merely reaction to the observed result.
Share this: ask how often an alarming signal appears when nothing is wrong.

puzzles.title: The Moving Standard
puzzles.question: A manager accepts weak evidence when it supports her strategy but demands flawless randomized evidence when it challenges the strategy. Even if every criticism she makes is individually possible, the asymmetric standard signals motivated belief maintenance.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Unequal evidential thresholds let a preferred conclusion survive by design rather than by consistently applied standards.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Any single study may deserve criticism, but accepting friendly evidence cheaply while taxing hostile evidence heavily reveals a directional rule for what gets believed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Motivated reasoning often appears as unequal scrutiny rather than explicit dishonesty.
A fair evidential standard should be chosen before knowing which side benefits.
Symmetry tests ask whether the same flaw would matter in favourable evidence.
Consistent thresholds make belief change answer to method instead of preference.
Share this: apply your strongest objection to evidence supporting your own side.

puzzles.title: The Quiet Advocate
puzzles.question: Writing an essay against one's private view should produce the same attitude change whether the writer freely chooses the position or is assigned it without choice, because the text itself is identical.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The identical essay has different implications for the self when chosen freely than when imposed externally.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Under low choice, assignment explains the advocacy; under high choice, the writer must reconcile voluntary authorship with the prior attitude, making internal change more likely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The meaning of behaviour depends on whether the actor experiences ownership of it.
Identical actions can produce different internal pressure under choice and coercion.
Experimental designs manipulate perceived freedom to test this difference.
Observable output alone does not reveal the psychological account attached to it.
Share this: ask whether a statement you heard reflects belief, role, incentive, or compulsion.

puzzles.title: The Honest Prediction
puzzles.question: A forecaster records probabilities before outcomes and is rewarded for calibration rather than rhetorical certainty. This structure should make genuine belief updating easier to distinguish from post-hoc rationalization.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Timestamped probabilities preserve prior beliefs, while calibration rewards appropriately scaled revision instead of a convincing retrospective story.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Without a prior record, memory can convert uncertainty into 'I knew it'; scored forecasts reveal both the original confidence and how later evidence changed it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Belief updating cannot be measured if the earlier belief is allowed to drift in memory.
Probabilities preserve uncertainty better than binary declarations.
Calibration rewards confidence that matches outcome frequencies over time.
Decision records turn hindsight stories into checkable learning.
Share this: timestamp three probabilistic forecasts and score them next month.

puzzles.title: The Sour Source
puzzles.question: When credible evidence threatens a costly belief, attacking the source's character can reduce dissonance without addressing the evidence's logic. Therefore feeling relief after discrediting the source does not show the claim was refuted.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Source derogation can restore consistency psychologically while leaving the argument's evidential content untouched.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Source reliability can legitimately matter, but a character attack that does not change the data or inference may function mainly to remove the messenger from consideration.
puzzles.lessonContent:
People can protect beliefs by downgrading whoever delivers unwelcome information.
Source evaluation is relevant only where credibility affects the evidence.
An argument's structure can remain intact even when its advocate is unpleasant.
Relief is evidence that tension changed, not that a proposition became false.
Share this: restate one disliked person's argument without mentioning the person.

puzzles.title: The Effort Trap
puzzles.question: Someone keeps funding a failing project because abandoning it would make years of sacrifice feel wasted. This can involve both a forward-looking sunk-cost error and dissonance reduction through protecting the meaning of past effort.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The decision rule wrongly counts unrecoverable costs, while continued commitment can also defend a self-story in which the sacrifice was justified.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The concepts overlap but answer different questions: one concerns which costs should guide future action, and the other concerns why admitting waste threatens psychological consistency.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One behaviour can reflect both a decision error and a self-protective motive.
Sunk costs are past resources that no future option can recover.
Effort justification explains why declaring those resources wasted feels threatening.
A fresh-start test separates future value from the need to honour prior sacrifice.
Share this: ask of one commitment, 'Would I begin it today with what I now know?'.

puzzles.title: The Pleasant Update
puzzles.question: A founder rapidly accepts weak good news about her company but demands repeated confirmation of strong bad news. Because she eventually considers both, her belief updating is necessarily unbiased.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Different acceptance thresholds for desirable and undesirable evidence produce systematically biased updating even when neither side is completely ignored.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Bias can operate through update size and evidential standards: favourable signals receive full weight immediately while threatening signals are discounted pending impossible certainty.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Biased updating need not look like total blindness to contrary facts.
People can assign different weights to evidence according to its emotional direction.
Equal methodological standards matter more than merely seeing both sides.
Tracking numerical confidence exposes asymmetric revisions that prose can conceal.
Share this: record how far good and bad news move one confidence estimate this week.

puzzles.title: Identity Insurance
puzzles.question: If accepting a factual correction would threaten someone's membership in a valued group, supplying stronger evidence alone may fail; reducing the identity cost of revision can sometimes improve updating without weakening evidential standards.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. When a conclusion carries social penalties, people may defend belonging rather than assess evidence; making correction compatible with identity can remove that extra motive.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The evidence should remain rigorous, but the communication can show that changing one factual belief need not require betrayal of the whole group or self.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Beliefs can function as badges of loyalty as well as descriptions of reality.
Social costs alter the incentives surrounding acknowledgement of evidence.
Identity-safe framing separates factual revision from total group rejection.
Better communication removes defensive stakes without changing what counts as proof.
Share this: frame one correction as consistent with a value your listener already holds.

puzzles.title: The Counterfeit Cause
puzzles.question: After making a difficult choice, participants feel tension. Researchers give half a harmless pill described as calming; that group shows less revaluation of the options. This pattern can support the idea that attributed discomfort helps drive dissonance reduction.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. If discomfort is attributed to an external source, less attitude change may be needed to explain or relieve it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The pill need not pharmacologically work: an available alternative explanation for arousal can reduce the pressure to reinterpret the choice, linking felt discomfort to the consistency process.
puzzles.lessonContent:
People interpret bodily arousal using the explanations available in context.
Misattribution can redirect discomfort away from a threatening inconsistency.
If tension seems externally caused, changing an attitude may feel less necessary.
Placebo-style designs can test explanations without requiring an active drug.
Share this: before defending a decision, check whether fatigue or stress is colouring the discomfort.

puzzles.title: Facts After Failure
puzzles.question: When a prediction fails, inventing an untestable auxiliary explanation preserves the original belief but counts as strong updating because the belief now accommodates more facts.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. An explanation that can absorb every outcome without risky predictions protects a belief from evidence rather than updating it responsibly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Genuine updating should change confidence or generate new tests; adding an escape clause that forbids no future observation makes the theory less vulnerable, not better supported.
puzzles.lessonContent:
An explanation earns evidential value by ruling out some possible observations.
Ad hoc additions can save a belief while reducing its testability.
Accommodation after the fact is weaker than successful prediction in advance.
A revised theory should state what evidence would now count against it.
Share this: ask what future result a newly patched explanation would fail to explain.

puzzles.title: Rewarded Honesty
puzzles.question: An organization wants employees to admit failed assumptions. Rewarding accurate correction and preserving status after revision should reduce dissonance-driven defence more effectively than punishing anyone whose public view changes.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Making revision safe lowers the reputational cost of inconsistency and aligns social incentives with accurate updating.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Punishing reversals teaches people to protect prior claims; rewarding documented correction lets consistency attach to being a careful learner rather than never being wrong.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cultures determine whether correction signals competence or humiliation.
Punishing changed conclusions rewards hidden errors and elaborate defence.
Status can be attached to process fidelity rather than unwavering positions.
Visible revision norms make updating socially compatible with a coherent identity.
Share this: recognize one person for changing course promptly when evidence shifted.

puzzles.title: The Costly Badge
puzzles.question: Members who buy an expensive symbol of a movement later express stronger belief. This observation alone distinguishes effort justification from the simpler possibility that stronger believers chose to buy the symbol.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The correlation is compatible with reverse causation: prior conviction may produce both the costly purchase and later reported strength.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. To isolate justification, researchers need prior belief measures or exogenous variation in cost; otherwise sacrifice may be the consequence of commitment rather than its cause.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Costly signals can reveal existing commitment as well as deepen commitment.
Cross-sectional correlations cannot establish which variable moved first.
Baseline measures show whether groups already differed before the sacrifice.
Exogenous cost changes offer stronger evidence about effects of investment itself.
Share this: ask whether a sacrifice created devotion or merely revealed devotion already present.

puzzles.title: Confidence by Degrees
puzzles.question: After strong evidence lowers a hypothesis from 80% plausible to 35%, continuing to investigate it can be rational; belief updating does not require treating every serious setback as proof of impossibility.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. A substantial downward update can leave meaningful uncertainty, and further investigation may still have value.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Rational confidence is graded: evidence can sharply weaken a claim without eliminating it, and the decision to investigate also depends on stakes and the value of resolving uncertainty.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Uncertainty is continuous even when language tempts us toward yes-or-no conclusions.
Large updates need not end at zero or one.
Actions depend on both probability and consequence, not probability alone.
Continued inquiry can coexist with honest acknowledgement that a claim became less likely.
Share this: replace one binary opinion with a percentage and name what would move it.

puzzles.title: The Membership Mirror
puzzles.question: A rule permits a collection for every condition. Let R collect exactly the collections that are not members of themselves. What happens when the condition is tested on R?
choices: R must be an empty collection
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Membership makes R fail its own entry condition, while non-membership makes R satisfy it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'Either assumption reverses itself': putting R in excludes it, and leaving R out qualifies it. The unrestricted collection rule, not a missing fact, creates the contradiction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unrestricted comprehension turns any verbal condition into a proposed collection.
Self-application is a stress test for conditions that mention membership or exclusion.
A contradiction can expose a defective construction rule rather than a mysterious object.
Modern set theories restrict which conditions are allowed to form sets.
Share this: test one rule today by asking what happens when the rule is applied to itself.

puzzles.title: The Loose Index
puzzles.question: An archive index lists every bound catalogue in the archive that does not list itself. The index is a loose sheet, not a bound catalogue. Must asking whether it lists itself create a paradox?
choices: No, the rule's domain excludes the index
Yes, every index is automatically a catalogue
Yes, because all negative rules contradict themselves
No, because an index can never list documents
puzzles.correctAnswer: No, the rule's domain excludes the index
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The self-test never starts because the rule quantifies only over bound catalogues, and the loose index is outside that domain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 'No, the rule's domain excludes the index.' Russell-style trouble needs the defining rule to range over the object doing the defining; a genuine domain boundary blocks that step.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A quantified rule applies only to objects inside its stated domain.
Many apparent paradoxes smuggle the classifier itself into a class it was never said to occupy.
Domain restrictions work only when they are principled, not invented after trouble appears.
Checking type and scope should come before testing a rule on itself.
Share this: underline the domain words in one policy before deciding whom it covers.

puzzles.title: Floors of Truth
puzzles.question: A typed language lets level-1 predicates describe level-0 objects, level-2 predicates describe level-1 predicates, and so on. A level-1 predicate is then asked whether it applies to itself. What is the system's response?
choices: It applies to itself as false
It applies to itself as true
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The hierarchy prevents a predicate from taking an argument at its own level, so the dangerous sentence cannot be formed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close, but the answer is 'The expression is not well-typed.' Type theory does not solve the loop by choosing a truth value; it blocks same-level self-application before evaluation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Type hierarchies separate objects from predicates that describe those objects.
An ill-typed expression is rejected as malformed rather than labelled true or false.
This strategy prevents vicious circles by limiting same-level self-application.
Programming-language type systems use the same broad idea to rule out invalid operations early.
Share this: find one category error today and state which two levels were confused.

puzzles.title: Words Judge Words
puzzles.question: Call an adjective autological if it describes itself: 'English' is English. Call it heterological if it does not describe itself. Under those definitions, how should 'heterological' be classified?
choices: Both, because every adjective has both properties
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. If the word is heterological, it describes itself and becomes autological; if it is not, it fails to describe itself and becomes heterological.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'Neither classification remains stable.' Each proposed label changes whether the adjective satisfies its own definition, recreating a Russell-like reversal with words.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Semantic predicates can classify expressions by features those expressions themselves possess.
Trouble begins when a classification is both self-applicable and defined by negation.
Grelling's paradox transfers a set-membership pattern into ordinary language.
Changing the subject matter does not remove a contradiction's logical shape.
Share this: invent one adjective that clearly describes itself and explain why.

puzzles.title: The Short Description
puzzles.question: Define N as 'the smallest positive integer not describable in fewer than twelve English words.' The quoted phrase itself uses fewer than twelve words and appears to describe N. Which diagnosis best fits?
choices: English contains only finitely many integers
The definition undermines its own description limit
The smallest integer cannot be positive
puzzles.correctAnswer: The definition undermines its own description limit
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. If the phrase successfully picks out N, it supplies the very short description that N was defined not to have.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's subtler than a calculation. The answer is 'The definition undermines its own description limit': the act of identifying the supposedly undescribable number violates the condition used to identify it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Berry-style paradoxes mix counting with an informal notion of describability.
Natural language cannot always be treated as a perfectly fixed formal code.
Definitions may become part of the evidence against what they define.
Formal complexity theory avoids this looseness by fixing a language and encoding scheme.
Share this: rewrite one vague claim about what is 'easy to describe' using a measurable limit.

puzzles.title: The Missing Decimal
puzzles.question: Someone claims to list, in alphabetical order of their finite English descriptions, every describable infinite decimal. A diagonal procedure then specifies a decimal differing from entry n at digit n. Which claim is most vulnerable?
choices: Finite descriptions form a clean complete list
Infinite decimals cannot differ at one digit
Alphabetical order cannot include any numbers
Diagonal procedures always repeat an entry
puzzles.correctAnswer: Finite descriptions form a clean complete list
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The newly specified decimal is itself described finitely yet differs from every listed entry, exposing instability in the supposed enumeration of informal descriptions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 'Finite descriptions form a clean complete list.' Diagonal change guarantees difference from each row; the paradox targets the assumption that informal definability can be exhaustively and unambiguously enumerated.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Diagonal arguments construct an outsider by changing one feature associated with each listed item.
The method proves incompleteness only when the proposed list and construction are precisely specified.
Informal phrases such as 'describable in English' can hide ambiguity and circularity.
Richard's paradox shows why formal languages matter when definitions are counted.
Share this: diagonalize a three-row binary list by flipping its first, second, and third diagonal bits.

puzzles.title: Beyond the Gap
puzzles.question: A theory handles 'This sentence is false' by assigning it no truth value. A new sentence says, 'This sentence is not true.' Why does the original repair face renewed pressure?
choices: Every sentence without a value is grammatically false
Negation can only be used in mathematics
The new sentence refers to the older sentence
Being valueless appears to make the new claim accurate
puzzles.correctAnswer: Being valueless appears to make the new claim accurate
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. If the sentence is neither true nor false, then it is indeed not true, which seems to make it true and revives the loop.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'Being valueless appears to make the new claim accurate.' The strengthened Liar targets the broader predicate 'not true,' so merely adding a truth-value gap does not automatically contain it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A proposed paradox solution must survive versions that target the solution's new category.
Truth-value gaps separate failure of truth from ordinary falsity.
Strengthened formulations can describe themselves as false, untrue, or defective.
Robust theories explain why their semantic vocabulary cannot simply be reinserted into the object language.
Share this: stress-test one exception today by rewriting a rule to mention the exception itself.

puzzles.title: The Truth Teller
puzzles.question: Consider only the sentence 'This sentence is true.' Unlike a sentence asserting its own falsity, what does classical consistency alone determine about its truth value?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Calling it true agrees with its content, but calling it false also makes its claim of truth false; consistency does not select between them.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is 'It permits either assignment.' Positive self-reference can create underdetermination rather than contradiction because each truth assignment supports itself.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-reference does not always generate an outright contradiction.
Positive feedback can support multiple fixed points instead of none.
Consistency asks whether an assignment works, not whether it is uniquely forced.
Separating existence from uniqueness prevents many logical overclaims.
Share this: when a rule has one solution, check whether a second solution also satisfies it.

puzzles.title: The Crossed Cards
puzzles.question: Card A says, 'Card B is false.' Card B says, 'Card A is true.' Assuming each card is either true or false, which result follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. B must match A, while A must oppose B, so every attempted assignment demands its own reversal.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'No assignment satisfies both.' One card enforces sameness and the other enforces opposition, producing incompatible constraints across the pair.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reference loops can run through several statements rather than one sentence pointing directly at itself.
Translate 'is true' as sameness and 'is false' as opposition between truth values.
A loop with incompatible parity has no stable assignment.
Constraint diagrams make indirect semantic cycles easier to inspect.
Share this: draw arrows between two claims today and label each arrow 'same' or 'opposite'.

puzzles.title: The Endless Accusation
puzzles.question: Sentence 1 says every later sentence is false; sentence 2 says every sentence after it is false; and so on forever. No sentence mentions itself. What lesson does the resulting Yablo-style instability support?
choices: Circular dependence can exist without direct self-naming
Infinite lists make every sentence false
Only the first sentence can mention truth
puzzles.correctAnswer: Circular dependence can exist without direct self-naming
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Each sentence points only forward, yet the infinite dependency pattern recreates the pressure usually blamed on explicit self-reference.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 'Circular dependence can exist without direct self-naming.' The global structure, not a word such as 'this,' can supply the loop-like dependency that defeats a stable assignment.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Direct self-naming is one route to circularity, not the only one.
Infinite dependency chains can have global properties absent from every local link.
Yablo-style constructions test whether semantic circularity is structural rather than grammatical.
Inspecting a dependency graph can reveal feedback hidden by one-way sentences.
Share this: map the dependencies in one circular workplace process without using people's names.

puzzles.title: The Conditional Trap
puzzles.question: Let C say, 'If C is true, then the alarm is justified.' A naive truth rule allows C exactly when what C says holds. Without independent evidence about the alarm, what makes this Curry-style sentence dangerous?
choices: It denies that C has any words
It requires the alarm to be false
It contains no conditional at all
It can bootstrap the conclusion from self-application
puzzles.correctAnswer: It can bootstrap the conclusion from self-application
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Unrestricted self-referential truth principles can turn the conditional back on itself and derive the alarm claim without evidence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'It can bootstrap the conclusion from self-application.' Curry's pattern is alarming because it can produce an arbitrary conclusion without using explicit negation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Curry's paradox combines self-reference with a conditional rather than a direct denial.
Not every semantic paradox depends on saying that a sentence is false.
Rules that freely move between a sentence and 'the sentence is true' can become explosive.
Formal systems control contraction, implication, or truth rules to block the bootstrap.
Share this: challenge one conclusion today by asking what evidence enters besides the conclusion itself.

puzzles.title: Front and Back
puzzles.question: The front of a card says, 'The sentence on the back is true.' The back says, 'The sentence on the front is false.' Under two-valued logic, which assessment is correct?
choices: No stable pair of values exists
puzzles.correctAnswer: No stable pair of values exists
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The front requires the values to match, while the back requires them to differ, so neither possible pairing works.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: the answer is 'No stable pair of values exists.' Treat one side as an equality constraint and the other as an inequality constraint; they cannot both hold.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mutual reference distributes a paradox across objects without changing its logical force.
Statements about another statement's truth can be translated into value constraints.
Sameness and opposition cannot both govern the same pair.
Reducing prose to constraints often makes a semantic puzzle mechanical.
Share this: translate one verbal dependency today into an equals or not-equals relation.

puzzles.title: Language Above Language
puzzles.question: A base language can discuss snow but cannot call its own sentences true. A metalanguage can state which base-language sentences are true. Why does this hierarchy help with semantic paradoxes?
choices: It makes every base sentence true
It removes negation from ordinary speech
It prevents one level from applying its truth predicate to itself
It proves that metalanguage sentences need no interpretation
puzzles.correctAnswer: It prevents one level from applying its truth predicate to itself
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Truth is evaluated from a higher level, so the base language cannot construct its own Liar using that predicate.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'It prevents one level from applying its truth predicate to itself.' Tarski's hierarchy controls where truth talk occurs rather than declaring troublesome sentences true or banning ordinary negation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
An object language makes claims; a metalanguage describes those claims.
Tarskian hierarchies place each truth predicate above the sentences it evaluates.
The separation blocks semantic closure at a single level.
Any higher language that discusses its own truth may require another level in turn.
Share this: distinguish a claim from a claim about that claim in one conversation today.

puzzles.title: Inside the Quotes
puzzles.question: Which sentence talks about an expression rather than using that expression to talk about weather?
choices: Expected rain may cancel the match
Rain refers to falling water outdoors
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Quotation turns the words themselves into the subject, while the other sentences use words to discuss rain or meaning.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is ''Rain is expected' contains three words.' Quotation marks signal mention of a linguistic object, a distinction that keeps object-level claims separate from claims about language.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Using a word talks through it; mentioning a word talks about the word itself.
Quotation marks often mark the shift from object to expression.
Use-mention confusion can make harmless linguistic facts look like worldly facts.
Semantic reasoning depends on tracking which level a term occupies.
Share this: write one sentence that uses your name and another that mentions the written name.

puzzles.title: The Diagonal Name
puzzles.question: A formal system can substitute a formula's own code number into a blank within that formula. What is the crucial result of this diagonal move?
choices: A sentence can assert a property of its own code
puzzles.correctAnswer: A sentence can assert a property of its own code
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Diagonal substitution creates disciplined self-reference inside arithmetic without relying on an informal phrase such as 'this sentence.'
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'A sentence can assert a property of its own code.' Coding syntax as numbers plus self-substitution lets a formal sentence indirectly speak about itself.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Diagonalization links an item to the position or code that represents that item.
Gödel numbering lets arithmetic encode formulas and proofs as ordinary integers.
A fixed-point construction can reproduce self-reference without semantic pronouns.
The technique powers both limitation theorems and computability results.
Share this: explain diagonalization to someone using a list and one changed diagonal entry.

puzzles.title: Proof Looks Inward
puzzles.question: In a consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic, G effectively says, 'G is not provable here.' If the system proved G, what would follow?
choices: G would become an axiom of every system
The system would prove a false claim about its own proof
Arithmetic would contain no true sentences
G would cease to be a grammatical formula
puzzles.correctAnswer: The system would prove a false claim about its own proof
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A proof of G would make G's internal claim of unprovability false, conflicting with the assumed consistency and sound encoding of proof.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is 'The system would prove a false claim about its own proof.' The key is the gap between truth and provability: consistency prevents this self-referential sentence from being proved within the system.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Formal truth and provability are different notions.
Arithmetic can encode claims about the existence of arithmetic proofs.
Diagonalization creates a sentence tied to its own provability status.
Incompleteness limits sufficiently expressive consistent systems, not arithmetic reasoning in general.
Share this: label one belief today as proven, supported, or merely true-looking.

puzzles.title: The Bottomless Call
puzzles.question: A function immediately calls itself with the same input and has no base case. Assuming unlimited resources, what is the primary defect?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The definition generates nontermination, not a proposition that is both true and false.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'It never reaches a result.' Computational self-reference can loop forever without creating a logical contradiction; termination and consistency are separate properties.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Recursion defines a process in terms of smaller or later instances of itself.
A base case supplies a stopping point for evaluation.
Self-calls that make no progress cause divergence rather than semantic contradiction.
Separating nontermination from inconsistency improves debugging and proof design.
Share this: inspect one recursive process and identify both its progress step and stopping rule.

puzzles.title: The Expanding Initials
puzzles.question: The name GNU expands to 'GNU's Not Unix,' so the first word invokes the acronym being expanded. Why is this recursive definition harmless?
choices: It supplies a reusable expansion without asserting its own negation
It proves GNU and Unix are identical
It prevents the initials from being pronounced
It assigns GNU alternating truth values
puzzles.correctAnswer: It supplies a reusable expansion without asserting its own negation
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The expansion is recursive but does not impose incompatible truth conditions; self-reference alone is not enough for paradox.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 'It supplies a reusable expansion without asserting its own negation.' A recursive acronym points back to a label, but nothing requires the label both to have and lack a property.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Recursion and paradox are not synonyms.
Benign self-reference can abbreviate, reproduce, or constrain without contradiction.
Negation and unrestricted classification often supply the dangerous extra ingredient.
Always identify the exact incompatible requirements before declaring a loop paradoxical.
Share this: find one harmless self-reference in a document, program, or organization today.

puzzles.title: The Printing Program
puzzles.question: A program outputs its own source code exactly and then halts. Which conclusion is best?
choices: The output must be logically false
The program secretly reads its source file
No finite program can describe itself
Self-description can have a stable fixed point
puzzles.correctAnswer: Self-description can have a stable fixed point
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. A quine demonstrates coherent self-reproduction: the generated text matches the generator without any contradiction.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'Self-description can have a stable fixed point.' Carefully arranged code can produce its own representation, showing that the troublesome ingredient in paradox is not self-reference by itself.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A fixed point is an input or description left unchanged by an operation.
Quines are programs whose output is their own source representation.
Self-reproduction can be finite and terminating when quotation and data are handled carefully.
Constructive examples are powerful tests against claims of impossibility.
Share this: look up the structure of a tiny quine and identify its code part and data part.

puzzles.title: Three in a Loop
puzzles.question: A says B is false. B says C is false. C says A is false. If each statement must be true or false, what follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Following three reversals around the loop makes A require the opposite of itself, so every starting value fails.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is 'No assignment is consistent.' Each 'false' flips the value; an odd number of flips returns to the start demanding the opposite value.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Truth-reference networks can be solved by tracking flips around cycles.
Each assertion of falsity reverses the next statement's value.
An odd cycle of reversals is inconsistent because it returns with opposite parity.
Parity reasoning replaces trial-and-error with a short structural test.
Share this: mark an odd social blame cycle with plus and minus signs and multiply the signs.

puzzles.title: Four in a Loop
puzzles.question: A says B is false, B says C is false, C says D is false, and D says A is false. How many consistent truth assignments exist?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Four reversals return to the starting value, permitting the two alternating assignments that begin with either true or false.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'Exactly two.' An even number of flips is consistent, but choosing A fixes every other value, leaving only the two opposite alternating patterns.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Even reversal cycles return a value to itself rather than its opposite.
Consistency does not imply uniqueness; a constraint network may admit several models.
Once one node is chosen, connected equality and opposition constraints propagate mechanically.
Counting free starting choices reveals how many assignments remain.
Share this: solve a four-seat alternating constraint by trying each possible first seat.

puzzles.title: The Mixed Notice
puzzles.question: A card contains two statements: (1) 'Every statement on this card is false.' (2) 'Two plus two equals four.' Which evaluation is consistent?
choices: Statement 1 is false and statement 2 is true
Statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false
Neither statement can receive a value
puzzles.correctAnswer: Statement 1 is false and statement 2 is true
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The true arithmetic statement makes the universal claim false, and that falsehood causes no reversal because the claim did not say merely that it itself was false.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 'Statement 1 is false and statement 2 is true.' A self-including universal can fail because of another member, so its self-reference need not force contradiction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A universal statement is false when even one covered instance fails.
Self-inclusion does not guarantee paradox if another fact settles the broader claim.
Evaluate quantifier scope before isolating the self-referential fragment.
Counterexamples can stabilize claims that initially resemble the Liar.
Share this: test one 'everything here' statement by looking for a single counterexample.

puzzles.title: The Diagonal Guest
puzzles.question: Suppose each member of a set S is paired with a subset of S. Form D from exactly those members not contained in their paired subset. Why can D not be the subset paired with any member d?
choices: D contains no members of S
Every subset must contain its label
Pairing is impossible only when S is finite
At d, membership in D reverses membership in the paired subset
puzzles.correctAnswer: At d, membership in D reverses membership in the paired subset
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. If D were paired with d, then d would belong to D exactly when d did not belong to D, so that pairing is impossible.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'At d, membership in D reverses membership in the paired subset.' The diagonal construction differs from each candidate at that candidate's own element, proving the list misses D.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cantor's diagonal method proves that a proposed enumeration omits a constructed case.
The new object differs from candidate d specifically at coordinate d.
Russell-like reversals often arise as local versions of diagonal arguments.
Power sets therefore cannot be completely paired with their underlying sets.
Share this: create a missing binary row by flipping the diagonal of a small table.

puzzles.title: The Membership Committee
puzzles.question: A club admits every organization that is not a member of itself, but its charter defines 'organization' to include the club. Which minimal change directly blocks the Russell-style conflict?
choices: Exclude the club from the rule's eligible domain
Let the chair decide after each application
puzzles.correctAnswer: Exclude the club from the rule's eligible domain
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Removing the classifier from the class it classifies prevents the self-membership test that creates opposite requirements.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The answer is 'Exclude the club from the rule's eligible domain.' Delay, discretion, and renaming do not alter the contradictory condition; a genuine level or domain restriction does.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Repairing a paradox requires changing the premise that licenses the contradiction.
Domain stratification can separate a governing object from the objects it governs.
Cosmetic wording changes do nothing if the same self-application remains possible.
Minimal repairs should block the bad inference while preserving ordinary cases.
Share this: repair one overbroad rule by stating a principled domain boundary.

puzzles.title: The Amendment Clause
puzzles.question: A constitution says, 'This clause may be amended only by a unanimous vote.' The assembly unanimously amends the clause. Why is no paradox forced?
choices: Constitutions cannot refer to their own clauses
The self-reference imposes a compatible procedure
An amended clause was never part of the constitution
puzzles.correctAnswer: The self-reference imposes a compatible procedure
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The clause refers to itself but sets a satisfiable condition, and the unanimous action meets that condition.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 'The self-reference imposes a compatible procedure.' Self-reference becomes paradoxical only when the resulting requirements conflict; here the rule and action fit together.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-governing rules can be coherent when their requirements have a fixed point.
Reference to oneself is not equivalent to denial of oneself.
Institutional rules often regulate their own amendment, interpretation, or expiry.
The correct test is satisfiability: can all stated conditions hold together?
Share this: inspect one policy that governs its own revision and test whether its procedure can be met.

puzzles.title: The Tolerant Chain
puzzles.question: A paint strip changes imperceptibly from red to orange. If every adjacent pair must receive the same color label because their difference is tiny, then transitivity forces the two visibly different endpoints to receive the same label.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Local tolerance plus transitivity propagates one label across the entire chain, producing the sorites conflict at the endpoints.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Each tiny step preserves the label under the tolerance premise; chaining all those equivalences makes the distant endpoints match even though the setup says they plainly differ.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sorites reasoning combines plausible local tolerance with repeated inference across a long series.
Transitivity can turn negligible pairwise differences into an implausible global verdict.
The contradiction pressures the tolerance rule, endpoint judgments, or classical inference.
Continuous transitions make the hidden cost of repeated categorization visible.
Share this: inspect a gradient today and ask which adjacent step supposedly changes its label.

puzzles.title: Induction Misfires
puzzles.question: If a predicate such as 'young' applies at age 20 and changing age by one day never changes its application, mathematical induction validly proves that every possible age is young.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Induction would be valid only if the universal one-day preservation premise were true; vagueness makes that tolerance premise tempting, not guaranteed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Mathematical induction faithfully transmits a genuine step rule, but the sorites problem is precisely whether 'one day can never matter' holds without exception across the whole range.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Induction requires both a base case and a universally valid successor step.
Formal validity cannot rescue a plausible but false or unstable premise.
Vague predicates tempt us to promote local similarity into exceptionless preservation.
Audit the induction step rather than blaming the inference rule that uses it.
Share this: when someone says 'one more cannot matter,' ask whether that remains true at every stage.

puzzles.title: The Hidden Cutoff
puzzles.question: Epistemicism about vagueness can consistently claim that one exact millisecond separates 'soon' from 'not soon' even though speakers could never discover which millisecond it is.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Epistemicism preserves a sharp extension while treating its boundary as unknowable because linguistic use cannot reveal it precisely.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The view distinguishes metaphysical sharpness from epistemic access: there is a last qualifying instant, but no feasible evidence tells speakers where it lies.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Epistemicism treats vague predicates as sharply divided despite our ignorance of the divide.
Unknown boundaries need not be nonexistent boundaries on this account.
The view preserves classical truth values at the cost of radical semantic ignorance.
Its central challenge is explaining why the cutoff is both real and systematically inaccessible.
Share this: separate 'there is no fact' from 'we cannot know the fact' in one uncertain claim.

puzzles.title: Either Side
puzzles.question: Under supervaluationism, a borderline coat may be neither definitely blue nor definitely not blue, while 'the coat is blue or it is not blue' remains true on every admissible sharpening.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Different precisifications may disagree on the coat, yet each classical precisification makes the disjunction true, so it is supertrue.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Supervaluationism permits truth-value gaps for borderline atomic claims while preserving some classical compounds that hold under every acceptable way of drawing the boundary.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Supervaluationism evaluates vague language across multiple admissible precisifications.
A claim is supertrue when every acceptable sharpening makes it true.
Borderline atomic claims may lack a settled value even when classical tautologies survive.
This separates determinacy of parts from validity of a compound.
Share this: list two reasonable cutoffs for one vague category and test a disjunction under both.

puzzles.title: Confidence or Degree
puzzles.question: In fuzzy logic, assigning 0.7 truth to 'the room is warm' necessarily means there is a 70% chance that the room is fully warm and a 30% chance it is not warm at all.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. A fuzzy degree represents graded membership or truth, whereas probability represents uncertainty about which state obtains.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Seventy-percent warm can model partial satisfaction of a predicate even with complete information; a 70% probability instead measures uncertainty over alternatives.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Degrees of truth and degrees of belief answer different questions.
Fuzzy logic models partial category membership along a graded scale.
Probability models uncertainty about facts or outcomes.
The numbers may look identical while carrying different logical roles.
Share this: label one percentage today as either uncertainty or degree before interpreting it.

puzzles.title: Standards on Court
puzzles.question: A 190-centimeter person can count as tall among all adults but not tall among professional basketball centers without contradiction, because contextualism lets the comparison standard shift.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The predicate's threshold is supplied partly by the conversational comparison class, so the two utterances evaluate against different standards.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The person's height stays fixed, but 'tall' can select different thresholds in ordinary-adult and elite-center contexts; no single proposition is both affirmed and denied.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Context-sensitive predicates draw standards from a comparison class or practical purpose.
Changing context can change content without changing the underlying object.
Apparent contradictions may disappear once hidden standards are made explicit.
Contextualism explains flexible use but must still constrain which shifts are legitimate.
Share this: add an explicit comparison class to one use of 'large,' 'fast,' or 'expensive' today.

puzzles.title: A Line by Decree
puzzles.question: A city defines 'high-rise' for taxes as any building at least 35 meters tall. This legal precisification proves that ordinary 'high-rise' had a naturally sharp 35-meter boundary all along.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The city creates an operational boundary for a purpose; it does not discover a pre-existing semantic joint in ordinary usage.
