Choice overload is conditional rather than a universal threshold effect.
Expertise compresses many details into a few meaningful patterns.
High stakes amplify the cost of uncertainty and the desire to compare everything.
Set size matters through the cognitive task it creates for a particular chooser.
Share this: ask an expert which three filters they use in a category that overwhelms you.

puzzles.title: No Returns Allowed
puzzles.question: Two stores offer the same large selection, but one makes every sale final. The no-return policy will always simplify choice because it prevents shoppers from reconsidering later.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Irreversibility can raise pre-choice anxiety and anticipated regret, making a large set harder rather than easier to navigate.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Closing the door after purchase may end later switching, but before purchase it raises the penalty for error and can intensify exhaustive comparison.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reversibility changes both the cost of mistakes and the timing of doubt.
Final choices can create closure after commitment while increasing anxiety beforehand.
Words such as 'always' hide these competing stages of a decision.
Good choice design considers anticipation as well as post-choice behaviour.
Share this: notice whether a return policy changes how long you compare before buying.

puzzles.title: Expert Immunity
puzzles.question: A sommelier can compare more wines than a novice, so expertise makes a person immune to choice overload in that domain regardless of time pressure or how similar the options are.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Expertise raises capacity, but severe time pressure and near-identical alternatives can still make marginal comparisons costly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Experts possess better filters, not unlimited attention; a badly structured or time-starved choice can exceed even a skilled chooser's useful capacity.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Expertise improves categorization and eliminates irrelevant comparisons.
Time limits constrain how much even good filters can process.
Highly similar alternatives demand finer distinctions than clearly separated ones.
Capacity is shaped by person, set, and situation together.
Share this: ask a skilled chooser what conditions still make their own field overwhelming.

puzzles.title: The Helpful Default
puzzles.question: An employer offers 40 retirement funds but preselects a diversified default that employees may freely replace. The default can reduce decision burden without literally removing any option.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. A reversible default supplies a workable path while preserving access to the full set for employees who want to compare it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Choice architecture can lower the cost of choosing through a starting point, even when formal freedom remains unchanged.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Defaults answer what happens when a chooser takes no additional action.
They reduce search and setup costs while leaving opt-out freedom intact.
Their power creates a duty to choose defaults transparently and for defensible reasons.
Preserving options does not require presenting every option with equal friction.
Share this: inspect one default setting today and decide whether it serves your actual goal.

puzzles.title: Curated Freedom
puzzles.question: A software team hides obsolete plans and shows three relevant subscriptions, with a link to view all. Because fewer plans appear first, users necessarily have less meaningful freedom.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Layered presentation can make relevant choice easier while preserving access to the wider set for unusual needs.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Meaningful freedom concerns access and agency, not whether every alternative occupies identical visual space on the first screen.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Curation can organize freedom rather than simply reduce it.
Progressive disclosure shows common choices first and detail on demand.
The ethical test is whether hidden options remain accessible and whether ranking serves the user.
Presentation changes cognitive cost even when the underlying set stays fixed.
Share this: reorganize one crowded digital menu into common, specialized, and obsolete choices.

puzzles.title: The Perfect Laptop
puzzles.question: Mara insists on finding the single best laptop across every specification, while Theo stops at the first model meeting his important requirements. Mara is more exposed to prolonged comparison and post-purchase doubt.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. A maximizing rule keeps every superior possibility relevant, whereas a threshold rule permits the search to end once core needs are met.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Searching for the absolute best expands both the evidence required before choosing and the alternatives available for second-guessing afterward.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Maximizing searches for the best available option; satisficing searches for one that clears a standard.
The best-option rule becomes expensive when attributes conflict and inventories change.
Thresholds provide a stopping condition before comparison becomes endless.
Higher search effort does not guarantee higher experienced satisfaction.
Share this: define three must-haves before your next purchase and stop when they are met.

puzzles.title: Good Enough Means Lazy
puzzles.question: A doctor chooses the first treatment that meets explicit safety and effectiveness thresholds. This is necessarily careless because responsible decisions must compare every available treatment.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. A well-designed threshold can embody rigorous evidence and stop low-value comparison; 'good enough' need not mean unexamined.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Satisficing is careless only when the standard is careless; explicit, evidence-based requirements can make it a disciplined stopping rule.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A stopping rule determines when further search is no longer worth its cost.
Threshold quality matters more than the casual phrase 'good enough' suggests.
Professional standards often encode extensive prior comparison into a usable rule.
Exhaustive search can consume time needed for action without changing the decision.
Share this: create one evidence-based stopping rule for a decision you keep postponing.

puzzles.title: Fifty Tiny Comparisons
puzzles.question: A hiring manager compares 50 candidates across 12 weakly prioritized traits. Even if each comparison is easy, the total search burden can grow enough to encourage delay or shortcuts.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Many small comparisons accumulate, especially when no clear weighting tells the chooser which differences deserve attention.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Choice difficulty can emerge from the number of pairings and attributes, not from any single alternative being hard to understand.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Decision cost grows with both alternatives and attributes.
Unclear priorities force the chooser to revisit trade-offs repeatedly.
Accumulated comparison can produce deferral, arbitrary filtering, or reliance on vivid cues.
Predefined criteria reduce burden and protect relevant evidence.
Share this: rank your criteria before opening the full list in your next comparison task.

puzzles.title: Algorithmic Peace
puzzles.question: A streaming service recommends one film from thousands. If the recommendation is accurate, the viewer cannot experience choice-related regret because the algorithm removed the need to compare.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The viewer may still imagine better unseen options, distrust the recommendation, or continue browsing after accepting it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Recommendation reduces search but does not erase awareness of the larger catalogue or guarantee psychological closure.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Recommendation tools outsource part of search, not the whole experience of agency.
Trust in the recommender determines whether its shortlist feels helpful or constraining.
Visible abundance can preserve imagined alternatives after a recommendation is accepted.
Closure often requires a stopping commitment as well as a good suggestion.
Share this: accept one recommendation today without reopening the catalogue afterward.

puzzles.title: The Forgone Shelf
puzzles.question: After choosing one of 30 appealing courses, a student keeps picturing the benefits of the other 29. The larger set can lower satisfaction by making opportunity costs more vivid.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Every attractive rejected option contributes a possible benefit the chosen course does not provide, feeding comparison after commitment.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. More attractive alternatives can make the selected option feel costly even when its own quality has not changed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone by a choice.
Large attractive sets make sacrificed possibilities easier to imagine.
Post-choice attention can therefore change satisfaction without changing the chosen object.
Commitment improves when attention shifts from unavailable branches to value within the selected one.
Share this: after one choice today, name what you gained before revisiting what you declined.

puzzles.title: Preference Under Construction
puzzles.question: Nikhil has no fixed preference between complex insurance plans until he sees how deductibles, premiums, and exclusions are presented. His eventual preference can be partly constructed during comparison rather than merely retrieved from within.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. For unfamiliar trade-offs, people often build priorities in response to framing and available contrasts instead of consulting a complete internal ranking.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Many preferences become definite only when a choice environment makes particular attributes and trade-offs salient.
puzzles.lessonContent:
People do not carry stable rankings for every unfamiliar decision.
Comparison can create weights for attributes while appearing merely to reveal them.
Framing and ordering matter most when prior preferences are weak.
Reflecting on goals before viewing plans can anchor priorities in needs rather than presentation.
Share this: write your priorities before opening options in one unfamiliar category.

puzzles.title: The Highest Stakes
puzzles.question: Because medical choices matter greatly, patients should always receive every technically possible option at once; withholding any detail from the first conversation necessarily worsens autonomy.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Autonomy can be supported by staged explanation, decision aids, and relevant filtering, provided options and trade-offs remain honestly accessible.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Dumping undifferentiated information can obstruct understanding; informed choice concerns usable comprehension, not maximum simultaneous detail.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Information quantity and informed understanding are not interchangeable.
High-stakes decisions need accuracy, relevance, and time for questions.
Staged disclosure can preserve detail while controlling cognitive load.
Ethical guidance supports deliberation without secretly replacing the chooser's values.
Share this: ask an expert to separate must-know facts from details that can wait until a second conversation.

puzzles.title: Architecture Everywhere
puzzles.question: A benefits form must list plans in some order and select some outcome for an unanswered field. Therefore avoiding choice architecture entirely is impossible; the design question is how to use it responsibly.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Order, defaults, grouping, and friction exist even when designers claim neutrality, so their effects require deliberate scrutiny.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A choice must be presented somehow, and presentation inevitably changes attention and effort; responsibility cannot be escaped by leaving those effects accidental.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Choice architecture is the environment in which alternatives are encountered.
Order, defaults, categories, and required steps all guide attention and effort.
Neutral presentation is rarely literal because some arrangement must be chosen.
Responsible design makes its goals visible and preserves meaningful exit routes.
Share this: inspect the ordering and default in one form before accepting its apparent neutrality.

puzzles.title: Advice Is Abdication
puzzles.question: A patient asks a doctor to recommend one treatment after discussing the patient's priorities. Accepting that recommendation necessarily means surrendering autonomy to the doctor.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Choosing to delegate expert filtering under stated values can itself be an exercise of autonomy, especially when the recommendation remains rejectable.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Agency includes deciding how to decide; informed, voluntary delegation differs from having a choice silently made on one's behalf.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Meta-choice concerns who will search, filter, or decide and under what constraints.
Delegation can conserve attention while keeping values and consent with the chooser.
The right to ask for guidance is part of autonomy, not its opposite.
Good advisers explain reasoning and leave room for refusal or revision.
Share this: tell an adviser which values should govern any recommendation you request.

puzzles.title: Three Useful Bins
puzzles.question: A job site groups hundreds of listings into three user-chosen priorities before showing individual roles. Meaningful categories can reduce overload even though the number of jobs in the database is unchanged.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Categories compress the comparison task by letting users eliminate whole regions of the option space according to relevant goals.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Cognitive burden depends on how options are structured and filtered, not only on how many records exist behind the interface.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Chunking combines many details into a smaller number of meaningful units.
User-relevant categories turn browsing into staged elimination rather than all-at-once comparison.
Poor categories merely hide options; good ones map to actual goals.
Information structure can lower burden without shrinking inventory.
Share this: group one long personal list into three decision-relevant categories before choosing.

puzzles.title: Nothing Chosen
puzzles.question: A shopper leaves a wall of nearly identical televisions without buying. This proves that none of the televisions met the shopper's needs.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Deferral can result from comparison burden, uncertainty, or fear of choosing badly even when many options are acceptable.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Failure to choose reveals that the decision process stalled, not necessarily that every available product was unsuitable.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Choice deferral has multiple causes: poor fit, high effort, uncertainty, and anticipated regret.
Observed inaction does not identify which cause produced it.
Similar alternatives can be harder to distinguish despite many meeting the same need.
Diagnostic questions should test both product fit and process burden.
Share this: when someone postpones a choice, ask whether the problem is options, criteria, or consequences.

puzzles.title: The Open Tab
puzzles.question: Lena buys refundable tickets but keeps comparing routes for two weeks. Reversibility can preserve flexibility while also delaying psychological commitment and extending search.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. An open exit lowers the cost of error but can keep alternatives mentally alive and make the decision feel unfinished.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Reversible choice offers practical protection, yet the same openness can invite continued comparison instead of closure.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Flexibility has option value because it protects against uncertain future information.
Open options also carry attention costs when they remain under continuous review.
Closure may require a self-imposed date even when formal reversal remains possible.
The best policy balances error costs against the cost of prolonged indecision.
Share this: set a final review date for one reversible choice that keeps consuming attention.

puzzles.title: Everyone Chose Better
puzzles.question: After selecting a phone, Arman sees friends praising different models and becomes less satisfied. Social comparison can amplify choice regret by continually supplying attractive alternatives he rejected.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Other people's visible choices refresh counterfactuals and make the selected option compete long after the purchase is complete.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Satisfaction depends partly on the comparison set kept in view, and social feeds can make that set unusually large and vivid.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Counterfactual thinking imagines how a different choice might have produced a better result.
Social visibility continually refreshes alternatives that would otherwise fade.
People display benefits more readily than hidden costs, skewing comparison.
Post-choice attention is therefore part of experienced value.
Share this: mute product comparisons for a week after your next considered purchase.

puzzles.title: Known Taste, Broad Shelf
puzzles.question: A reader knows the exact author and edition wanted. The bookstore's million-title inventory must still create choice overload because the total number of available books is enormous.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. A precise preference and effective search can collapse a huge inventory into one relevant result, leaving little comparison burden.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. What matters is the live consideration set, not every item technically stocked; clear goals and search tools can make abundance useful.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The consideration set contains options a chooser actually evaluates.
Clear preferences can shrink that set before comparison begins.
Search tools make large inventories valuable when they retrieve rather than merely display.
Abundance is most burdensome when goals are vague and filtering is weak.
Share this: state your target precisely before entering one very large marketplace.

puzzles.title: The Middle Plan
puzzles.question: A company adds an overpriced premium plan that few customers want. Even though no existing plan changes, the new comparison can shift customers toward the formerly expensive middle plan.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Options are evaluated relationally, so a new extreme can change which existing alternative appears moderate or valuable.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The added plan can serve as a reference point, altering the frame around unchanged alternatives rather than winning customers itself.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Preferences can depend on the comparison set rather than only on isolated features.
An extreme option can make a neighbouring choice look moderate.
Decoys reveal that adding an option may change choices among existing ones.
Evaluating each alternative against prior needs reduces contextual steering.
Share this: remove the most extreme plan from one pricing table and see whether the middle still looks natural.

puzzles.title: More Facts, Less Fog
puzzles.question: A buyer overwhelmed by 20 mortgage offers can always solve the problem by collecting more facts about every offer, because additional information necessarily makes comparison easier.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. More facts can add attributes and conflicts; what often helps is prioritization, standardization, or elimination rather than raw volume.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Information is useful only when it changes a relevant distinction or supports a decision rule; undigested detail can deepen overload.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Information has value when it can alter a choice or confidence appropriately.
Extra attributes increase comparison cost when priorities remain undefined.
Standardized summaries expose relevant differences better than scattered detail.
The remedy for overload is often structure, not another page of facts.
Share this: delete one comparison column that cannot realistically change your current decision.

puzzles.title: The Search Boundary
puzzles.question: Before apartment hunting, Rosa sets non-negotiable criteria, a budget, and a date after which she will choose the best qualifying option seen. Such a stopping rule can improve decisions by preventing endless expansion of the search.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Advance criteria preserve what matters and define when further search is unlikely to justify its time and attention costs.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A stopping rule does not guarantee perfection; it protects a good decision from an unlimited hunt for hypothetical improvement.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Search has costs in time, attention, delay, and lost opportunities.
Advance criteria prevent every newly seen feature from rewriting priorities.
A deadline can convert an open-ended maximization problem into a tractable one.
Stopping wisely is part of decision skill, not evidence of failure.
Share this: set criteria and a final decision date before beginning one upcoming search.

puzzles.title: Browsing After Buying
puzzles.question: After ordering a camera, Dev continues reading rankings for every competing model. Even if the purchase cannot be changed, this continued comparison can reduce satisfaction without improving the decision.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Once no useful action remains, comparison may only highlight forgone advantages and feed counterfactual regret.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Search has value while it can inform action; after an irreversible choice, the same activity can become a machine for generating alternatives without benefits.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The value of information depends on whether it can still guide a useful action.
Post-decision search often emphasizes features the chosen option lacks.
Every alternative has advantages, so continued comparison can always manufacture doubt.
Attention invested in using a choice can create more value than attention spent reopening it.
Share this: close reviews after one irreversible purchase and learn one feature of what you chose instead.

puzzles.title: One Approved Provider
puzzles.question: Because too many pension providers can overwhelm employees, allowing only the employer's own provider is automatically the best remedy for the paradox of choice.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Reducing burden does not justify eliminating competition or creating conflicts of interest; defaults, shortlists, and comparison tools can preserve alternatives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Choice overload identifies a design problem, not a blank cheque for monopoly; the remedy must also protect quality, transparency, and exit.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A diagnosis of overload does not determine a single ethical remedy.
Removing options can simplify choice while also reducing competition and protection against poor providers.
Defaults, curated sets, and standardized comparisons offer less restrictive tools.
Good architecture reduces cognitive cost while preserving meaningful challenge and exit.
Share this: when someone proposes fewer choices, ask who selects the survivors and who benefits.

puzzles.title: Forecasted Fortune
puzzles.question: A reliable model puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box when it predicts you will take only that box; a clear box always holds $10,000. In past cases, P(full | opaque-only) = 0.99 and P(full | both) = 0.01. Which act has the higher expected payout?
choices: Take only the opaque box, with an expected $990,000
Take both boxes, with an expected $20,000
Either act, because the past prediction is already fixed
puzzles.correctAnswer: Take only the opaque box, with an expected $990,000
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Conditioning on the contemplated act gives $990,000 for opaque-only versus $20,000 for both, so the observed act-outcome link overwhelms the clear-box bonus.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - take only the opaque box, with an expected $990,000. The relevant conditional payoffs are 0.99 x $1,000,000 and 0.01 x $1,000,000 + $10,000; saying the prediction is fixed does not make those evidential expectations equal.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Evidential decision rules compare outcomes conditional on each available act.
A strong act-outcome correlation can outweigh a smaller guaranteed addition.
Conditional expectation multiplies each possible payoff by its probability under that choice.
This reasoning evaluates what an action indicates, not only what it physically changes.
Share this: calculate two conditional expected values before trusting a verbal intuition about a risky choice.

puzzles.title: The Accuracy Line
puzzles.question: An opaque box pays $1,000,000. A clear box pays $10,000. A symmetric predictor is correct with probability p: it fills the opaque box for predicted one-boxers. Using conditional expected value, above what p does opaque-only beat taking both?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Opaque-only yields pM, while both yields (1-p)M + $10,000; solving pM > (1-p)M + $10,000 gives p > 0.505.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the threshold is any p greater than 0.505. The comparison is not merely whether the predictor beats chance: its advantage over chance must also cover the clear box's one-percent-sized bonus.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Decision thresholds occur where two expected-payoff expressions are equal.
A small guaranteed bonus shifts the break-even point above bare predictive chance.
Symmetric accuracy makes a contemplated act alter which prediction error matters.
Writing the inequality prevents vague words such as reliable from deciding the problem.
Share this: turn one verbal risk trade-off into an inequality and find its break-even probability.

puzzles.title: Frozen Box Contents
puzzles.question: The predictor has left and both boxes are sealed. You reason causally: your hand movement cannot alter either box now. Holding their contents fixed, what does dominance reasoning recommend?
choices: Take opaque-only because it signals the richer state
Randomize because neither act changes the past
Take both because it adds the clear-box money in either state
Refuse because prediction makes agency incoherent
puzzles.correctAnswer: Take both because it adds the clear-box money in either state
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. If the opaque box is full, both pays the bonus more; if it is empty, both still pays the bonus more, so causal state-by-state comparison favors both.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Take both because it adds the clear-box money in either state. Correlation with the hidden state motivates the rival view, but dominance deliberately holds that already-set state constant across the two acts.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dominance compares actions within every possible fixed state of the world.
An action dominates when it does at least as well in all states and better in some.
Causal reasoning holds past variables fixed when evaluating a present intervention.
Newcomb-style cases become difficult because evidential and causal comparisons hold different things fixed.
Share this: make a state-by-state payoff table for one choice whose evidence and causal effects seem to conflict.

puzzles.title: Random Hands Trial
puzzles.question: After predictors fill boxes, researchers randomly assign participants to take one or both. The opaque box is full in 60% of each assigned group; the clear box holds $5,000. What result best isolates the causal effect of taking both?
choices: The one-box group earns $5,000 more on average
Random assignment makes both acts pay equally
The two-box group earns $5,000 more on average
puzzles.correctAnswer: The two-box group earns $5,000 more on average
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Random assignment breaks the usual selection link, and equal opaque-fill rates leave the clear-box amount as the entire average causal difference.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is that the two-box group earns $5,000 more on average. With the hidden-box distribution balanced by random assignment, the groups differ only in whether they also collect the clear box.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Random assignment severs common causes between a chosen action and an outcome.
Observational conditioning can mix an action's effect with the traits that predict the action.
A balanced hidden-state rate lets the remaining payoff difference identify the intervention effect.
Causal evidence asks what changes when the action is assigned rather than merely observed.
Share this: ask whether one persuasive comparison came from self-selection or random assignment.

puzzles.title: Signature Before Prediction
puzzles.question: Tomorrow a 99%-accurate predictor will inspect whether you signed an enforceable opaque-only contract, then fill a $1,000,000 box accordingly. Staying flexible lets you take both tomorrow but will be predicted as such. The clear box has $1,000. What should a payoff-maximizer do today?
choices: Sign the opaque-only contract before inspection
Stay flexible and take both boxes tomorrow
Decline both boxes to avoid manipulation
puzzles.correctAnswer: Sign the opaque-only contract before inspection
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The commitment is made while it can still affect the predictor's evidence, making the likely million far more valuable than preserving tomorrow's small local bonus.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - sign the opaque-only contract before inspection. Flexibility has local value after the boxes are filled, but here it changes what the predictor sees and therefore sharply reduces the chance that the valuable box is funded.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Commitment can change an earlier observer's forecast by changing future feasible actions.
The value of flexibility is not always positive when others condition rewards on reliability.
An ex ante policy comparison includes consequences that disappear from an ex post act comparison.
Contracts and public promises often work by deliberately narrowing later choice.
Share this: identify one goal where a modest loss of future flexibility would improve incentives today.

puzzles.title: Tomorrow's Temptation
puzzles.question: Today you may bind tomorrow's choice before a perfect predictor fills the opaque box. Tomorrow, after filling, taking both adds $1,000 whatever happened. Which pair describes the time conflict?
choices: Decline commitment today; take opaque-only tomorrow
Commit to opaque-only today; prefer both when tomorrow arrives unbound
Commit to both today; prefer opaque-only when tomorrow arrives
Randomize today; decline all money tomorrow
puzzles.correctAnswer: Commit to opaque-only today; prefer both when tomorrow arrives unbound
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Before prediction, commitment secures the funded box; after prediction, an unbound causal comparison sees only the extra $1,000, producing dynamic inconsistency.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: commit to opaque-only today, but prefer both when tomorrow arrives unbound. The information structure changes between stages, so a policy that is best before prediction need not be the act favored after the prediction is fixed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dynamic inconsistency occurs when plans favored at one time are rejected at another.
Information and causal timing can change what a local comparison counts as fixed.
Commitment devices let an earlier policy survive a later temptation.
Reflective decision rules aim to choose plans their future versions can predictably execute.
Share this: find one recurring choice where your advance plan and moment-of-action preference diverge.

puzzles.title: The Copied Program
puzzles.question: A predictor runs an exact copy of your deterministic decision program, then fills the opaque box if the copy outputs ONE. Your live program receives the same inputs. Which counterfactual best captures their logical link?
choices: Changing your output leaves the copied output fixed by definition
Only physical signals sent after prediction can connect the outputs
A different program output would occur in both matching computations
Exact copying makes every counterfactual meaningless
puzzles.correctAnswer: A different program output would occur in both matching computations
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The outputs need not communicate through time; they covary because they instantiate the same computation on the same input.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, a different program output would occur in both matching computations. Holding the simulation fixed while changing the identical live computation breaks the stipulated logical identity, even though the earlier physical box remains fixed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Logical dependence can connect matching computations without a physical signal between them.
Counterfactual reasoning must decide whether copies of one algorithm vary together.
Simulation-based predictors make source-code policy relevant to later rewards.
Physical causation and mathematical covariation answer different comparison questions.
Share this: distinguish a shared-rule correlation from a message-passing connection in one system you use.

puzzles.title: No Message Backward
puzzles.question: A neuroscientist predicts your box choice from yesterday's brain scan, then fills the box. Today your choice strongly correlates with yesterday's prediction. What best explains this without backward causation?
choices: Today's hand movement changes yesterday's scan
The sealed box transmits a signal into your motor cortex
Correlation itself proves a future-to-past causal arrow
The scan and choice reflect the same earlier decision-making state
puzzles.correctAnswer: The scan and choice reflect the same earlier decision-making state
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. A common prior state can generate both the forecast and the later act, creating predictive dependence without any influence traveling backward in time.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is that the scan and choice reflect the same earlier decision-making state. Predictability requires shared information or structure, not a causal message from the later action into the past.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A common cause can make two events informative about each other without either causing the other.
Prediction exploits traces of a process that later produces behaviour.
Temporal correlation alone does not identify the direction of causation.
Causal diagrams force proposed arrows and shared causes to be stated separately.
Share this: draw a common-cause explanation for one correlation that is often described causally.

puzzles.title: Unequal Prediction Errors
puzzles.question: An opaque box holds $1,000,000 when the model predicts ONE. It predicts ONE for 90% of actual one-boxers but also for 5% of actual two-boxers. A clear box holds $5,000. Under observed conditional payoff, which choice wins?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The relevant rates are conditional on each actual act: 0.90 x $1,000,000 versus 0.05 x $1,000,000 + $5,000.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - opaque-only yields $900,000 versus $55,000. Sensitivity and false-positive rate enter different action columns, so they must not be added or mistaken for one symmetric accuracy figure.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Asymmetric predictors have separate error rates for different actual behaviours.
Expected payoff uses the error rate conditional on the act being evaluated.
A single accuracy percentage can conceal strategically important asymmetry.
Confusion matrices keep true and false predictions in the correct columns.
Share this: request separate false-positive and false-negative rates for one classifier you encounter.

puzzles.title: Ninety Nine Percent
puzzles.question: A report says a predictor is 99% accurate overall, but gives neither how often people choose each act nor its error rate for each act. Can you derive P(opaque full | you take both) from that headline alone?
choices: No; base rates and the two conditional error rates are missing
No; overall accuracy contains no information whatsoever
puzzles.correctAnswer: No; base rates and the two conditional error rates are missing
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Overall accuracy is a weighted average, and many combinations of act prevalence and asymmetric errors produce the same 99% headline.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, no; base rates and the two conditional error rates are missing. One percent is the total error share, not necessarily the error probability within the subgroup of people who take both.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Aggregate accuracy averages performance across groups using their prevalence as weights.
A rare class can have poor conditional prediction while barely moving the headline number.
Decision payoffs usually require class-specific conditional probabilities.
Bayesian reasoning keeps overall, joint, and conditional rates distinct.
Share this: challenge one accuracy claim by asking for class frequencies and both kinds of error.

puzzles.title: Large Clear Box
puzzles.question: P(full | opaque-only) = 0.75 and P(full | both) = 0.20. The opaque box pays $200,000 and the clear box pays $150,000. Which act maximizes conditional expected money?
choices: Opaque-only, because predictor accuracy always dominates bonuses
Both, because its opaque box is more likely to be full
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Opaque-only averages $150,000, while both averages $40,000 from the opaque box plus the guaranteed $150,000.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is both, because $190,000 exceeds $150,000. A predictive advantage is not decisive by itself; its monetary value must be compared with the size of the certain bonus.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Probabilities and payoff magnitudes jointly determine expected value.
A more favorable signal can lose to a sufficiently large guaranteed component.
Decision labels should never replace multiplication and addition of outcomes.
Sensitivity analysis asks how a recommendation changes as stakes change.
Share this: vary one payoff in a decision table until the preferred action switches.

puzzles.title: Utility Bends Money
puzzles.question: Opaque-only gives a 60% chance of $1,000,000 and otherwise $0. Both gives a 10% chance of $1,400,000 and otherwise a guaranteed $400,000. For utility u(x) = sqrt(x), which has greater expected utility?
choices: Opaque-only, because its expected money is $600,000
Opaque-only, because utility preserves every money ranking
They tie because both can include the opaque prize
Both boxes, because about 688 utility units exceed 600
puzzles.correctAnswer: Both boxes, because about 688 utility units exceed 600
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Opaque-only gives 0.6 x 1000 = 600 utility units, while both gives 0.1 x sqrt(1,400,000) + 0.9 x sqrt(400,000), about 688.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Both boxes gives about 688 utility units, exceeding 600. Concave utility values the reliable $400,000 floor enough to reverse the ranking by expected dollars.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Expected utility applies probabilities to experienced value rather than raw money.
Concave utility represents diminishing marginal value and aversion to payoff spread.
Two acts can reverse order when evaluated by dollars and by utility.
A stated utility function turns vague risk preference into a checkable calculation.
Share this: compare one gamble by both expected money and a concave value scale.

puzzles.title: Perfect Peek
puzzles.question: Before choosing, you may learn for free whether the already-sealed opaque box is full. In either revealed state, taking both adds $10,000 and changes nothing else. For a causal decision-maker, what is the peek's decision value?
choices: Zero, because the same act is best after either signal
$10,000, because information is worth the clear box
$500,000, because uncertainty is cut in half
$1,000,000, because the opaque state becomes certain
puzzles.correctAnswer: Zero, because the same act is best after either signal
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Information has instrumental value only when it can improve the contingent action; here both remains better whether the opaque box is full or empty.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - the peek's decision value is zero, because the same act is best after either signal. Learning a hidden fact may satisfy curiosity, but it cannot improve this decision when it never changes the chosen branch.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The value of information comes from choosing different actions after different signals.
Perfect certainty can be worthless when one action dominates in every revealed state.
Information value is measured against the best decision available without the signal.
Curiosity value and instrumental decision value should be kept separate.
Share this: before buying information, name the action that each possible result would change.

puzzles.title: Admission Price
puzzles.question: A 90%-reliable Newcomb game charges $100,000 before prediction. Opaque-only conditionally pays $1,000,000 with probability 0.9; both gets that prize with probability 0.1 plus $10,000. Your outside option is $700,000. Which plan has greatest expected money after the fee?
choices: Decline and keep the $700,000 outside option
Enter and choose opaque-only for an expected net $800,000
Enter and take both for an expected net $10,000
Enter and randomize for an expected net $405,000
puzzles.correctAnswer: Enter and choose opaque-only for an expected net $800,000
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The fee reduces the opaque-only expectation from $900,000 to $800,000, which still beats the outside option; the two-box net is only $10,000.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The best plan is to enter and choose opaque-only for an expected net $800,000. Entry and action are separate decisions, so each in-game expectation must be reduced by the common fee and then compared with declining.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sequential choices require comparing complete plans rather than isolated moves.
Entry costs affect every participating strategy but not the outside option.
A game can contain an attractive act yet be unattractive to enter, or vice versa.
Decision trees keep fees, branches, and fallback payoffs in the correct order.
Share this: include the cost of access before comparing the advertised rewards of one opportunity.

puzzles.title: Forecast in Public
puzzles.question: A predictor publicly announces whether you will take one or both. You have precommitted to do the opposite of its announcement. What follows about a claimed perfect deterministic predictor in this setup?
choices: It remains perfect if it announces opaque-only
It remains perfect if it announces both boxes
No announcement can be correct under the opposite-act rule
It can restore perfection by announcing at random
puzzles.correctAnswer: No announcement can be correct under the opposite-act rule
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Either announcement triggers the other act, so public access plus a guaranteed contrarian response diagonalizes against every deterministic forecast.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is that no announcement can be correct under the opposite-act rule. Predicting either branch causes the committed agent to select its complement; random announcing changes frequencies but cannot make each forecast perfect.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A prediction can alter the system when the predicted agent observes it.
Diagonal strategies construct an output specifically different from a proposed forecast.
Perfect prediction claims need assumptions about secrecy, response, or restricted agents.
Self-reference often turns passive measurement into an interactive loop.
Share this: ask what changes when the subject of a forecast gets to read it before acting.

puzzles.title: Seeded Coin Flip
puzzles.question: You plan to use a hardware coin to hide your box choice, but the predictor reads both its physical state and your decision rule before filling the box. What does randomization accomplish against a perfect physical simulation?
choices: It guarantees the opaque prize on half the trials
It makes taking both dominate without affecting prediction
It forces the predictor to leave both boxes empty
It adds no unpredictability because the simulated seed fixes the flip
puzzles.correctAnswer: It adds no unpredictability because the simulated seed fixes the flip
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. A process can look random to you while remaining predictable to a model that knows the relevant physical seed and rule.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - it adds no unpredictability because the simulated seed fixes the flip. Randomization helps only relative to an observer missing the random source; stipulating complete state access removes that informational advantage.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Randomness is often defined relative to what an observer can know or compute.
A pseudorandom or physically seeded act is predictable to an agent with the seed and rule.
Mixed strategies gain value by concealing realization from an opponent.
Adding a coin does not help when the prediction model includes the coin.
Share this: identify what information makes one supposedly random process predictable.

puzzles.title: Rewarding Surprise
puzzles.question: A model predicts your act correctly 90% of the time. An opaque box gets $100,000 only when the model is wrong; a clear box always gets $20,000. The model has the same error rate for either act. Which choice maximizes expected money?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Either act gets the opaque reward only on the 10% error, worth $10,000 in expectation, while taking both adds the certain $20,000.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, take both for an expected $30,000. Because the miss rate is stipulated equal for both acts, neither choice improves the opaque-box chance; only the clear-box addition distinguishes them.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reversing a reward rule can remove the correlation that favored a familiar strategy.
Equal conditional error rates give both actions the same expected hidden reward.
A guaranteed component then decides the comparison by simple addition.
Decision procedures should follow the stated mechanism rather than the story's familiar surface.
Share this: reverse one incentive in a familiar puzzle and recompute instead of reusing its usual answer.

puzzles.title: The Craving Gene
puzzles.question: A gene causes both a harmless craving to smoke and cancer; assume smoking itself has no effect on cancer. Smoking gives a small pleasure. Population data show smokers get more cancer. What does causal decision theory recommend for a carrier deciding now?
choices: Avoid smoking because the act is evidence of cancer
Smoke if the pleasure exceeds its stipulated non-cancer costs
Randomize because the gene and act are correlated
Avoid the choice because genetic causes remove agency
puzzles.correctAnswer: Smoke if the pleasure exceeds its stipulated non-cancer costs
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Once the common gene and the stipulated absence of a smoking-to-cancer arrow are respected, intervening on smoking does not change cancer risk, so only actual causal costs and benefits remain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - smoke if the pleasure exceeds its stipulated non-cancer costs. The observed association is generated by the gene; treating the act as a cause would confuse evidence about an already-set risk with an effect on that risk.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A common cause can make an act predict harm even when the act does not produce it.
Causal decision rules evaluate interventions that break incoming arrows into the chosen action.
Evidence about hidden traits and effects of present behaviour are different quantities.
The conclusion depends on the causal assumptions, which real health cases must establish empirically.
Share this: separate predictive association from intervention evidence in one health headline.

puzzles.title: The Bitter Marker
puzzles.question: A harmless bitter tablet has no biological effect. A hidden biomarker independently causes recovery and a willingness to swallow it, so tablet-takers recover more often. You already know your biomarker status cannot change. Which conclusion follows causally?
choices: Taking the tablet improves recovery because takers recover more
Refusing the tablet worsens recovery by signaling the marker
The tablet choice cannot alter recovery under the stated graph
The better choice depends only on the population recovery rate
puzzles.correctAnswer: The tablet choice cannot alter recovery under the stated graph
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The biomarker explains both willingness and recovery, while the problem explicitly removes a causal path from the tablet to health.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is that the tablet choice cannot alter recovery under the stated graph. Choosing differently may be surprising evidence about what sort of person you are, but it cannot rewrite the fixed biomarker or create a missing biological effect.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Medical Newcomb cases contrast diagnostic evidence with treatment effects.
A marker can predict both uptake and outcome, creating selection bias.
Intervention questions ask what forcing treatment changes while holding prior causes fixed.
Real treatment decisions require trials or credible causal designs, not uptake correlations alone.
Share this: ask whether patients chose a treatment before interpreting their outcome difference.

puzzles.title: Membership as Evidence
puzzles.question: A gym is free to use, but buying a $200 badge strongly predicts who will attend because committed people buy it. The badge itself changes neither access nor motivation. How do evidential and causal reasoning differ?
choices: Both buy because attendance and purchase are correlated
Both decline because prediction never matters to decisions
Causal reasoning buys, while evidential reasoning declines
Evidential reasoning may buy, while causal reasoning declines
puzzles.correctAnswer: Evidential reasoning may buy, while causal reasoning declines
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Buying is favorable evidence about attendance but, by stipulation, does not cause attendance; the causal comparison therefore sees only its $200 cost.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Evidential reasoning may buy, while causal reasoning declines. The disagreement comes from whether conditioning on a self-chosen signal should count its correlation with a valuable outcome when the signal has no causal route to that outcome.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-signaling choices can correlate with success because underlying traits produce both.
Evidential rules may value an act for the favorable type it indicates.
Causal rules ignore diagnostic value when intervention leaves the outcome mechanism unchanged.
Practical commitments often have real motivational effects, so causal stipulations must be checked.
Share this: ask whether one paid commitment changes behaviour or merely identifies people already likely to act.

puzzles.title: Arrows Into Choice
puzzles.question: A diagram has stable trait T pointing to both predictor output P and your choice C; P points to box content B. There is no arrow from C to B. Under an intervention do(C = both), what happens to B?
choices: It stays governed by P while the incoming T-to-C link is cut
It becomes full because both includes the opaque box
It becomes empty because intervention disproves P
It changes only if C remains correlated with T
puzzles.correctAnswer: It stays governed by P while the incoming T-to-C link is cut
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The intervention replaces the normal causes of C but creates no new path to B, which remains determined upstream by P.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - B stays governed by P while the incoming T-to-C link is cut. Intervention semantics alter the chosen node's generating equation, not every correlated ancestor or downstream variable elsewhere in the graph.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A causal intervention sets one node while removing its ordinary incoming arrows.
Other structural equations remain intact unless a directed path carries the intervention onward.
Correlation through a shared ancestor disappears when the action is externally set.
Graph surgery makes the phrase holding everything else fixed more precise.
Share this: draw one action-outcome graph and mark which arrows an intervention would cut.

puzzles.title: Visible Commitment Badge
puzzles.question: For $20,000 you can wear an enforceable badge requiring opaque-only. A 95%-accurate predictor sees badges before filling a $1,000,000 box; flexible players intending both get the prize 5% of the time plus $10,000. Which policy pays more in expectation?
choices: Buy the badge, worth $930,000 after its cost
puzzles.correctAnswer: Buy the badge, worth $930,000 after its cost
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The visible commitment yields 0.95 x $1,000,000 - $20,000 = $930,000, far above the flexible two-box expectation of $60,000.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is to buy the badge, worth $930,000 after its cost. Its expense must be subtracted, but its effect on the predictor's forecast makes it an investment rather than a mere restriction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Observable commitments can alter other agents' predictions and responses.
Their value equals the induced payoff change minus the cost of lost flexibility and enforcement.
Credibility matters because an unenforceable signal may not move a sophisticated observer.
Institutions often sell trust by making later defection expensive or impossible.
Share this: find one bond, deposit, or deadline whose cost creates a valuable credible signal.

puzzles.title: Empty Despite Wisdom
puzzles.question: A decision rule selects opaque-only because P(full | opaque-only) = 0.8 and the alternative's expected payoff is far lower. This time the opaque box is empty. What is the soundest evaluation?
choices: The empty box proves taking both was rational all along
Any rule that sometimes loses is irrational
The policy can be rational despite this unlucky outcome
Prediction accuracy must be recomputed as zero
puzzles.correctAnswer: The policy can be rational despite this unlucky outcome
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Rationality under uncertainty grades the choice using available probabilities and payoffs, not by demanding that the higher-value gamble win on every trial.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the policy can be rational despite this unlucky outcome. An 80% event fails one time in five, and observing a loss does not retroactively change the information or expected values available at choice time.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Decision quality and outcome quality separate whenever uncertainty remains.
A good probabilistic policy can lose, while a poor one can get lucky.
Outcome bias imports information revealed later into evaluation of an earlier choice.
Fair review reconstructs the evidence and alternatives available at the decision point.
Share this: reassess one past choice using only what was knowable before its outcome.

puzzles.title: Buying Better Foresight
puzzles.question: Before prediction, you can upgrade a symmetric predictor from 60% to 90% accuracy. You will use opaque-only, the opaque prize is $1,000,000, and there is no other payoff. Ignoring risk attitudes, what is the upgrade's maximum fair price?
choices: $60,000, the original error probability times the prize
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Expected prize rises from $600,000 to $900,000, so any fee above $300,000 consumes more value than the accuracy upgrade creates.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite - the maximum fair price is $300,000, the increase in expected prize. Pricing an improvement uses the difference between optimized expectations, not the new total reward or an unscaled percentage-point count.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The value of a forecasting improvement is its marginal effect on expected payoff.
Accuracy percentages acquire economic meaning only when combined with stakes and decisions.
A fair fee compares the best achievable expectation before and after the upgrade.
Total value and incremental value answer different purchasing questions.
Share this: price one information upgrade by estimating how much it can change your actual decision outcome.

puzzles.title: Rich One Boxers
puzzles.question: Records show voluntary one-boxers averaged $900,000 while two-boxers averaged $20,000. A critic says this proves physically taking the clear box destroys $880,000. What is the strongest reply?
choices: The groups were selected by predictable choice, so earnings do not identify the act's causal effect
The average gap proves the clear box contained negative money
A larger sample would necessarily make the causal claim true
Voluntary data cannot contain any useful predictive information
puzzles.correctAnswer: The groups were selected by predictable choice, so earnings do not identify the act's causal effect
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The predictor deliberately creates different hidden-box distributions for people disposed toward different acts, so the observational earnings gap mixes selection with any causal effect.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The strongest reply is that the groups were selected by predictable choice, so earnings do not identify the act's causal effect. The records can strongly predict earnings while still failing to show that adding the clear-box action physically empties a sealed box.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Selection bias occurs when compared groups differ before the focal action is applied.
Prediction mechanisms can engineer enormous observational gaps without matching intervention effects.
More data reduce sampling noise but do not repair a biased comparison design.
Predictive usefulness and causal identification should be judged separately.
Share this: identify the selection rule behind one dramatic average difference before calling it an effect.

puzzles.title: The Discounted Confession
puzzles.question: Two suspects each choose Silence or Confess. Against Silence, Confess gives 0 years instead of 1; against Confess, it gives 5 years instead of 8. Yet mutual Silence gives 1 year each, better than mutual Confess at 5. This payoff structure is a prisoner's dilemma.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Confessing reduces each suspect's sentence under either action by the other, while both would prefer the mutual-silence outcome to mutual confession.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Comparing each column shows Confess is individually better, but comparing the two symmetric outcomes shows the dominant-strategy result is collectively worse.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A prisoner's dilemma combines an individual incentive to defect with a shared gain from mutual cooperation.
The defining payoff order is temptation above reward above punishment above the sucker outcome.
Dominance is checked separately against each possible opposing action.
The social trap appears only after individual and joint comparisons are both made.
Share this: write a two-by-two payoff table for one situation people casually call a dilemma.

puzzles.title: Insurance Changes Sides
puzzles.question: Two firms can Maintain or Cut safety spending. If the rival Maintains, Cut pays 6 versus Maintain's 4; if the rival Cuts, Maintain pays 3 versus Cut's 1 because insurance penalizes joint cutting. Cutting is still a dominant strategy for each firm.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Cutting is better against Maintain, but Maintaining is better against Cut, so neither action dominates across both cases.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A dominant strategy must beat the alternative for every opposing move; the insurance penalty reverses the comparison when the rival cuts.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dominance requires one action to outperform another in every relevant contingency.
One favorable column is not enough to establish a dominant strategy.
Policies can transform a dilemma by changing only one strategically decisive payoff.
Best-response arrows reveal whether incentives point the same way across the table.
Share this: compare both opponent columns before calling one workplace tactic inevitable.

puzzles.title: Stable Yet Wasteful
puzzles.question: In a one-shot game, each airline gains by cutting price whether its rival holds or cuts, but both earn more if both hold. Mutual price-cutting can therefore be both a Nash equilibrium and Pareto-inferior to mutual restraint.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Neither airline can improve alone from mutual cutting, making it stable, even though coordinated restraint would make both better off.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Nash equilibrium tests unilateral deviation, while Pareto comparison asks whether another outcome benefits everyone; those tests can point to stability and waste at once.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Nash equilibrium means no player benefits by changing alone.
Pareto improvement means at least one player gains and nobody loses.
A stable outcome need not maximize welfare or total payoff.
Coordination problems often persist precisely because the better move must be joint.
Share this: find one stable routine where no individual can profitably improve it alone.

puzzles.title: Solo Escape Route
puzzles.question: At mutual defection in a standard prisoner's dilemma, either player can move the pair to the mutually cooperative payoff simply by cooperating alone while the other keeps defecting.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. A unilateral cooperator receives the sucker payoff while the other receives temptation; reaching mutual cooperation requires both actions to change.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Changing one action moves to an asymmetric outcome, not the cooperative corner, and makes the lone cooperator worse off under the defining payoff order.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A payoff matrix outcome is determined by the combination of all players' actions.
Changing one coordinate cannot directly reach a corner that differs in both coordinates.
The sucker payoff makes unilateral moral effort strategically vulnerable.
Escaping a social trap often needs coordination, enforcement, or repeated incentives.
Share this: ask which other actions must change before proposing an individual fix to a shared trap.

puzzles.title: Contracted Restraint
puzzles.question: Two suppliers face a one-shot prisoner's dilemma over quality. They sign an enforceable contract imposing a penalty larger than the gain from secretly cutting quality. The contract can remove defection's dominance by changing the effective payoffs.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. A sufficiently large enforceable penalty makes the tempting deviation less profitable, so the strategic game after contracting is no longer the original dilemma.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Enforcement is not mere persuasion: it subtracts from the deviation payoff and can reverse the best response that generated the trap.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Institutions change behaviour by changing consequences attached to actions.
An enforceable penalty must exceed the private gain it is meant to deter.
When effective payoffs change, the resulting strategic game may change category.
Contracts convert promises into incentives only when breach is detectable and costly.
Share this: identify the monitoring and penalty that make one real agreement credible.

puzzles.title: Promise Over Coffee
puzzles.question: Before a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, both players sincerely promise to cooperate, but promises are nonbinding and do not alter preferences, information, or reputation. Their conversation alone logically guarantees mutual cooperation.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The promise may influence beliefs or values in real life, but under the stated unchanged game each player still gains by defecting after any verbal agreement.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Cheap talk can coordinate when interests partly align, but it cannot logically erase a dominant deviation while every payoff and consequence remains unchanged.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cheap talk is communication that carries no direct enforcement cost.
Messages can reveal intentions without making those intentions incentive-compatible.
A promise is strategically reliable only when preferences, reputation, or penalties support keeping it.
Separating sincerity from incentive prevents hopeful words from being treated as guarantees.
Share this: ask what makes one promise costly to break rather than merely easy to say.

puzzles.title: Last Round Shadow
puzzles.question: Two perfectly rational players know their standard prisoner's dilemma will end after exactly ten rounds, and all rationality is common knowledge. Backward induction by itself predicts cooperation in round one because nine future punishments remain.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Defection is dominant in the final round; removing that round's leverage repeats the argument backward until the first round.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. With a known final round, there is no later punishment there, and common knowledge lets that unravel every earlier threat by backward induction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Backward induction solves a finite game from its final decision point.
A last round with no future consequences restores the one-shot incentive.
Common knowledge lets players carry that conclusion into every preceding round.
Real finite relationships may cooperate because rationality, horizons, or information are imperfect.
Share this: locate the final enforceable consequence before relying on a repeated threat.

puzzles.title: Unknown Final Meeting
puzzles.question: If partners believe each round may be followed by another and care enough about future gains, a threat to stop cooperating after betrayal can make present cooperation rational even though one-shot defection dominates.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. A sufficiently valuable shadow of the future can make the stream of cooperative rewards exceed the one-time temptation followed by punishment.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Uncertain continuation prevents a known final round from unraveling the relationship, allowing future losses to discipline a profitable betrayal today.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Repeated games add future consequences to an action's effective payoff.
Continuation probability and patience determine the size of the future shadow.
Conditional strategies can reward cooperation and punish observed betrayal.
The stage game stays unchanged while the strategy across time changes incentives.
Share this: identify one relationship where expected future contact supports trust today.

puzzles.title: Patient Partners
puzzles.question: Each cooperative round pays 3. Defecting once pays 5, then punishment pays 1 forever. With continuation weight 0.8, cooperation is sustainable because 3/(1-0.8) exceeds 5 + 0.8/(1-0.8).
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Continued cooperation is worth 15, while deviation followed by punishment is worth 9, so the threat makes restraint optimal.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The discounted cooperative stream is 15, and the tempting 5 plus the discounted stream of 1s totals only 9.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Discounted value adds future payoffs with progressively smaller weights.
A deviation comparison includes its immediate gain and the continuation it triggers.
Cooperation is sustainable when its full stream beats temptation plus punishment.
Explicit sums reveal how patience changes strategic incentives.
Share this: calculate how many future benefits are needed to outweigh one short-term gain.

puzzles.title: Short Future
puzzles.question: Using the same payoffs - cooperation 3 forever, deviation 5 then punishment 1 - a continuation weight of 0.2 is enough to sustain cooperation under the threat.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Cooperation is worth 3.75, while deviation is worth 5.25, so a weakly valued future cannot outweigh the immediate temptation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Substituting 0.2 gives 3/(0.8) = 3.75 versus 5 + 0.2/(0.8) = 5.25, leaving betrayal profitable.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Future punishment works only when future payoffs receive enough weight.
Low continuation probability shrinks both future rewards and future sanctions.
The same strategy can be stable in a lasting relationship and unstable in a fleeting one.
Threshold calculations replace the vague claim that repetition always creates cooperation.
Share this: estimate whether one threatened future cost is large enough to change today's incentive.

puzzles.title: Echoing Mistake
puzzles.question: Two players use strict tit-for-tat: start by cooperating, then copy the other's previous move. After one accidental defection by only one player, perfect copying can make them alternate cooperation and defection indefinitely rather than immediately restore mutual cooperation.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Each player answers the other's last move, so the accidental defection bounces back and forth one round out of phase.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The mistaken defection is copied by the victim next round while the original player copies the victim's earlier cooperation, creating an alternating echo.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reciprocal strategies use recent behaviour as both reward and punishment.
Implementation noise can make a fair response target an accidental move.
Symmetric retaliation may propagate an error instead of cancelling it.
Robust cooperation needs a recovery path as well as a deterrent.
Share this: trace three rounds after one mistaken action before judging a reciprocal rule resilient.

puzzles.title: One Forgiving Move
puzzles.question: In a noisy repeated dilemma, occasionally cooperating after the opponent's defection can stop accidental retaliation loops, though excessive forgiveness may invite deliberate exploitation.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Limited forgiveness creates a route back to mutual cooperation, but making punishment too unreliable weakens deterrence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Noise makes some defections unintentional, so a strategy needs both enough retaliation to deter and enough forgiveness to recover.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Error tolerance and deterrence pull repeated strategies in opposite directions.
Forgiveness can absorb noise by resetting a cycle of retaliation.
Unlimited forgiveness removes the future cost that disciplines opportunism.
Good rules balance responsiveness with a credible path back to trust.
Share this: design one response rule that distinguishes a first mistake from repeated exploitation.

puzzles.title: Grim but Credible
puzzles.question: In an infinitely repeated standard prisoner's dilemma, grim trigger prescribes permanent defection after any betrayal. Once punishment starts, continuing to defect is credible because mutual defection is already a stage-game equilibrium.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. During the punishment phase, neither player gains by unilaterally cooperating, so carrying out the threat is sequentially rational under the standard payoffs.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A threat deters only if players will execute it later; here the prescribed punishment coincides with the one-shot equilibrium once cooperation has ended.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A credible threat must remain rational when the time comes to carry it out.
Subgame reasoning tests strategies after histories that may never occur on the intended path.
Stage-game equilibria often supply credible punishment states.
Severity alone does not create credibility; future incentives do.
Share this: test whether you would really carry out one threat after its triggering event.

puzzles.title: Costly Empty Threat
puzzles.question: A manager threatens to impose a punishment that would cost the manager more than tolerating a supplier's defection, with no reputational or future benefit. The punishment is credible merely because it was announced in advance.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. If carrying it out is worse when the moment arrives and no commitment changes that calculation, the announcement is dynamically incredible.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Advance words do not bind later incentives; a rational supplier can anticipate that the manager will prefer not to execute a self-harming sanction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Threat credibility is evaluated at the future decision node, not when words are spoken.
A costly punishment may need commitment, delegation, or reputation to become believable.
Empty threats fail when the target can reason backward from later incentives.
Strategic promises and threats share the need for incentive compatibility.
Share this: ask what would make one announced consequence rational to enforce later.

puzzles.title: Glass-Walled Choices
puzzles.question: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, making both choices perfectly observable before payoffs are delivered automatically removes defection's dominance, even if neither player can revise and no payoff changes.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Observation after simultaneous irrevocable choice may aid accountability elsewhere, but it does not change either payoff comparison inside the stated one-shot game.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Transparency affects strategy only through consequences such as revision, reputation, punishment, or changed preferences; bare visibility does not rewrite the matrix.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Information changes incentives only when some action or payoff can respond to it.
Observability after an irreversible move differs from observation before a revisable move.
Transparency can matter through reputation or enforcement without being magic itself.
A mechanism should specify the causal route from seeing to strategic consequence.
Share this: ask what anyone can do differently with one proposed transparency measure.

puzzles.title: Taxing Betrayal
puzzles.question: A prisoner's-dilemma payoff table is T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0. A tax of 2 applies whenever a player defects. After the tax, defection is no longer strictly dominant.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Against cooperation, taxed defection ties cooperation at 3; against defection, taxed defection gives -1 while cooperation gives 0, so strict dominance disappears.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Subtracting 2 from each defection payoff creates a tie in one column and makes cooperation better in the other, defeating strict dominance.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Taxes and penalties modify the payoff attached to the targeted action.
Strict dominance requires a strict advantage in every opponent contingency.
A policy need not make cooperation dominant to remove defection's dominance.
Recomputing every affected cell prevents intuitive but incorrect mechanism claims.
Share this: adjust one payoff table with a proposed fine and redraw its best responses.

puzzles.title: Tiny Green Bonus
puzzles.question: For T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0, giving a bonus of 1 whenever a player cooperates makes cooperation strictly dominant.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Against cooperation, cooperating rises to 4 but defection still pays 5; against defection, cooperation and defection tie at 1.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The bonus improves both cooperation cells, but not enough to beat defection in either column strictly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
An incentive must be tested against every strategic response, not merely added symbolically.
A small subsidy can weaken a trap without fully reversing it.
Strict dominance is stronger than being competitive or tied.
Minimum effective incentive size follows from the largest relevant payoff gap.
Share this: calculate the smallest bonus that would reverse one unwanted private incentive.

puzzles.title: Crowded Pasture
puzzles.question: Ten herders each gain privately from adding one animal, while the resulting pasture damage is shared across all ten and eventually leaves everyone worse off if all add. This is a many-player social dilemma even though it is not literally a two-player matrix.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Each herder captures the concentrated benefit but bears only part of the shared cost, so individually attractive additions can aggregate into collective loss.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The number of players changes the formal model, but the conflict between private marginal gain and shared damage preserves the social-dilemma logic.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Many-player dilemmas distribute the cost of one action across a group.
Private benefits can exceed a person's share of harm while total harm exceeds total benefit.
The tragedy emerges through aggregation rather than one uniquely malicious actor.
Quotas, ownership, and pricing can align marginal private and social costs.
Share this: identify who captures the benefit and who shares the cost in one common resource.

puzzles.title: One Different Player
puzzles.question: A game is automatically a standard prisoner's dilemma whenever mutual cooperation beats mutual defection, even if one player prefers cooperating when the other cooperates.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The standard dilemma requires defection to be each player's dominant strategy; one player's cooperative best response breaks that defining condition.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A collectively better cooperative outcome is necessary but not sufficient; the individual best-response pattern must also create the trap for both players.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Social inefficiency alone does not identify a particular game form.
Each player's best response must be checked because asymmetric incentives matter.
Games with conditional cooperation may instead resemble coordination or assurance problems.
Correct classification predicts which remedies can work.
Share this: check every player's incentives before applying a familiar game-theory label.

puzzles.title: Caring Changes Payoffs
puzzles.question: If players begin valuing the other's welfare as part of their own utility, an unchanged table of cash payments may no longer represent the same strategic prisoner's dilemma.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Strategic payoffs represent what players value, not merely cash; concern for the other can reorder outcomes and change best responses.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The monetary consequences may stay fixed while utility changes, so calling the cash table the complete payoff table would misdescribe the players' actual objectives.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Game-theoretic payoffs encode preferences over outcomes, not necessarily money alone.
Fairness, guilt, loyalty, and identity can enter utility alongside material reward.
Changing preferences can transform a game without changing external cash flows.
Observed cooperation does not by itself prove a calculation error.
Share this: list one nonmonetary value that changes how people respond to a financial incentive.
