puzzles.title: Punched and Folded
puzzles.question: A sheet is folded in half five times, then a single hole is punched straight through the stack. When unfolded, how many holes appear?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Each fold doubles the layers, so five folds produce thirty-two layers and thirty-two holes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 32. Doubling repeats five times, giving two to the fifth power. Counting layers rather than imagining unfolding is the reliable shortcut.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Folding doubles the layer count each time.
Repeated doubling is exponentiation.
Counting layers predicts the unfolded result.
many small operations compound surprisingly fast.

puzzles.title: Layers of Paper
puzzles.question: How many layers thick is a sheet of paper after being folded in half three times?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Each fold doubles the stack, so three folds multiply one layer into eight.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Doubling three times gives two cubed. The common mistake is adding three rather than doubling three times.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Repeated doubling grows faster than addition.
Model growth processes as multiplication, not sums.
Small exponent differences matter quickly.
Practical folding limits are physical, not mathematical.

puzzles.title: Squares in Three
puzzles.question: In a three-by-three grid of small squares, how many squares of every possible size are there in total?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Nine single squares, four two-by-two squares, and one three-by-three square total fourteen.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 14. Counting only the small cells misses the larger squares formed by their combination. Working size by size, from largest to smallest, prevents omissions.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Composite shapes hide inside simple grids.
Count systematically by size to avoid misses.
Patterns of squares form familiar sequences.
Explicit enumeration beats visual estimation.

puzzles.title: Squares in Four
puzzles.question: In a four-by-four grid of small squares, how many squares of all sizes are there altogether?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Sixteen singles, nine doubles, four triples, and one large square total thirty.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 30. Each size contributes a shrinking count of positions, and the totals add up. Recognising the pattern of decreasing-square counts speeds the work enormously.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Larger grids follow the same size-by-size logic.
Square counts form a recognisable sequence.
Pattern recognition converts counting into formula.

puzzles.title: Pyramid Corners
puzzles.question: How many corners does a square-based pyramid have?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The four base corners plus the single apex make five.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. The apex must be counted separately from the base, which is the step people most often forget. Naming each corner one by one prevents the omission.

Pyramids merge two shapes into one solid.
Count base features and apex features separately.
Naming each point guards against double counting.
Compound solids reward methodical enumeration.

puzzles.title: Pyramid Edges
puzzles.question: Counting the line segments where two faces of a square-based pyramid meet, what is the total?

Grouping features by type simplifies counting.
Base and side counts often add cleanly.
Compound solids hide two families of edges.
Structured enumeration prevents errors.

puzzles.title: Prism Faces
puzzles.question: How many faces does a triangular prism have in total?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Two triangular ends plus three rectangular sides make five faces.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Both end triangles count, and the three connecting rectangles complete the total. Forgetting one end is the usual slip.

Prisms pair matching end faces with connecting sides.
Count ends and sides as separate groups.
Matching pairs are easy to overlook.
Naming each face out loud prevents omission.

puzzles.title: Four-Sided Solid
puzzles.question: The simplest closed solid is bounded entirely by identical triangles that meet three at each corner. How many triangles enclose it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Four triangles enclose the simplest possible solid, with three meeting at each corner.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Its name literally records the count, and each vertex is shared by three faces. The smallest solid in existence has no rectangular sides at all.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Names sometimes encode structural facts.
Minimal solids reveal how faces close a volume.
Shared vertices create elegant symmetries.
Simplicity still requires careful counting.

puzzles.title: Cuts Into Eight
puzzles.question: What is the minimum number of straight cuts needed to divide a cube into eight equal smaller cubes?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. One cut through each of the three axes divides the cube into eight pieces.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Each plane cut splits every existing piece, so three perpendicular planes generate two-by-two-by-two pieces. Cutting each small cube individually would require far more.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Each cut multiplies the number of pieces.
Planes cut along axes, not individual pieces.
Doubling twice per axis reaches eight in three steps.

puzzles.title: Ant Across Two
puzzles.question: An ant crawls along a cube's surface from one corner to the diagonally opposite corner by the shortest route. How many faces does the route cross?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Flattening two adjacent faces into one rectangle makes the shortest path a straight line.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. The trick is to unfold the two faces the ant must use, turning a twisting route into a plain diagonal. Any three-face route is longer because it bends around an extra edge.

Unfolding converts curved paths into straight ones.
The shortest route often crosses a shared edge.
Flattening is a standard geometric technique.

puzzles.title: Pentagon Diagonals
puzzles.question: How many diagonals does a regular pentagon have?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Every corner connects to two non-adjacent corners, and the doubled count halves to five.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Each vertex links to two others that are not neighbours, and dividing by two avoids counting each line twice. The star pattern inside a pentagon traces exactly these lines.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Diagonals skip neighbours and connect distant vertices.
Counting both directions forces a division by two.
Overcounting then correcting is a standard technique.
Geometry and sequences interconnect repeatedly.

puzzles.title: Hexagon Diagonals
puzzles.question: In a regular six-sided figure, how many straight lines join pairs of corners that are not already neighbours?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Each of six vertices connects to three non-neighbours, and halving the doubled count gives nine.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. Progressing from five-sided to six-sided shapes shows the pattern growing by one connection per vertex. Counting per vertex, then halving, is the cleanest path.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Connection counts grow with the number of vertices.
Per-vertex counting followed by halving avoids errors.
Simple formulas summarise polygon features.
Sequences connect shapes of growing size.

puzzles.title: Square Symmetry
puzzles.question: How many lines of symmetry does a non-square rectangle have?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The horizontal and vertical midlines each fold the rectangle onto itself.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. The diagonals do not work because unequal sides fail to overlap, leaving only the two midlines. The square, with equal sides, has four.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Symmetry counts depend on proportion, not shape name.
Unequal sides eliminate diagonal folds.
Test each candidate line by folding mentally.
Small property changes alter symmetry deeply.

puzzles.title: Turned-Over Letter
puzzles.question: Turning a lowercase letter b through one hundred and eighty degrees produces which lowercase letter?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The bowl and stem swap sides and directions, turning the b into a q.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is q. A half-turn moves both the stem and the bowl, unlike a mirror flip which would produce a different letter. Tracking both parts of the shape is what makes the rotation reliable.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rotation and reflection produce different results.
Track every part of a shape during transformation.
Letters are shapes with orientation properties.
Half-turns reverse both axes at once.

puzzles.title: Eternal Return
puzzles.question: Nietzsche's thought of eternal recurrence asks whether you could will to live this exact life again and again, forever.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The idea works as a test of affirmation: a life you could will to repeat without end is one you have genuinely embraced.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The question is not whether the cycle is literally real but whether your attitude could bear it. The demon's whisper in The Gay Science turns a cosmological fancy into a personal examination.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Thought experiments can test character, not just facts.
A hypothesis can function as an ethical mirror.
Ask what a claim reveals about your stance.
Repetition magnifies the weight of each choice.

puzzles.title: Amor Fati
puzzles.question: Amor fati is the attitude of loving one's fate and wanting nothing different, whether about the past or the future.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Loving fate means no longer wishing reality were otherwise, a stance Nietzsche treats as the mark of a well-turned soul.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The opposite attitude keeps one foot braced against what already is, and that resistance drains energy better spent on creation. Acceptance here is active, not resigned.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Resistance to the unchangeable spends energy that cannot return.
Acceptance frees attention for what can still be done.
Loving what is differs from merely tolerating it.
An attitude can be chosen and practised.
Share this: name tonight one fixed fact and try wanting it exactly as it is.

puzzles.title: The Demon Test
puzzles.question: Nietzsche presents the demon who announces eternal recurrence purely as a curse, allowing no possibility of a joyful response.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The demon asks whether you would crash down or answer that you are a god, so joy is the whole point of the test.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. The passage explicitly imagines a listener who could reply, 'I am a god, and I never heard anything more divine.' The whisper is a challenge, not a sentence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A thought experiment's drama can conceal its invitation.
Read the possible responses an author leaves open.
Framing shapes whether an idea empowers or crushes.
One passage can carry both threat and opportunity.
Share this: look tonight for the hidden choice inside a discouraging idea.

puzzles.title: Slave Morality
puzzles.question: In Nietzsche's account of the origin of morals, slave morality begins with the strong declaring their own strength to be good.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. That describes master morality; slave morality begins with the powerless branding the strong as evil and their own weakness as good.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. The noble path starts with self-affirmation, while the reactive path starts with resentment projected outward. Nietzsche's point is that the two moralities arise from opposite directions.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Systems of value have origins worth tracing.
Reactive and self-affirming ethics start from different places.
Naming who begins a moral vocabulary reveals its logic.
Origins do not settle current worth, but they inform it.
Share this: trace tonight where one of your own values first came from.

puzzles.title: The Resentful Reframe
puzzles.question: Ressentiment is the resentful reframing by which the powerless declare weakness good and strength evil.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Nietzsche coins the French term for a creative but covert revenge, in which defeat is relabelled as virtue.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The move is not mere complaint but a revaluation that flips the winners' values upside down. Its hallmark is that the reversal is never admitted as revenge.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Values can be reshaped by resentment rather than reason.
A revaluation may hide its motive even from itself.
Ask who benefits from a sudden reversal of worth.
Covert motives deserve as much scrutiny as stated ones.
Share this: notice tonight a value that might be dressed-up grievance.

puzzles.title: God Is Dead
puzzles.question: The announcement 'God is dead' is made by a madman in The Gay Science and lands on listeners who mock him.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The madman cries his news in the marketplace and is met with ridicule, because his audience has not yet felt the consequences.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Nietzsche's point is about timing: the deed is done in culture long before the culture registers the loss. The madman's frustration is that he arrives too early.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Consequences can outrun public awareness of them.
A messenger may be mocked before being understood.
Events and their meanings arrive on different clocks.
Cultural change lags the acts that produce it.
Share this: name tonight a change already underway that most people have not yet felt.

puzzles.title: Perspectives All the Way
puzzles.question: Nietzsche's perspectivism holds that knowing always occurs from some perspective and that there is no view from nowhere.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Every claim is made from a position, and Nietzsche thinks the pretence of a neutral eye is the real illusion.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Multiple perspectives are not simply errors to be cancelled; they are the only access there is. The honest move is to name the vantage, not to fake its absence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
All knowing has a location and an interest.
Pretending to neutrality can hide a stronger bias.
More perspectives widen rather than corrupt a picture.
State your vantage instead of hiding it.
Share this: name aloud tonight the perspective behind one opinion you hold.

puzzles.title: Will to Pleasure
puzzles.question: Nietzsche reduces all human striving to the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. He treats pleasure and pain as side effects, not the aim, and mocks the idea that humans are fundamentally comfort-seekers.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Nietzsche argues people often pursue growth, mastery, or meaning past comfort and even past survival. Reducing motive to pleasure is exactly the flattening he attacks.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Motives are more varied than a single currency.
Side effects can be mistaken for goals.
Assuming one master-drive flattens human behaviour.
Test explanations against lives that seek hardship.
Share this: consider tonight why someone you know chose the harder path.

puzzles.title: The Overman
puzzles.question: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, the overman is an ideal humanity might surpass itself toward rather than a biological race.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The overman is a figure of aspiration — the meaning of the earth that humanity could grow toward — not a genetic category.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Zarathustra speaks of humanity as a rope stretched between beast and overman, an image of self-transcendence. Reading it as a bloodline distorts the metaphor entirely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Metaphors of aspiration are easily literalised and misused.
An ideal points beyond the present without being a species.
Aim higher than present arrangements, not narrower ones.
Ask what a symbol was meant to move you toward.
Share this: name tonight one way you could outgrow your current self.

puzzles.title: The Last Man
puzzles.question: Zarathustra's 'last man' is a contented, comfort-seeking figure who has stopped striving and blinks blankly at great ambition.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The last man invents happiness and asks for no more, a warning portrait of a humanity that has traded longing for safety.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Zarathustra offers the last man as the most contemptible outcome, precisely because nothing is risked or desired. The image is a diagnosis of comfortable stagnation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Comfort can quietly replace aspiration.
Every ideal casts a shadow of its failure mode.
Ask what a culture trades away for stability.
Contentment unexamined may be decline in disguise.
Share this: check tonight whether one comfort has quietly meant one abandonment.

puzzles.title: Endless Overcoming
puzzles.question: For Nietzsche, the will to power shows itself in self-overcoming — the drive to surpass one's present form.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Power for Nietzsche is not domination alone but the expansion of one's own capacities, expressed most purely in self-overcoming.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Growth here is a process with no final rung, because every attainment creates a new horizon. The target is continuous transformation rather than a finished state.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Growth is a process, not a destination.
Each achievement reveals a further reach.
Mastery of self and mastery of others are not the same.
Motion can be the point rather than the prize.
Share this: choose tonight one habit to deliberately surpass next week.

puzzles.title: Become Who You Are
puzzles.question: The maxim 'become who you are' tells you to stop striving and simply accept whatever you already happen to be.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The maxim is a task, not a licence: you are to fashion a unified self from raw material, not passively endorse it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Nietzsche sets a goal of giving style to one's character, which takes discipline and struggle. Acceptance of the given is closer to what he criticises.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Identity can be a project rather than a possession.
Raw tendencies need shaping to become a self.
Giving style to character is active work.
Being and becoming do not exclude each other.
Share this: journal tonight on one trait worth shaping rather than indulging.

puzzles.title: Apollonian and Dionysian
puzzles.question: In The Birth of Tragedy, the Apollonian names dreamlike form and the Dionysian names intoxication and the dissolving of boundaries.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The two impulses stand for disciplined image and ecstatic dissolution, and tragedy fuses them.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Apollo contributes shape, individuation, and dream; Dionysus brings rapture and loss of self. Nietzsche argues the greatest art needs both tensions held together.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Creative work draws on opposed energies.
Structure and ecstasy need not cancel each other.
Naming two poles clarifies a whole spectrum.
Tension frequently produces the finest results.
Share this: identify tonight one project that needs both more order and more abandon.

puzzles.title: Revaluing Values
puzzles.question: Nietzsche's call for a revaluation of all values meant preserving the existing moral rankings and merely adding new ones on top.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Revaluation means reweighing the values themselves, including the ones long assumed to be beyond question.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Adding layers would leave the inherited table intact, which is exactly what Nietzsche refuses. The task is to examine and reconstitute the ranking from the ground up.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Inherited rankings can be questioned rather than patched.
Adding to a system leaves its assumptions untouched.
Re-evaluation requires examining first principles.
Some tasks demand rebuilding, not extending.
Share this: pick tonight one inherited value and ask what justifies its rank.

puzzles.title: Free Spirits
puzzles.question: Nietzsche's free spirits are experimenters with values who can think against the herd.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The free spirit is not merely a nonconformist but one who can hold values provisionally and test them.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Freedom here is a capacity for experiment and endurance of uncertainty, not the mere flouting of rules. Nietzsche prizes the discipline such independence requires.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Independence of mind is a skill, not a mood.
Holding values provisionally allows testing.
Dissent without discipline becomes mere contrarianism.
Courage is often required to think against a crowd.
Share this: examine tonight one majority opinion you have never personally tested.

puzzles.title: Herd Morality
puzzles.question: Nietzsche regarded herd morality as the highest achievement of culture and thought the exceptional should submit to it.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. He saw herd morality as a leveler that protects the many by taming the few, and he resisted its claim to universal authority.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Its utility in maintaining order is precisely what Nietzsche grants and then warns against absolutising. He feared a single morality would flatten the possibility of higher types.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A norm can be useful yet not universally binding.
Weigh what a rule protects against what it suppresses.
Universal systems can erase worthwhile exceptions.
Grant a value's utility before questioning its scope.
Share this: find tonight one rule that serves most people but not everyone.

puzzles.title: The Pity Critic
puzzles.question: Nietzsche criticised pity partly because he thought it can multiply suffering and obscure the sufferer's own strength.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. He worried that pity spreads the feeling of suffering and can treat the sufferer as merely passive.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Nietzsche distinguishes help from the contagion of sorrow, and he wants room for the sufferer's capacity to rise. His target is the sentiment, not the offer of aid.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Compassion can help or can spread distress.
Treating someone as helpless may weaken them.
Distinguish the emotion from the practical response.
Respect the strength even in someone struggling.
Share this: offer tonight practical help rather than only shared sorrow.

puzzles.title: Suffering Required
puzzles.question: For Nietzsche, suffering is merely an obstacle to greatness that the strong should simply avoid.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. He treats discipline and hardship as necessary conditions for depth, not as accidents to be dodged.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Nietzsche praises hardness and the growth that comes through difficulty, seeing ease as a risk to development. What he rejects is useless suffering, not struggle itself.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Difficulty can be formative rather than merely harmful.
Avoiding all discomfort may stunt growth.
Distinguish pointless pain from productive struggle.
Ask what a hardship is teaching before fleeing it.
Share this: reflect tonight on how one past difficulty shaped your strength.

puzzles.title: Dancing Star
puzzles.question: Nietzsche writes that one must still have chaos in oneself to give birth to a dancing star.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The line from Zarathustra links inner disorder to the birth of something radiant, unlike the calm of mere order.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The chaos is raw material, and the star is what disciplined creation makes of it. The image honours tension rather than trying to remove it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Disorder can be the raw material of creation.
Tension channelled well becomes energy.
Seeking calm first may erase the spark.
Transformation begins with unintegrated material.
Share this: note tonight one restless feeling and ask what it could build.

puzzles.title: Unknown to Ourselves
puzzles.question: Beyond Good and Evil opens by suggesting that we knowers are unknown to ourselves.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The book begins by placing the knower, not the world, as the first mystery.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Nietzsche suggests we have never sought ourselves and that our stored knowledge may be the very thing hiding us. Self-knowledge is framed as the harder problem.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The observer is part of what must be understood.
Accumulated knowledge can conceal self-ignorance.
Turn the investigative lens inward sometimes.
Some questions have no neutral examiner.
Share this: ask tonight what you have never seriously examined about yourself.

puzzles.title: Army of Metaphors
puzzles.question: Nietzsche describes truths as a mobile army of metaphors — coins whose images have worn away.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. In the early essay on truth and lies, truths are metaphors that have lost their sensory force and now pass as literal.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The metaphor of worn coins suggests that familiarity turns a created image into a supposed fact. Nietzsche asks us to notice the human act inside what feels given.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Familiarity can make an invention seem like a fact.
Language carries buried metaphors worth recovering.
What feels literal may once have been figurative.
Notice the human act inside the given.
Share this: trace tonight the original image inside one abstract word you use.

puzzles.title: Value Creators
puzzles.question: Nietzsche thought a higher human being creates values rather than merely conforming to inherited ones.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Creation of values is his mark of the higher type, as opposed to the passive inheritance of a ready-made table.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. This does not mean ignoring all norms but rather legislating for oneself with awareness and responsibility. The contrast is between authorship and mere conformity.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Received values can be adopted or authored.
Creation brings responsibility along with freedom.
Awareness of inheritance precedes genuine choice.
Legislating for oneself demands discipline.
Share this: decide tonight one value you will consciously own rather than inherit.

puzzles.title: No to Life
puzzles.question: Nietzsche's philosophy ultimately ends in pessimism, concluding that life is not worth living.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. He attacks pessimism as a symptom while offering a tragic affirmation that says yes to life including its pain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Nietzsche's target is resignation, and his aim is a cheerfulness hard-won through facing the worst. Saying yes despite suffering is the endpoint, not despair.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Acknowledging pain is not the same as surrendering to it.
A position can be bleak in detail yet affirmative overall.
Distinguish diagnosis from prescription.
A hopeful conclusion may pass through a dark middle.
Share this: name tonight one hard truth you can still say yes to.

puzzles.title: Zarathustras Model
puzzles.question: The prophet of Thus Spoke Zarathustra is modelled on Zoroaster, whose moral dualism Nietzsche partly seeks to invert.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Nietzsche chose the name deliberately, casting a founder of moral dualism as the herald of its overcoming.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The choice is ironic and strategic: the original Zarathustra invented the good-versus-evil scheme, so his namesake is fit to be its undoer. The echo is part of the argument.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Names and allusions can carry arguments.
Historical figures can be recast to reverse a legacy.
Irony can advance a philosophical point.
Choose teachers whose limits you also address.
Share this: notice tonight a tradition worth honouring by revising.

puzzles.title: Philosophy as Confession
puzzles.question: Nietzsche held that a philosopher's style and life are inseparable from the philosophy, so thought is an involuntary confession.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. He saw metaphysical claims as symptoms of the thinker's constitution, making philosophy a species of autobiography.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. On this view the philosopher's body, habits, and temperament leave fingerprints on every doctrine. Reading a system therefore means reading its author too.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Thoughts are shaped by the life that produces them.
Biography can illuminate a doctrine.
Style is evidence about the thinker.
No system is entirely impersonal.
Share this: consider tonight what one of your opinions reveals about your life.

puzzles.title: Same Shape Trap
puzzles.question: A chef argues that because a cook must taste food while preparing it, a surgeon should operate on their own body during surgery. What is the central flaw?
choices: A shared surface word masks a relevant difference
The conclusion rests on a tested mechanism
The analogy is strong because both are skilled trades
The reasoning is circular but still convincing
puzzles.correctAnswer: A shared surface word masks a relevant difference
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Tasting is sampling for quality, not operating on yourself — the shared word hides wildly different actions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a shared surface word masks a relevant difference. The two roles share a vocabulary, not a method, and the whole conclusion rides on that coincidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Surface wording can disguise a deep difference in action.
Analogy transfers only when the underlying mechanism matches.
Test whether the shared term means the same thing twice.
Name the relevant feature the comparison ignores.
Share this: find tonight one comparison that survives only on a shared word.

puzzles.title: Old Law New Phone
puzzles.question: A legislator says a rule for organising a bookshelf is so obviously sensible that the same plan must work for a national economy. Why does the comparison fail?
choices: The systems differ in complexity and feedback
The two cases follow exactly equal rules
The argument was never meant as a comparison
puzzles.correctAnswer: The systems differ in complexity and feedback
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A shelf is static and small; an economy is adaptive, with countless actors reacting to every rule.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the systems differ in complexity and feedback. Scale and feedback turn a tidy principle into a warning, because people respond to the plan in ways shelves never do.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scale can change what a rule actually does.
Systems with feedback behave unlike static ones.
Check whether both cases respond to intervention.
Complexity is a relevant difference, not a detail.
Share this: name tonight one plan that needs a different version at a larger scale.

puzzles.title: Both Sides Wrong
puzzles.question: Someone breaks a promise and someone else cheats on a test. Because both acted wrongly, an arguer concludes the two offences are equally serious. What is the mistake?
choices: Equal labels do not make equal magnitude
Broken promises are always the graver act
Cheating is never a matter of wrongdoing
Only one of the two sides was at fault
puzzles.correctAnswer: Equal labels do not make equal magnitude
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Calling both acts wrong says nothing about how wrong each one is — severity is a separate question.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: equal labels do not make equal magnitude. Sharing a category is not sharing a weight, and treating the two as identical erases the very trade-offs morality needs.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sharing a category is not sharing a degree.
Separate whether an act is wrong from how wrong it is.
Magnitude needs its own evidence and scale.
Watch for labels that flatten important differences.
Share this: weigh tonight two wrongs you know without using the same word for both.

puzzles.title: One Shared Feature
puzzles.question: Two plans both use the colour blue, and a manager concludes that whichever plan works better here will also work better abroad. What is the reasoning error?
choices: One shared feature is doing all the work
The plans are identical in every respect
Colour has no bearing on anything at all
Foreign markets should not be compared
puzzles.correctAnswer: One shared feature is doing all the work
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Blue is irrelevant to performance, so the resemblance proves nothing about how either plan behaves.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: one shared feature is doing all the work. An analogy needs relevant overlap, and an irrelevant trait cannot carry a conclusion about outcomes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Analogies need overlap that bears on the conclusion.
Irrelevant similarities are noise, not evidence.
Ask which shared feature could actually cause the result.
Distinguish decorative likeness from causal likeness.
Share this: spot tonight one argument that leans on a purely decorative similarity.

puzzles.title: Irrelevant Disanalogy
puzzles.question: An enthusiast says a bicycle and a corporation are alike because both have spokespeople, so a bike manual should guide a boardroom. Which reply best diagnoses the analogy?
choices: The comparison ignores the relevant domain difference
Corporations and bicycles share no traits at all
Repair manuals are useful in every setting
The analogy is sound but the conclusion is rude
puzzles.correctAnswer: The comparison ignores the relevant domain difference
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The shared word 'spokes' is a pun, and the domains of machines and governance behave nothing alike.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the comparison ignores the relevant domain difference. It is not that nothing is shared, but that what is shared cannot support the transfer of one domain's methods to the other.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some similarities are real yet useless for transfer.
A pun is not a structural resemblance.
Test whether the shared trait could bear the conclusion's weight.
Name the domain difference the analogy skips.
Share this: separate tonight a genuine similarity from a merely verbal one.

puzzles.title: Precedent Transfer
puzzles.question: A lawyer argues that a ruling about noisy neighbours settles a case about industrial pollution because both involve disturbance. When does the precedent actually transfer?
choices: Precedent transfers only when the mechanism transfers
Precedent always transfers whenever judges feel it fits
Noisy neighbours and polluters are legally identical
Precedent never transfers between distinct settings
puzzles.correctAnswer: Precedent transfers only when the mechanism transfers
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A ruling follows the legal reasoning that produced it, so the new case must share the mechanism, not just the mood.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: precedent transfers only when the mechanism transfers. Noise and toxic discharge may both annoy, but the duties, harms, and standards they trigger are entirely different.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rules travel with reasons, not with vibes.
A shared effect does not guarantee a shared mechanism.
Identify the principle a ruling actually rests on.
Match that principle to the new facts before transferring.
Share this: apply tonight one rule by first stating the reason behind it.

puzzles.title: Same Outcome Same Cause
puzzles.question: Two students both fail an exam. One never studied; the other was ill. A teacher blames laziness in both cases. What is the flaw?
choices: Similarity of outcome does not prove similarity of cause
Illness always explains every academic failure
Both students cannot possibly have failed fairly
Laziness is never a real explanation for anyone
puzzles.correctAnswer: Similarity of outcome does not prove similarity of cause
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. One result can have many routes, so matching failures says nothing about matching reasons.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: similarity of outcome does not prove similarity of cause. Diagnosis requires looking at each path, not inferring the cause from the shared finish line.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Results can converge from unrelated causes.
Never infer one cause from one shared outcome.
Investigate each case before generalising.
Treat correlation and causation as distinct tools.
Share this: ask tonight about two similar failures before assuming one reason.

puzzles.title: Vivid Not Evidence
puzzles.question: To prove a diet works, a speaker shows a dramatic before-and-after photo and asks the audience to be convinced. What is wrong with this argument?
choices: The vivid comparison substitutes for evidence
Photographs are always honest and reliable
Dieting has no measurable effects on anyone
The audience failed to appreciate the image
puzzles.correctAnswer: The vivid comparison substitutes for evidence
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A striking image is memorable, but a single anecdote cannot stand in for controlled results.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the vivid comparison substitutes for evidence. Vividness is a feature of presentation, not of proof, and it can make weak claims feel overwhelming.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Vividness persuades without proving.
Memorable examples still need systematic support.
Separate presentation strength from evidential strength.
Ask what data would confirm the claim beyond one case.
Share this: notice tonight where a striking image is doing an argument's work.

puzzles.title: Asymmetric Wrongs
puzzles.question: An arguer says you cannot criticise a small theft by a citizen because a bank also broke the law. What is the defect in this comparison?
choices: Both sides are not symmetric because both erred somewhere
Banks are inherently more honest than citizens
Small thefts are the most serious of all crimes
Citizens are never permitted to commit crimes
puzzles.correctAnswer: Both sides are not symmetric because both erred somewhere
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Two wrongs of different size and character do not cancel out; the reply changes the subject instead of answering.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: both sides are not symmetric because both erred somewhere. The offender's own fault does not erase the citizen's, and treating them as equal is the real distortion.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A counter-wrong does not nullify a first wrong.
Symmetry must be argued, not assumed from shared guilt.
Notice when a reply dodges rather than answers.
Compare like with like in scale and kind.
Share this: watch tonight for a defence that only changes the subject.

puzzles.title: Map Is Not Territory
puzzles.question: A strategist treats a simplified diagram of a city as if every feature of the real streets were captured in it. What mistake is being made?
choices: The map is not the territory it describes
Diagrams are useless for any real planning
Cities never change once they are mapped
The strategist should ignore the real streets
puzzles.correctAnswer: The map is not the territory it describes
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Every model omits something, and mistaking the abridgement for the place itself is what leads plans astray.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the map is not the territory it describes. The diagram is useful precisely because it leaves things out, but usefulness is not completeness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
All models simplify by necessity.
Forgetting the omissions turns a tool into a trap.
Match the model's purpose to your question.
Return to the terrain before betting on the plan.
Share this: name tonight one thing a favourite model of yours leaves out.

puzzles.title: Metaphor as Mechanism
puzzles.question: Someone explains memory by saying the brain is a filing cabinet, then concludes memories must be stored in alphabetical order. What error has occurred?
choices: A metaphor is being treated as a mechanism
Filing cabinets are poorly understood devices
Memory research has produced no useful results
The brain contains no physical structures at all
puzzles.correctAnswer: A metaphor is being treated as a mechanism
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The cabinet is a helpful image, but an image has no gears, so its incidental features carry no real predictions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a metaphor is being treated as a mechanism. Pictures aid intuition, yet only an actual mechanism can license claims about how something must work.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Metaphors illuminate without explaining.
Do not infer details from a figure of speech.
Ask what independent process could produce the result.
Keep illustration separate from mechanism.
Share this: catch tonight one metaphor you have started taking literally.

puzzles.title: Question-Begging Analogy
puzzles.question: A speaker claims that since a good team is a family, members owe absolute obedience, because families demand absolute obedience. What is the flaw?
choices: The analogy begs the question it was meant to answer
Teams and families have nothing in common at all
Obedience is always required inside every group
The speaker has proven the conclusion properly
puzzles.correctAnswer: The analogy begs the question it was meant to answer
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The claim to be supported is smuggled into the comparison, so the argument assumes what it set out to show.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy begs the question it was meant to answer. The disputed feature is loaded into the premise, which turns the reasoning into a circle.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Check whether the premise already contains the conclusion.
Analogiests can smuggle in the very point at issue.
A valid argument cannot assume its own result.
Restate the claim without the analogy to test it.
Share this: strip tonight an argument of its metaphor and see what remains.

puzzles.title: Scale Changes Properties
puzzles.question: Because a paper boat floats, a child concludes that a steel ship of the same shape must also float. The reasoning needs which correction?
choices: Scale changes the properties being compared
Steel vessels are simply paper in disguise
Nothing large can ever be made to float
The child's conclusion was fully justified
puzzles.correctAnswer: Scale changes the properties being compared
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The child's conclusion happens to be true, but not for the reason given — material and buoyancy behave differently at scale.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: scale changes the properties being compared. Weight grows with volume while the hull's support grows differently, so an inference from a small model needs more than shape.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Properties can shift as size increases.
Shape alone rarely determines behaviour at scale.
Small models test feasibility, not certainty.
Recheck assumptions whenever magnitude changes.
Share this: notice tonight one thing that behaves differently when made much bigger.

puzzles.title: Fallacy of One Case
puzzles.question: One rainy Monday had low sales, so a manager declares that rain always depresses sales everywhere. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The analogy commits the fallacy of the single case
Rain reliably lowers sales in every market
One Monday cannot be measured at all
Sales data should never be collected
puzzles.correctAnswer: The analogy commits the fallacy of the single case
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A single observation cannot support a universal rule, no matter how tidy it looks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy commits the fallacy of the single case. One rainy Monday might be a coincidence or a local quirk, so generality needs many cases and a comparison group.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A single instance cannot ground a universal rule.
Generality needs many cases and a contrast.
Watch for confident claims built from one observation.
Ask for the base rate before accepting a trend.
Share this: question tonight one sweeping claim that rests on a lone example.

puzzles.title: One Example Rule
puzzles.question: A traveller meets one rude waiter in a city and concludes that everyone there is rude. What is the reasoning error?
choices: One example is stretched into a general rule
Waiters are the best judges of a whole city
Cities can have only one waiter each
puzzles.correctAnswer: One example is stretched into a general rule
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A sample of one says almost nothing about a population, however striking the encounter felt.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: one example is stretched into a general rule. The traveller generalises from an unrepresentative moment, and strong feelings make small samples feel conclusive.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Samples must be large enough to support a claim.
Emotion can disguise a tiny sample as proof.
Ask how representative the example really is.
Withhold general verdicts until the evidence widens.
Share this: catch tonight one broad conclusion drawn from a single person.

puzzles.title: Whatabout Conduct
puzzles.question: Asked about a company's emissions, a spokesperson replies that another firm littered last year, so the question should be dropped. What is this manoeuvre?
choices: Whataboutism compares conduct rather than the argument
The spokesperson answered the question directly
Littering is worse than every other offence
Companies should never be asked about emissions
puzzles.correctAnswer: Whataboutism compares conduct rather than the argument
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The reply shifts attention to a different party instead of addressing the question that was asked.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: whataboutism compares conduct rather than the argument. Even a genuine fault elsewhere is irrelevant to whether this company's emissions are a problem.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Changing the subject is not answering.
Another's conduct cannot settle this question.
Notice when a reply redirects rather than replies.
Return the discussion to the original claim.
Share this: hold tonight one conversation to its original question.

puzzles.title: Smuggled Value
puzzles.question: An article calls one method clean and another dirty before presenting any data, then argues the first is superior. What is the problem?
choices: The comparison smuggles in a value judgment
Data are irrelevant to every comparison
Cleanliness is a measurable physical property
The second method is definitely the better one
puzzles.correctAnswer: The comparison smuggles in a value judgment
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Loading the labels with approval does the arguing before a single fact arrives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the comparison smuggles in a value judgment. Word choice prejudges the question, so the reader is persuaded by framing rather than by evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Labels can carry hidden verdicts.
Choose neutral terms before weighing evidence.
Notice framing that steers conclusions in advance.
Separate description from evaluation.
Share this: rewrite tonight one loaded description in neutral words.

puzzles.title: Natural Is Good
puzzles.question: A label claims a product is superior because its ingredients are natural rather than synthetic. What is the inferential gap?
choices: Natural is not a synonym for good
Labels are legally required to be true
Nature contains nothing dangerous at all
puzzles.correctAnswer: Natural is not a synonym for good
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Origin says nothing about safety or quality — many natural things are deadly and many synthetic ones are beneficial.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: natural is not a synonym for good. The argument slides from a descriptive fact about origin to a value judgment about worth, which needs its own support.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Origin and value are separate questions.
Natural does not imply safe, and synthetic does not imply harmful.
Demand evidence for the leap from source to quality.
Watch for pleasant words doing logical work.
Share this: examine tonight one 'natural' claim and ask what it actually guarantees.

puzzles.title: Trying Same Way
puzzles.question: When a study method failed for one student, a coach says the student simply must try harder and repeat exactly the same routine. What is the flaw?
choices: Trying harder is not the same as trying the same way
Effort is completely irrelevant to all learning
Study methods can never be improved by anyone
The student's failure proves the method works
puzzles.correctAnswer: Trying harder is not the same as trying the same way
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. More effort on a faulty method often deepens the rut, since intensity cannot repair an inappropriate approach.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: trying harder is not the same as trying the same way. Persistence matters, but repeating an unsuitable routine just spends more energy on the same mistake.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Effort and method are different variables.
More intensity on a bad method wastes resources.
Diagnose the approach before demanding more grit.
Change one variable at a time when progress stalls.
Share this: review tonight one struggle where the method, not the effort, needs changing.

puzzles.title: Middle Not True
puzzles.question: Two experts disagree about a medical dose, so a journalist concludes the correct amount is exactly halfway between their numbers. What is the error?
choices: The middle option is not automatically the true one
Experts never disagree about medical doses
Halfway values are always the safest choice
Journalists should not report on medicine
puzzles.correctAnswer: The middle option is not automatically the true one
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Splitting a difference feels fair but has no evidential basis — one expert may simply be mistaken.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the middle option is not automatically the true one. Truth is not a compromise between positions, and averaging them can land on a dose neither side supports.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fairness is not the same as accuracy.
A midpoint between claims is not thereby true.
Weigh the evidence behind each position separately.
Do not let conflict resolution settle empirical questions.
Share this: resist tonight the urge to split a disagreement down the middle.

puzzles.title: Anecdote Not Mechanism
puzzles.question: A supplement seller cites one customer who felt better after taking it as proof that the product works for everyone. What is missing?
choices: An anecdote is not a mechanism
Supplements always work for every person
Feeling better proves a product is effective
puzzles.correctAnswer: An anecdote is not a mechanism
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Feeling better may come from time, expectation, or coincidence, and none of those paths are the product working.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: an anecdote is not a mechanism. A single recovery story cannot show why the outcome occurred or whether the product caused it at all.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Personal stories cannot isolate a cause.
Recovery has many possible explanations besides a product.
Mechanisms require controlled comparison.
Ask what would have happened without the intervention.
Share this: question tonight one testimonial about what actually caused the improvement.

puzzles.title: Irrelevant Domain
puzzles.question: A debater argues that because chess rewards patience, the same patience must win every negotiation. Why is the analogy weak?
choices: The analogy's domain is irrelevant to the claim
Chess and negotiation are the same activity
Patience never helps in any board game
puzzles.correctAnswer: The analogy's domain is irrelevant to the claim
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Patience may help in both, but the claim covers all negotiations, and the chess setting cannot support that scope.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy's domain is irrelevant to the claim. Similar virtues can appear in different activities without one guaranteeing success in the other.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A virtue's value is relative to its setting.
Different activities reward the same trait differently.
Check whether the borrowed domain covers the conclusion.
Test the claim inside the target setting.
Share this: list tonight one skill that helps in one arena but not another.

puzzles.title: Proves Too Much
puzzles.question: A defence of astrology notes that its predictions feel accurate, which would equally justify any fortune-telling system. What is the flaw?
choices: The analogy proves too much to be useful
Fortune-telling systems are all scientifically sound
Feeling accurate is the best test of truth
Astrology has no competitors of any kind
puzzles.correctAnswer: The analogy proves too much to be useful
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A test that passes every system cannot distinguish the good from the worthless, so it supports nothing in particular.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy proves too much to be useful. When the same reasoning would validate any rival, it has no discriminating power and cannot establish the claim.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A test must be able to fail something.
Evidence that fits every outcome distinguishes nothing.
Ask whether a rival could use the same reasoning.
Prefer criteria with discriminating power.
Share this: check tonight whether one of your standards could ever rule anything out.

puzzles.title: The Word Just
puzzles.question: An arguer says a hospital is just a business, therefore it should cut every unprofitable ward. What does the word just conceal?
choices: The word just hides an unsupported equivalence
Profit is the only measure of any value
Wards are never expensive to operate
puzzles.correctAnswer: The word just hides an unsupported equivalence
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. 'Just' asserts that hospitals are nothing more than businesses, which is the very claim that needed proving.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the word just hides an unsupported equivalence. The little word flattens a contested comparison into a premise, smuggling the conclusion into the setup.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Small words can smuggle large claims.
'Just' and 'merely' often assert an unproven reduction.
Notice when equivalence is assumed rather than argued.
Remove the qualifier and test the claim plainly.
Share this: spot tonight one 'just' that quietly assumes the point at issue.

puzzles.title: Kinds Apart
puzzles.question: A reviewer says a hammer is like a lawyer because both handle problems, then argues a hammer should be allowed to advise clients. What is the fundamental error?
choices: The two items belong to different logical categories
Hammers and lawyers are essentially interchangeable
Legal advice is a form of manual labour
The reviewer correctly matched two professions
puzzles.correctAnswer: The two items belong to different logical categories
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A tool and a professional are different kinds of thing, so capacities belonging to one cannot be reassigned to the other.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the two items belong to different logical categories. Comparing across kinds can suggest shared abilities that the categories themselves rule out.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Comparisons must respect what kind of thing each item is.
Capacities do not transfer across category boundaries.
Ask whether the two belong to the same logical type.
Beware analogies that blur object with agent.
Share this: name tonight one comparison that quietly crosses between kinds.

puzzles.title: Cold All Night
puzzles.question: I hum without a song, I am cold without a winter, and I keep your dinner safe until morning. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The kitchen appliance stays cold around the clock and glows softly when its door opens.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is refrigerator. Continuous cold, a hum, and a little interior light all point to the appliance that preserves food, not an oven or a freezer alone.
puzzles.hintText:
I never sleep, and I work hardest in silence.
Open my door and a small light greets you.
Leftovers trust me more than the counter.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Identify an object by the job it performs.
Continuous work often hides in plain sight.
Setting narrows the field quickly.
Test each clue against the candidate.

puzzles.title: Morning Bread Pop
puzzles.question: I wait for bread, then warm it until it launches itself at me. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The toaster takes slices, browns them, and springs them up when done.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is toaster. The leap of the bread and the darkness dial rule out an oven or a microwave.
puzzles.hintText:
Two or four slots are my only rooms.
A dial decides how dark things get.
Breakfast is my whole career.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Functional clues describe what an object does.
Precise verbs narrow a category fast.
Odd details are often the most identifying.
Match every clue, not just the first.

puzzles.title: Floor Swallower
puzzles.question: I eat crumbs, dust, and stray hair, yet I never get full. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The vacuum consumes debris from floors and stores it in a bag or canister.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is vacuum. Rolling motion, a wide noisy mouth, and collected dirt distinguish it from a broom or a mop.
puzzles.hintText:
I roll across the floor on small wheels.
My mouth is wide and noisy.
When I am done, a bag or a bin sits heavier.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cause and function can identify an object.
Notice what a thing takes in and where it goes.
Noise and motion are useful clues.
Reject candidates that match only one hint.

puzzles.title: Handle Left Alone
puzzles.question: Turn me and water obeys; leave me and it waits patiently. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The faucet releases water on demand and is notorious for dripping when worn.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is faucet. Sitting by the basin, controlling temperature, and dripping at night set it apart from a shower head or a pipe.
puzzles.hintText:
I live at the edge of a basin.
Hot or cold depends on which way you move me.
A drip from me at night is a famous annoyance.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Objects are defined by the control they exert.
Small fault symptoms can identify a device.
Location narrows possibilities.
Match the setting as well as the action.

puzzles.title: Daylight Gate
puzzles.question: I hang still, yet I decide whether morning enters your room. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The curtain hangs on a rod and controls how much light and view enter a room.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is curtain. Cloth, pleats, a rod, and control of light fit a window covering, not a door or a wall.
puzzles.hintText:
I am cloth that folds in pleats.
A rod holds me above a window.
Pull me shut and the world disappears.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Objects can be identified by what they block or allow.
Material and mounting are strong clues.
Consider what an object separates.
Use the whole clue set before deciding.

puzzles.title: Silent Number Keeper
puzzles.question: I hold a number you rarely see, and I argue with the weather on your behalf. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The thermostat senses temperature and switches heating or cooling to hold a set point.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is thermostat. It reads temperature and commands the system, unlike a thermometer that only reports.
puzzles.hintText:
I sit on a wall and watch the temperature.
Turn my dial and a furnace or fan responds.
Your comfort is my only concern.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some devices act on information rather than matter.
Distinguish measuring from controlling.
A set point is a goal an object maintains.
Think of what responds when a device changes.

puzzles.title: Button Without a Body
puzzles.question: I have buttons but no body, and I command a box from across the room. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The remote control sends invisible signals to operate a television or similar device.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is remote control. Handheld buttons and an invisible beam distinguish it from a phone or a game controller.
puzzles.hintText:
I run on small batteries and point with light you cannot see.
Lose me and the couch becomes a prison.
My buttons change channels and volumes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
An object can act at a distance.
Invisible signals still count as effects.
Form follows the function of controlling another thing.
Consider what a device is pointed at.

puzzles.title: Tether of Life
puzzles.question: I am limp and useless alone, but connected, I bring something back from the dead. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The charging cable carries power from a source into a battery-powered device.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is charging cable. Only a power lead links a socket to a device and revives it, unlike earphones or a data drive.
puzzles.hintText:
One end plugs into a wall or a port.
The other end fits a small socket.
Without me a device slowly loses its voice.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some objects function only in a connection.
A bridge between two things has a distinct role.
Consider the direction of flow.
Power and information are different loads.

puzzles.title: Private Whisperer
puzzles.question: I speak into ears no one else can hear, and a wire sometimes keeps me on a leash. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! Earphones deliver sound directly to the listener's ears, keeping it private.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is earphones. Paired speakers worn at the ears and the habit of tangling point to personal audio, not a radio or a speaker.
puzzles.hintText:
Two small speakers sit at my ends.
I turn a shared room into a private one.
Tangle me in a pocket and you will regret it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Objects can be defined by their audience.
Private versus shared use is a strong clue.
Small form often signals personal function.
Match every hint before committing.

puzzles.title: Paper Storyteller
puzzles.question: I take silent instructions and cover paper with them. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The printer turns digital instructions into marks on paper.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is printer. Converting data into a warm sheet distinguishes it from a scanner, which works the other way.
puzzles.hintText:
I sit on a desk and tremble as I work.
Ink or powder is my only voice.
Something warm and flat comes out of me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some devices translate between media.
Direction of conversion identifies the machine.
Heat and sound are clues to a working process.
Know what goes in and what comes out.

puzzles.title: Little Metal Bite
puzzles.question: I bite paper and leave two small marks behind. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The stapler drives a metal staple through sheets to bind them.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is stapler. Biting sheets and leaving a bent wire bracket is unique to it, unlike a hole punch or a paperclip.
puzzles.hintText:
I hold a strip of wire inside my jaw.
Press my top and I clinch a small bracket.
Teachers and clerks keep me within reach.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mechanism plus result identifies a tool.
The material consumed is a strong clue.
A small action can have a lasting effect.
Distinguish joining from puncturing.

puzzles.title: Glowing Marker
puzzles.question: I am bright and transparent at once, and I make words shout without changing them. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The highlighter lays a translucent bright band that makes text stand out.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is highlighter. A broad see-through stroke over existing words is its signature, unlike a pen or a crayon.
puzzles.hintText:
I have a wide tip and a cap that snaps.
My colour is loud but my line is see-through.
Students drag me across important sentences.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some tools emphasise rather than replace.
Transparency makes a useful visual clue.
Colour can carry a function.
Think of what remains visible underneath.
Share this: notice tonight how you mark what matters in a text.

puzzles.title: Bent Wire Grip
puzzles.question: I am a single wire folded twice, and I hold pages without leaving a wound. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The paperclip grips sheets by spring tension and can be removed without damage.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is paperclip. Its bent double loop and gentle hold distinguish it from a staple, which pierces the page.
puzzles.hintText:
I slip over a corner and squeeze gently.
Unbend me and I stop being useful.
Offices pour me out by the boxful.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Temporary solutions differ from permanent ones.
Shape can reveal a mechanism.
Reversibility is a design property.
Distinguish holding from fastening.
Share this: find tonight one object you can use and undo cleanly.

puzzles.title: Stretch and Snap
puzzles.question: I am small, dull, and endlessly flexible, and I can snap back from any insult. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The rubber band stretches elastically and returns to shape, holding bundles together.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is rubber band. Elastic springiness and decay in sunlight mark it as rubber, unlike string or tape.
puzzles.hintText:
Stretch me and I store energy.
A bundle of pens and a rolled newspaper both obey me.
I crumble and perish if left in the sun.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Materials have characteristic behaviours.
Elasticity is a property worth naming.
Environmental weakness can be a clue.
Notice what an object does when released.
Share this: spot tonight one object whose power lives in its stretch.

puzzles.title: Unseen Pull
puzzles.question: I reach across a gap and pull metal toward me without a hand. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The magnet exerts an invisible force that attracts iron and some metals across space.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is magnet. Action at a distance through materials is its signature, unlike glue which must touch.
puzzles.hintText:
My power passes through paper and glass.
Two of us can repel as easily as attract.
Doors and notes cling to me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Forces can act without contact.
Invisible influences are still real effects.
Polarity creates attraction and repulsion.
Consider what works through a barrier.

puzzles.title: Popping Field
puzzles.question: I am a sheet of tiny pillows, and people squeeze me just for the sound. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! Bubble wrap cushions fragile items with sealed air pockets that pop under pressure.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is bubble wrap. Rows of air-filled pockets and the irresistible popping distinguish it from foam or paper padding.
puzzles.hintText:
I protect what is fragile inside a box.
Each of my pockets holds a puff of air.
Nobody can resist pressing just one.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Packaging is designed around fragility.
Many small units can cushion a whole.
Sensory appeal can reveal an object's identity.
Think of what protects by absorbing.

puzzles.title: Straight and Numbered
puzzles.question: I am long, straight, and covered in small marks that settle arguments about size. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The ruler provides a straight edge and a marked scale for measuring length.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ruler. A straight edge with numbered units measures length, unlike a tape measure's flexible case or a protractor's arc.
puzzles.hintText:
My edge is true and my numbers march in order.
Some of me fold or roll away.
Builders and students keep me close.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Measurement turns comparison into numbers.
A standard scale lets people agree.
Straightness has uses beyond measuring.
Notice the units an object carries.

puzzles.title: Fast Thumb Helper
puzzles.question: I hold no thoughts, yet I win arithmetic races against almost everyone. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The calculator performs arithmetic instantly from keyed input and shows the result.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is calculator. Digital keys and an instant display separate it from an abacus, which needs a moving hand and beads.
puzzles.hintText:
I am small enough for a pocket or a desk.
My face is covered in digits and signs.
Press me and a screen answers instantly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tools can outsource a mental task.
Speed is a clue to a dedicated device.
Input and output shape an object's form.
Know what a machine replaces.

puzzles.title: Ancient Counting Frame
puzzles.question: I count without electricity, using beads that slide on rods. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The abacus is a manual counting frame whose sliding beads represent numbers.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is abacus. Wooden beads on rods and no power source distinguish it from an electronic calculator.
puzzles.hintText:
I am a frame with parallel wires.
Each row of beads stands for a place value.
Traders used me centuries before screens.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Old tools encode knowledge in their structure.
Place value can be represented physically.
Absence of power is itself a clue.
Think of how a device stores meaning.

puzzles.title: Falling Sands
puzzles.question: I measure time by losing what I hold, and I must be flipped to start again. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The hourglass measures a fixed interval by sand draining from one bulb to the other.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is hourglass. Twin glass chambers and falling sand mark it as a timer, unlike a clock face or a candle.
puzzles.hintText:
I am two glass bulbs joined at the waist.
Sand runs from top to bottom.
I am useless lying on my side.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Time can be measured by a changing quantity.
Physical processes can serve as standards.
Orientation can be essential to function.
Notice what must reset a device.

puzzles.title: Mouth Gardener
puzzles.question: I work in a wet, dark place twice a day, and I leave it cleaner than I found it. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The toothbrush scrubs teeth and gums with bristles during a daily routine.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is toothbrush. Bristles, a handle, and a home by the sink identify it, unlike a comb or a razor.
puzzles.hintText:
I am long and thin with a bristled head.
I live near a tube of paste.
My owner replaces me every few months.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Routines create familiar objects.
Bristles imply scrubbing.
Location and timing narrow the field.
Think of what an object cleans.

puzzles.title: Drain Rescuer
puzzles.question: I press and pull where nobody wants to look, and I restore the flow. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The plunger uses suction to clear a blocked drain or toilet.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is plunger. A rubber cup on a handle and a suction action distinguish it from a brush or a mop.
puzzles.hintText:
I have a rubber cup on a stick.
I work by suction and a firm seal.
Plumbers call on me when water refuses to leave.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Pressure differences can move stubborn things.
Tools are shaped by the problem they solve.
A firm seal enables a force.
Notice what a tool pushes or pulls.

puzzles.title: Wet Floor Dancer
puzzles.question: I glide across a wet floor and leave it cleaner, though I never dance on my own. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The mop absorbs and scrubs liquid from floors with a long handle and strands.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is mop. A handle with wet absorbent strands sets it apart from a broom, which works dry, or a rag used by hand.
puzzles.hintText:
I am a long stick with soft strands at the bottom.
I am soaked in a bucket before I work.
I follow spills and footprints.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Think of what an object absorbs.
Handle length tells you how it is used.
Dry and wet cleaning are different jobs.
Match the tool to the substance.

puzzles.title: Thirsty Square
puzzles.question: I drink a great deal, but only so I can give it all back. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The sponge soaks up liquid in its porous structure and releases it when squeezed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sponge. A soft porous block that absorbs and wrings out is distinct from a cloth or a brush.
puzzles.hintText:
I am soft, full of holes, and often yellow or green.
Squeeze me and water pours out.
I live near a sink and dislike being left damp.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Porosity explains absorbency.
An object can be defined by what it holds temporarily.
Squeezing returns what was taken in.
Notice the texture that enables a function.

puzzles.title: Pocket Sun
puzzles.question: I hold a tiny sun in my hand and point it wherever I choose. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes! The flashlight projects a beam from a battery-powered bulb or LED.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is flashlight. A handheld, battery-lit beam separates it from a lamp or a candle.
puzzles.hintText:
I run on batteries and shine a narrow beam.
Twist or click me to switch on.
I am vital when the power fails.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Portable light changed how people move at night.
A beam is directed, not ambient.
Power source shapes a device's role.
Think of what an object makes possible.

puzzles.title: Inside View
puzzles.question: A team estimates a project will take three months, reasoning only from the plan in front of them. Which forecasting error does this illustrate?
choices: The estimate came from the inside view
The estimate borrowed from finished projects
The estimate used a wide confidence range
The estimate ignored the current details
puzzles.correctAnswer: The estimate came from the inside view
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The team reasoned only from the plan's details rather than comparing with comparable finished work.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the estimate came from the inside view. The outside view would anchor on how long comparable work actually took.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Plans are built from imagined steps.
Imagined steps rarely match lived ones.
Anchor estimates on completed comparable work.

puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 7000. Seven days per week times one thousand weeks gives seven thousand.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7000. Multiplying the weekly unit by the count is the simplest route.

puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 1209600. The daily 86400 seconds doubled gives the fortnight.

Use powers of ten for large totals.

puzzles.question: Reading twenty pages per hour, how many hours are needed to finish a five-hundred-page book?

Chain small rates into large totals.

puzzles.question: Starting with a single sheet, how many times can most people fold it in half before it becomes practically impossible?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 7. Each fold doubles the layers, so thickness explodes and the stack resists further folding.

Repeated doubling grows faster than intuition suggests.

puzzles.question: Sleeping eight hours every night, how many hours of sleep does a person get in one non-leap year?

puzzles.title: Weeks in a Year
puzzles.question: How many whole weeks fit into a non-leap year of 365 days?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 52. Seven times 52 is 364, leaving just one spare day.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 52. Dividing 365 by seven gives 52 with a remainder of one.

Division with remainder clarifies cycles.
A near-miss remainder is worth noticing.
Calendars are arithmetic in disguise.

puzzles.title: Hand Overlaps
puzzles.question: On a twelve-hour clock face, how many times do the hour and minute hands overlap?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 11. The overlap skips once in twelve hours, so the familiar twelve becomes eleven.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 11. The pair meets slightly less than once an hour, so one of the twelve possible points is missed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Continuous motion breaks neat hourly assumptions.
Relative speed, not absolute speed, decides meetings.
Off-by-one surprises are common in counting.

puzzles.title: Pizza Count
puzzles.question: Twelve people each want three slices, and each pizza provides eight slices. How many pizzas must be ordered?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. Thirty-six slices are needed, and four pizzas give only thirty-two, so you round up.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Division leaves a remainder, and food cannot be served in fractions of a pizza.

Round up when the supply comes in whole units.
Compute the total demand first.
Remainders matter in real logistics.

puzzles.title: Decade of Books
puzzles.question: Reading twelve books a year, how many books does a person finish in ten years?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 120. Multiplying the yearly rate by ten years is the whole calculation.

Multiply rates by the number of periods.

puzzles.question: A tap drips once every second. How many drips fall in one hour?

puzzles.lessonContent:
Testing discomfort builds tolerance.
Wanting less increases freedom.
Choose mild challenges, not self-punishment.
Notice that comfort is optional.
Share this: deliberately skip one small comfort today.

puzzles.title: View From Above
puzzles.question: The Stoic exercise of imagining your life from a great height is meant to give what?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Zooming out restores proportion and shrinks the apparent size of troubles.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is perspective. Seeing your concerns against the whole reduces their grip without dismissing them.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scale changes the feeling of a problem.
Zoom out to restore proportion.
Context reduces the power of a moment.
Return to your own size deliberately.
Share this: imagine tonight your day from far above, then continue it.

puzzles.title: Only True Good
puzzles.question: For the Stoics, what alone is genuinely good, independent of circumstance?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Virtue is the only unconditional good, since it cannot be taken away by fortune.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is virtue. Health, wealth, and reputation are preferred but not necessary for living well.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Distinguish unconditional goods from preferred ones.
Fortune cannot remove good character.
Rank values by dependability.
Invest in what cannot be confiscated.
Share this: name tonight one good no one can take from you.

puzzles.title: Only True Evil
puzzles.question: The Stoics held that only one condition corrupts a person no matter the circumstance. What is it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Vice, the corruption of character, is the only unconditional evil.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is vice. Pain and loss are unwelcome but not evils in the moral sense the Stoics mean.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Harm to character outweighs harm to comfort.
Rank misfortunes by what they damage.
Guard integrity above advantage.
Judge events by their effect on character.
Share this: weigh tonight one choice by its effect on your character.

puzzles.title: Only Now
puzzles.question: What do the Stoics advise regarding the past and the future?
