puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Knowing the original problem and builder clarifies whether the practice still serves a need.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ask who built this and why. Understanding the origin turns a mystery into a decision about present relevance.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Origins explain present form.
Understand the problem before judging the answer.
Designers faced constraints you may share.
History informs current choices.
Share this: learn the origin of one practice in your life.

puzzles.title: Bad Rules
puzzles.question: A rule is genuinely flawed yet persists. What might still be true of it?
choices: Even bad rules can do useful work
Bad rules help no one ever
puzzles.correctAnswer: Even bad rules can do useful work
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. An imperfect rule may yet provide stability or coordination worth preserving in a replacement.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is even bad rules can do useful work. Reform should carry over the function, not just remove the fault.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Faults and functions can coexist.
Reform should keep what works.
Total removal may lose hidden benefits.
Replace rather than merely delete.
Share this: identify a useful function inside one flawed rule.

puzzles.title: Preserve Function
puzzles.question: You replace an old rule with a better one. What should the new rule aim to keep?
choices: Reform should add as much as possible
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The point is to fix the flaw while retaining the job the old rule was doing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is reform should preserve function. Skipping this step repeats the original error in reverse.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Change should keep the good.
Identify the function before replacing it.
Reform is surgery, not demolition.
Check that the new version still works.
Share this: state the function a change must preserve.

puzzles.title: Invisible Reasons
puzzles.question: Why is it hard to judge whether an old arrangement should stay or go?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The original rationale may never have been documented and the context is long gone.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is historical reasons are often invisible. Missing records force careful inference rather than assumption.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reasons may never have been recorded.
Context disappears before explanations do.
Infer purpose from effects.
Ask people who remember.
Share this: recover the reason behind one undocumented practice.

puzzles.title: Reversible Steps
puzzles.question: When uncertain about a change, what property makes it safer to attempt?
choices: Reversibility is a virtue in reform
puzzles.correctAnswer: Reversibility is a virtue in reform
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A step you can undo allows learning without locking in the consequences.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is reversibility is a virtue in reform. Keeping options open reduces the cost of being wrong.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Undoable decisions are cheaper to try.
Reversibility limits downside risk.
Keep exits open under uncertainty.
Prefer steps you can retract.
Share this: design one change so it can be undone.

puzzles.title: Nash Basics
puzzles.question: A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies in which no player can improve by changing only their own move.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Each player's choice is the best response to the others', so no one gains from a solo change.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The definition concerns unilateral deviation — everyone is doing the best they can given what the others are doing.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stability means no profitable solo change.
Best responses hold each choice in place.
Equilibrium is about mutual consistency.
Check each player one at a time.
Share this: ask whether any party could improve by acting alone.

puzzles.title: Group Optimum
puzzles.question: If a set of strategies is a Nash equilibrium, it must also give every player the best outcome the group could achieve.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Stable arrangements can be collectively poor, as the prisoner's dilemma famously shows.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. No player can improve alone, yet all might improve together — that gap is the heart of the dilemma.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stable and optimal are different tests.
Joint improvement can be possible at equilibrium.
Efficiency requires cooperation, not just stability.
Ask whether everyone could gain together.
Share this: find one stable arrangement that everyone dislikes.

puzzles.title: Prisoners Choice
puzzles.question: The prisoner's dilemma shows that individually rational choices can leave everyone worse off than if they had cooperated.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Each player's safest individual move leads to a jointly inferior result.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Rationality at the individual level does not guarantee a good outcome for the pair, which is the paradox.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Individual and collective incentives can conflict.
Good personal choices may produce poor shared outcomes.
Structure, not character, drives the result.
Look for ways to change the incentives.
Share this: name one situation where acting safely hurts everyone.

puzzles.title: Mutual Cooperation
puzzles.question: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, mutual cooperation is the Nash equilibrium.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Mutual defection is the equilibrium; each player is tempted to defect whatever the other does.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Cooperation would be better for both, but each has an incentive to break it alone, so it cannot hold.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Equilibrium follows incentives, not desirability.
Temptation breaks otherwise good arrangements.
The best joint outcome may be unstable.
Check each player's temptation to defect.
Share this: note one agreement vulnerable to a solo defection.

puzzles.title: Dominant Move
puzzles.question: A dominant strategy is one that is best for a player no matter what the other players choose.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. It outperforms the alternatives across every possible response from others.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Dominance is a strong property: the choice does not depend on predicting what others will do.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dominance means never needing to predict.
A robust choice wins across scenarios.
Few real decisions have this property.
Look for options that are safe everywhere.
Share this: find one option that is reasonable whatever happens.

puzzles.title: How Many Equilibria
puzzles.question: Every game has exactly one Nash equilibrium.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Games can have none in pure strategies, one, or several.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Some games have multiple equilibria and others none until mixed strategies are allowed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Multiplicity is common in games.
Some games have no stable pure choice.
Mixed strategies can supply an equilibrium.
Check all the possibilities rather than assuming one.
Share this: consider whether a situation has more than one stable outcome.

puzzles.title: Matching Pennies
puzzles.question: Matching pennies has no Nash equilibrium in pure strategies.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Whatever pair of moves you pick, one player would rather switch, so only a mixed strategy stabilises it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Each pure pair invites a profitable deviation, so the equilibrium exists only in randomised play.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some games reward unpredictability.
Randomising can restore stability.
Pure choices may never settle.
Think in probabilities when no move is safe.
Share this: name one situation where being predictable is a disadvantage.

puzzles.title: Mixed Strategy
puzzles.question: A mixed strategy means choosing randomly among your available moves according to set probabilities.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Players randomise over options, often to keep an opponent from predicting them.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The randomness is deliberate and weighted, not careless, and it can be the stable way to play.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Deliberate randomness can be optimal.
Unpredictability protects against exploitation.
Probabilities can be tuned.
Mix only when pure choices fail.
Share this: notice one contest where surprise has value.

puzzles.title: Dominant Pair
puzzles.question: If both players have a dominant strategy, the resulting combination is the unique Nash equilibrium.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. When each picks their best-everywhere option, no one can gain by switching alone.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Mutual dominance pins the outcome down uniquely, which is why these games are easy to predict.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dominance simplifies prediction.
When both sides are locked in, the result is clear.
Strong structure reduces uncertainty.
Check dominance before forecasting.
Share this: identify one situation with a forced choice on both sides.

puzzles.title: Efficiency Promise
puzzles.question: A Nash equilibrium always produces an efficient, waste-free outcome.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Equilibria can be stable and still wasteful, as arms races and commons problems show.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Stability says nothing about whether resources are well used; everyone may be stuck in a poor but rational pattern.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stability can coexist with waste.
Rational behaviour may preserve inefficiency.
Efficiency needs its own analysis.
Distinguish a settled outcome from a good one.
Share this: find one stable practice that wastes something.

puzzles.title: Traffic Side
puzzles.question: Choosing which side of the road to drive on is a coordination game with more than one possible equilibrium.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Driving on the left or the right can both be stable, as long as everyone agrees.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Either convention works once adopted, which is why coordination games often have multiple equilibria.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some outcomes need agreement, not correctness.
Either convention can be stable.
The hardest part is choosing together.
Standardisation creates value on its own.
Share this: name one convention whose value lies only in everyone sharing it.

puzzles.title: Focal Point
puzzles.question: A focal point is an obvious option that helps players coordinate without communicating.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Shared expectations can settle an ambiguous coordination problem on one choice.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Prominence does the work: people converge on the option that stands out to everyone at once.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shared expectation can replace communication.
Prominence guides coordination.
Culture shapes what counts as obvious.
Look for the salient option.
Share this: pick where to meet a friend without discussing it.

puzzles.title: Repeated Game
puzzles.question: In a prisoner's dilemma played repeatedly, cooperation can be sustained as an equilibrium.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. When the game repeats, future consequences can make cooperation the better long-run choice.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The shadow of the future changes incentives, so reciprocity can hold where a single round would collapse.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Repetition changes incentives.
Future consequences discipline present temptation.
Trust can build through reciprocity.
The shadow of the future matters.
Share this: notice one relationship sustained by repeated interaction.

puzzles.title: Stag Hunt
puzzles.question: The stag hunt shows that a safe, moderate outcome can be a stable equilibrium even when a better one exists.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Fear of being let down can hold players at a lower but safer payoff.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Both the grand prize and the safe fallback can be equilibria, and risk attitudes decide which one settles.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Risk and reward trade off in games.
Safe fallbacks can trap players.
Trust enables better equilibria.
Ask what would justify the bolder choice.
Share this: weigh one safe option against a better but riskier one.

puzzles.title: Trust Not Required
puzzles.question: For a Nash equilibrium to hold, players must trust one another.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Trust is irrelevant to the definition; stability comes from incentives, not goodwill.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Even suspicious players stay put if switching would cost them, which is what equilibrium requires.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Incentives, not trust, stabilise outcomes.
People can settle while distrusting each other.
Goodwill is a separate question.
Look at payoffs, not intentions.
Share this: find one stable arrangement held by incentives rather than trust.

puzzles.title: Cheap Talk
puzzles.question: Cheap talk is communication that costs nothing and so may not be credible.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Words without a cost or commitment can be ignored, since anyone could say them.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Because talk is free, it carries little information unless backed by something at stake.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Free promises are weak signals.
Costly commitments carry information.
Ask what a speaker risks by talking.
Credibility must be earned or burned.
Share this: distinguish one commitment from mere talk.

puzzles.title: Commons Overuse
puzzles.question: In the tragedy of the commons, shared resources are overused even though everyone would gain from restraint.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Each user captures the full benefit of taking more while sharing the cost of depletion.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Private gain and shared loss push each individual toward overuse, leaving the group worse off.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shared costs and private gains invite overuse.
Individual logic erodes collective goods.
Rules or prices can realign incentives.
Design matters more than goodwill.
Share this: name one shared resource you use and its cost.

puzzles.title: Solve Backward
puzzles.question: Backward induction solves sequential games by reasoning from the final move back to the first.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Starting at the end pins down each earlier choice, because players anticipate what follows.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Working backwards removes options that would not be chosen later, narrowing the path from the start.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sequential games are solved from the end.
Later moves constrain earlier ones.
Anticipation shapes present choices.
Reason backward to find the path.
Share this: plan a multi-step decision starting from its last step.

puzzles.title: Credible Threats
puzzles.question: Subgame perfect equilibrium rules out threats that a player would not actually carry out.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Only promises and threats that are rational to execute survive the analysis.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. A threat you would not follow through on is discounted, so the equilibrium ignores it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Threats must be worth executing.
Talk that would not be carried out is discounted.
Credibility is checked at each decision point.
Test whether you would really follow through.
Share this: examine whether one of your threats is credible.

puzzles.title: Nested Games
puzzles.question: Every Nash equilibrium of a sequential game is also subgame perfect.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Some equilibria rely on non-credible threats and fail the stronger subgame perfect test.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. Subgame perfection is a stricter requirement, so it excludes equilibria that ordinary stability would allow.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some tests are stricter than others.
Stability can rest on empty threats.
Stronger criteria screen them out.
Nested reasoning exposes weaknesses.
Share this: find one plan that survives only through a bluff.

puzzles.title: Tit for Tat
puzzles.question: Tit for tat is a repeated-game strategy that starts by cooperating, then copies the opponent's previous move.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. It rewards cooperation and punishes defection in equal measure, which keeps it simple and effective.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The strategy is nice first, retaliatory when wronged, and forgiving once the other side cooperates again.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reciprocity can sustain cooperation.
Simple rules often outperform complex ones.
Forgiveness prevents endless feuds.
Respond to behaviour, not intentions.
Share this: apply one equal-and-opposite response in a repeating situation.

puzzles.title: Poor But Locked In
puzzles.question: A Nash equilibrium can be inefficient and still remain stable.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. No one can improve alone, which is enough to hold a wasteful arrangement in place.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Stability and efficiency are independent properties, so a poor but locked-in outcome is perfectly possible.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Independent standards can disagree.
Locked-in outcomes may be poor.
Collective improvement needs coordination.
Look for ways to change the whole game.
Share this: identify one stable situation everyone wishes were different.

puzzles.title: No Regret
puzzles.question: At a Nash equilibrium, each player regrets their choice given what the others did.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. By definition no player could have done better by switching alone, so there is no regret in that sense.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is false. A player might wish the whole outcome were different, but given the others' choices their own move was best.
puzzles.lessonContent:
No single change improves your position.
Regret concerns joint alternatives, not solo ones.
Distinguish your choice from the outcome.
Check each move against the others'.
Share this: ask whether you would change your move given the others'.

puzzles.title: Free Rider
puzzles.question: Free riding is an example of a collective action problem.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Benefiting without contributing undermines the group effort that produces the benefit.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. When contributions are voluntary and benefits shared, each individual gains by letting others pay the cost.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shared benefits invite non-contribution.
Voluntary efforts are vulnerable to free riding.
Excludability changes incentives.
Design rules that reward contribution.
Share this: notice one shared effort you benefit from without joining.

puzzles.title: Arms Race
puzzles.question: An arms race can be modelled as a prisoner's dilemma.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Each side arms to avoid falling behind, and both end up worse off than if neither had.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Mutual restraint would be better, but each side fears the other's advantage, producing the same dilemma structure.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Competition can trap both parties.
Fear of falling behind drives escalation.
Mutual restraint needs enforcement.
Look for ways to change the stakes.
Share this: find one escalation that both sides would prefer to stop.

puzzles.title: Carbs per Gram
puzzles.question: Roughly how many Calories does one gram of carbohydrate provide?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 4. Carbohydrate and protein share the same energy density per gram.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Knowing the per-gram values for each macronutrient makes label reading quick.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Each macronutrient has a known energy density.
Per-gram values make label maths fast.
Compare foods by composition, not just weight.
Small densities still add up over a day.
Share this: estimate the energy in one snack from its macronutrients.

puzzles.title: Protein per Gram
puzzles.question: One gram of protein supplies roughly how much energy to the body?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 4. Protein matches carbohydrate in energy density despite its different role.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Protein's main job is building tissue, but its energy content per gram equals carbohydrate's.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Function and energy density are separate facts.
Two nutrients can share a density but differ in role.
Compare roles, not just calories.
Use per-gram values for quick estimates.
Share this: compare the roles of two foods with the same energy density.

puzzles.title: Fat per Gram
puzzles.question: How much energy does a single gram of fat supply?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 9. This nutrient carries more than twice the energy of carbohydrate or protein per gram.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. Its high density explains why small amounts contribute large shares of a meal's energy.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Energy density varies widely between nutrients.
High density means small portions matter.
Read composition, not just portion size.
Compare densities before judging a food.
Share this: check the density of one food you eat daily.

puzzles.title: Alcohol per Gram
puzzles.question: Pure alcohol supplies roughly how much energy per gram?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 7. Alcohol sits between carbohydrate and fat in energy density.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7. Its energy is easy to overlook because drinks are not always thought of as food.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Not all energy sources appear on a plate.
Drinks can carry substantial energy.
Check what is easy to overlook.
Density tells you how much a small amount adds.
Share this: estimate the energy in one drink you might overlook.

puzzles.title: Kilogram of Fat
puzzles.question: Roughly how many Calories must be removed to lose one kilogram of body fat tissue?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 7700. Fat tissue is not pure energy, so the figure is lower than the raw density suggests.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7700. Tissue contains water and other material, so the energy cost per kilogram is not simply nine times a thousand.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Body tissue is a mixture, not a pure fuel.
Real-world figures differ from raw density.
Spread large deficits over time.
Check assumptions behind a rule of thumb.
Share this: plan one realistic weekly deficit instead of a crash.

puzzles.title: Mile of Running
puzzles.question: Roughly how many Calories does an average adult burn running one mile?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 100. The cost scales with body weight and distance more than with speed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 100. Distance and weight dominate, which is why fast and slow runners over the same mile differ little.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Energy cost tracks distance and mass.
Speed changes time, not the total much.
Estimate exercise cost from distance.
Compare effort with the food it offsets.
Share this: estimate the energy of one walk or run you take.

puzzles.title: Thirty Percent Fat
puzzles.question: On a 2000-Calorie daily diet, how many Calories come from fat at thirty percent?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 600. Thirty percent of two thousand is six hundred Calories.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 600. Multiplying the total by the fraction gives the share quickly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Percentages convert to amounts easily.
Know the total before taking a share.
Fractions and percentages are interchangeable.
Check the share against portion sizes.
Share this: compute one percentage of your daily energy target.

puzzles.title: Energy Currency
puzzles.question: What molecule do cells use as their immediate energy currency?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Cells spend this molecule to power almost every process.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ATP. It is the rechargeable unit cells exchange for work of all kinds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cells need a spendable form of energy.
One molecule serves as the common currency.
Energy is stored and released in small packets.
Biological systems reuse a standard unit.
Share this: think of one daily system that runs on a common unit.

puzzles.title: Cellular Burning
puzzles.question: What is the process called by which cells release energy from glucose using oxygen?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Cells combine glucose with oxygen to release usable energy, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is cellular respiration. It is a slow, controlled release rather than a flame, which is why it powers life without burning tissue.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Energy release can be controlled, not explosive.
Oxygen enables a more complete breakdown.
Waste products must be expelled.
Chemistry inside cells mirrors combustion safely.
Share this: notice one process that releases energy slowly and safely.

puzzles.title: Long Slow Effort
puzzles.question: What kind of exercise relies on oxygen over sustained periods, such as jogging or cycling?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Sustained effort that uses oxygen steadily builds endurance.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is aerobic exercise. Because oxygen is available throughout, this work can continue for a long time.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fuelling method shapes endurance.
With oxygen, effort can be steady and long.
Without it, bursts are short.
Match the activity to the energy system.
Share this: pick one long, steady activity for this week.

puzzles.title: Short Hard Effort
puzzles.question: What kind of exercise is intense and brief, working faster than oxygen can be supplied?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Very intense effort outstrips oxygen supply and can only be sustained briefly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is anaerobic exercise. Its intensity is its limit, since the body cannot keep it up for long.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Intensity and duration trade against each other.
Some efforts outrun oxygen delivery.
Bursts give way to recovery.
Choose the mode that fits your goal.
Share this: try one short, intense burst followed by rest.

puzzles.title: Stored Muscle Fuel
puzzles.question: What form of stored carbohydrate do muscles and the liver keep for quick energy?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. This branched storage form of glucose can be broken down quickly when demand rises.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is glycogen. It is the body's fast-access reserve, unlike fat which releases energy more slowly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Storage forms enable quick access.
Different reserves serve different speeds.
Bodies stockpile for predictable demand.
Refuel before and after hard effort.
Share this: plan one meal around an upcoming demanding activity.

puzzles.title: Burning Muscles
puzzles.question: What substance builds up and causes the burning feeling during very hard exercise?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Intense effort produces this byproduct faster than it can be cleared, contributing to the burn.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is lactic acid. It accumulates during hard work and dissipates with rest and oxygen.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Byproducts signal the limits of a process.
Hard effort outpaces clearing mechanisms.
Recovery restores balance.
Sensations are information about metabolism.
Share this: notice how one intense effort eases with rest.

puzzles.title: Label Unit
puzzles.question: Food labels use a 'Calorie' that is technically what larger unit?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The dietary unit equals a thousand small calories of physics.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a kilocalorie. The everyday name is a shortened form of the larger scientific unit.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Common names can hide precise units.
A factor of a thousand changes meaning.
Read definitions before comparing numbers.
Units are part of the claim.
Share this: check the exact unit on one label or meter.

puzzles.title: Resting Burn
puzzles.question: What does basal metabolic rate measure, in plain terms?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. It is the energy the body spends at complete rest just to stay alive.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is resting energy use. Even without movement, organs and cells consume energy continuously.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Bodies spend energy even at rest.
Baseline needs anchor daily estimates.
Most energy use happens below awareness.
Distinguish resting cost from activity.
Share this: estimate what your body burns without moving.

puzzles.title: Eating Less
puzzles.question: What is the gradual result of consistently taking in less energy than you use?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. A sustained gap between intake and use draws on stored reserves.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is weight loss. The change follows the arithmetic over time, not any single day.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Direction follows the energy balance.
Single days matter less than trends.
Slow changes are more sustainable.
Track the trend, not the day.
Share this: compare one week's intake and activity honestly.

puzzles.title: Eating More
puzzles.question: What usually follows from a lasting excess of intake over use?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. A sustained surplus is stored, mostly as reserve tissue.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is weight gain. The body banks the difference rather than discarding it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Surplus energy is stored, not discarded.
Storage happens gradually.
Trends beat single meals.
Balance awareness prevents drift.
Share this: notice one small daily surplus that could add up.

puzzles.title: Building Blocks
puzzles.question: What is the main role of protein in the body, beyond providing energy?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Protein supplies the raw material for muscles, organs, and repair.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is building tissue. Its structural role matters more than the energy it can eventually yield.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Nutrients have primary roles.
Structure and fuel are different functions.
Prioritise building over burning.
Match intake to the job a nutrient does.
Share this: name one food that supports repair rather than quick energy.

puzzles.title: Vitamin Carrier
puzzles.question: Which dietary component helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. These vitamins dissolve in fat, so some fat in a meal improves their absorption.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is dietary fat. Without it, fat-soluble vitamins pass through largely unused.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some nutrients need a carrier to absorb.
Solubility determines how vitamins travel.
Balance matters more than elimination.
Pair nutrients for better uptake.
Share this: check whether one healthy food is paired with a helpful carrier.

puzzles.title: Body Heat
puzzles.question: During exercise, most of the energy released from fuel is eventually lost as what?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Only a fraction becomes mechanical work; the rest escapes as warmth.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is heat loss. Inefficiency in energy conversion is why exercise raises body temperature.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Conversion is never perfectly efficient.
Wasted energy usually appears as warmth.
Inefficiency explains physical sensations.
Track where the remainder goes.
Share this: notice one process that warms things as a byproduct.

puzzles.title: Exercise Alone
puzzles.question: Why does exercise by itself often fail to produce large weight changes?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. A typical session burns far less than most people assume compared with daily intake.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is small energy cost. Exercise brings many benefits, but its direct energy use is modest relative to eating.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Effort and energy cost are not identical.
Perceived exertion can overstate expenditure.
Combine activity with intake changes.
Measure rather than assume.
Share this: compare one workout's cost with one snack's energy.

puzzles.title: Stored Surplus
puzzles.question: In what form does the body mainly store long-term surplus energy?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Fat is the body's dense, long-term energy reserve, packed efficiently for storage.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is body fat. It holds far more energy per gram than the short-term reserves used during exercise.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Long-term storage favours dense forms.
Different reserves serve different durations.
Storage efficiency matters for survival.
Balance intake with use over time.
Share this: name one long-term reserve you maintain.

puzzles.title: Lab Measurement
puzzles.question: What laboratory technique measures a food's energy content by burning it completely?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The sample is combusted in a sealed vessel and the released heat is measured.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is bomb calorimetry. It captures all the energy a food contains, which is more than the body can extract.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Measurement methods shape reported values.
Complete combustion overstates usable energy.
Distinguish what a food holds from what is absorbed.
Question how a number was obtained.
Share this: ask how one nutritional figure was actually measured.

puzzles.title: Richest Fuel
puzzles.question: Which macronutrient supplies the most energy per gram?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. At about nine Calories per gram it exceeds both carbohydrate and protein.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is fat. Its density is why even small amounts of rich foods carry substantial energy.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Energy density differs by nutrient.
Dense sources need smaller portions.
Composition matters as much as quantity.
Compare per-gram values before judging.
Share this: compare the density of two foods you often eat.

puzzles.title: Fibre per Gram
puzzles.question: How much energy does a gram of dietary fibre actually deliver?
puzzles.correctExplanation: About 2. Fibre resists full digestion, so it yields far less energy than other carbohydrates.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Because it is not fully broken down, its contribution is small and often counted separately.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Not everything eaten is absorbed.
Digestibility changes energy yield.
Count resistant components differently.
Expect lower values from fibre-rich foods.
Share this: note one food whose energy is only partly available.

puzzles.title: Some Versus All
puzzles.question: A claim says some students passed. A listener concludes that some students failed. What is the error?
choices: The claim says nothing at all
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. 'Some passed' leaves open the possibility that every last one passed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is some does not mean all. The word some guarantees at least one, not that any were left out.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Quantifiers carry exact logical force.
Some guarantees at least one, nothing more.
Do not read an exclusion into a partial claim.
Check what a statement actually rules out.
Share this: restate one everyday claim in strict logical terms.

puzzles.title: Existence Question
puzzles.question: A rule says all trespassers will be prosecuted. Does the rule have to be triggered at least once?
choices: All requires at least one case
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A universal rule can stand even if no case ever satisfies its condition.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is all does not imply existence. The statement constrains members of a set without asserting that the set is non-empty.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Universals constrain without guaranteeing cases.
Rules can be true yet never triggered.
Separate the condition from its instances.
Ask what a statement asserts exists.
Share this: find one rule that has never needed to apply.

puzzles.title: Middle Term
puzzles.question: Two premises in a syllogism never share a common term. What must be added for a valid conclusion?
choices: The middle term must be linked
puzzles.correctAnswer: The middle term must be linked
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A shared middle term is what connects the subject of one premise to the predicate of the other.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the middle term must be linked. Without that bridge, two true premises cannot yield a conclusion about a third thing.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Syllogisms rely on a connecting term.
No shared term means no reliable link.
Structure decides whether a conclusion follows.
Look for the bridge between premises.
Share this: identify the connecting term in one argument you use.

puzzles.title: Overlapping Circles
puzzles.question: In a Venn diagram, two circles overlap. What does the shared region represent?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Anything inside both circles belongs to each of the two groups at once.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is overlapping circles show shared members. The overlap is the intersection, the things both sets contain.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Diagrams make set relations visible.
Overlap marks shared membership.
Draw before arguing about groups.
Pictures expose hidden assumptions.
Share this: sketch two overlapping groups to test a claim.

puzzles.title: No Shared Members
puzzles.question: Two categories have no members in common at all. What are they called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Disjoint groups never overlap, so nothing can belong to both.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is disjoint sets share no members. Their circles on a diagram do not touch, which is a strong logical constraint.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some groups exclude each other entirely.
Naming the relation clarifies reasoning.
Exclusion can be tested case by case.
Draw the boundary before arguing.
Share this: find two categories that cannot both apply.

puzzles.title: Nested Sets
puzzles.question: Every member of one group is also a member of a larger group. How is the smaller group described?
choices: A subset lies entirely within another
puzzles.correctAnswer: A subset lies entirely within another
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A subset sits wholly inside a larger set without anything outside it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a subset lies entirely within another. Confusing subset with superset reverses the direction of containment.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Containment has a direction.
Subset and superset are not interchangeable.
State which is inside which.
Test membership to confirm the relation.
Share this: name one group that fits entirely inside another.

puzzles.title: Outside the Set
puzzles.question: What is the set of everything not included in a given group called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The complement contains every element outside the original set, relative to a universe.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is complement means everything outside. It depends on what universe of things you are considering, so context matters.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Negation has a scope.
The outside depends on the universe chosen.
Define the frame before using complements.
Ambiguity hides in unstated universes.
Share this: state the frame for one claim about what is outside.

puzzles.title: Negating All
puzzles.question: What is the correct negation of the statement 'all birds fly'?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. One counterexample suffices, so the negation is that at least one bird does not fly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is negating all gives some not. 'No birds fly' is far too strong and does not follow from a single exception.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Negation uses the minimum counterexample.
One exception refutes a universal.
Do not overshoot in the opposite direction.
Test a negation against a single case.
Share this: negate one sweeping claim with the weakest counterexample.

puzzles.title: Negating Some
puzzles.question: What is the correct negation of 'some people are left-handed'?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. To deny that at least one exists, you must claim there are none at all.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is negating some gives none. The opposite of 'at least one' is 'not even one', not merely 'not all'.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Existence claims negate to absence.
At least one opposes none at all.
Match the strength of the denial.
Avoid confusing contrary and contradictory.
Share this: write the exact denial of one existence claim.

puzzles.title: Combined Groups
puzzles.question: What operation collects every element that belongs to either of two groups, including the overlap?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The union gathers all members of both, counting the shared region only once.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is union combines both groups. Intersection is the opposite move, keeping only what both share.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Union gathers, intersection narrows.
Two operations mirror and and or.
Name the operation before computing.
Overlap is counted once in a union.
Share this: decide whether a question calls for combining or narrowing.

puzzles.title: Common Members
puzzles.question: What operation keeps only the elements shared by two groups?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The intersection is exactly the overlap between the two sets.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is intersection contains common members. It answers which things satisfy both conditions at once.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Intersection answers both-at-once questions.
It can be empty when groups are disjoint.
Narrowing reveals precise categories.
Check the overlap before concluding.
Share this: find what two of your commitments have in common.

puzzles.title: Universal Affirmative
puzzles.question: How is the proposition 'all S are P' classified in traditional logic?
choices: The universal affirmative states all S are P
The particular negative denies some S
The universal negative denies all S
The particular affirmative notes some S
puzzles.correctAnswer: The universal affirmative states all S are P
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. It is universal in quantity and affirmative in quality, embracing the whole subject class.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the universal affirmative states all S are P. Its quantity is universal and its quality affirmative.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Propositions have quantity and quality.
Universal covers all; particular covers some.
Affirmative joins; negative separates.
Classify before reasoning.
Share this: classify one claim by its quantity and quality.

puzzles.title: Particular Negative
puzzles.question: Which description fits the statement 'some S are not P'?
choices: The particular negative states some S are not P
The universal negative denies all S
The universal affirmative includes all S
The particular affirmative notes some S
puzzles.correctAnswer: The particular negative states some S are not P
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. It is particular in quantity, since it concerns some, and negative in quality.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the particular negative states some S are not P. The word some fixes the quantity while not fixes the quality.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Small words set logical classification.
Some marks particular scope.
Not marks negative quality.
Classify precisely before arguing.
Share this: rewrite one sentence into formal logical form.

puzzles.title: Shared Term Rule
puzzles.question: Two premises about entirely unrelated subjects cannot yield a conclusion about them. What is missing?
choices: A valid syllogism needs a shared term
A valid syllogism needs longer premises
A valid syllogism needs a negative
A valid syllogism needs three subjects
puzzles.correctAnswer: A valid syllogism needs a shared term
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The shared term is the bridge that lets a third claim follow.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a valid syllogism needs a shared term. Without a common term, the premises float free of each other.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Bridges connect premises.
No common term means no link.
Structure, not truth, drives validity.
Find the term the premises share.
Share this: check the bridge in one argument you hear today.

puzzles.title: Double Negative
puzzles.question: What is wrong with a syllogism whose two premises are both negative?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Two exclusions cancel into no connection, so no affirmative link survives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is two negatives cannot conclude positively. Since both premises deny, nothing is joined to support a positive claim.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Two denials leave nothing connected.
Validity depends on the form.
Check whether premises build a link.
Rewrite negatives to see the gap.
Share this: spot one argument that only states what is not.

puzzles.title: Middle Undistributed
puzzles.question: A syllogism's shared term is never applied to all its members. Which fallacy results?
choices: An undistributed middle is a fallacy
A distributed middle is a fallacy
puzzles.correctAnswer: An undistributed middle is a fallacy
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. If the bridge term never covers its whole class, the link can slip past the intended overlap.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an undistributed middle is a fallacy. The premises may be true while the connection between them is accidental.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shared terms must cover their range.
Partial links can mislead.
True premises do not save a broken form.
Check how much of the middle is used.
Share this: test whether a shared term is used fully.

puzzles.title: Illicit Terms
puzzles.question: A conclusion claims more about a term than the premises support. What is the violation?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A valid conclusion cannot assert something the premises never established about a term.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an illicit term breaks validity. The conclusion overreaches what the premises licensed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Conclusions cannot exceed their premises.
Every term must be earned.
Check scope before accepting a result.
Spot overreach by comparing claims.
Share this: find one conclusion that says more than its evidence.

puzzles.title: Quantity and Quality
puzzles.question: What two features together define the type of a categorical proposition?
choices: Quantity and quality define a proposition
Length and clarity define a proposition
Speaker and audience define a proposition
Tense and mood define a proposition
puzzles.correctAnswer: Quantity and quality define a proposition
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Whether it concerns all or some, and whether it affirms or denies, fixes its logical type.

Two axes classify categorical claims.

Quality: affirm or deny.

puzzles.title: Diagram Test

One valid arrangement is not enough.
A diagram can show what must follow.

puzzles.title: Chain of Alls
puzzles.question: If all A are B and all B are C, what follows about A and C?

puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Universal inclusion chains, so every A is also a C.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is chained universal statements transfer. Inclusion is transitive when the middle term is distributed throughout.

Chains require full coverage at each step.
Direction matters: the reverse does not follow.
Follow the links from start to finish.

puzzles.title: One Way Some
puzzles.question: From 'some A are B', what can you correctly conclude about B?

Converse inferences are risky.
Particular statements reverse only weakly.
Do not upgrade some into all.
State exactly what an overlap licenses.

puzzles.title: Enough Condition
puzzles.question: What is a condition that is enough on its own to bring about an outcome?
choices: A sufficient condition guarantees the outcome

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a sufficient condition guarantees the outcome. It may not be the only route, but it is always enough.

Conditions differ in strength.

puzzles.title: Required Condition
puzzles.question: What is a condition that must hold for an outcome, though it may not be enough alone?
choices: A necessary condition is required but not enough

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a necessary condition is required but not enough. Confusing it with sufficiency leads to the converse error.

Necessary means cannot do without.
It need not guarantee the result.
Separate requirement from guarantee.
Test by removing the condition.

puzzles.title: Denied Antecedent
puzzles.question: From 'if it rains, the ground is wet' someone concludes that because it did not rain, the ground is dry. What fallacy is this?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The ground could be wet for many other reasons, so the absence of rain proves nothing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is denying the antecedent is invalid. Other causes can produce the same outcome, so the denial does not follow.

One cause is not the only cause.
Absence of a trigger does not remove the effect.
Conditionals license only some inferences.
List rival causes before concluding.

puzzles.title: Affirming the Consequent
puzzles.question: Given that rain makes the ground wet, what is wrong with arguing that a wet ground proves it rained?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Other causes could wet the ground, so the effect does not prove that particular cause.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is affirming the consequent is invalid. The valid move is to deny the consequent, not to affirm it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Effects can have several causes.
Inferring one cause from an effect is unsafe.
The valid conditional move denies the consequent.
Look for other explanations first.

puzzles.title: Nine Coins Heavy
puzzles.question: You have nine identical coins and one is slightly heavier. Using a balance scale, what is the fewest weighings that guarantee finding it?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. A balance has three outcomes, so two weighings can distinguish among nine possibilities.

A balance yields three outcomes per use.
Each weighing can shrink options to a third.

Plan the split before weighing.

puzzles.title: Twenty Seven Coins
puzzles.question: Among twenty-seven coins, one is heavier. What is the minimum number of balance weighings needed to identify it for certain?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Three weighings can separate twenty-seven possibilities because three cubed is twenty-seven.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Dividing the set into thirds each time matches the three outcomes of the balance.

Capacity grows as three to the power of trials.
Three weighings handle up to twenty-seven.
Split into thirds at each step.
Match method to the tool's outcomes.

puzzles.title: Three Coins Heavy
puzzles.question: With three coins and one known to be heavier, how many balance weighings are needed at minimum?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. If one side drops, that coin is heavier; if they balance, the third is the culprit.

A single comparison can split three ways.
Balance, left-heavy, and right-heavy cover all cases.
Design the weighing to use every outcome.
Efficiency comes from full use of information.

puzzles.title: Twelve Unknown Coins
puzzles.question: Among twelve coins one is counterfeit and may be heavier or lighter. What is the fewest balance weighings that guarantee identifying it and its direction?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Twelve coins times two possible directions gives twenty-four cases, just within the twenty-seven that three weighings reach.

Unknown direction doubles the possibilities.
Keep within the tool's capacity.
Design each weighing to split the cases evenly.

puzzles.title: Four Coins Heavy

Overlooked failures hurt most.
Rare does not mean harmless.
Prepare a response before you need it.
Attend to the neglected case.

puzzles.title: Check Separately
puzzles.question: A buyer checks a claim with a second source that has no relationship to the first. Why?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is verify claims independently. Corroboration from a linked source is not real corroboration at all.

Linked sources share the same errors.
Independence gives real confirmation.

Test claims at the origin.

puzzles.title: Rules Can Bend

Assume rules are always followed in spirit

People optimise for the letter.
Wording creates loopholes.
Anticipate literal compliance.
Test a rule against its own purpose.

puzzles.title: Competence Assumed
puzzles.question: A strategist plans on the assumption that the opponent will act well, not badly. Why?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is assume competence in your opponent. Preparing for a capable rival produces a plan that holds even when they play well.

Do not rely on others' mistakes.
Assume a capable opponent.
Robust plans survive good play.
Prepare for the strong case.

puzzles.title: Review Beats Consensus
puzzles.question: A team invites harsh critique before a launch rather than seeking quick agreement. What does this improve?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is adversarial review beats optimistic consensus. Harmony feels good but it does not find the flaws that matter.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Harmony can hide flaws.
Invite critique before the launch.
Reward the person who finds the problem.
Make dissent safe and early.

puzzles.title: Between Two
puzzles.question: Three people stand in a row with A left of B and B left of C. How many people stand between A and C?

Order constraints fix a single arrangement.

Middle positions follow from endpoints.

puzzles.title: After Ann
puzzles.question: Ann finishes ahead of Ben, and Ben ahead of Cal. How many runners finish after Ann?

Transitive order chains settle ranks.

puzzles.title: Shortest of Three
puzzles.question: A is taller than B, and B is taller than C. Who is the shortest?

Transitive relations give a full ranking.
Follow the chain to its end.
One direction fixes the other.
Check the whole order for consistency.

puzzles.title: First and Last
puzzles.question: Four friends line up with D first and A last. How many people stand between them?

Endpoints reduce the count to inspect.
Subtract fixed positions from the total.
Picture the line before answering.

puzzles.title: All Labels Wrong
puzzles.question: Three boxes are labelled apples, oranges, and mixed, and every label is wrong. What is the fewest boxes you must open to fix all the labels?

Wrong information constrains strongly.
One clue can fix the whole system.
Choose the box with the most implications.
Use elimination, not guessing.

puzzles.title: Middle of Five
puzzles.question: Five houses stand in a row, numbered from one end. Which position is the middle house?

Middle positions follow from odd counts.

Adjacency shifts a position by one.

puzzles.title: Furthest South
puzzles.question: Town X is north of town Y, and town Y is north of town Z. Which town lies furthest south?

Direction words create an order.

One relation implies its reverse.

puzzles.title: Two Seat Swap
puzzles.question: Four people sit in fixed seats, and two of them swap places. How many people end up in a different seat?

Track each element's position.

Moves and changes are not the same count.

puzzles.title: One Trip
puzzles.question: Three switches outside a room control three bulbs inside, and you may enter only once. What is the fewest trips into the room needed to match every switch?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Using an extra property beyond on and off lets every switch be identified in one entry.

Add a property to gain information.
Heat, sound, and time can carry signals.
One visit can suffice with clever use of state.
Think beyond binary states.

puzzles.title: One Question
puzzles.question: Two guards stand at two doors, one always truthful and one always lying, and you may ask a single question. How many questions do you need to find the safe door?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Asking one guard what the other would say and then taking the opposite door settles it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. A question that routes through both guards cancels the lie and exposes the truth.

Design questions to cancel deception.
Route through both sources at once.
One well-built question beats many.
Think about how lies compose.

puzzles.title: Testing a Rule
puzzles.question: A rule claims every card with a vowel on one side has an even number on the other. Which cards must you turn over to test it?

Test a rule by seeking its violation.

puzzles.title: Middle of Seven

Balance equal numbers on both sides.
Compute the centre directly.
