puzzles.lessonContent:
Some things need effort; others need space.
Forcing deepens resistance.
Discern the difference.
Allow what you cannot steer.
Share this: stop controlling one thing that does not need it.

puzzles.title: Never the Same
puzzles.question: Which metaphor compares a life to a river that is never the same twice?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The image captures continuity and change at once, since the river is one yet always new.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the river of change. Identity and flux can coexist, as with a stream that is both itself and different.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Continuity and change can coexist.
Images communicate abstract ideas.
Use metaphor to see, then look past it.
Hold both sameness and flux.
Share this: notice one thing that is continuous and changing at once.

puzzles.title: Upside of Flux
puzzles.question: What positive opportunity does impermanence offer for difficult states?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Because all things change, even hard states are not final, which is a reason for hope.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the gift of impermanence. The very fact that things change means suffering also has an end.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Change works in both directions.
Painful states are not permanent either.
Hope follows from flux.
Remember transience in hard moments.
Share this: recall one difficulty that eventually changed.

puzzles.title: Flowing Awareness
puzzles.question: What does the teaching of change imply about the self or personality?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. If all conditioned things change, the self is better seen as an ongoing process than a fixed thing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the self is a process. This need not mean there is no person, only that the person is not a frozen object.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Persons can be processes, not objects.
Change applies inward as well as outward.
Reject frozen pictures of identity.
Notice how you differ from your past self.
Share this: name one way your sense of self has shifted over time.

puzzles.title: Rigid Shell
puzzles.question: What is the outer, rigid layer of the Earth that is broken into moving plates called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. This cool, brittle shell rides on a hotter, slowly deforming layer beneath it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the lithosphere. It includes the crust and the uppermost rigid mantle, unlike the softer layer below.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Layers can be defined by rigidity, not just depth.
Brittle shells can fracture and move.
Identify the layer by behaviour.
Distinguish similar-sounding geospheres.
Share this: name one material whose behaviour depends on temperature.

puzzles.title: Soft Layer Below
puzzles.question: On what layer do tectonic plates effectively glide?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. This hotter, weaker layer deforms slowly and allows the rigid plates above to move.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the asthenosphere. Its ductile behaviour provides the lubrication plates need to shift.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Movement needs a deforming substrate.
Softer layers enable rigid slabs to slide.
Temperature controls mechanical behaviour.
Match a motion to its mechanism.
Share this: find one system that moves because something beneath it yields.

puzzles.title: Pulling Apart
puzzles.question: What kind of boundary forms where two plates move away from each other?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Spreading plates create new crust along ridges as material rises to fill the gap.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a divergent boundary. Moving apart allows magma to rise and solidify into fresh crust.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Boundary types follow plate motion.
Moving apart creates new material.
Rising material fills the opening.
Classify by relative movement.
Share this: name one process where separation creates something new.

puzzles.title: Pushing Together
puzzles.question: What is created where an ocean plate meets a continental plate and sinks beneath it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The denser ocean plate descends, producing deep trenches and chains of volcanoes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a subduction zone. Sinking crust melts at depth and fuels the volcanism above it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Density decides which plate sinks.
Sinking crust drives melting and volcanism.
Trenches mark the descent.
Connect motion to surface features.
Share this: name one place where something denser sinks beneath something lighter.

puzzles.title: Side by Side
puzzles.question: What is a boundary where two plates slide past each other horizontally called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Here crust is neither created nor destroyed; the plates simply grind past one another.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a transform boundary. Sliding motion builds stress that releases as earthquakes rather than as new crust or volcanoes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some boundaries neither build nor destroy.
Horizontal motion stores stress.
Stress release appears as shaking.
Classify by the kind of motion.
Share this: name one system that stores energy by sliding rather than colliding.

puzzles.title: New Sea Floor
puzzles.question: What process creates new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Magma rises at the ridge, solidifies, and pushes older crust outward on both sides.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is seafloor spreading. The pattern of magnetic stripes records this steady outward growth.
puzzles.lessonContent:
New material forms where plates separate.
Outward growth pushes older parts away.
Symmetry around a ridge reveals the process.
Use patterns as evidence of motion.
Share this: notice one record that preserves a repeated process.

puzzles.title: Single Landmass
puzzles.question: What is the name of the ancient supercontinent that later broke apart?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Matching coastlines, fossils, and rocks across oceans record its break-up.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Pangaea. The matching evidence on separate continents is what first suggested the land had once been joined.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Present features can preserve past connections.
Matching evidence across gaps signals former unity.
Reconstruct history from scattered clues.
Weigh multiple lines of evidence.
Share this: find one sign that two separate things were once joined.

puzzles.title: Fossil Match
puzzles.question: Why do identical fossils appear on continents now separated by an ocean?
choices: The ocean was once dry land
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Distributed species could not cross wide oceans, so the land must have been connected when they lived.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the continents were once joined. Matching fossils across wide water is strong evidence of former proximity.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Distribution puzzles imply past connections.
Organisms that cannot cross water suggest a land bridge.
Combine geology with biology.
Use inexplicable facts as clues.
Share this: find one fact best explained by a past connection.

puzzles.title: Driving Motion
puzzles.question: What mainly drives the movement of tectonic plates?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Heat from the interior sets up slow circulation that carries plates along with it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is convection in the mantle. Rising hot rock and sinking cool rock transfer heat and momentum to the plates above.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Heat differences drive circulation.
Moving fluids can carry solid cargo.
Slow motions can still be powerful.
Connect a driver to the motion it causes.
Share this: name one system powered by a temperature difference.

puzzles.title: Rocks Break
puzzles.question: What causes most earthquakes at plate boundaries?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Stress builds where rock is stuck, then releases suddenly when it breaks and slides.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sudden slip along a fault. The stored elastic energy radiates as seismic waves when the rock finally moves.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stress accumulates at locked boundaries.
Sudden release radiates energy.
Stored strain explains sudden events.
Link a slow build-up to a fast release.
Share this: name one event caused by stored pressure releasing.

puzzles.title: Underground Origin
puzzles.question: What is the point inside the Earth where an earthquake begins called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The focus lies at depth, while the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the focus. Confusing it with the surface point reverses the relationship between depth and the map location.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Interior origins project to surface points.
Distinguish depth from map location.
Define terms precisely.
Relate an object to its projection.
Share this: distinguish the source of an event from where it is felt.

puzzles.title: Surface Point
puzzles.question: What is the point on the surface directly above an earthquake's origin called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. It marks where the released energy is usually felt most strongly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the epicentre. It sits on the surface, directly above the deeper point where the rupture occurred.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Surface projections name a separate point.
Locate both origin and projection.
Map coordinates need a reference.
Relate depth to surface location.
Share this: mark where one deep event would be felt at the surface.

puzzles.title: Two Wave Types
puzzles.question: Which seismic waves arrive first at a distant station?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. These compressional waves travel fastest, so they are recorded before the others.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is primary waves. Their speed advantage is why the arrival order of wave types reveals distance to the origin.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Speed differences create arrival order.
Timing reveals distance.
Use sequence as a measuring tool.
Fast signals arrive before slow ones.
Share this: use an arrival delay to estimate one distance.

puzzles.title: Seismic Strength
puzzles.question: What does earthquake magnitude measure?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Magnitude is a single figure for the source, while damage varies with distance and local conditions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is energy released at the source. Confusing it with local damage mixes a source property with a site effect.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Source and site effects differ.
One number may describe the origin only.
Damage depends on more than strength.
Separate cause from local impact.
Share this: distinguish the strength of an event from its local effects.

puzzles.title: Tidal Wave
puzzles.question: What usually generates a tsunami?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Sudden vertical movement of the seabed pushes the whole water column, sending long waves across the ocean.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is displacement of the seafloor. The wave travels through the full depth of water, which is why it crosses oceans with little loss.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Large water waves need a large sudden push.
Deep disturbance carries energy far.
Distinguish wind waves from displaced-water waves.
Connect cause to scale.
Share this: name one hazard caused by a sudden vertical shift.

puzzles.title: Where Plates Sink
puzzles.question: What deep feature typically marks a subduction zone?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The descending plate bends the seafloor down, producing the deepest parts of the oceans.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an ocean trench. The bend at the point of descent creates a long, narrow depression.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sinking creates a deep low.
Map features reveal underlying motion.
Connect a landform to a process.
Read topography as evidence.
Share this: link one deep feature to the process that shaped it.

puzzles.title: Underwater Chain
puzzles.question: What long feature forms where plates pull apart on the ocean floor?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Rising magma builds a long elevated chain along the spreading boundary.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a mid-ocean ridge. New crust added at the boundary creates a raised ridge that runs for thousands of kilometres.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Spreading raises new terrain.
Growth leaves a raised seam.
Long features follow long boundaries.
Connect creation to topography.
Share this: find one feature created by material being added.

puzzles.title: Magnetic Record
puzzles.question: What do the alternating magnetic stripes on the seafloor record?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. New crust locks in the field direction at the time it forms, creating a striped record as the field flips.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is reversals of Earth's magnetic field. The symmetrical pattern on both sides of a ridge also confirms spreading.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some materials record conditions when they form.
Symmetry reveals a shared origin.
Natural archives preserve history.
Read patterns as timelines.
Share this: name one natural record that stores past conditions.

puzzles.title: Hawaii Chain
puzzles.question: A chain of volcanoes forms over a stationary deep source as a plate moves. What is that source called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The plate drifts over a fixed plume, leaving a line of progressively older volcanoes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a hot spot. The age progression along the chain shows the plate moving over a stationary source.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fixed sources leave trails.
Age order along a chain reveals motion.
Relative motion explains patterns.
Use progressions as evidence.
Share this: find one trail that records something moving over time.

puzzles.title: Building Mountains
puzzles.question: What process raises large mountain ranges such as the Himalayas?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Where two continental plates meet, the crust crumples and thickens into high ranges.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is collision of continental plates. Neither plate sinks easily, so the crust piles up instead.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Collisions can lift terrain.
When neither side sinks, material piles up.
Connect compression to elevation.
Read ranges as evidence of collision.
Share this: name one feature formed by two things pressing together.

puzzles.title: Splitting a Continent
puzzles.question: What feature forms where a continent is being pulled apart?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Stretching thins the crust and drops a long block down between faults.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a rift valley. Tension pulls the crust apart, and the sunken block becomes a long depression.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tension thins and drops crust.
Stretching creates lows, not highs.
Match a landform to its stress.
Contrast compression and tension.
Share this: contrast one feature made by pulling with one made by pushing.

puzzles.title: Ring of Fire
puzzles.question: Why are so many volcanoes and earthquakes concentrated around the Pacific Rim?
choices: It is closest to the equator
The core is nearer the surface
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Several plates converge along the rim, producing frequent subduction, volcanism, and quakes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is many plate boundaries meet there. Concentration of hazards follows concentration of plate interaction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Hazards cluster where boundaries cluster.
Geography follows underlying structure.
Look for a common cause behind a pattern.
Map activity to detect structure.
Share this: find one pattern explained by a shared underlying cause.

puzzles.title: Slow Drift
puzzles.question: How fast do tectonic plates typically move each year?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The pace matches the growth of a fingernail, yet over millions of years it reshapes the planet.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a few centimetres. Imperceptibly slow motion accumulates into enormous change across geological time.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Slow rates can produce large results.
Time multiplies small movements.
Do not equate slow with insignificant.
Estimate cumulative effects.
Share this: compute one huge result from a tiny annual change.

puzzles.title: Inner Heat
puzzles.question: Where does most of the Earth's internal heat come from today?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The decay of long-lived isotopes, plus leftover primordial heat, keeps the interior hot.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is radioactive decay in the interior. This steady source drives the convection that moves plates.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Internal heat needs an internal source.
Decay supplies energy over long timescales.
Trace a driver to its origin.
Distinguish surface from interior energy.
Share this: identify the source behind one long-lived process.

puzzles.title: Ocean Age
puzzles.question: Why is oceanic crust generally much younger than continental crust?
choices: It is continually recycled by subduction
It was formed more recently by humans
It is made of younger minerals only
puzzles.correctAnswer: It is continually recycled by subduction
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Dense ocean plates sink back into the mantle, so little ancient seafloor survives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it is continually recycled by subduction. Continental crust is buoyant enough to avoid the same fate.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Recycling resets ages.
What can be destroyed does not accumulate.
Buoyancy decides what survives.
Explain age distributions by process.
Share this: name one material whose age reflects constant renewal.

puzzles.title: From the Antecedent
puzzles.question: Given that if it rains the streets flood, and that it is raining, what follows validly?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Affirming the antecedent lets the consequent be concluded with certainty.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Q follows by modus ponens. This is the most basic valid conditional inference.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One conditional plus its antecedent yields the consequent.
This form is always valid.
Recognise it quickly.
Apply it without hesitation.
Share this: spot one everyday inference of this form.

puzzles.title: From the Denial
puzzles.question: Suppose that whenever the sprinkler runs the grass becomes damp, and tonight the grass stayed dry. What follows validly?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Denying the consequent forces the denial of the antecedent, so the sprinkler cannot have run.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the sprinkler did not run. This is the second valid conditional inference, and it is equally reliable.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One conditional plus the negation of its consequent yields the negation of its antecedent.
This form is also always valid.
Pair it with the affirm-the-antecedent form.
Recognise both patterns.
Share this: find one conclusion you drew by ruling out an outcome.

puzzles.title: Given the Consequent
puzzles.question: A kettle whistles whenever it boils, and right now it is whistling. What follows about whether it boiled?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The whistle could have other causes, so hearing it does not prove the kettle boiled.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no conclusion about the boiling. Treating the consequent as proof of the antecedent is the fallacy of affirming it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
An effect can have many possible causes.
The consequent does not imply the antecedent.
Resist the pull of this fallacy.
List rival causes before concluding.
Share this: name an alternative cause for one effect you assume.

puzzles.title: Given No Rain
puzzles.question: If a number is divisible by four then it is even. This number is not divisible by four. What follows about whether it is even?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Six is even but not divisible by four, so the absence of one condition proves nothing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the converse does not follow. Concluding the opposite of the consequent from the opposite of the antecedent is invalid.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Denying a cause does not remove an effect.
Rival causes break the inference.
Avoid reversing the conditional.
Check whether other paths exist.
Share this: find one outcome with more than one route.

puzzles.title: Reversing Terms
puzzles.question: What is the converse of the statement that if it rains the streets flood?
choices: If the streets flood it rained
If it does not rain the streets do not flood
If the streets do not flood it did not rain
puzzles.correctAnswer: If the streets flood it rained
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The converse swaps the two halves, which is why it does not always preserve truth.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is if the streets flood it rained. Swapping antecedent and consequent creates a new claim that needs its own proof.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The converse swaps the parts.
A swap does not preserve truth.
Learn the named transformations.
Distinguish converse from contrapositive.
Share this: write the converse of one rule you follow and test it.

puzzles.title: Negating Both
puzzles.question: What is the inverse of the rule that if the alarm sounds the doors lock?
choices: If the alarm is silent the doors stay open
If the doors lock the alarm sounded
If the doors are open the alarm was silent
puzzles.correctAnswer: If the alarm is silent the doors stay open
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The inverse negates both halves without swapping them, and it is not logically equivalent to the original.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is if the alarm is silent the doors stay open. Negating both parts changes the claim and usually weakens it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Negation alone creates a new statement.
Inverse and contrapositive differ.
Only one of them preserves truth.
Compare the named forms.
Share this: contrast the inverse and contrapositive of one rule.

puzzles.title: Swapping and Negating
puzzles.question: Which statement is the contrapositive of 'if a plant gets no light it turns pale'?
choices: If a plant is not pale it is getting light
If a plant turns pale it gets no light
If a plant gets light it turns green
puzzles.correctAnswer: If a plant is not pale it is getting light
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Swapping and negating both halves yields a statement equivalent to the original.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is if a plant is not pale it is getting light. This is the one transformation that preserves the original's truth exactly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One transformation preserves equivalence.
Swap and negate both parts.
Use it to rewrite a claim safely.
Know which transformation is valid.
Share this: rewrite one conditional as its contrapositive.

puzzles.title: Equivalent Form
puzzles.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to 'if it rains the streets flood'?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Only the contrapositive has exactly the same truth conditions as the original.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is its contrapositive. The converse and inverse can be false even when the original is true.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Equivalence is a strong relation.
Only one transformation preserves it.
Do not confuse similar rewrites.
Test truth conditions to check.
Share this: verify one rewrite really means the same thing.

puzzles.title: Only If
puzzles.question: What does 'you pass only if you sit the exam' tell you about sitting the exam?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The exam is required, but sitting it does not by itself guarantee a pass.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Q is necessary for P. Only-if introduces a requirement, not a guarantee.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Only-if signals a requirement.
Necessary conditions can be met without success.
Parse wording before reasoning.
Distinguish required from enough.
Share this: find one requirement that is not a guarantee.

puzzles.title: If Clause
puzzles.question: What does 'you pass if you score above ninety' tell you about scoring above ninety?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Passing the threshold is enough for a pass, though other routes might also exist.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Q is sufficient for P. The plain if introduces a guarantee, so meeting it settles the outcome.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A plain if signals a guarantee.
Enough differs from required.
At least one route suffices.
Parse the phrasing carefully.
Share this: name one condition that is enough on its own.

puzzles.title: Both Ways
puzzles.question: What does 'you pass if and only if you score above ninety' add beyond a simple if?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The biconditional binds the two outcomes together in both directions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is both necessary and sufficient. It rules out any other route to the outcome, unlike a one-way condition.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Biconditionals bind both directions.
No alternative route remains.
Recognise the stronger claim.
Use it to simplify reasoning.
Share this: find one situation with a strict either-or rule.

puzzles.title: Hidden Negation
puzzles.question: How is 'unless you hurry, you will be late' best rewritten as a conditional?
choices: If you are not quick then you will be late
If you hurry then you will be late
If you are late then you hurried
puzzles.correctAnswer: If you are not quick then you will be late
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Unless introduces the exception, so its negation becomes the antecedent.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is if you are not quick then you will be late. Reading unless as a plain if changes the meaning entirely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unless hides a negation.
Translate it into a conditional carefully.
Paraphrase before reasoning.
Avoid mistaking exception for condition.
Share this: rewrite one unless sentence as a clear conditional.

puzzles.title: No Rain No Flood
puzzles.question: Someone argues that because the alarm did not sound, the doors cannot be locked, given that the alarm always sounds when they lock. Which error is this?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The doors might be locked by another mechanism, so the silent alarm does not rule out locked doors.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the antecedent is denied wrongly. The error is reasoning from the denial of the antecedent to the denial of the consequent.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One cause is not the only cause.
Absence of a trigger does not remove an effect.
Name the fallacy to avoid it.
List rival causes first.
Share this: catch yourself ruling out one cause for an outcome today.

puzzles.title: Wet Streets Rain
puzzles.question: Someone argues that because the grass is damp, the sprinkler must be running, given that the sprinkler always makes the grass damp. Which error is this?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Rain or dew could have dampened the grass, so the effect does not prove that particular cause.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the consequent is affirmed wrongly. The valid move would be to deny the consequent, not to affirm it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Effects can have several causes.
Inferring one cause from an effect is unsafe.
The valid conditional move denies the consequent.
Look for other explanations.
Share this: find one effect you blamed on a single cause.

puzzles.title: Dry Ground
puzzles.question: A rule says that whenever ice forms the pond freezes over. Tonight the pond is not frozen. What follows validly?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. An unfrozen pond rules out ice having formed, since ice would have frozen it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ice did not form. Denying the consequent validly forces the denial of the antecedent.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Ruling out an outcome rules out its necessary cause.
This is a valid inference.
Contrast it with the invalid opposite.
Use consequences as tests.
Share this: rule out one cause by ruling out its effect.

puzzles.title: All as If
puzzles.question: How is 'all swans are white' best expressed as a conditional?
choices: If something is a swan then it is white
If something is white then it is a swan
If something is not a swan it is not white
puzzles.correctAnswer: If something is a swan then it is white
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Universal statements translate into conditionals running from the subject to the predicate.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is if something is a swan then it is white. Reversing the direction creates the converse, which is a different claim.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Universals become conditionals.
Keep the direction from subject to predicate.
Avoid reversing the terms.
Translate before testing.
Share this: turn one universal claim into a conditional.

puzzles.title: Single Exception
puzzles.question: What would refute the claim that all swans are white?
choices: A case where P is true and Q is false
A case where both are true
A case where both are false
puzzles.correctAnswer: A case where P is true and Q is false
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. One swan that is not white is enough to break a universal claim.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a case where P is true and Q is false. Confirming cases cannot establish a universal the way a single counterexample can refute it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Universals fall to a single counterexample.
Confirmation is weaker than refutation.
Hunt for the exception.
Design tests that could fail.
Share this: name one observation that would disprove a general claim you hold.

puzzles.title: When False
puzzles.question: Under exactly what conditions is a conditional claim false?
choices: P is true and Q is false
P is false and Q is true
Both P and Q are true
Both P and Q are false
puzzles.correctAnswer: P is true and Q is false
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A conditional promises something given its antecedent, and it fails only when the promise is broken.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is P is true and Q is false. Every other combination leaves the conditional intact, which is why its logic surprises people.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A conditional breaks only one way.
When the antecedent holds and the consequent fails.
Other cases leave the promise unbroken.
Learn the truth conditions precisely.
Share this: test one if-then claim against this single failure case.

puzzles.title: Oxygen Needed
puzzles.question: Oxygen is required for a fire to burn, but alone it does not start one. What role does oxygen play?
choices: Oxygen is necessary but not sufficient
Oxygen is sufficient but not necessary
Oxygen is both necessary and sufficient
puzzles.correctAnswer: Oxygen is necessary but not sufficient
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Without it no fire burns, yet fuel and heat are also required.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is oxygen is necessary but not sufficient. Missing its presence guarantees no fire, but its presence does not guarantee one.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Necessary and sufficient come apart.
Required is weaker than enough.
Check both directions of a condition.
Test by adding and removing.
Share this: classify one requirement as necessary, sufficient, or both.

puzzles.title: Guarantee Condition
puzzles.question: What is a condition that always brings about the outcome, though other routes may exist?
choices: A sufficient condition guarantees the result
A necessary condition guarantees the result
puzzles.correctAnswer: A sufficient condition guarantees the result
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Meeting it is always enough, even if it is not the only way to reach the outcome.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a sufficient condition guarantees the result. It can coexist with other sufficient routes without losing its guarantee.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sufficient means always enough.
Other routes may also lead there.
Necessary means required, not enough.
Name the condition's role.
Share this: identify one sufficient route to a goal you want.

puzzles.title: Stronger Claim
puzzles.question: How does 'if and only if' compare with a plain 'if'?
choices: The biconditional is the stronger claim
puzzles.correctAnswer: The biconditional is the stronger claim
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. It adds the reverse direction, excluding any alternative route.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the biconditional is the stronger claim. More is asserted, so more can go wrong when testing it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stronger claims say more.
More content means more to test.
Note where a claim adds a reverse condition.
Compare strength before accepting.

puzzles.title: Basic Valid Form
puzzles.question: How is the inference that affirms the antecedent and concludes the consequent classified?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. This form is valid in every interpretation of the conditional.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is valid by modus ponens. It cannot fail as long as the premise conditional is true.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One conditional form is always valid.
Recognise it by its shape.
Apply it with confidence.
Contrast it with invalid lookalikes.

puzzles.title: Second Valid Form
puzzles.question: A rule says the pond freezes whenever ice forms, and the pond is not frozen. How is the step to 'no ice formed' classified?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. This form is valid, unlike its tempting lookalike that affirms the consequent.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is valid by modus tollens. It is the counterpart to modus ponens and is equally reliable.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Two conditional forms are valid.
One affirms, one denies.
Learn both by their shapes.
Avoid their invalid twins.

puzzles.title: Reversed Fallacy
puzzles.question: What is the fallacy of concluding the antecedent from the consequent called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Treating the consequent as evidence for the antecedent reverses the conditional's direction.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is affirming the consequent. It is the mirror image of denying the antecedent, and both are invalid.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The converse tempts constantly.
Effects do not prove their causes.
Name the fallacy to resist it.
Check the direction of inference.

puzzles.title: Chain Conclusion
puzzles.question: Given that if P then Q, and if Q then R, what follows validly?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Conditionals chain together, carrying the antecedent to the final consequent.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is if P then R. The reverse chain does not follow, since the links are one-directional.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Conditionals can be linked.
Carry the start to the end.
Direction is preserved, not reversed.
Build long chains carefully.

puzzles.title: At Least One
puzzles.question: In a group, 20 people like tea, 15 like coffee, and 10 like both. How many like at least one of the two?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 25. Adding the two groups double-counts the overlap, so subtract it once.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 25. Adding the counts plainly would count the shared people twice.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Overlaps cause double counting.
Add the groups, then subtract the shared part.
Inclusion and exclusion handles overlaps.

puzzles.question: Of those who like tea or coffee, 20 like tea, 15 like coffee, and 10 like both. How many like tea alone?

puzzles.title: Science Alone

puzzles.title: Neither Subject
puzzles.question: In a class of 30 with 18 maths and 20 science students and 12 taking both, how many take neither?

puzzles.question: What is the name of the principle that adds set sizes and subtracts their overlaps to count a union?

puzzles.title: Readers Together
puzzles.question: Of 40 people, 25 read newspaper A, 20 read newspaper B, and 10 read both. How many read at least one?

puzzles.title: Cyclists Only
puzzles.question: A survey finds twenty cyclists, ten of whom also drive. How many cycle without driving?

puzzles.question: If every member of set A is also in set B, how large is the union of A and B?

puzzles.question: Why must the shared members be subtracted when adding the sizes of two overlapping groups?

puzzles.title: Money M
puzzles.question: In the classic puzzle SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, each letter is a distinct digit. Which digit does M stand for?

puzzles.lessonContent:
Notation should avoid ambiguity.
Similar shapes invite misreading.
Design choices reduce errors.
Choose clear symbols.
Share this: notice one symbol that could be misread in your own notes.

puzzles.title: Puzzle Name
puzzles.question: What is the standard name for a letter-arithmetic puzzle where letters stand for digits?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The name covers puzzles where words encode a hidden arithmetic equation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a cryptarithm. The other terms describe letter arrangements, not digit substitutions.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Names organise a family of puzzles.
Learn the term to find resources.
Distinguish similar-sounding forms.
Use precise vocabulary.
Share this: name one puzzle type you enjoy and its defining rule.

puzzles.title: Eleven Letters
puzzles.question: Why can a standard cryptarithm not use eleven distinct letters in base ten?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Ten digits cannot be assigned distinctly to eleven letters.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is not enough digits. The distinctness rule makes eleven letters impossible in base ten.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Resource limits bound assignments.
Count symbols against available values.
Test a scheme against its constraints.
Recognise impossible cases early.
Share this: check whether one substitution scheme is even possible.

puzzles.title: Mauvaise Foi
puzzles.question: In Sartre's philosophy, what does the French term for self-deception about one's own freedom describe?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. It names the flight from freedom by pretending our choices are not ours.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is bad faith. The self-deception hides from the very freedom that defines us.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-deception can be a philosophical stance.
We may deny our own freedom to escape responsibility.
Naming the evasion is the first step past it.
Notice where you claim you had no choice.
Share this: catch one moment today when you said you had no choice.

puzzles.title: Forced Freedom
puzzles.question: What does Sartre mean by saying humans are condemned to be free?
choices: Freedom is a punishment from others
People are never free in practice
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. We did not choose to be free, yet we cannot stop choosing, even by refusing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is freedom cannot be escaped. Even refusing to choose is itself a choice, which is the weight he describes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some conditions arrive without consent.
Even refusal is a decision.
Responsibility follows from unavoidable choice.
Own the choices you would rather deny.
Share this: note one refusal that was itself a decision.

puzzles.title: Existence First
puzzles.question: What does the slogan that existence precedes essence mean for humans?
choices: We are born with a fixed nature
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Unlike a manufactured object, a person first exists and then defines what they are through action.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is we create ourselves through choices. There is no blueprint to fall back on, which is both the freedom and the burden.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some things are made to a plan.
People are not; they become through action.
No fixed nature excuses a choice.
Self-definition is ongoing work.
Share this: name one trait you are actively choosing rather than inheriting.

puzzles.title: The Waiter
puzzles.question: Why does Sartre use a café waiter to illustrate bad faith?
choices: He performs his role as if it fixed him
He refuses to work at all
He has no freedom to choose
puzzles.correctAnswer: He performs his role as if it fixed him
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The waiter plays at being a waiter, treating a role as an inescapable essence rather than a chosen activity.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is he performs his role as if it fixed him. The exaggerated performance reveals the flight from freedom into a persona.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Roles can become hiding places.
Playing a part rigidly may mask a choice.
Distinguish what you do from what you are.
Notice when a role does your deciding.
Share this: observe one role you slip into as an escape.

puzzles.title: Anguish of Choice
puzzles.question: What kind of distress does Sartre associate with recognising our freedom?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Facing that we alone author our choices produces a vertigo of responsibility.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is anxiety about responsibility. It is not fear of harm but the weight of being the source of one's own values.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Freedom carries weight.
Responsibility can feel like vertigo.
Anxiety is a signal of authorship.
Do not let it push you into denial.
Share this: sit with one decision you are avoiding out of its weight.

puzzles.title: No Excuses
puzzles.question: What does Sartre say about blaming one's nature or upbringing for one's actions?
choices: It is a form of bad faith
puzzles.correctAnswer: It is a form of bad faith
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Explaining ourselves away through causes denies the freedom that remains regardless of background.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it is a form of bad faith. Background shapes the situation, yet the response to it is still chosen.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Causes can explain without excusing.
Circumstances set the scene, not the answer.
Watch for explanations that erase agency.
Acknowledge influence without surrendering choice.
Share this: separate one influence on you from the choice you still make.

puzzles.title: Being for Itself
puzzles.question: What does Sartre mean by consciousness being for-itself rather than in-itself?
choices: It is a fixed physical object
It has no existence at all
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Consciousness is not a thing that simply is; it is directed beyond itself and aware of its own awareness.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it is aware and self-transcending. Objects are in themselves, while consciousness always relates to something beyond it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Two modes of being can be distinguished.
Things simply are; awareness relates.
Consciousness is always about something.
Distinguish substance from activity.
Share this: notice how your attention is always directed at something.

puzzles.title: Fixed Facts
puzzles.question: What does Sartre call the facts about our situation that we did not choose?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Birth, body, and past are given facts that limit without determining us.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is facticity. It names what is simply given, as opposed to what we do with it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some givens cannot be chosen.
Limits are real but not total.
Distinguish the given from the response.
Work within facts without surrendering to them.
Share this: list one unchangeable fact and one choice it still leaves open.

puzzles.title: Going Beyond
puzzles.question: What does Sartre call our capacity to surpass the given facts of our situation?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. We can project beyond what is given, which is the active side of freedom.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is transcendence. It is the movement past the fixed toward what we make of it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Facts are not the whole story.
We project beyond the given.
Freedom lies in the surpassing.
Balance limits with possibility.
Share this: name one way you could surpass a limit you currently accept.

puzzles.title: Living Truthfully
puzzles.question: What does Sartre call the attitude that owns one's freedom and responsibility?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Authentic existence acknowledges that one is the author of one's choices.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is authenticity. It is not a permanent state but an ongoing honesty about one's freedom.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Honesty with oneself is a practice.
Own your authorship.
It is a direction, not a finished badge.
Return to it after lapses.
Share this: name one area where you will own your choices this week.

puzzles.title: Life Project
puzzles.question: What does Sartre mean by a fundamental project?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Beneath particular choices lies a basic orientation that gives them shape.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an overarching choice of self. The project unifies many decisions into a coherent direction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Many choices can share a theme.
A unifying direction shapes particular acts.
Review the pattern behind your decisions.
Adjust the project, not just the steps.
Share this: name the direction most of your recent choices point toward.

puzzles.title: Serious World
puzzles.question: What does Sartre criticise in the attitude that treats values as fixed objects in the world?
choices: It hides human authorship of values
It respects other people too much
puzzles.correctAnswer: It hides human authorship of values
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Treating values as given things avoids the burden of having chosen them.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it hides human authorship of values. Projecting our values outward lets us claim they were imposed rather than chosen.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Values can be treated as discovered facts.
That framing hides the choices behind them.
Owning authorship is uncomfortable.
See values as commitments, not objects.
Share this: name one value you hold and the choice that sustains it.

puzzles.title: Determinism Excuse
puzzles.question: Why does Sartre consider a rigid belief in determinism a form of bad faith?
choices: It denies the freedom we experience
puzzles.correctAnswer: It denies the freedom we experience
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Using causality as an excuse pretends that our deliberation makes no difference.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it denies the freedom we experience. The belief conveniently removes responsibility for what we do.
puzzles.lessonContent:
An excuse can take a philosophical form.
Denying choice removes accountability.
Notice when theory serves avoidance.
Hold explanations and agency together.
Share this: find one belief that conveniently excuses a habit.

puzzles.title: The Look
puzzles.question: What happens to a person when they become aware of being looked at by another, in Sartre's account?
choices: They become an object for the other
puzzles.correctAnswer: They become an object for the other
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Being seen turns us into something judged, introducing a tension between subject and object.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is they become an object for the other. The gaze reveals that others define us in ways we cannot control.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Others see us in ways we cannot fully govern.
Being looked at changes self-awareness.
Identity is partly shaped from outside.
Balance inner authorship with outer perception.
Share this: notice how you change when someone is watching.

puzzles.title: Shared Responsibility
puzzles.question: Why does Sartre say that choosing for oneself is also choosing for humanity?
choices: A choice models a universal norm
No one is ever truly free
puzzles.correctAnswer: A choice models a universal norm
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. In choosing, we affirm that this is how one ought to act, which carries weight beyond ourselves.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a choice models a universal norm. Every act tacitly proposes an example, which is why responsibility is so heavy.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Personal choices imply general claims.
Acting suggests what others should do too.
Responsibility extends beyond yourself.
Weigh the example your action sets.
Share this: consider what example one of your habits sets for others.

puzzles.title: The Coward
puzzles.question: How does Sartre treat the person who claims to have been born a coward?
choices: They are not cowardly by nature
puzzles.correctAnswer: They are not cowardly by nature
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. He says people make themselves cowardly through their acts, not by an inborn essence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is they are not cowardly by nature. The claim of a fixed disposition is exactly the bad faith he criticises.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Character is made through action.
Labels of fixed nature excuse inaction.
People can remake what they have become.
See traits as patterns, not essences.
Share this: name one trait you think you cannot change, and test it.

puzzles.title: Paradox of Sincerity
puzzles.question: Why is sincerity alone not sufficient to escape bad faith for Sartre?
choices: It can become a new fixed role
puzzles.correctAnswer: It can become a new fixed role
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Being true to a supposed fixed self can itself be a way of dodging change and responsibility.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it can become a new fixed role. Clinging to a permanent identity can be as evasive as any other form of self-deception.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Even virtues can become escapes.
A fixed self-image can prevent growth.
Watch for identities that block change.
Stay open to revising who you are.
Share this: question one label you use to explain yourself.

puzzles.title: Committed Freedom
puzzles.question: How does Sartre connect freedom with commitment?
choices: Freedom is realised through engaged choice
puzzles.correctAnswer: Freedom is realised through engaged choice
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Freedom is not idle detachment but the act of committing to something in the world.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is freedom is realised through engaged choice. Withdrawing from all commitment would be another evasion of responsibility.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Freedom needs engagement to be real.
Choosing to do nothing is still a choice.
Commitment gives freedom direction.
Avoid the flight into detachment.
Share this: commit to one small thing you have been holding back from.

puzzles.title: Situated Choice
puzzles.question: What does Sartre mean by saying freedom is situated?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. We choose within circumstances we did not pick, so freedom is always concrete rather than abstract.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is choice always occurs within limits. The situation shapes the options without eliminating the act of choosing.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Freedom works through particular conditions.
Constraints shape the options available.
A limited field still requires choosing.
Do not confuse limits with absence of choice.
Share this: name one constraint and the choice it still allows.

puzzles.title: Hell Is Others
puzzles.question: What did Sartre mean by the famous line that hell is other people?
choices: Others fix us in their judgments
puzzles.correctAnswer: Others fix us in their judgments
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The line concerns how the gaze of others can freeze us into identities we did not choose.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is others fix us in their judgments. It is a claim about the power of being seen, not a condemnation of company.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Others can define us against our will.
Judgment fixes what we feel is fluid.
The line is about the gaze, not hatred.
Notice when others' views trap you.
Share this: reflect on one label others place on you.

puzzles.title: Free Refusal
puzzles.question: Could someone escape freedom by refusing to choose at all, according to Sartre?
choices: No, refusing is itself a choice
Yes, if they try hard enough
puzzles.correctAnswer: No, refusing is itself a choice
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Declining to decide is a way of deciding, so freedom cannot be dodged.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no, refusing is itself a choice. Even passivity expresses a stance, which is why responsibility cannot be evaded.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Inaction expresses a stance.
Avoidance is a form of action.
You cannot step outside choosing.
Accept that passivity has consequences.
Share this: notice one non-decision that has already made a choice for you.

puzzles.title: Without a Script
puzzles.question: What does Sartre call the condition of being responsible for everything without having chosen one's existence?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Without pre-given guidance, we are left to create values ourselves, which brings both freedom and forlornness.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is abandonment. It names the vertigo of having no fixed rulebook to lean on.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Absence of guidance is a condition.
Freedom can feel like forlornness.
We must generate values without a script.
Accept the discomfort rather than flee it.
Share this: name one area where you must supply the rule yourself.

puzzles.title: Choosing Self
puzzles.question: What does Sartre say we are continually doing through our choices?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Each decision contributes to the person we are becoming, with no blueprint to follow.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is making ourselves. The self is the sum of choices rather than a pre-existing given.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The self is built through action.
Choices accumulate into character.
No blueprint relieves us of authorship.
Attend to the pattern of your decisions.
Share this: name one small choice that is shaping who you are.

puzzles.title: Roles and Freedom
puzzles.question: How should one hold a social role, on Sartre's view?
choices: As a chosen performance to own
As the whole of one's identity
puzzles.correctAnswer: As a chosen performance to own
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Roles can be played consciously without being mistaken for one's entire essence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is as a chosen performance to own. Treating the role as an unchangeable fate is precisely the bad faith he warns against.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Roles are performances, not essences.
Play them without being swallowed.
Awareness keeps freedom intact.
Separate the part from the person.
Share this: name one role you play and how you might hold it more consciously.

puzzles.title: Responsibility Weight
puzzles.question: Why is authenticity difficult to sustain, according to Sartre?
choices: It means constant awareness of freedom
puzzles.correctAnswer: It means constant awareness of freedom
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Living without the comfort of excuses is demanding, so bad faith is a constant temptation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it means constant awareness of freedom. The difficulty is the ongoing responsibility, not any material condition.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Honesty with oneself takes effort.
Comfortable excuses are tempting.
Authenticity is a continual return.
Expect lapses without abandoning the effort.
Share this: recommit to one honest choice you have been avoiding.

puzzles.title: Straight Path
puzzles.question: How does light travel through a uniform medium such as air?
choices: It does not travel at all
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. This straight-line travel is why shadows and sharp edges form.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is in straight lines. It is why a barrier casts a sharp shadow rather than a blurred pile of light.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Straight paths create sharp shadows.
Obstacles block what travels in lines.
Observe edges to infer path shape.
Simple models explain many effects.
Share this: notice how a sharp shadow reveals the path of light.

puzzles.title: Bouncing Off
puzzles.question: When light reflects off a smooth mirror, how does the outgoing angle compare with the incoming one?
choices: The outgoing angle is always larger
The outgoing angle is always zero
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The outgoing angle is measured from the same normal line and matches the incoming angle.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is they are equal. This predictable rule is what lets mirrors form images we can rely on.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reflection is symmetric about the normal.
Measure angles from the same reference.
Predictable rules allow precise design.
Use the pattern to trace light paths.
Share this: trace how a mirror redirects a torch beam.

puzzles.title: Bending Light
puzzles.question: Why does light bend when it passes from air into water?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A change of speed at the boundary makes the direction shift, which is why a straw looks broken in a glass.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it changes speed. The direction changes only at the boundary, not while travelling within one medium.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Speed changes shift direction.
Bending happens at the boundary.
Everyday illusions follow from simple rules.
Observe carefully, then explain.
Share this: notice how an object looks bent in a full glass of water.

puzzles.title: Bringing Together
puzzles.question: Which lens shape can focus parallel light rays to a point?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Its outward-curving surfaces bend rays inward toward a focus.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a convex lens. The inward-bending shape concentrates light, which is why it magnifies and focuses.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shape determines how light bends.
Curved surfaces gather or spread rays.
Converging and diverging are opposites.
Link geometry to optical effect.
Share this: use a lens to focus sunlight and observe the bright spot.

puzzles.title: Splitting White
puzzles.question: What happens when a narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Different colours bend by different amounts, so the beam fans into a spectrum.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it spreads into colours. White light is a mixture, and the prism separates its components by how much each bends.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mixtures can be separated by a property.
Different components bend differently.
A simple tool reveals hidden structure.
Connect observation to composition.
Share this: look for a rainbow formed by a glass edge or water spray.

puzzles.title: Seeing Colour
puzzles.question: What determines the colour an object appears to have?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. We see the wavelengths a surface sends back to our eyes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the light it reflects. Change the lighting and the apparent colour changes with it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Perceived colour depends on what returns.
Absorbed light is not seen.
Objects do not glow with an inner hue.
Test colour under different lights.
Share this: compare one object's colour indoors and in daylight.

puzzles.title: Dark Surface
puzzles.question: Why does a black surface look black?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Little light returns to the eye, so the surface appears dark.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it absorbs most light. Absorption also explains why dark surfaces warm up faster in sunshine.
puzzles.lessonContent:
What is absorbed cannot be seen.
Darkness follows from strong absorption.
Energy absorbed becomes heat.
Connect appearance to energy.
Share this: compare how two colours warm in the sun.

puzzles.title: Bright Surface
puzzles.question: Why does a white surface look bright in sunlight?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Most wavelengths bounce back, so the surface appears bright and colourless.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it reflects most light. High reflection is also why pale surfaces stay cooler in the sun.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Brightness follows from reflection.
A surface can return almost everything.
Reflected energy does not become heat.
Relate appearance to energy balance.
Share this: notice which surfaces stay cool on a sunny day.

puzzles.title: Coloured Filter
puzzles.question: What does a red filter do to white light passing through it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The filter absorbs other wavelengths and lets red through.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it transmits only red. Stacking filters removes more colours and can leave no light at all.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Filters select by wavelength.
Absorption removes what does not pass.
Combining filters multiplies restrictions.
Predict which colours survive.
Share this: look through coloured materials at a light source.

puzzles.title: Light Primaries
puzzles.question: Which three colours combine additively to make white light?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Screens use these three because mixing them at full strength gives white.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is red, green, and blue. Pigment mixing follows different rules from mixing beams of light.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Light and pigment mix differently.
Additive mixing brightens toward white.
Subtractive mixing darkens toward black.
Do not confuse the two systems.
Share this: examine the tiny dots on a screen with a magnifier.

puzzles.title: All Primaries
puzzles.question: What colour appears when the three additive primaries are mixed at full strength?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Combining red, green, and blue beams recreates the full daylight mix.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is white light. Adding light works opposite to adding pigments, which would darken toward black.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Adding light increases brightness.
The three beams together give white.
Contrast with pigment behaviour.
Choose the system that matches the medium.
Share this: predict the result of overlapping coloured light beams.

puzzles.title: Pigment Mix
puzzles.question: What colour results from mixing all the usual paint pigments together?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Each pigment absorbs more wavelengths, so the mixture darkens and dulls.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a muddy dark shade. Subtractive mixing removes light, which is why pigments darken rather than brighten.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Pigments subtract from the light.
More pigments mean more absorption.
Mixing paints darkens toward neutral.
Contrast with light mixing.
Share this: mix two paint colours and note how the brightness changes.

puzzles.title: Opposite Colour
puzzles.question: Which light colour is complementary to red, producing white when combined?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Cyan is the mixture of the other two primaries, so it completes red to white.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is cyan. Complementary pairs are found by combining the remaining primaries.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Complements complete a mix to white.
Find them from the remaining primaries.
Colour wheels encode these relations.
Use pairs deliberately in design.
Share this: identify the complement of one colour you often use.

puzzles.title: Blue Sky
puzzles.question: Why does the daytime sky appear blue?
choices: The sun emits only blue light
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Tiny air molecules scatter blue light across the sky more than red.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is short wavelengths scatter more. Scattered light reaches your eyes from every direction, making the whole dome look coloured.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Small particles scatter some wavelengths more.
Scattered light arrives from all directions.
Colour can arise from scattering, not only pigment.
Connect physics to a familiar view.
Share this: explain one everyday colour by scattering.

puzzles.title: Red Sunset
puzzles.question: Why do sunsets look red?
choices: The sun cools in the evening
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A longer path through the atmosphere scatters away the blue, leaving reds and oranges.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is light travels further through air. More scattering removes the shorter wavelengths before they reach your eyes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Path length changes what survives.
More travel means more scattering away.
The same cause explains blue days and red evenings.
Track how conditions alter an effect.
Share this: watch a sunset and describe the colour shift.

puzzles.title: Rainbow Maker
puzzles.question: What produces the colours of a rainbow?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Droplets bend and reflect sunlight, spreading it into its component colours.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is refraction inside water droplets. Airborne water acts like countless tiny prisms.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Everyday objects can act as optical tools.
Droplets behave like prisms.
The observer's position matters.
Connect a sighting to its mechanism.
Share this: find how your position changes what you see in a rainbow.

puzzles.title: Mirror Image
puzzles.question: What kind of image does a flat mirror form?
choices: A virtual image behind the mirror
puzzles.correctAnswer: A virtual image behind the mirror
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The light appears to come from behind the glass, so no screen can capture the image.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a virtual image behind the mirror. Real images can be projected, while virtual ones cannot.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Images can be real or virtual.
Virtual images cannot be caught on a screen.
Trace where light appears to come from.
Distinguish appearance from source.
Share this: compare a mirror image with one projected by a lens.

puzzles.title: Spreading Rays
puzzles.question: What does a concave lens do to parallel light rays?
choices: It focuses them to a point
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Its inward-curving shape spreads rays apart, making objects look smaller.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it diverges them. This is the opposite effect to a convex lens, which gathers light together.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Lens shapes have opposite effects.
Converging gathers; diverging spreads.
Choose the lens for the task.
Predict before you test.
Share this: predict the effect of one lens, then check it.

puzzles.title: Magnifying Lens
puzzles.question: Which everyday use relies on a convex lens?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The converging lens makes an object appear larger when held at the right distance.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a magnifying glass. The same shape also concentrates sunlight and is used in cameras and spectacles.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One principle serves many devices.
Spot the shared component across uses.
Link a tool to its optical basis.
Recognise converging lenses in daily life.
Share this: find one more device that uses a converging lens.

puzzles.title: Making Shadows
puzzles.question: Why does an opaque object cast a shadow?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Light travels in straight lines, so an obstacle leaves a dark region behind it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it blocks the light. Transparent objects cast faint shadows because they let much of the light through.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Blocking creates darkness.
Straight paths leave a clear gap.
Transparency affects shadow strength.
Relate shape to the object causing it.
Share this: compare shadows from clear and solid objects.

puzzles.title: Darkest Shadow
puzzles.question: What is the darkest central part of a shadow called?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. This region receives no direct light at all, unlike the surrounding partial shade.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the umbra. The softer outer region, where light is partly blocked, is the penumbra.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shadows have internal structure.
Total and partial blocking differ.
Source size widens the partial region.
Examine edges to see the effect.
Share this: inspect the edge of a shadow cast by a lamp.

puzzles.title: Soft Light
puzzles.question: How does a translucent material affect light passing through it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. It lets light through while diffusing it, so objects behind appear blurred rather than clear.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it scatters some light. Transparent materials transmit clearly, while opaque ones block entirely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Materials vary in how they pass light.
Clear, cloudy, and blocking are three cases.
Diffusion softens what is seen.
Classify by the effect on light.

puzzles.title: Colour Detectors

puzzles.title: Speed of Light

puzzles.title: Why Colour

A physical quantity maps to a perception.

Investment can trap rather than liberate.

puzzles.title: Not the Same Plane

Treat each step on its own merits.

puzzles.question: What principle says decisions should compare only the additional costs and benefits of the next step?

puzzles.title: Forgone Alternative

puzzles.title: Stopping the Bleed

Closure has an emotional price.

puzzles.title: Justifying the Past
puzzles.question: What psychological pressure pushes people to act in ways that justify earlier choices?

puzzles.title: Public Promise
puzzles.question: Why does announcing a commitment publicly make abandoning it harder?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Going back on a stated commitment invites embarrassment, which can outweigh a sensible exit.

Public stakes add pressure.

Allow room to change your mind.

puzzles.title: Valuing What We Own

Ownership changes perceived value.

puzzles.title: Keeping Things As Is
puzzles.question: What bias favours continuing with the current arrangement even when a better one is available?

puzzles.title: Zero Based

Shared decisions can share the blind spot.

puzzles.title: The Thirty-Six Percent
puzzles.question: In 2015 a consortium re-ran 100 prominent psychology studies with larger samples and preregistered analysis plans. About 36% replicated clearly. What is the most reasonable takeaway?
choices: Roughly two-thirds of the original researchers committed outright fraud
Many published findings were weaker or more fragile than they looked
Psychology therefore contains no trustworthy findings at all
The replications failed mainly because their samples were too large
puzzles.correctAnswer: Many published findings were weaker or more fragile than they looked
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. A failed replication usually means the original effect was smaller, noisier, or context-dependent — not that anyone cheated. Most non-replications trace to flexible analysis and small samples.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that many published findings were weaker or more fragile than they looked. Fraud is rare; the bigger culprits are small samples, flexible analyses, and journals preferring splashy positives. One failed replication rarely kills a claim — a pattern of them demotes it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A single replication is a data point; a pattern across labs is the verdict.
Failed replications usually signal inflated effects, not fraud.
Preregistration and larger samples are the standard fixes.

puzzles.title: The Expansive Pose
puzzles.question: A famous study claimed two minutes of expansive posture raised testosterone and risk-taking. Large preregistered replications found no hormonal change and little behavioral effect. What should a careful reader conclude?
choices: Posture research is pseudoscience and all of it should be discarded
Standing tall cures anxiety and every clinic should prescribe it
The hormone mechanism failed, though confident posture can still feel subjectively better
The replications must have coached participants to slouch on purpose
puzzles.correctAnswer: The hormone mechanism failed, though confident posture can still feel subjectively better
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The specific hormonal pathway did not survive retesting, which kills the original claim — but a weaker claim (people report feeling bolder) is a different hypothesis needing its own test.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that the hormone mechanism failed, though confident posture can still feel subjectively better. Killing one mechanism does not prove the opposite extreme, and it does not license a vaguer wellness claim without fresh evidence. Separate the falsified claim from any replacement claim.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Falsifying a mechanism is not the same as proving nothing is happening.
