puzzles.title: The Willpower Battery
puzzles.question: Early studies said self-control runs down like a battery (ego depletion). Later, a 23-lab preregistered replication found essentially zero effect. Which response best fits the evidence?
choices: The depletion model is settled law and the 23 labs conspired
Treat depletion as unproven and look for better-supported models of self-control
Willpower is infinite so effort never impairs later performance
Discard all of psychology because one model stumbled
puzzles.correctAnswer: Treat depletion as unproven and look for better-supported models of self-control
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. A multilab null with high power demotes the model from fact to unproven. Motivation, beliefs, and attention now explain the old results better — science updates instead of mourning.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close, but the answer is to treat depletion as unproven and look for better-supported models of self-control. A big clean null does not prove willpower is limitless either — fatigue is real, but the specific glucose-battery story lost its evidence. Update the model, don't flip to the opposite extreme.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Multilab preregistered nulls are how weak models get retired.
'Unproven' is a verdict too — absence of evidence after strong tests matters.
Old results often get re-explained by motivation and attention effects.
Hold models loosely and mechanisms tightly.
Share this: test your own focus across the day and notice what actually drains it.

puzzles.title: The Slow Prime
puzzles.question: A classic paper said flashing words like 'wrinkled' made students walk slower. Multiple direct replications, some larger than the original, found no such effect. What is the sharpest lesson?
choices: Subliminal influence is impossible under every condition
Priming researchers fabricated all of their data
Even elegant effects need direct replication before they become textbook facts
Walking speed can never be measured reliably in a hallway
puzzles.correctAnswer: Even elegant effects need direct replication before they become textbook facts
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Elegance is not evidence. Direct replications — same recipe, bigger sample — are the admission ticket from 'intriguing result' to 'reliable phenomenon'.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that even elegant effects need direct replication before they become textbook facts. The failure does not prove subliminal influence is impossible everywhere, nor does it prove fraud; it proves one famous demonstration was fragile. Charm at first telling is the weakest form of evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Direct replication means rerunning the same recipe, not a loose remix.
Textbook status should require surviving at least one independent rerun.
Fragility is about the effect size and noise, not the researchers' honesty.
Ask 'was this directly replicated?' before quoting any classic.
Share this: pick a beloved classic study and check its replication record tonight.

puzzles.title: The Pen Smile
puzzles.question: Holding a pen in your teeth (forcing a smile) was said to make cartoons funnier. A 17-lab replication found no effect, though a later meta-analysis found a tiny one. What is the fair summary?
choices: Facial feedback is a proven large effect after all
Any effect is at best tiny, so the original claim was greatly overstated
The 17 labs all used the wrong brand of pen
Smiling never influences mood under any circumstances
puzzles.correctAnswer: Any effect is at best tiny, so the original claim was greatly overstated
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A huge original effect plus a near-zero replication pattern equals inflation. A later tiny meta-analytic signal, if real, is a different and far humbler claim.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that any effect is at best tiny, so the original claim was greatly overstated. Neither 'proven large' nor 'smile science is dead' fits: the honest update is shrinkage. Science communication failed here by reporting the first splash and ignoring the seventeen reruns.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Compare effect sizes across studies, not just significant-or-not.
Meta-analytic crumbs are not vindication of the original feast.
Media covers the splash; the correction never trends.
Shrinkage across replications is the signature of an inflated claim.
Share this: when a headline cites one study, search for its meta-analysis instead.

puzzles.title: The Marshmallow Revision
puzzles.question: The famous marshmallow test linked childhood delay to later success. A 2018 replication with a larger, more diverse sample found the link shrank sharply after accounting for family background. What follows?
choices: Self-control in children is meaningless and unteachable
Family background fully determines every life outcome
The celebrated direct link was mostly a proxy for socioeconomic context
The 2018 team must have used stale marshmallows
puzzles.correctAnswer: The celebrated direct link was mostly a proxy for socioeconomic context
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The replication did not deny that waiting correlates with outcomes — it showed the correlation rides mostly on background factors. Confounders, not willpower magic, carried the effect.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that the celebrated direct link was mostly a proxy for socioeconomic context. This is the classic third-variable story: trust in adults, home stability, and resources predict both waiting and later scores. Control for the confounder before praising the marshmallow.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Correlation needs a confounder hunt before it becomes advice.
Diverse, larger samples often shrink famous effects — that is progress.
'Mostly a proxy' still leaves room for a small real effect.
Ask what hidden third variable could drive both sides of any link.
Share this: name a famous correlation and brainstorm its third variables aloud.

puzzles.title: The Garden of Forking Paths
puzzles.question: A researcher tries five analysis choices and reports only the one giving p < 0.05, without mentioning the others. Even with honest intent, what does this practice do?
choices: It guarantees the published result is exactly true
It inflates false positives, because hidden tries multiply the chance of a fluke
It is harmless as long as the sample was randomly assigned
It only matters in physics, never in psychology
puzzles.correctAnswer: It inflates false positives, because hidden tries multiply the chance of a fluke
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — this is p-hacking. Five undisclosed tries at 5% error each give roughly a 23% chance of at least one fluke 'hit'. Preregistration closes the garden of forking paths.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that it inflates false positives, because hidden tries multiply the chance of a fluke. Intent is irrelevant: unreported flexibility turns the 5% error rate into fiction. This is why preregistered analysis plans now anchor credible work.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unreported choices quietly multiply your false-positive rate.
Preregistration separates confirmatory tests from exploration.
Exploration is fine — secret exploration sold as confirmation is not.
Count the tries, not just the reported hit.
Share this: explain p-hacking to someone using a coin-flip analogy.

puzzles.title: The Hypothesis Aftermath
puzzles.question: After seeing the data, a team writes its hypothesis as if it had predicted the exact pattern all along. What is wrong with presenting exploration as confirmation?
choices: Nothing — a correct prediction is correct whenever it is written
It hides how many patterns were tried, so the result looks far more surprising than it is
It is only a problem if the data were fabricated
Journals actually require hypotheses to be written last
puzzles.correctAnswer: It hides how many patterns were tried, so the result looks far more surprising than it is
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — HARKing (hypothesizing after results are known) launders exploration into confirmation. A pattern that 'would have been predicted' after ten peeks is far less impressive than one predicted before a single peek.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close, but the answer is that it hides how many patterns were tried, so the result looks far more surprising than it is. The sin is statistical, not moral: post-hoc stories fit noise beautifully. Label exploration as exploration and the problem vanishes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Predictions count only when they precede the peek.
Post-hoc stories fit noise as easily as signal.
HARKing turns ten tries into one apparent bullseye.
Reward papers that label exploration honestly.
Share this: ask whether a surprising claim was predicted or narrated afterward.

puzzles.title: The Drawer of Nulls
puzzles.question: Journals publish striking positives far more often than boring nulls. If twenty labs test a useless pill and only the one fluke positive gets published, what does the literature show?
choices: An accurate picture, since peer review filters all flukes
A distorted shelf where a dead pill looks promising
Proof that the pill works in exactly 5% of patients
Nothing at all, because unpublished work cannot bias anyone
puzzles.correctAnswer: A distorted shelf where a dead pill looks promising
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the file-drawer effect. Publication bias means the visible literature is a highlight reel. Meta-analyses must hunt unpublished nulls or they inherit the distortion.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a distorted shelf where a dead pill looks promising. Peer review cannot fix what it never sees, and nineteen silent nulls do not cancel one loud fluke in readers' minds. Registered reports, which accept papers before results exist, were built for this.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The published record is a filtered sample, not a census.
Null results are data — file drawers full of them warp every field.
Registered reports judge the question and method, not the outcome.
Distrust literatures where every arrow points the same way.
Share this: point out one field where only positive results ever seem to appear.

puzzles.title: The Locked Plan
puzzles.question: Two teams test the same claim. Team A posts its hypotheses, sample size, and analysis code before collecting data; Team B decides everything afterward. Team A's positive result is:
choices: Guaranteed true because posting plans magically improves data
More credible, because it closed off undisclosed flexibility
Less creative and therefore scientifically worthless
Identical in evidential weight to Team B's
puzzles.correctAnswer: More credible, because it closed off undisclosed flexibility
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Preregistration does not bless results — it constrains the researchers' own wiggle room, so a hit cannot be one of many hidden tries. Same data, higher credibility, purely from process.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that it is more credible, because it closed off undisclosed flexibility. Preregistration is a commitment device, not a truth spell: it keeps the false-positive rate honest. Exploration remains welcome — it just gets labeled as exploration.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Process quality is evidence quality.
Commitment devices beat good intentions against self-deception.
Preregistration distinguishes testing a claim from discovering one.
Weight preregistered hits above flexible ones.
Share this: challenge someone to preregister their next prediction, even casually.

puzzles.title: The Tiny Net
puzzles.question: A lab tests a subtle effect with 15 people per group, finds p < 0.05, and celebrates. Why should a methodologist stay cautious even about this 'significant' result?
choices: Small samples make statistics illegal to compute
Tiny studies can only detect huge effects, so any hit is likely inflated or lucky
Fifteen per group guarantees the null hypothesis is true
Significance from small samples is always stronger than from large ones
puzzles.correctAnswer: Tiny studies can only detect huge effects, so any hit is likely inflated or lucky
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — low power plus significance equals the winner's curse: only lucky overestimates clear the bar. Small significant studies systematically exaggerate, which is why replication teams demand bigger nets.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close, but the answer is that tiny studies can only detect huge effects, so any hit is likely inflated or lucky. This is the winner's curse: underpowered designs filter for flukes. Significance tells you a threshold was crossed, not that the net was wide enough.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Power is the chance your design could catch a real effect.
Underpowered hits exaggerate — the winner's curse is mathematical.
Ask every sample size: enough power for what effect?
Big claims need nets, not thimbles.
Share this: check the sample size the next time a tiny study makes news.

puzzles.title: The Campus Species
puzzles.question: Most classic social-psychology findings came from Western undergraduates — a narrow slice of humanity. What is the principled worry about generalizing them?
choices: Undergraduates are incapable of honest questionnaire answers
The effects may depend on culture, age, and context rather than being universal
Only neuroscience may generalize; behavior never can
WEIRD is a compliment, so sampling is ideal
puzzles.correctAnswer: The effects may depend on culture, age, and context rather than being universal
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. WEIRD samples (Western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic) are outliers on many traits. A finding can be real in the lab and still fail to travel — replication across populations is part of the claim.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that the effects may depend on culture, age, and context rather than being universal. The worry is not dishonesty but narrowness: humanity varies, and campus sophomores are a peculiar tribe. Generalize only as far as your samples have actually roamed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Humans do X' requires humans, plural and varied.
Campus samples are convenient, not representative.
Cross-cultural replication is part of finishing the job.
Scope every claim to the populations actually tested.
Share this: notice how many cited studies sampled only students.

puzzles.title: The Psychic Files
puzzles.question: In 2011 a top journal published evidence for precognition. Larger preregistered attempts then failed to replicate it, and critics found analytical flexibility. What is the correct update?
choices: Precognition is disproven with absolute logical certainty
The original claim lost its evidential support and reverts to unproven
Journals should never publish surprising results again
Failed replications prove the replicators lack psychic ability
puzzles.correctAnswer: The original claim lost its evidential support and reverts to unproven
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence; when the support collapses under preregistered scrutiny, the claim reverts to unproven — not 'refuted forever', but no longer something to believe.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that the original claim lost its evidential support and reverts to unproven. Science rarely delivers logical disproof; it withdraws belief when evidence evaporates. The Bem episode is now taught as a stress test that improved methods across psychology.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Extraordinary claims carry extraordinary burdens of proof.
One flexible positive cannot outweigh preregistered nulls.
'Unproven' is the honest shelf for collapsed claims.
Strong methods matter most exactly when results amaze.
Share this: explain why scientists demand more evidence for weirder claims.

puzzles.title: The Basement Revisited
puzzles.question: Archival digging later showed guards in the famous 1971 prison study were coached and participants played roles they thought were expected. What does this change?
choices: Nothing — coaching makes experiments more realistic
It downgrades the study from spontaneous cruelty to partly staged performance
It proves prisons have no psychological effects on anyone
It shows archives should stay sealed forever
puzzles.correctAnswer: It downgrades the study from spontaneous cruelty to partly staged performance
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Demand characteristics — participants performing the expected role — offer a rival explanation the original narrative ignored. The study becomes a cautionary tale about experimenter influence, not a law of human nature.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that it downgrades the study from spontaneous cruelty to partly staged performance. Situations do shape behavior, but this particular demonstration was contaminated by coaching. Iconic does not mean evidentially clean.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Demand characteristics can manufacture the very behavior studied.
Famous demonstrations deserve the same audits as obscure ones.
Rival explanations must be ruled out, not merely unmentioned.
Teach the controversy, not just the legend.
Share this: retell a famous experiment including what later audits found.

puzzles.title: The Thirty-Eight Witnesses
puzzles.question: Textbooks long said 38 witnesses watched a 1964 murder and did nothing. Later reporting showed the witness count was inflated and several people did call or intervene. What is the methodological moral?
choices: Secondhand retellings calcify; check primary sources before building theories on anecdotes
Newspapers never make errors about numbers
Intervention always happens, so the bystander effect cannot exist
puzzles.correctAnswer: Secondhand retellings calcify; check primary sources before building theories on anecdotes
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The bystander effect itself survived controlled experiments — but the founding anecdote was journalistic embroidery. Theories should rest on data, and origin stories need source-checking.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that secondhand retellings calcify, so check primary sources before building theories on anecdotes. Note the subtlety: the lab phenomenon replicated while the legend decayed. Separate the anecdote from the evidence at all times.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Founding anecdotes are marketing, not data.
Trace famous stories to primary sources before citing them.
A phenomenon can be real while its legend is false.
Legends calcify fast; corrections travel slowly.
Share this: verify one famous origin story and report what you find.

puzzles.title: The Watching Factory
puzzles.question: The Hawthorne illumination experiments supposedly proved workers speed up when observed. Reanalyses found the data were messy, shifts coincided with other changes, and the effect was largely myth. What follows?
choices: Observation never affects behavior in any setting
Workplace studies are impossible in principle
Named effects need data audits too — labels can outlive their evidence
The factories should have used brighter bulbs throughout
puzzles.correctAnswer: Named effects need data audits too — labels can outlive their evidence
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Eponymous effects gain immunity by familiarity; the Hawthorne audit shows labels can survive their data by decades. Audit the evidence behind every named effect you invoke.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that named effects need data audits too, since labels can outlive their evidence. Reactivity is real in some settings, but this particular label rested on confounded, cherry-picked records. Fame is not a replication.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Familiar labels borrow credibility they may not have earned.
Confounded originals (rest breaks, pay changes) masquerade as pure effects.
Reanalysis of old data is replication too.
Retire labels whose evidence retired first.
Share this: name an effect everyone cites and ask what its data actually show.

puzzles.title: The Hot Hand Returns
puzzles.question: For decades textbooks said the basketball 'hot hand' was a pure fallacy. A 2017 analysis showed the classic test itself was biased, and corrected studies found small real streakiness. What does this teach?
choices: Textbooks are always wrong about everything
Failed replications only ever destroy; they never refine
Debunkings need the same scrutiny as the claims they debunk
Streaks prove players should always force contested shots
puzzles.correctAnswer: Debunkings need the same scrutiny as the claims they debunk
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The original debunking contained its own statistical bias (selection on makes). Skepticism is not exempt from methods — audit the audit, and let corrected tests have the last word.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that debunkings need the same scrutiny as the claims they debunk. The 2017 correction did not prove giant hot hands; it proved the famous refutation was flawed and a modest effect survives. Nobody's methods get a free pass, including the skeptics'.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Apply equal rigor to claims and to their takedowns.
Famous refutations can harbor their own biases.
Replication can resurrect as well as bury.
Follow the corrected analysis, not the louder headline.
Share this: find a famous debunking and check whether it survived audit.

puzzles.title: The Silent Sonata
puzzles.question: The 1993 'Mozart effect' paper reported a brief spatial-task boost after listening to Mozart. Follow-ups found the boost tiny, transient, and reproducible by any enjoyable stimulus. What is the honest headline?
choices: Mozart permanently raises children's IQ by large margins
Any pleasant arousal briefly helps; there is nothing Mozart-specific
Only silence improves test scores from now on
puzzles.correctAnswer: Any pleasant arousal briefly helps; there is nothing Mozart-specific
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — arousal-and-mood, not Mozart magic. The policy craze (state-funded Mozart CDs for babies) outran an effect that was small, short-lived, and generic. Mechanism-checking beats composer worship.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that any pleasant arousal briefly helps and there is nothing Mozart-specific. The original result was real but misattributed; controls with other enjoyable stimuli erased the specialness. Billions in baby-Mozart products were sold on a misread mechanism.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Real effect, wrong mechanism is the commonest misread.
Control conditions decide what a finding is actually about.
Policy should wait for mechanism checks, not first splashes.
Enjoyment confounds more studies than anyone admits.
Share this: explain the Mozart story before anyone buys genius-building CDs.

puzzles.title: The Matching Myth
puzzles.question: Schools spend heavily matching lessons to 'visual' or 'auditory' learners. Controlled reviews find no benefit of such matching over good instruction for everyone. What should schools do?
choices: Keep spending, because students enjoy the labels
Drop the matching and invest in methods with replicated support
Test learning styles more often until benefits appear
Teach only through the teacher's own preferred style
puzzles.correctAnswer: Drop the matching and invest in methods with replicated support
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The learning-styles hypothesis made a testable prediction — matched instruction beats mismatched — and it failed. Preferences are real; their instructional payoff is not. Fund retrieval practice and spacing instead.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to drop the matching and invest in methods with replicated support. Liking a label is not evidence it helps learning. This is opportunity cost in action: every pound spent on debunked matching is a pound not spent on spacing or testing effects.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Preferences are not aptitudes — test the payoff, not the label.
Failed predictions should retire programs, not just papers.
Opportunity cost makes debunked fads actively harmful.
Fund the unglamorous methods that replicate.
Share this: tell a teacher which study methods actually survived testing.

puzzles.title: The Ten-Thousand Shortcut
puzzles.question: Popular books reduced expertise research to '10,000 hours of practice makes a master.' The underlying work stressed a specific kind of practice and found it explains only part of performance variance. What is the accurate version?
choices: Hours never matter and talent explains everything
Deliberate, feedback-rich practice matters, but genes, coaching, and opportunity matter too
Anyone reaching 10,000 hours is guaranteed world-class status
The researchers retracted every word they ever wrote
puzzles.correctAnswer: Deliberate, feedback-rich practice matters, but genes, coaching, and opportunity matter too
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Ericsson studied deliberate practice — designed, feedback-heavy, coached — and even that leaves much variance unexplained. The pop number kept the hours and dropped the adjectives that did the work.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that deliberate, feedback-rich practice matters, but genes, coaching, and opportunity matter too. Popularization amputated the qualifiers: not all hours count, and practice is necessary without being sufficient. Read the paper, not the poster.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Popularization preserves numbers and deletes qualifiers.
'Necessary but not sufficient' describes most success factors.
Variance explained is the honest measure of any factor.
Check what the original researchers actually claimed.
Share this: correct someone quoting the 10,000-hour rule this week.

puzzles.title: The Split Brain Story
puzzles.question: Pop psychology sorts people into 'left-brained' (logical) and 'right-brained' (creative). Brain imaging shows both hemispheres collaborate on virtually every complex task. What is the verdict?
choices: The sorting is a valid diagnostic used in neurology wards
Hemispheres differ in style of processing, but the personality sorting is myth
The right hemisphere is entirely silent during logic tasks
Creativity lives only in the right frontal lobe
puzzles.correctAnswer: Hemispheres differ in style of processing, but the personality sorting is myth
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Lateralization is real (language leans left, spatial attention leans right) — but leaping from processing biases to personality types is fiction. Networks, not halves, do the thinking.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that hemispheres differ in style of processing, but the personality sorting is myth. A grain of neuroscience got inflated into horoscopes with lab coats. Keep the genuine finding (lateralized processing) and discard the personality merch.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Grains of truth grow the hardiest myths.
Networks collaborate; halves do not freelance personalities.
Ask which exact claim the imaging actually supports.
Neuro-babble borrows lab coats for marketing.
Share this: deflate one left-brain/right-brain quiz with the facts.

puzzles.title: The Retracted Link
puzzles.question: A 1998 paper linking a common childhood vaccine to autism was retracted for falsified data and ethical violations, yet the scare persists. Later studies of millions of children found no link. What is the rational position?
choices: One retracted paper outweighs millions of studied children
The vaccine-autism link is unsupported; the scare rests on fraud
Retraction proves all vaccine research is corrupt
Anecdotes of timing prove causation regardless of data
puzzles.correctAnswer: The vaccine-autism link is unsupported; the scare rests on fraud
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Wakefield's paper was fraud, not error — and massive subsequent studies found nothing. Timing anecdotes (symptoms noticed near vaccination age) are base-rate illusions, not evidence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that the vaccine-autism link is unsupported and the scare rests on fraud. Retraction here meant fabrication, and epidemiology at million-child scale then confirmed the null. Fear outlived its only source by decades — a lesson in asymmetric outrage.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fraud and error need different responses — retract, then re-test at scale.
Coincidence of timing is the engine of most health scares.
Large nulls deserve more weight than vivid anecdotes.
Misinformation outlives its source; corrections need repeating.
Share this: explain base-rate timing to someone sharing a scare story.

puzzles.title: The Copied Digits
puzzles.question: Investigators noticed impossible statistical patterns — identical variances across unrelated conditions, duplicated number strings — in a social psychologist's papers, exposing fabrication. What is the general lesson?
choices: Statistics can never detect fraud, only replication can
Fabricated data often fails basic sanity checks that real noisy data would pass
Peer reviewers should repeat every experiment personally
puzzles.correctAnswer: Fabricated data often fails basic sanity checks that real noisy data would pass
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — the Stapel case. Real data are messy in lawful ways; invented data are suspiciously tidy (identical means, impossible rotations). Forensic statistics now screens for too-perfect patterns.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that fabricated data often fails basic sanity checks that real noisy data would pass. Fraudsters imagine data cleaner than reality produces. Replication catches false claims; forensics catches false data — science needs both nets.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Real noise has fingerprints; invented data often lacks them.
Too-perfect patterns are a red flag, not a triumph.
Forensic statistics complements replication.
Trust systems that assume verification, not virtue.
Share this: explain how duplicate digits once toppled a famous career.

puzzles.title: The Loose Cable
puzzles.question: In 2011 a detector reported neutrinos arriving faster than light. Months later the team found a loose fiber-optic cable had skewed the timing. What did the episode demonstrate at its best?
choices: That relativity was finally overthrown by one reading
That announcing early and inviting scrutiny is how error gets caught fast
That physicists should never publish anomalous results
That cables are immune to scientific interest
puzzles.correctAnswer: That announcing early and inviting scrutiny is how error gets caught fast
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. OPERA published precisely so others could find the flaw — and they did. Open anomaly-handling turned a potential embarrassment into a demonstration of self-correction working at full speed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that announcing early and inviting scrutiny is how error gets caught fast. The team asked for help checking an impossible result instead of hiding it. Contrast this with cold fusion's press-conference-first route: process decides whether anomalies enlighten or mislead.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Publish the anomaly with the methods, then let the pack attack it.
Extraordinary readings demand equipment checks before theory funerals.
Self-correction is a designed process, not a lucky accident.
Reward teams that report their own undermining evidence.
Share this: contrast OPERA's openness with a hype-first announcement.

puzzles.title: The Press-Conference Fusion
puzzles.question: In 1989 two chemists announced tabletop fusion at a press conference before peer review. Labs worldwide tried, failed to replicate, and the claim collapsed. What was the core procedural failure?
choices: They used water that was insufficiently heavy
Going public before independent replication could check the work
They published in journals with too high an impact factor
Other labs were simply jealous of chemistry's triumph
puzzles.correctAnswer: Going public before independent replication could check the work
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Cold fusion's sin was sequence: publicity first, verification later. Peer review is slow, but press conferences are not peer review — replication before announcement is the norm that prevents fiascos.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is going public before independent replication could check the work. Some labs saw marginal excess heat, but nothing nuclear-scale or reproducible. Announcement order matters: verify, then trumpet — never the reverse.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Announcement order is a method choice: verify first, trumpet later.
Press conferences are not peer review.
Failed worldwide replication is decisive, not a conspiracy.
Skepticism of hype-first science is earned.
Share this: explain why scientists distrust breakthroughs announced on stage.

puzzles.title: The Finger's Command
puzzles.question: One raised finger summons me; night nurses post me on every ward. I am the word that means no more words. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Hush, exactly. The raised finger is its emblem, night wards enforce it, and it is uniquely a word whose meaning is no more words.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is hush. One finger commands it, hospitals post it after dark, and it doubles as both the command and the state. Command-words that erase speech are a tiny club with one famous member.
puzzles.hintText:
A raised forefinger is my universal symbol.
Night wards post me on every door.
I am a word commanding wordlessness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Some words perform actions instead of describing them.
A raised finger works across languages because gesture predates speech.
Commands that demand quiet are obeyed fastest when whispered themselves.
Enforced quiet is social long before any rulebook mentions it.
Share this: quiet a room with one finger and watch compliance spread.

puzzles.title: The Hungry Storm
puzzles.question: Empty stomachs make me before lunch; dark clouds make me after lightning. I warn of hunger and of rain alike. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Rumble, exactly. The belly growl and the storm growl share one word, and both are advance warnings — of hunger and of rain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is rumble. Empty stomachs growl it before meals; clouds deliver it after lightning. One word living in the belly and the sky is the hinge — warnings come in growls whatever their source.
puzzles.hintText:
Your belly makes me when lunch runs late.
Distant storms send me after the flash.
I warn before meals and tempests alike.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One word can live in the belly and the sky at once.
Body-and-weather pairings are a classic riddle hinge.
Warnings arrive as growls whatever their source.
Hunger and storms both announce themselves early.
Share this: catch your stomach answering a riddle about weather.

puzzles.title: The Bronze Throat
puzzles.question: I have a tongue yet never taste, and I speak only when struck. Towns once set their hours by my voice. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A bell. The tongue-that-never-tastes is the clapper, and the town-hours line recalls church bells marking the day.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is bell. A bell's clapper is literally called its tongue, it sounds only when struck, and communities ran their schedules by tower bells. 'Throat' plus 'tongue' pushes you toward a mouth — the reframe is toward metal.
puzzles.hintText:
My tongue is the clapper inside me.
Towns told time by my voice for centuries.
I speak only when something hits me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Body-part metaphors in riddles point at named components, not bodies.
'Only when struck' is a passivity clue: the thing never acts alone.
Historical-use lines date the object and narrow the field.
Replace each metaphor with its literal twin and reread.
Share this: find another object with a body-part name and riddle it.

puzzles.title: The Stretched Singer
puzzles.question: My skin is pulled tight so my voice runs deep. Hands beat me and crowds move to my rhythm. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A drum. Stretched skin over a shell, played by striking, leading marches — every line is literal once the musical frame clicks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is drum. The skin is the drumhead, beating is how it sounds, and rhythm moves crowds and soldiers alike. 'Singer' misleads toward voices; the instrument frame resolves everything at once.
puzzles.hintText:
My skin is an animal hide pulled over a shell.
Beating me is the entire technique.
Marching feet follow my lead.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Occupation words (singer, worker, guard) smuggle the wrong category in.
Material clues (skin, shell, hide) are usually literal — trust them.
When every clue fits two frames, pick the frame that fits all of them.
Action verbs name the playing technique in disguise.
Share this: riddle an instrument using only its materials and verbs.

puzzles.title: The Half Complaint
puzzles.question: I am complaint spoken halfway; brooks perform me over stones. Crowds do me before the verdict lands. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Murmur, exactly. Half-spoken complaint, water over stones, and the crowd's pre-verdict sound share one low-voiced word.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is murmur. Brooks murmur over stones, crowds do it before verdicts, and complaint-half-spoken defines the register. Water metaphors for quiet speech are the oldest trick in the riddle book.
puzzles.hintText:
Brooks perform me over smooth stones.
Spectators produce me before decisions land.
I am speech kept deliberately low.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Water metaphors (brooks, streams, ripples) voice quiet sounds.
'Halfway' qualifiers mark lowered registers, not broken ones.
Crowd scenes stage collective low voices precisely.
Nature and human versions of one sound share every clue.
Share this: stand by running water and list what else it resembles.

puzzles.title: The Chest Drummer
puzzles.question: I thump without hands inside a cage of bone, faster when you run, louder when you fear. Doctors read me like a clock. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Your heartbeat. The bone cage is the ribs, exertion and fear both raise it, and the pulse check is the doctor's clock.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is heartbeat. It thumps without hands, quickens with running, pounds with fear, and physicians literally count it against time. 'Drummer' suggests an outsider; the twist is the musician lives inside you.
puzzles.hintText:
My cage is the ribcage.
Running speeds me; fear amplifies me.
Doctors time me with two fingers.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Location prepositions ('inside a cage') are the load-bearing clue.
Body riddles pair a container image with a behavior change.
'Faster when, louder when' lines are stimulus-response pairs — map both.
The solver's own body is always on the suspect list.
Share this: check your pulse, then describe it as a riddle for someone.

puzzles.title: The Begged Return
puzzles.question: I am the shout that begs repetition; stages grant me by replaying themselves. No performer plans me, yet all rehearse for me. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Encore, exactly. The shout begging repetition, granted by replay, planned by nobody yet rehearsed for by all — the unlisted final number.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is encore. Audiences demand it, stages grant it by replaying themselves, and its absence from every setlist is the paradox. Unplanned traditions hide inside the most scripted evenings.
puzzles.hintText:
Audiences shout me to prolong the night.
Stages answer by replaying themselves.
No setlist ever schedules me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unplanned traditions hide inside the most scripted events.
'Begs repetition' marks rituals audiences control, not performers.
Absence from every plan is itself the sharpest clue.
Ask who commands the moment when nobody scheduled it.
Share this: demand a replay of anything tonight and name the ritual.

puzzles.title: The Nightly Sawmill
puzzles.question: Each night I saw logs that never fall. My worker sleeps on the job and wakes denying everything. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A snore. Sawing logs is the classic idiom, the sleeper is the unwitting worker, and the denial is every morning-after ever.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is snore. The idiom 'sawing logs' is doing all the work — logs that never fall can only be imaginary timber. Sleeping on the job plus denial sketches the sleeper exactly.
puzzles.hintText:
'Sawing logs' is the old slang for my sound.
My worker is unconscious while producing me.
Morning denials are part of the joke.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Idioms are riddle engines: take one literally and build around it.
'Worker' plus unconsciousness points at involuntary body acts.
Denial and embarrassment are social fingerprints of the answer.
Translate slang back to literal and the image collapses correctly.
Share this: turn one idiom literal and watch someone solve it.

puzzles.title: The Hiccuping Ghost
puzzles.question: My throat jumps though nothing startles it, and frights are prescribed to cure me though fear never caused me. I come in fits and leave unannounced. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Hiccups. The cure-versus-cause flip is the signature: scares treat what no scare started, and fits that vanish describe the bout pattern.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is hiccup. The diaphragm spasms without startling, folk cures prescribe frights anyway, and bouts end as mysteriously as they begin. Cure/cause asymmetry is the clue most solvers underuse.
puzzles.hintText:
Being startled is the folk cure, not the cause.
I arrive in fits and stop without farewell.
My home is a jumping diaphragm.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cure-versus-cause mismatches expose involuntary body events.
'Comes in fits, leaves unannounced' fits spasms, giggles, and sneezes.
Folk remedies are clue material, not medical advice.
Ask what condition a cure treats without resembling its cause.
Share this: collect three folk cures and riddle their ailments.

puzzles.title: The Porch Musician
puzzles.question: I hang idle until the air decides to play me. Glass and brass, I gossip with every breeze yet know no words. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Wind chimes. They hang silent until breezes strike glass or brass tubes — a musician played entirely by weather.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is wind chimes. Hanging idle plus air-as-performer leaves few candidates, and glass-and-brass names the materials outright. 'Musician' tricks you into picturing a person; the instrument plays itself.
puzzles.hintText:
I hang on porches and wait for weather.
Glass and brass are my common materials.
Only moving air can perform on me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Played by weather' marks passive instruments — chimes, flags, aeolian harps.
Material pairs (glass and brass) are near-giveaways; trust them.
Person-words for objects signal category misdirection.
Ask who the performer is when no human appears.
Share this: hang a question in moving air and see who answers.

puzzles.title: The Struck Disc
puzzles.question: I am a bronze moon that answers blows with a long slow dawn of sound. Temples hang me; orchestras save me for the climax. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A gong. Bronze disc, temple-hung, reserved for climaxes, with a slow blooming tone — the dawn-of-sound image seals it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is gong. A flat bronze disc that blooms into a long tone fits temples and finales alike. 'Moon' gives the shape, 'dawn' gives the slow attack — two metaphors, one object.
puzzles.hintText:
Temples hang me by the entrance.
Orchestras keep me for the biggest moment.
My sound dawns slowly and fades slowly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shape-plus-sound metaphors (moon, dawn) each carry half the answer.
Ceremonial settings (temples, finales) mark instruments of gravity.
Slow-attack descriptions separate gongs from bells and drums.
Split compound images and solve each half.
Share this: describe a sound using only sky metaphors.

puzzles.title: The Wailing Herald
puzzles.question: I cry without sadness to clear the road ahead. Red lights borrow my voice, and every driver knows my name without lessons. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A siren. Crying without grief to clear roads, paired with flashing lights — emergency vehicles are the only fit.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is siren. The emotion verb (cry) is pure acoustics here, and road-clearing plus red lights names emergency response. Knowing its name 'without lessons' hints how deeply alarms are learned in childhood.
puzzles.hintText:
I clear roads without saying a word.
Red lights and I always travel together.
Crying without sadness is my whole job.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Emotion verbs for machines (cry, scream, wail) describe pitch contours.
Paired signals (light plus sound) identify warning systems fast.
'Without lessons' marks knowledge absorbed, not taught.
Strip feelings from verbs and hear the physics.
Share this: imitate three warning sounds and name their jobs.

puzzles.title: The Borrowed Cone
puzzles.question: Quiet voices borrow my cone to cross the field. Coaches wear me like a muzzle; lifeguards aim me like a trumpet. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A megaphone. Borrowed cone, coach's muzzle, lifeguard's trumpet — one cone lending loudness it never owned.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is megaphone. Quiet voices borrow its cone to cross fields, and the muzzle-plus-trumpet pair names its shape and aim. Borrowed-power tools are a whole riddle family: ladders, lenses, and cones.
puzzles.hintText:
Coaches carry me to every practice.
Lifeguards aim my cone across beaches.
I lend loudness I do not own.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Borrowed-power tools (ladders, lenses, cones) lend what they lack.
'Muzzle' and 'trumpet' sketch one flared shape twice.
Occupation pairs (coaches, lifeguards) triangulate the user.
Ask what the tool lends that it never owned.
Share this: cup your hands around a shout and name the tool you became.

puzzles.title: The Empty Broadcast
puzzles.question: Turn my dial and I fill the room with the sound of nothing arriving. Sailors once feared me; insomniacs now pay for recordings of me. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Static. Between-station hiss is literally the sound of nothing arriving, and white-noise sleep products made it a purchase.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is static. The dial places it on a radio, 'nothing arriving' defines an empty carrier, and the insomniac market confirms the modern sleep-aid twist. Sailors feared dead air; we now stream it.
puzzles.hintText:
A dial summons me between stations.
I am the sound of no signal arriving.
Sleepless people now buy recordings of me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Sound of nothing' paradoxes resolve into carriers without content.
Dial, tuner, and antenna words place any riddle on a radio.
Old fear turned modern product is a favorite riddle arc.
Ask what fills a channel when the message is missing.
Share this: tune between stations and describe what you hear.

puzzles.title: The Held Flower
puzzles.question: Before batteries, I gathered voices into deaf ears; ladies held me like a bouquet at concerts. Flared brass, no wires, borrowed hearing. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: An ear trumpet. Flared brass held like a bouquet, funneling voices to hard-of-hearing ears before electronics existed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ear trumpet. Before hearing aids, a flared horn gathered voices the way a bouquet gathers stems — held, not worn. Brass without wires marks every pre-electric aid.
puzzles.hintText:
Victorian ladies held me like flowers.
I gathered voices without wires or batteries.
Flared brass carried sound to deaf ears.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Pre-electric aids borrowed shape instead of power.
Held-not-worn marks the earliest assistive tools.
Flowers-to-ears imagery hides acoustics in etiquette.
Need plus physics predicts the invention before history does.
Share this: cup a hand behind your ear and feel the gain.

puzzles.title: The Morning Yell
puzzles.question: I yell one syllable until a hand silences me; the punctual both love and hate me. Fire employs my loudest cousin. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: An alarm. One syllable yelled till slapped silent, loved and hated by the punctual, with the fire siren as its loudest kin.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is alarm. The slapped hand is the snooze button's dawn ritual, and love-plus-hate is every commuter's relationship with it. Cousin-across-contexts (bedroom versus burning building) stretches one word over two volumes.
puzzles.hintText:
Punctual people both love and hate me.
A slapped hand is my daily defeat.
Fire employs my loudest cousin.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Love-plus-hate marks tools that serve and torment at once.
Daily rituals (the slapped snooze) are clue gold.
Cousin-across-contexts stretches one word over two volumes.
Ask what both rescues mornings and ruins them.
Share this: ask someone whether they love or hate their wake-up call.

puzzles.title: The Choral Key
puzzles.question: No bigger than a pocket harmonica, I lend choirs their first true note. Conductors puff me once and thirty voices align. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A pitch pipe. Pocket harmonica size, one puff lending thirty voices their starting note — the choir's reference standard.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is pitch pipe. Conductors carry the thirteen-reed pipe to hand every singer the same first note. Lending-one-true-note marks reference tools: forks, pipes, and dial tones.
puzzles.hintText:
Conductors pocket me before rehearsals.
One puff tunes thirty voices.
Thirteen reeds hide in my small body.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reference tools lend one true value and nothing else.
Pocket-size plus professional use equals a working standard.
'Lends its note' separates givers from players.
Count the reeds, keys, or marks — numbers name small tools.
Share this: hum a starting note and ask a choir how they find theirs.

puzzles.title: The Eye Closer
puzzles.question: I am a song whose success is measured in sleep. Parents perform me nightly to an audience of one who never applauds awake. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A lullaby. A song scored by sleep, performed nightly for one drowsy listener — success measured in unconsciousness inverts every concert norm.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is lullaby. The paradox (a song that succeeds when unheard) resolves the moment you place it in a nursery. Audience-of-one plus nightly performance leaves cradle songs alone on stage.
puzzles.hintText:
My success is a sleeping listener.
Parents sing me to audiences of one.
No one stays awake to applaud me.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Success-inversion ('succeeds when unheard') marks bedtime artifacts.
Audience-size clues (one, drowsy, nightly) stage the scene precisely.
Paradoxes dissolve when you relocate the performance.
Ask where a song could triumph by putting listeners out.
Share this: sing someone to sleep with a riddle about it.

puzzles.title: The Knuckled Question
puzzles.question: I ask entry without a voice, and wood translates me. Opportunity performs me, say the proverbs, though doors answer most. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A knock. Voiceless entry-request translated by wood, with opportunity's famous proverb as corroboration.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is knock. Asking without a voice plus wood-as-translator leaves raps and rings; the opportunity proverb settles it. Thresholds speak in percussion, not words.
puzzles.hintText:
Proverbs say opportunity performs me.
Wood translates me into summons.
Knuckles are my usual instrument.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Proverb guests ('opportunity does it') smuggle famous phrases in.
Thresholds speak in percussion: raps, rings, and buzzers.
'Without a voice' plus a surface names every impact signal.
Translate the proverb literally and the action appears.
Share this: perform the proverb the next time you visit someone.

puzzles.title: The Purchased Hush
puzzles.question: I sound like rain on a window that never opens. Offices pipe me through ceilings so strangers cannot be overheard. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: White noise. Rain-like masking sound piped through offices to blur conversations — privacy sold by the decibel.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is white noise. It resembles rain, carries no message, and its office job is acoustic camouflage. Bought-and-piped marks it as a modern utility, not weather.
puzzles.hintText:
Offices pump me through ceiling speakers.
I mask conversations without uttering words.
Rain on glass is my closest natural twin.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Resemblance-plus-function ('like rain, masks speech') splits twins apart.
Piped, purchased, and ceiling-mounted mark modern utilities.
Masking is a job description — ask what hires it.
Compare candidates on function when sounds resemble each other.
Share this: notice the hush layered under your office air.

puzzles.title: The Looping Howl
puzzles.question: Point me at my own voice and I scream. Speakers dread me; guitarists sometimes tame me into song. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Microphone feedback squeal. A mic hearing its own amplified output loops into a howl — dreaded in speeches, occasionally ridden by guitarists.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is microphone squeal. Self-hearing loops explain the scream, and the split reaction (dreaded versus tamed) separates speeches from rock solos. Loops that amplify themselves are the whole physics.
puzzles.hintText:
Pointing me at a speaker wakes me.
Speakers dread me; guitarists ride me.
I am a loop screaming at itself.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-reference ('hearing its own voice') marks feedback systems.
Split reactions to one thing reveal two different contexts.
Loop-plus-amplifier always ends in a howl or a crash.
Ask what happens when an output becomes its own input.
Share this: explain why speakers fear the very tool they hold.

puzzles.title: The Blessed Explosion
puzzles.question: I erupt from faces without anger, and strangers bless me for it. Suppressing me is said to be unwise. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A sneeze. Erupting without anger, blessed by strangers ('bless you'), and famously unwise to stifle — three social fingerprints, one reflex.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sneeze. The blessing custom is the giveaway hiding in etiquette: only one bodily eruption earns 'bless you' from strangers. Eruption-without-anger rules out every emotional outburst.
puzzles.hintText:
Strangers bless me though I am not holy.
Holding me in is famously unwise.
I erupt from faces without any anger.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Etiquette customs ('bless you') are answer fingerprints in disguise.
'Erupts without anger' separates reflexes from emotions.
Folk warnings (never stifle) corroborate body-event suspects.
Mine manners for clues — politeness remembers old causes.
Share this: ask someone why strangers say bless you and watch the story unfold.

puzzles.title: Three Detonations
puzzles.question: Balloons end with me, charts rank me, and corn becomes snack through me. One syllable, three explosions. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Pop. Balloon bursts, chart music, and popcorn share one syllable — three explosions wearing the same tiny word.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is pop. Endings (balloons), rankings (charts), and heated corn each detonate the same syllable. One short word living three loud lives is the whole puzzle.
puzzles.hintText:
Balloons conclude with me.
Charts rank my musical namesake.
Heated corn performs me by the thousand.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One syllable can live three loud lives at once.
Endings, rankings, and snacks share more words than you'd guess.
Short words carry the heaviest riddle loads.
Collect the three lives before naming the word.
Share this: find another syllable with three separate jobs.

puzzles.title: The Needle's Complaint
puzzles.question: Drag a diamond across my black spirals and I sing decades. One violent skid across me became rock's favorite punctuation. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A record scratch. Diamond stylus on grooved vinyl plays decades of music, and the skid-sound became hip-hop and rock punctuation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is record scratch. Diamond-on-spiral names the stylus and groove exactly; the violent skid is the DJ's favorite mark. 'Complaint' voices the sound while hiding the disc.
puzzles.hintText:
A diamond stylus reads my black spirals.
Decades of music sleep in my grooves.
One skid across me punctuates rock songs.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tool-plus-medium pairs (diamond, spiral) name obsolete tech precisely.
One famous misuse can outshine a device's intended purpose.
'Punctuation' marks sounds borrowed as transitions.
Date the technology and the decade arrives unasked.
Share this: play a vinyl crackle and ask what the needle reads.

puzzles.title: The Mountain Call
puzzles.question: I am singing that breaks its own voice on purpose, leaping valleys between chest and head. Alpine herders invented me to cross distances. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A yodel. Deliberate voice-breaks leaping registers, invented by herders to carry across mountains — distance-shaped singing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is yodel. Breaking one's voice is normally failure; done deliberately across valleys it becomes technique. Herders plus leaping registers leave Alpine song-calls alone on the peak.
puzzles.hintText:
Alpine herders threw me across valleys.
I leap between chest voice and head voice.
Breaking voice on purpose is my technique.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Deliberate-failure techniques (breaking, cracking, missing) mark folk arts.
Landscape shaped the art: valleys demand carried sound.
Register leaps are anatomy made audible.
Ask what flaw becomes a feature when done on purpose.
Share this: attempt one valley-leap note and feel the break.

puzzles.title: The Rainy Ticket
puzzles.question: You paid $60 for an outdoor concert ticket. On the day, it pours rain and you feel a cold coming on. The money is nonrefundable. What is the rational choice?
choices: Go and suffer, so the $60 is not wasted
Go for exactly 60 minutes to earn the money back
Stay home and rest, treating the $60 as already gone
Sell the ticket at a loss to punish yourself
puzzles.correctAnswer: Stay home and rest, treating the $60 as already gone
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The $60 is gone whether you go or not — only tonight's comfort versus misery is still decided. Rational choice compares futures, not pasts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to stay home and rest, treating the $60 as already gone. Going 'so it isn't wasted' spends a miserable evening trying to rescue money that is unrescuable. Compare the two futures: cozy rest versus cold rain.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Money already spent is gone from every future you can still choose.
Compare only what differs between your options going forward.
'Not wasting it' usually means wasting an evening on top.
Notice the tug: honoring past payments feels loyal but decides nothing.
Share this: name one ticket or booking you should skip this month.

puzzles.title: The Dull Movie
puzzles.question: Twenty minutes into a two-hour film, you are bored and checking your watch. Leaving now frees your whole evening. What should decide it?
choices: How you will spend the next hundred minutes
The price of the ticket you already paid
How annoyed the row behind you looks
The director's reputation from past films
puzzles.correctAnswer: How you will spend the next hundred minutes
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Only the remaining hundred minutes are still yours. The ticket, the reviews, and the director's past cannot be changed by staying.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is how you will spend the next hundred minutes. The ticket is sunk, the row's feelings are not yours to manage, and reputations don't refund evenings. Ask only: is this film the best use of the time I still hold?
puzzles.lessonContent:
Time already spent is sunk exactly like money.
Ask what the next hour earns you, not what the last one cost.
Quitting fast is a skill, not a character flaw.
Boredom twenty minutes in reliably predicts the rest.
Share this: walk out of something dull this week — practice quitting.

puzzles.title: The Heavy Book
puzzles.question: You are 100 pages into a 400-page novel you dislike. Finishing takes six more hours you could spend on books you love. What is the smart move?
choices: Finish it, because 100 pages must not go to waste
Skim the ending so the 100 pages count double
Reread the 100 pages until you like them
Abandon it and read something you will actually enjoy
puzzles.correctAnswer: Abandon it and read something you will actually enjoy
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The 100 pages bought information — this book isn't for you — and that information says stop. Six good hours beat six dutiful ones.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to abandon it and read something you will actually enjoy. The 100 pages already paid for their lesson by revealing the book's quality. Reading on converts a small sunk cost into a large one.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A bad book's opening chapters are a paid sample, not a contract.
'Life's too short' is a decision rule, not a cliché.
Abandoning fast multiplies lifetime good books.
Track joy per hour and quit below your bar.
Share this: shelve one book you are enduring, today.

puzzles.title: The Failing Project
puzzles.question: Your team spent four months on a product that tests badly with every user group. Pivoting now saves the next six months. What argues for pivoting?
choices: The four months already invested in the current design
What the next six months will produce under each plan
The launch date printed on old slides
How hard everyone worked last quarter
puzzles.correctAnswer: What the next six months will produce under each plan
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The four months are identical in every future — only the next six differ. Effort and old slides don't convert into user love.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is what the next six months will produce under each plan. Past effort is sunk; honoring it with more doomed effort doubles the loss. Kill criteria written in advance make pivots painless.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Projects need kill criteria before attachment grows.
Past quarters never appear in any future you can pick.
Pivoting is redirecting, not failing.
Bad test results are cheap information — use them early.
Share this: write a kill rule for one project you own.

puzzles.title: The Cold Meal
puzzles.question: You ordered an expensive dish that arrives overcooked and unpleasant. Eating it will only spoil your evening further. What is rational?
choices: Stop eating and order something you will enjoy
Eat it all, since it cost so much
Eat half to recover half the value
Complain loudly until dessert is free
puzzles.correctAnswer: Stop eating and order something you will enjoy
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The bill is fixed; only your evening's pleasure is still variable. Forcing down bad food adds a ruined night to a wasted dish.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to stop eating and order something you will enjoy. The price cannot be uneaten, and half-measures recover no value at all. Fix the future (your evening), not the past (the bill).
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fixed bills and variable evenings belong in separate columns.
Forcing consumption never refunds anything.
Half-measures split the difference between two bad options.
Speak up early: kitchens fix mistakes cheaper than stomachs do.
Share this: send back one bad dish instead of enduring it.

puzzles.title: The Long Queue
puzzles.question: You waited 30 minutes in a slow line, then spot an empty till across the store. Switching means losing your spot but checking out in two minutes. What matters?
choices: How annoyed the people behind you look
The principle of never switching lines
The minutes each option still requires
puzzles.correctAnswer: The minutes each option still requires
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The 30 minutes are spent in all futures; only remaining wait differs. Switching 'wastes' nothing — it buys back your time.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the minutes each option still requires. Loyalty to a line is loyalty to sunk minutes. Compare forward waits only, and the empty till wins by a mile.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Queues charge in forward minutes, not past ones.
Line loyalty is sunk-cost loyalty with a trolley.
Switching lines feels disloyal and is usually brilliant.
Recompute waits whenever new information arrives.
Share this: switch one queue this week and time the savings.

puzzles.title: The Sinking Stock
puzzles.question: You bought shares at $100; they now trade at $40 and the company's prospects worsened. Fresh analysis says similar money earns more elsewhere. What should you do?
choices: Hold until $100 to avoid admitting the loss
Buy more to lower the average at any cost
Sell and move the money where prospects are better
Never look at the price again
puzzles.correctAnswer: Sell and move the money where prospects are better
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The $60 loss is realized in every future; only the $40's future growth is still choosable. 'Getting back to even' is nostalgia priced in dollars.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to sell and move the money where prospects are better. The purchase price is history; each dollar should work where it grows best. Averaging down on worsening prospects throws good money after bad.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Every dollar should work where it grows best, regardless of its history.
'Back to even' is an emotional target, not a strategy.
Losses are tuition only if they change future behavior.
Re-underwrite every holding as if you bought it today.
Share this: ask of one holding — would I buy it fresh today?

puzzles.title: The Costly Auction
puzzles.question: Bidding passes what the antique is worth to you, but you have already bid five times and hate losing. What is the disciplined move?
choices: Keep bidding to defend your earlier bids
Stop bidding, since earlier bids cannot be recovered by overpaying
Bid once more to scare the rival off
Ask the auctioneer to cancel your bids
puzzles.correctAnswer: Stop bidding, since earlier bids cannot be recovered by overpaying
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Past bids are sunk; overpaying now converts a lost auction into an expensive trophy. Set your max before bidding and let rivals overpay.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to stop bidding, since earlier bids cannot be recovered by overpaying. Hating to lose is exactly the lever auctions pull. Your max price decided calmly beats your pride decided publicly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Set your walk-away price before the adrenaline starts.
Auctions monetize the hatred of losing — budget for it.
Each bid should stand alone, not defend its predecessors.
Winning an overpayment is just losing with applause.

puzzles.title: The Membership Trap
puzzles.question: You prepaid a year of gym visits, then moved across town. Each trip now costs an hour you resent. What is the clear-eyed view?
choices: Treat the fee as gone and exercise near home
Go three times weekly to honor the payment
Drive across town angrily every single week
Cancel fitness entirely out of spite
puzzles.correctAnswer: Treat the fee as gone and exercise near home
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The fee is identical in all futures; weekly resentment is optional. Honoring payments with suffering is the sunk-cost signature.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to treat the fee as gone and exercise near home. Forced cross-town trips convert one sunk fee into fifty resented hours. Pay for the future you will actually use.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Prepayments buy options, not obligations.
Resented compliance costs more than the fee ever did.
Re-optimize whenever your address, schedule, or body changes.
The best gym is the one your future self attends.

puzzles.title: The Overfull Plate
puzzles.question: At a buffet you already paid for, you feel full but keep eating 'to get your money's worth.' What is this logic doing?
choices: Beating the restaurant at its own game
Training your stomach for future buffets
Trading comfort and health for money already gone
puzzles.correctAnswer: Trading comfort and health for money already gone
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The entry fee is sunk; extra bites purchase only discomfort. 'Money's worth' at a buffet is measured in enjoyment, which peaks before fullness.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is trading comfort and health for money already gone. No bite refunds the entry fee. Restaurants price buffets knowing full stomachs stop — the house banks on exactly this fallacy.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Getting your money's worth' peaks before discomfort begins.
Buffets are priced against this exact fallacy.
Fullness is a stop signal, not a challenge.
Worth is enjoyment per bite, and late bites score negative.

puzzles.title: The Awful Layover
puzzles.question: You booked a $200 flight with miserable layovers. Later a direct flight for the same trip appears at $180. The $200 is nonrefundable either way. What is rational?
choices: Endure the layovers so the $200 counts for something
Book the direct flight and let the $200 go
Buy the direct flight and also take the miserable one
Skip the trip to avoid deciding
puzzles.correctAnswer: Book the direct flight and let the $200 go
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The $200 is gone in all futures; the choice is between comfort and misery at $180. Enduring layovers 'for the money' spends hours to honor a sunk fare.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to book the direct flight and let the $200 go. The old fare cannot be flown into value. Compare total futures: $200 lost plus comfort versus $200 lost plus exhaustion.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Nonrefundable means the money is gone, not that the trip is fixed.
Rebook whenever a better option beats the old total.
'Getting use' from a bad booking spends good hours after bad dollars.
Separate the purchase (past) from the journey (future).

puzzles.title: The Half Rewrite
puzzles.question: Your team rewrote half the app before discovering a maintained library that does it better. Continuing wastes three months; switching wastes the rewrite. What is best?
choices: Finish the rewrite to justify the months spent
Rewrite the other half twice as fast out of pride
Adopt the library and scrap the rewrite
Hide the library so nobody feels embarrassed
puzzles.correctAnswer: Adopt the library and scrap the rewrite
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The rewrite months are sunk; the next three are still yours. Scrapping feels wasteful but saves a quarter — pride is the most expensive dependency.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to adopt the library and scrap the rewrite. Sunk engineering effort is not architecture. The discovery is good news arriving late, not an insult — celebrate finding the shortcut in month two instead of month five.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'We built it ourselves' is not a technical argument.
Discoveries that obsolete your work are gifts with awkward timing.
Prototype to learn, then be willing to throw the prototype away.
Measure remaining cost, never invested cost.

puzzles.title: The Silent Campaign
puzzles.question: Half the ad budget is spent with zero qualified leads, and the data shows the channel mismatches your buyers. What should happen to the other half?
choices: Pause the campaign and reallocate the rest
Spend it identically so the first half was not wasted
Double the same ads to overwhelm the data
Spend it on office decorations instead
puzzles.correctAnswer: Pause the campaign and reallocate the rest
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The spent half bought a lesson — wrong channel — and lessons say redirect. Spending the rest identically turns tuition into arson.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to pause the campaign and reallocate the rest. Zero leads from half a budget is data, not bad luck to average out. Every budget needs a stop-loss written before launch.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Zero results from half a budget is an answer, not a streak.
Stop-losses belong in marketing plans as well as trading ones.
Tuition spending teaches; continuation spending burns.
Reallocate fast — channels rarely fix themselves.

puzzles.title: The Doubled Quote
puzzles.question: Your kitchen is half renovated when the contractor doubles the remaining price. A rival quotes the whole job, from scratch, at the original total. What is rational?
choices: Pay double to protect the half-finished work
Finish it yourself with no skills to save face
Beg the contractor to feel ashamed
Switch contractors despite the half-done kitchen
puzzles.correctAnswer: Switch contractors despite the half-done kitchen
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The half-done kitchen exists in all futures; only remaining cost differs. Paying double 'protects' nothing — it ransoms your own project.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to switch contractors despite the half-done kitchen. Progress-to-date is sunk leverage the contractor is exploiting. Get completion quotes, not sympathy, and let the rival finish it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Half-done work is sunk leverage — never let it become a ransom.
Always price completion, not continuation.
Mid-project repricing is information about the contractor.
Competitive quotes are the antidote to capture.

puzzles.title: The Wrong Major
puzzles.question: Two years into an accounting degree you dread, switching to design adds one extra year but fits you far better. What does clear thinking say?
choices: Stay, because two years must not be wasted
Switch majors and accept the extra year
Stay and be miserable out of loyalty to sunk semesters
Pick whichever annoys your advisor most
puzzles.correctAnswer: Switch majors and accept the extra year
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The two years are spent in all futures; the choice is between three content years and two miserable ones. One extra year is cheap against a forty-year career.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to switch majors and accept the extra year. Sunk semesters feel enormous at twenty and tiny at forty. Compare careers, not transcripts — the degree serves the life, not vice versa.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Degrees serve lives, not transcripts.
Two painful years are a scouting report, not a life sentence.
One extra year is trivial against a forty-year career.
Choose the future self you want to inhabit.

puzzles.title: The Weak Hand
puzzles.question: The poker pot is huge, but your cards are weak and one more bet is required to stay. The chips you already committed cannot be retrieved. What is disciplined?
choices: Stay in, because the pot is huge
Call to defend everything you already committed
Fold and ignore the chips already committed
Borrow money to win it all back
puzzles.correctAnswer: Fold and ignore the chips already committed
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Pot size tempts, but your cards decide — and committed chips are gone either way. 'Pot committed' with a dead hand is just donating with drama.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to fold and ignore the chips already committed. Big pots lure weak hands the way deep water lures weak swimmers. Decide on card strength and price, never on chips already pushed forward.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Chips pushed forward belong to the pot's past, not your future.
Pot size advertises; card strength decides.
'Pot committed' is often just sunk-cost with a poker face.
Fold early, fold often — survival compounds.

puzzles.title: The Cold Curb
puzzles.question: You waited 25 minutes for a late friend who now says 20 more. A warm café next door beats the freezing curb, and they can join you there. What is sensible?
choices: Head to the café and meet them later
Stand freezing so the 25 minutes meant something
Wait exactly 25 more minutes for symmetry
puzzles.correctAnswer: Head to the café and meet them later
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The 25 minutes are spent; only the next 20 are choosable, and warm beats freezing. Suffering to validate waiting validates nothing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to head to the café and meet them later. Freezing to honor the wait converts sunk minutes into a cold. Redirect the meeting point instead of enduring the curb.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Waiting validates nothing — comfort is still choosable.
Redirect plans instead of enduring them.
Sunk minutes feel like investments; they are weather.
Propose the warm alternative before resentment arrives.

puzzles.title: The Tired Engine
puzzles.question: Your old car worth $800 needs a $900 repair, with the mechanic warning more is coming. What is the clear-eyed call?
choices: Repair it, because you already spent so much on it before
Repair it twice to show the car who is boss
Sell it for parts and start over
Retire the car instead of funding another repair
puzzles.correctAnswer: Retire the car instead of funding another repair
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Past repairs are sunk; this $900 buys a fraction of an $800 car plus looming bills. Price the car's future, not its history with you.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to retire the car instead of funding another repair. Every old repair is gone, and warnings of more are forward costs in disguise. Compare repair bills against replacement, never against nostalgia.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Price the machine's future, not your history together.
Repair-versus-replace is arithmetic wearing overalls.
'Just one more fix' is the car's favorite sentence.
Looming warnings are costs arriving early — heed them.

puzzles.title: The Final Season
puzzles.question: You endured five bad seasons of a show, and the final season just dropped. Watching costs eight hours; everyone agrees it stays bad. What is smart?
choices: Watch it, or the five seasons were pointless
Watch it at double speed to halve the waste
Skip the finale and reclaim your evenings
Rewatch season one to remember why you started
puzzles.correctAnswer: Skip the finale and reclaim your evenings
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The five seasons are unwatched-able history; only eight future hours are at stake. Completionism is sunk-cost with a trophy screen.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to skip the finale and reclaim your evenings. Endured seasons don't obligate future ones — quitting at the finale still banks every hour saved. Spoil yourself with a summary instead.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Completionism is sunk-cost with a trophy screen.
Summaries exist precisely for shows you should quit.
Hours saved at the finale spend identically to any others.
Abandon franchises, not just books.
