puzzles.title: The Expiring Points
puzzles.question: Your loyalty points expire soon, tempting you toward a trip you don't want on bad dates. What is the points-smart move?
choices: Take the trip so the points do not die in vain
Let the points expire rather than take a trip you dislike
Book the trip and resent every mile of it
Buy overpriced merchandise to rescue the balance
puzzles.correctAnswer: Let the points expire rather than take a trip you dislike
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Points are sunk discounts, not obligations — spending a miserable week to 'save' them buys the most expensive free trip ever. Expiry is a feature that frees you.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to let the points expire rather than take a trip you dislike. Loyalty programs monetize exactly this dread of waste. A free trip you hate costs a week of your life.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Loyalty currencies buy loyalty, not value.
Expiry dread is the program working as designed.
Free things that cost weeks are the priciest of all.
Let balances die before they spend your life.

puzzles.title: The Split Sauce
puzzles.question: Your sauce split, and rescuing it needs pricey saffron with poor odds. Restarting from scratch costs little and twenty minutes. What is wise?
choices: Restart the sauce instead of rescuing it expensively
Pour saffron after pride and hope loudly
Serve it split and blame the recipe
Throw the whole dinner away in despair
puzzles.correctAnswer: Restart the sauce instead of rescuing it expensively
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The split batch is sunk; compare rescue cost against restart cost. Cheap restarts beat expensive rescues nearly every time.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to restart the sauce instead of rescuing it expensively. Pride prescribes saffron; arithmetic prescribes twenty minutes. Rescue spending should beat restart spending, or restart wins.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Compare rescue cost against restart cost, not against zero.
Pride prescribes premium ingredients; arithmetic prescribes fresh starts.
Split sauces and sunk projects share one decision rule.
Restarting is a skill disguised as defeat.

puzzles.title: The Bare Soil
puzzles.question: Your seedlings never sprouted after a month, but daily watering continues from habit. Fresh seeds plus two weeks beats another month of hope. What now?
choices: Water twice as much to encourage the soil
Buy a garden gnome to supervise
Replant the bed instead of watering bare soil
puzzles.correctAnswer: Replant the bed instead of watering bare soil
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The month of watering is sunk; bare soil plus hope is not a crop. Replanting converts ritual into results in two weeks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to replant the bed instead of watering bare soil. Habit waters; evidence replants. A month with zero sprouts is the soil's verdict — appeal it with fresh seeds, not more water.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Habit waters; evidence replants.
Zero results over a full cycle is a verdict, not a delay.
Rituals feel productive while producing nothing.
Appeal bad verdicts with fresh starts, not more of the same.

puzzles.title: The Silent Guitar
puzzles.question: You bought a pricey guitar but dislike practicing; selling it funds piano lessons you would love. What is the music-smart move?
choices: Keep the guitar as expensive wall decoration
Practice miserably to justify the purchase
Sell the guitar and fund piano lessons
Buy a second guitar for motivation
puzzles.correctAnswer: Sell the guitar and fund piano lessons
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The purchase price is sunk; the guitar's value now is whatever it funds. Loving piano beats resenting strings at any price.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to sell the guitar and fund piano lessons. Justifying purchases with misery converts one sunk cost into years of dull practice. Instruments serve players, never the reverse.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Possessions serve players, never the reverse.
Resale converts mistakes into tuition for better ones.
Loving the instrument beats affording it.
Miserable practice justifies nothing — redirect it.

puzzles.title: The Second Day
puzzles.question: You paid $500 for a two-day conference; day one was useless and day two promises the same speakers. What buys the most value?
choices: Attend day two so the $500 counts
Sleep through day two in the back row
Skip day two and work on what matters
Heckle the speakers to recover value
puzzles.correctAnswer: Skip day two and work on what matters
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The $500 is gone; day two is a fresh eight hours. Spending it proving attendance wastes the only asset left — your time.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to skip day two and work on what matters. Attendance theater recovers no value. Day one was the sample; its verdict is the gift — accept it and redeploy.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Day one of anything is a paid sample.
Attendance theater recovers zero value.
Redeploy rescued hours immediately or they dissolve.
Bad conferences teach decisiveness as a side effect.

puzzles.title: The Third Rescue
puzzles.question: Executives funded two rescue rounds for a failing product; both flopped. Now a third rescue is requested with the same plan. What is disciplined?
choices: Cancel the project despite the two rescue rounds
Fund round three because the first two must pay off
Fund it to avoid admitting the rescues failed
Rename the product and fund it quietly
puzzles.correctAnswer: Cancel the project despite the two rescue rounds
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Two failed rescues are evidence, not investment — the same plan failing twice predicts the third. Escalation ends when evidence outranks embarrassment.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to cancel the project despite the two rescue rounds. Failed rescues are data about the plan, and identical plans don't improve with repetition. This is the Concorde trap: flying on because so much was spent.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Failed rescues are evidence, not installments toward success.
Identical plans do not improve with repetition.
Escalation ends when evidence outranks embarrassment.
Famous money pits (Concorde!) all flew on sunk fuel.

puzzles.title: The Upside-Down Moon
puzzles.question: Capital letters H, I, N, O, S, X, and Z look the same upside down. How many letters of the word MOON survive being flipped?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Three — both O's and the N survive rotation; only M breaks. Check each letter against the survivor list.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 3. Test MOON letter by letter: M breaks, but O, O, and N all look identical upside down. Flipping words letter-by-letter beats guessing from the whole shape.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rotation symmetry hides in seven capital letters.
Test candidates one by one instead of judging wholes.
Lists of survivors turn flips into checklist work.
What breaks often matters more than what holds.

puzzles.title: The Vowel Census
puzzles.question: How many vowels (A, E, I, O, U) appear in the word BOOKKEEPER?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Five — O, O, E, E, E. Walk the word left to right and tally; doubles count twice.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 5. March through BOOKKEEPER: B (no), O, O, K (no), K (no), E, E, P (no), E, R (no). Doubled vowels each count, giving O-O-E-E-E.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Counting tasks reward left-to-right discipline.
Doubled letters count twice — never collapse them early.
Say each letter aloud to slow your eyes down.
Tallies beat impressions for every census task.

puzzles.title: The Third of Seven
puzzles.question: Spell out the number 7 as a word. What is its third letter?
puzzles.correctExplanation: V — S-E-V-E-N, and the third seat belongs to V. Spelling first, then indexing, is the whole method.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is V. Write SEVEN fully, then count seats: S is first, E is second, V is third. Two tiny steps in order beat one rushed guess.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Index puzzles split into spell-then-count.
Number words are just letter strings in disguise.
Off-by-one errors die when you write positions down.
Slow two-step routines beat clever leaps.

puzzles.title: The Midpoint Letter
puzzles.question: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, and so on. Which letter sits exactly halfway between B and H?
puzzles.correctExplanation: E — B is 2, H is 8, and the midpoint 5 is E. Convert, average, convert back.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is E. Number the letters (B = 2, H = 8), average to 5, and convert back to E. Alphabet math is just arithmetic wearing letters.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Letters become numbers the moment you fix A at 1.
Midpoints need the average, not a guess between neighbors.
Convert there and back — never average the shapes.
Alphabet positions underlie codes, puzzles, and spreadsheets.

puzzles.title: The Loyal Vowel
puzzles.question: The word STRENGTHS is famous among word lovers. How many vowels does it contain?
puzzles.correctExplanation: One — just the E hiding among eight consonants. Fame or not, count what is there.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 1. STRENGTHS carries a single E through nine letters, which is exactly its claim to fame. Length impresses; the census decides.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Long words can carry almost no vowels at all.
Fame never changes a letter count — verify anyway.
Single-vowel giants reward the patient counter.
Check consonant clusters instead of assuming balance.

puzzles.title: The Missing Seat
puzzles.question: A, B, C, E, F, G — one letter is missing from this run. Which one?
puzzles.correctExplanation: D — the run skips from C to E. Walk the alphabet alongside and the gap announces itself.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is D. Recite A through G beside the list: A, B, C match, then E appears where D should be. Gaps hide until you lay the full ruler down.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Gap hunts need the complete ruler laid alongside.
Skips announce themselves only against full sequences.
Recite, don't scan — rhythm exposes breaks.
Missing-middle items hide better than missing ends.

puzzles.title: The Salesman Demo
puzzles.question: TYPEWRITER is the longest common word typed using only a keyboard's top letter row. Verify it: which row does every one of its letters live on?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Top — T, Y, P, E, W, R, I, T, E, R all sit on QWERTY's upper row. The machine's name was no accident.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is top. Check each letter of TYPEWRITER against the keyboard: every one lives on the upper row. Salesmen allegedly typed it to prove the machine — legend or not, the letters check out.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Keyboards are geography — words have addresses on them.
Verify letter claims against the actual rows.
Product names sometimes encode demonstrations.
Constraints (one row only) turn typing into puzzling.

puzzles.title: The Left-Hand Parade
puzzles.question: STEWARDESSES is the longest common word typed with the left hand alone on QWERTY. Count its letters to confirm the record length.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Twelve letters, all left-hand keys. Count them: S-T-E-W-A-R-D-E-S-S-E-S. Records are just verified counts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 12. Spell STEWARDESSES and tally: twelve seats, every one reachable by the left hand. Long-word records fall to anyone willing to count.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Records are verified counts, not rumors.
Hand-zone maps turn keyboards into puzzle boards.
Longest-word hunts reward systematic trying.
Count first, marvel second.

puzzles.title: The Sweet Right Hand
puzzles.question: LOLLIPOP is often cited as the longest word typed with only the right hand. How many letters does it hold?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Eight — L-O-L-L-I-P-O-P, every key on the right side. Sweet and one-handed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 8. Count LOLLIPOP out: eight letters, all right-hand territory. Citations are starting points; your own count is the proof.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cite, then verify — even famous claims earn a recount.
Right-hand territory covers Y, U, I, O, P and below.
Short words can still hold records in tight categories.
Symmetry hunts (left versus right) organize the keyboard.

puzzles.title: The Mirrored Organ
puzzles.question: What 3-letter body part reads exactly the same forward and backward?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Eye — E-Y-E mirrors perfectly. The organ of reading reads the same both ways.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is eye. Only one three-letter body part mirrors: E-Y-E. Palindrome hunting means testing reversals, and this one passes on sight.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Palindromes read identically in both directions.
Test reversals mechanically — never trust the look.
Body parts hide neat wordplay (eye, noon-like pop).
Short words mirror most easily; start there.

puzzles.title: The Scrambled Swimmer
puzzles.question: Rearrange the letters C, I, F, A, I, P, C to name an ocean. What word do they spell?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Pacific — P-A-C-I-F-I-C uses every tile exactly once. Count letters first, then hunt familiar shapes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is Pacific. Arrange C-I-F-A-I-P-C into P-A-C-I-F-I-C and every tile is used once. Anagram solving means counting letters first, then hunting familiar shapes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Anagrams yield to letter counts before inspiration.
Count each letter's frequency, then match candidates.
Familiar proper nouns hide inside scrambled tiles.
Use every tile exactly once — leftovers mean retry.

puzzles.title: The Stargazing Anagram
puzzles.question: Rearrange ASTRONOMER to reveal what astronomers proverbially are. What two-word phrase appears?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Moon starer — A-S-T-R-O-N-O-M-E-R reshuffles into M-O-O-N-S-T-A-R-E-R exactly. The profession describes itself.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is moon starer. All ten letters of ASTRONOMER rebuild M-O-O-N S-T-A-R-E-R with none left over. Classic anagrams comment on their own subject — that self-reference is the confirmation signal.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-describing anagrams confirm themselves by meaning.
Ten-letter shuffles need frequency counts, not staring.
Hyphens and spaces are free — only letters must balance.
Meaning-fit is the checksum after letter-fit.

puzzles.title: The Ordered Vowels
puzzles.question: What common word contains the vowels A, E, I, O, U in that exact order?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Facetious — F-A-C-E-T-I-O-U-S lines all five vowels up in order. Order constraints make rare words findable.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is facetious. Walk it slowly: A, then E, then I, O, U — alphabetical vowels in sequence. Few words obey positional rules; those few are memorable.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Positional rules (in order!) shrink huge searches fast.
Walk candidate words vowel by vowel.
Rare obedient words earn their fame honestly.
Constraints are searchlights, not obstacles.

puzzles.title: The Ghost's Census
puzzles.question: The letters B and O both enclose space (B holds two pockets, O holds one). How many enclosed pockets appear in the word BOO?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Four — B brings two, each O brings one: 2 + 1 + 1. Letters have architecture if you look.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 4. Score BOO piece by piece: B's two pockets plus one per O gives 2 + 1 + 1. Enclosed-space counting turns spelling into geometry.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Letters have architecture: pockets, sticks, and curves.
Score words piece by piece, never by impression.
B counts double — its two pockets surprise everyone.
Geometry hides inside every spelled word.

puzzles.title: The Triple Mirror
puzzles.question: What 4-letter time word reads the same forward, backward, and upside down?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Noon — N-O-O-N mirrors forward-backward and survives rotation, since N and O both flip cleanly. Triple symmetry in four letters.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is noon. Check all three: forward NOON, backward NOON, upside-down NOON — N and O each survive the flip. Rare words pass every mirror you hold up.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stack symmetries: forward, backward, and rotated.
Test every claimed mirror mechanically.
N and O are the flipping elite — build from them.
Rare triple-passers earn their fame.

puzzles.title: The Calculator Greeting
puzzles.question: Type 0.7734 on a calculator and turn it upside down. What greeting appears?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Hello — 0.7734 flipped reads hELLO on seven-segment digits. Old calculators doubled as greeting cards.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is hello. Flip 0.7734 over: 4 becomes h, 3 becomes E, 7 becomes L, 7 becomes L, 0 becomes O. Segment digits were built for exactly this mischief.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Seven-segment digits double as an upside-down alphabet.
Flip-and-read is a physical transformation, not a guess.
Constraints of display shape the possible words.
Old tech hid whole puzzle genres in its limits.
Share this: flip 0.7734 for someone with a calculator app.

puzzles.title: The Neighbor Letter
puzzles.question: In the alphabet, what single letter sits directly between J and L?
puzzles.correctExplanation: K — J, K, L runs unbroken. Neighbors in sequences answer instantly when recited.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is K. Recite the stretch: J, then K, then L. Between-questions dissolve under direct recitation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Between-questions need recitation, not reasoning.
Say the sequence aloud and point at the middle.
Skipping ahead causes most off-by-one slips.
Anchor on known neighbors and step once.
Share this: ask for the letter between Q and S.

puzzles.title: The Reversed Seven
puzzles.question: Spell the word SEVEN backward, letter by letter. What string results?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Neves — N-E-V-E-S reversed is S-E-V-E-N backwards... reversed letter by letter: S,E,V,E,N becomes N,E,V,E,S. Backward spelling is pure mechanics.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is Neves. Write SEVEN, then read right to left: N, E, V, E, S. Reversal puzzles punish skippers and reward writers.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reversals demand writing, not mental flips.
Read right-to-left one seat at a time.
Palindromic middles (EVE here) anchor the work.
Mechanics beat memory for every backward task.
Share this: reverse your name and pronounce the result.

puzzles.title: The Longest Month
puzzles.question: Among the twelve month names, how many letters does the longest one hold?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Nine — SEPTEMBER's nine letters top every month. Extremes fall to exhaustive comparison.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 9. Line the months up and measure: SEPTEMBER reaches nine, and nothing beats it. Superlative hunts need the full field, not the famous few.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Superlatives need the whole field measured.
Famous candidates still require verification.
Count lengths, don't eyeball them.
Exhaustion is a legitimate solving method.
Share this: race someone to the longest weekday name.

puzzles.title: The Midweek Syllables
puzzles.question: Clap out the beats in WEDNESDAY. How many syllables does it carry?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Two — WEDNES-day, two claps. Spelling suggests three, but the mouth knows better.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 2. Clap it: WEDNES (one), DAY (two). Silent letters inflate the look; syllables follow sound, not spelling.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Syllables follow sound, never spelling.
Clapping turns hearing into counting.
Silent letters inflate words visually.
Trust the mouth over the eye for beats.
Share this: clap WEDNESDAY for a doubter.

puzzles.title: The Flipped Swimmer
puzzles.question: What English word reads exactly the same when turned upside down?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Swims — rotate S-W-I-M-S 180 degrees and it returns itself. Thematically perfect: it stays afloat either way.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is swims. Flip each letter: S, W, I, M, S all survive rotation as a set, spelling SWIMS again. Whole-word flips need every letter to cooperate.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Whole-word flips need unanimous letters.
Test the set, then test the order.
Meaning that matches the trick confirms the find.
Rotation words are a tiny elite club.
Share this: flip SWIMS on paper for a skeptic.

puzzles.title: The Shortest Month
puzzles.question: Which month name uses the fewest letters?
puzzles.correctExplanation: May — three letters, shorter than every rival. Extremes at both ends fall to exhaustive comparison.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is May. Line the months up and measure: MAY reaches only three letters, beating June and July at four. Shortest-hunts need the same full field as longest-hunts.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Minimums deserve the same full-field method as maximums.
Short famous answers still require verification.
Three-letter months are a club of one.
Pair longest with shortest for a complete picture.
Share this: race someone to the shortest weekday name.

puzzles.title: The Self Question
puzzles.question: How many letters spell the word ANSWER?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Six — A-N-S-W-E-R runs six letters. The question answers itself if you count.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 6. Spell ANSWER and tally: A, N, S, W, E, R — six. Self-referential questions still demand the mechanical count.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-referential questions still need mechanical work.
Count the asker, not just the asked.
Six letters hiding in plain sight reward counters.
Never let cleverness skip the tally.
Share this: count the letters in QUESTION for a friend.

puzzles.title: The Triple Double
puzzles.question: What common word contains three pairs of consecutive doubled letters in a row?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Bookkeeper — OO, KK, EE march consecutively through B-OO-KK-EE-PER. Triple doubles are vanishingly rare.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is bookkeeper. Scan it slowly: OO, then KK, then EE — three doubled pairs back to back. Bookkeeping qualifies too, which is why both are accepted.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Consecutive doubles are rare; triple runs nearly unique.
Scan slowly — doubles hide inside familiar words.
Accept near-twins when both satisfy the rule.
Rarity plus verifiability makes classics endure.
Share this: hunt the doubles in BOOKKEEPER aloud.

puzzles.title: The Near-Alphabet
puzzles.question: What common six-letter word has all of its letters in alphabetical order?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Almost — A-L-M-O-S-T never steps backward. Six ordered letters in everyday clothing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is almost. Walk A-L-M-O-S-T pair by pair: every step climbs. Ordinary words rarely file themselves so neatly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Order checks run pair by pair, never by glance.
Everyday words can hide perfect sequences.
Six ordered letters is the common-word ceiling.
Neatness in language rewards the checker.
Share this: test BEGIN for the same property.

puzzles.title: The Lottery Year
puzzles.question: Studies following big lottery winners find their happiness typically spikes, then drifts back near its old level within about a year. What does this suggest?
choices: Money permanently sets your happiness level
Winners secretly give all the money away
Joy from windfalls usually fades as life renormalizes
Happiness cannot be studied at all
puzzles.correctAnswer: Joy from windfalls usually fades as life renormalizes
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the hedonic treadmill. New circumstances thrill, then become the new normal, and happiness drifts home. Circumstances rent joy; they rarely buy it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that joy from windfalls usually fades as life renormalizes. Winners don't stay ecstatic; ordinary days reclaim them. This is adaptation at work: minds normalize both jackpots and setbacks.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Big wins thrill, then become background.
Minds renormalize circumstances with quiet efficiency.
Expectation, not events, sets the daily tone.
Plan for the fade before chasing the spike.
Share this: ask a friend what thrill faded fastest for them.

puzzles.title: The Raise That Vanished
puzzles.question: Maya's 10% raise delighted her for weeks — until it became just her salary, and she started eyeing the next bump. What happened?
choices: How her new normal swallowed the gain
Proof that raises always reduce happiness
A payroll error shrinking her checks
puzzles.correctAnswer: How her new normal swallowed the gain
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The raise reset her baseline, so the same money now feels ordinary. Treadmill logic: satisfaction tracks changes, not levels.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is how her new normal swallowed the gain. Nothing shrank except the thrill — adaptation converted a gain into background. Raises rent delight for weeks, then the lease renews at a higher price.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Satisfaction tracks changes, not levels.
Every gain quietly reprograms what counts as normal.
The next bump is already priced into today's mood.
Savor deliberately or adaptation spends the gain for you.
Share this: recall a raise whose thrill you can no longer feel.

puzzles.title: The New Car Smell
puzzles.question: Leo adored his new car for a month; by season's end it was just the car. Which idea best explains the fade?
choices: New tires secretly ruin the experience
Adaptation turns thrilling upgrades into ordinary background
puzzles.correctAnswer: Adaptation turns thrilling upgrades into ordinary background
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — hedonic adaptation. The car didn't change; Leo's reference point did. Upgrades deliver a burst, then membership in the new normal.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that adaptation turns thrilling upgrades into ordinary background. The vehicle is identical; the driver renormalized. Expect the fade and you can plan around it instead of financing it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Upgrades deliver bursts, then background membership.
Reference points move faster than odometers.
The fade is about the perceiver, not the purchase.
Lease delight knowingly or buy experiences instead.
Share this: name a purchase that became invisible within months.

puzzles.title: The Bigger House
puzzles.question: The Patels upsized for happiness, felt great for a season, then started wanting the next street over. What pattern is this?
choices: The treadmill: each new normal births a new want
puzzles.correctAnswer: The treadmill: each new normal births a new want
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — the hedonic treadmill. Each arrival becomes the baseline from which the next lack is measured. Square footage can't outrun a moving reference point.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the treadmill: each new normal births a new want. The house delivered exactly what was asked, then the asking moved. Wants escalate to match means — that is the mechanism, not a housing defect.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Arrivals become baselines; baselines breed new lacks.
Wants escalate to match means automatically.
Bigger rarely means better for long.
Contentment is a practice, not a purchase.
Share this: notice one want that grew to fit your means.

puzzles.title: The Promotion Plateau
puzzles.question: After months of wanting a promotion, Priya got it — and within weeks was stressed about the next level. What best describes her arc?
choices: Evidence her boss planned it cruelly
A rare medical condition of achievers
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — arrival fallacy plus treadmill. The summit becomes base camp instantly, and ambition re-anchors higher. Achievement satisfies; it rarely satiates.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is how arrival resets ambition upward. The promotion worked — then worked itself into the background. Ambition is a horizon: walking toward it moves it. Celebrate arrivals before re-anchoring.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Summits become base camps with startling speed.
Ambition re-anchors upward after every arrival.
Achievement satisfies; it rarely satiates.
Pause to inhabit wins before chasing sequels.
Share this: celebrate one past win you sprinted past.

puzzles.title: The Phone Cycle
puzzles.question: Each new phone thrills Jamal for days, then becomes the phone he complains about. What would most reliably slow this cycle?
choices: Longer gaps and gratitude for what it already does
puzzles.correctAnswer: Longer gaps and gratitude for what it already does
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Longer upgrade gaps let the baseline settle, and gratitude interrupts adaptation's erasure. You can't stop the treadmill, but you can step off the fast belt.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is longer gaps and gratitude for what it already does. Pricier phones just raise the baseline faster. Adaptation is fought with attention — noticing what works — not with specifications.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Attention interrupts adaptation's quiet erasure.
Longer gaps let baselines settle downward.
Gratitude is treadmill resistance training.
Specifications never satisfy; noticing does.

puzzles.title: The Neighbor's Lawn
puzzles.question: Chen was content with his car until the neighbor's gleaming SUV arrived. His car hadn't changed — what had?
choices: His reference point, now parked next door
puzzles.correctAnswer: His reference point, now parked next door
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — comparison reset his baseline. Satisfaction is relative: the same car feels poorer beside a richer signal. The Joneses live in your head rent-free.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is his reference point, now parked next door. The car is identical; the measuring stick moved. Comparison is the treadmill's engine — curate inputs and the baseline behaves.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Satisfaction is computed against neighbors, not absolutes.
Reference points move when the street changes.
Comparison is the treadmill's engine room.
Curate what you measure yourself against.

puzzles.title: The Trip Afterglow
puzzles.question: Asha's dream vacation glowed for weeks in memory, while her new sofa faded in days. What does research suggest about experiences versus things?
choices: Experiences typically resist adaptation better than possessions
puzzles.correctAnswer: Experiences typically resist adaptation better than possessions
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Experiences become storied parts of identity and are compared less; possessions sit around inviting comparison. Money buys more lasting joy as doing than as having.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that experiences typically resist adaptation better than possessions. Trips become stories you retell; sofas become furniture you stop seeing. Comparison shopping applies to things far more than to memories.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Doing beats having for durable delight.
Stories appreciate; objects depreciate into background.
Experiences dodge comparison — nobody benchmarks your sunset.
Spend marginal money on memory, not material.

puzzles.title: The Grade Horizon
puzzles.question: Sam swore a B+ would make him happy; it did for a day, then only A's would do. What shifted?
choices: His internal bar, rising to meet each win
The grading scale at his school
puzzles.correctAnswer: His internal bar, rising to meet each win
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the goalposts moved with him. Each win redefines acceptable, so satisfaction stays one step ahead. Name the bar and you can stop it drifting.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is his internal bar, rising to meet each win. The B+ didn't fail; the measuring system updated. Drifting standards guarantee permanent near-miss — unless you anchor them deliberately.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Internal bars rise to meet every win.
Drifting standards manufacture permanent near-miss.
Name your 'enough' before the win, not after.
Satisfaction needs an anchored finish line.

puzzles.title: The Follower Count
puzzles.question: Reaching 10,000 followers thrilled Noor for a weekend; soon only 50,000 would satisfy her. What is the healthiest reframe?
choices: Delete the app and move to the woods
Judge the work by its craft, not the counter
puzzles.correctAnswer: Judge the work by its craft, not the counter
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Counters are pure treadmill — every milestone expires on arrival. Craft standards endure because they live outside the numbers game.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to judge the work by its craft, not the counter. Follower milestones have a half-life of days. Internal scorecards (did I make it well?) don't renormalize the way public counters do.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Public counters expire on arrival; craft endures.
Milestones with half-lives of days are treadmills.
Internal scorecards resist renormalization.
Make for the work, count for curiosity.

puzzles.title: The Expectation Tax
puzzles.question: Two friends get identical bonuses. The one who expected double feels robbed; the one who expected nothing feels rich. What sets their joy?
choices: Expectations, taxing or gifting the same event
puzzles.correctAnswer: Expectations, taxing or gifting the same event
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — joy equals reality minus expectations. Identical events pay different happiness depending on the forecast. Manage the forecast and you keep more of every win.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is expectations, taxing or gifting the same event. The money is equal; the surprise differs. Happiness arithmetic subtracts the forecast first — low expectations are a wealth of a kind.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Joy equals reality minus expectations.
Forecasts tax or gift every identical event.
Expectation management is happiness budgeting.
Hope specifically, not vaguely, to calibrate well.
Share this: lower one forecast and enjoy the surplus.

puzzles.title: The Gratitude Lever
puzzles.question: Writing down three good things nightly reliably lifts reported well-being in studies. Why would such a tiny habit work?
choices: It tricks the brain with false memories
It redirects attention to gains adaptation would erase
It only works for naturally cheerful people
puzzles.correctAnswer: It redirects attention to gains adaptation would erase
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Adaptation erases gains from awareness; gratitude re-presents them. The habit doesn't change life — it changes what gets noticed, which is where joy lives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that it redirects attention to gains adaptation would erase. Circumstances stay fixed; the spotlight moves. Noticing is the cheapest treadmill brake ever tested.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Awareness is where joy actually lives.
Adaptation erases; attention restores.
Tiny nightly habits compound into baselines.
Noticing beats acquiring, daily.
Share this: text someone three good things tonight.

puzzles.title: The Brickman Study
puzzles.question: A 1978 study compared lottery winners, accident victims, and controls — and found all groups surprisingly close in everyday happiness. What is the core message?
choices: Humans adapt powerfully to both windfalls and misfortunes
Tragedy and fortune leave no mark at all
Controls are always the happiest group
puzzles.correctAnswer: Humans adapt powerfully to both windfalls and misfortunes
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Both extremes drifted toward ordinary — winners down, victims up. Adaptation is symmetric: it softens tragedy and taxes triumph. Resilience is the species' default setting.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that humans adapt powerfully to both windfalls and misfortunes. The shock isn't that events don't matter — they do, intensely, at first. It's that minds pull both peaks and valleys toward the middle over time.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Adaptation softens tragedy and taxes triumph alike.
First intensity always exceeds lasting impact.
Resilience is the default, not the exception.
Both peaks and valleys regress toward ordinary.
Share this: recall a valley you adapted out of.

puzzles.title: The Sabbatical Test
puzzles.question: Omar took a dream month off and felt transformed — then normal life reabsorbed him in weeks. What should he conclude?
choices: Breaks are pointless, so never rest
He rested incorrectly and should feel guilty
Lasting change needs systems, since states fade
puzzles.correctAnswer: Lasting change needs systems, since states fade
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. States (rested, inspired) fade; systems (habits, routines) persist. The sabbatical's gift is information about what to systematize, not a permanent mood.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that lasting change needs systems, since states fade. The month worked perfectly as a diagnostic — it showed which changes matter. Import two routines home instead of mourning the vanished glow.
puzzles.lessonContent:
States fade; systems persist.
Treat peaks as diagnostics, not destinations.
Import routines home from every escape.
Design beats inspiration over any horizon.
