puzzles.title: The Arrival Fallacy
puzzles.question: 'I'll be happy when I land the job' — then the job lands and happiness doesn't. What error did the wish contain?
choices: Locating lasting joy in the next arrival
puzzles.correctAnswer: Locating lasting joy in the next arrival
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the arrival fallacy. Lasting joy was assigned to a future event, but events deliver bursts, not baselines. Happiness lives in practices, not arrivals.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is locating lasting joy in the next arrival. The job can satisfy without satiating — that was never its job. Assign joy to daily practices and let arrivals be pleasant weather.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Events deliver bursts, never baselines.
'When X, then happy' mislocates joy by design.
Practices hold what arrivals only visit.
Want the job; don't invoice it for happiness.
Share this: catch yourself saying 'when X, then happy' once today.

puzzles.title: The Variety Spice
puzzles.question: Eating a favorite dessert daily dulled it; rotating treats kept each one special. What principle kept the joy alive?
choices: Sugar works better on a schedule
Variety and spacing slow adaptation's erasure
Favorites should be eaten only yearly
puzzles.correctAnswer: Variety and spacing slow adaptation's erasure
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Adaptation feeds on repetition; variety starves it. Spacing pleasures keeps each occurrence surprising — the same dessert, un-dulled.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that variety and spacing slow adaptation's erasure. Daily repetition trains the thrill away; rotation preserves novelty. Design your pleasures with gaps and they keep paying.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Repetition trains thrill away; rotation preserves it.
Spacing is savoring made structural.
Novelty can be scheduled, not just stumbled upon.
Same pleasures, arranged wisely, pay repeatedly.
Share this: rotate one daily pleasure this week.

puzzles.title: The Comparison Diet
puzzles.question: After unfollowing luxury influencers, Ana felt richer on the same salary. What changed?
choices: Her comparison set shrank to real life
puzzles.correctAnswer: Her comparison set shrank to real life
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Same salary, saner yardstick. Feeds curate impossible reference points; removing them lets ordinary sufficiency register again.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is her comparison set shrank to real life. Nothing material moved — the measuring stick did. Comparison diets work because baselines are built from inputs, and inputs are editable.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Baselines are built from daily inputs.
Curated feeds manufacture impossible yardsticks.
Sufficiency registers once comparison quiets.
Edit inputs; the baseline follows.
Share this: unfollow one account that taxes your contentment.

puzzles.title: The Set Point
puzzles.question: Twin studies suggest people have happiness 'set points' they drift back toward. What is the most hopeful accurate reading?
choices: Effort is useless, so abandon all growth
Set points are fixed and identical for everyone
Habits can nudge the range even if gravity pulls home
puzzles.correctAnswer: Habits can nudge the range even if gravity pulls home
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Set points describe gravity, not prison — practices like gratitude, exercise, and connection measurably shift the band. Drift home, but renovate home.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that habits can nudge the range even if gravity pulls home. Heritability is not immutability. The hopeful science: sustained practices move baselines modestly but really.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Gravity describes pull, not prison.
Heritable is not immutable.
Sustained practices shift baselines for real.
Renovate home instead of fighting the drift.
Share this: pick one baseline habit for the next month.

puzzles.title: The Anticipation Bonus
puzzles.question: Research finds people often enjoy looking forward to trips more than the trips themselves. Where is the practical lesson?
choices: Cancel all trips and only imagine them
Never plan anything to avoid disappointment
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Anticipation is free happiness paid in advance — plan early, countdown visibly, discuss eagerly. The wait can be designed as part of the gift.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to stretch and savor anticipation deliberately. Imagining-only misses the trip's own joys; the lesson is addition, not substitution. Countdowns, planning nights, and shared excitement are happiness with no price.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Anticipation is happiness paid in advance.
Countdowns convert waiting into savoring.
Plan early and discuss eagerly — it counts double.
The wait is designable part of every gift.
Share this: start a countdown for something small and sweet.

puzzles.title: The Giving High
puzzles.question: Spending $20 on a friend reliably lifts mood more than spending it on oneself in experiments. Why would giving beat getting?
choices: Giving dodges adaptation by connecting rather than acquiring
puzzles.correctAnswer: Giving dodges adaptation by connecting rather than acquiring
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Acquisitions join the baseline; connections refresh meaning. Giving spends money on relationship, which adaptation erodes far more slowly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that giving dodges adaptation by connecting rather than acquiring. Objects normalize; bonds compound. The $20 buys a story and a smile — assets the treadmill can't easily repossess.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Connections compound; acquisitions normalize.
Stories and smiles resist the treadmill's repossession.
Prosocial spending buys meaning, not material.
Give small and often rather than grandly once.
Share this: spend a little on someone today and watch your mood.

puzzles.title: The Nostalgia Trap
puzzles.question: Ravi insists college was pure bliss, though his journals from then record heavy stress. What is memory doing?
choices: Rosy retrospection: fading negatives, keeping highlights
Recording the past with perfect fidelity
puzzles.correctAnswer: Rosy retrospection: fading negatives, keeping highlights
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — rosy retrospection. Negatives fade faster than positives in recall, so the past glows. Compare with records, not feelings, before declaring eras golden.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is rosy retrospection: fading negatives, keeping highlights. Journals beat nostalgia because writing freezes the unedited mix. The past wasn't better — it is better remembered selectively.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Memory edits: negatives fade, highlights keep.
Journals freeze the unedited mix — trust them over glow.
'Golden eras' are often just well-filtered ones.
Check records before ranking decades.
Share this: reread one old journal entry tonight.

puzzles.title: The Enough Line
puzzles.question: Which habit most directly resists the treadmill's pull?
choices: Defining 'enough' in advance and honoring it
puzzles.correctAnswer: Defining 'enough' in advance and honoring it
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. A predefined 'enough' line stops the baseline from drifting — arrival gets recognized instead of re-anchored. The treadmill needs a moving target; enough starves it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is defining 'enough' in advance and honoring it. Every other option feeds the mechanism: bigger goals, upward comparison, scheduled upgrades. Enough is the only brake that works by design.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Enough' is a line drawn before arrival, not after.
Recognized arrivals satisfy; re-anchored ones don't.
Starve the treadmill of moving targets.
Honor the line publicly to make it stick.
Share this: declare one 'enough' out loud this week.

puzzles.title: The Savoring Lens
puzzles.question: Lingering over morning coffee — noticing aroma, warmth, taste — measurably lifts mood. What is savoring fighting?
choices: Adaptation's habit of making pleasures invisible
puzzles.correctAnswer: Adaptation's habit of making pleasures invisible
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Daily pleasures go invisible fastest; savoring re-renders them. Attention is the anti-adaptation — the same cup, seen again for the first time.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is adaptation's habit of making pleasures invisible. The coffee never changed; perception dulled. Savoring restores the first-cup experience to cup number thousand.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Daily pleasures go invisible fastest of all.
Attention re-renders the familiar as new.
Savoring is noticing with intent.
First-cup experiences can be reissued daily.
Share this: savor one routine thing fully tomorrow morning.

puzzles.title: The Minimalist Dividend
puzzles.question: After decluttering, Dana felt lighter and stopped browsing stores. What dividend did owning less pay?
choices: Fewer reference points for comparison and upkeep
puzzles.correctAnswer: Fewer reference points for comparison and upkeep
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Fewer possessions mean fewer comparison triggers and fewer maintenance taxes on attention. Lightness is the felt absence of treadmill fuel.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is fewer reference points for comparison and upkeep. Each object is a comparison candidate and a chore. Decluttering removes both at once — the dividend is attention returned.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Objects are comparison candidates and chores at once.
Fewer things mean fewer baselines to defend.
Lightness is attention returned to its owner.
Decluttering removes treadmill fuel by the bag.
Share this: remove five objects and notice the quiet.

puzzles.title: The Honeymoon Clock
puzzles.question: New relationships glow; then ordinary days arrive and couples call it fading love. What is usually fading?
choices: Novelty — while deeper attachment can be growing
puzzles.correctAnswer: Novelty — while deeper attachment can be growing
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The glow was novelty; its fade is adaptation, not verdict. Couples who mistake calm for loss chase new sparks instead of building warmth.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is novelty, while deeper attachment can be growing. Ordinary days are the relationship maturing, not dying. Measure warmth and trust, not butterflies — caterpillars were never the pet.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Novelty fades by design; attachment grows by practice.
Calm is maturation, not malfunction.
Measure trust and warmth, not butterflies.
New sparks entertain; built warmth sustains.
Share this: thank a partner for one ordinary-day kindness.

puzzles.title: The Two-Thirds Switch
puzzles.question: Three doors hide one car and two goats. You pick a door, the knowing host opens a different door revealing a goat, and you switch. Your winning chance is 2/3.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time; in the other 2/3 the host's forced reveal leaves the car behind the remaining door. Switching collects all of that 2/3.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, it is true. Count the three equally likely car positions: switching wins in two of them and loses in one. The reveal doesn't split 1/3–1/3 into 1/2–1/2 — it concentrates the 2/3 onto the door you can switch to.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Count positions, not doors standing open.
The host's forced move transfers probability to one door.
'Feels fifty-fifty' is the famous illusion here.
Enumerate all cases before trusting symmetry.
Share this: deal three cards and play ten rounds of switch.

puzzles.title: The Loyal Door
puzzles.question: In the classic setup, refusing to switch and staying with your first pick wins with probability 1/3.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Staying wins exactly when the first pick was right, which happens 1/3 of the time. Loyalty to a guess is never rewarded by the math.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Staying can only win if the original guess hit the car — a 1-in-3 event the reveal cannot improve. Everything the host does afterward is irrelevant to the staying player.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Staying freezes your odds at the first guess.
Later information helps only players who use it.
Loyalty to a pick is sunk-cost in disguise.
Separate the decision's two branches and score each.
Share this: ask a friend what staying wins before revealing the answer.

puzzles.title: The Even Split
puzzles.question: Once the host reveals a goat, two doors remain, so each must now hold the car with probability 1/2.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False — the classic trap. The two survivors are not symmetric: your door was picked blind (1/3) while the other survived a knowledgeable filter (2/3). Counting doors is not counting probability.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Two doors remaining does not mean two equal chances. Your door keeps its original 1/3; the host's filtering loads the other with 2/3. Symmetry must be earned by the process, never assumed from the scenery.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Equal counts of options never imply equal odds.
Ask how each survivor reached the final two.
Filtering processes load probability unevenly.
Scenery symmetry is the oldest trap in probability.
Share this: catch one 'two options so fifty-fifty' error this week.

puzzles.title: The Hundred Doors
puzzles.question: With 100 doors, you pick one, the knowing host opens 98 goats, and you switch to the last door. Your winning chance is 99/100.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Your pick is right 1/100; the host's 98 forced reveals funnel the other 99/100 onto the survivor. Bigger stages make the mechanism obvious.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Scale is the intuition pump: nobody believes their blind 1-in-100 guess beats the door that survived 98 deliberate reveals. The 3-door game runs the identical logic at smaller scale.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scale up thought experiments until intuition surrenders.
Ninety-eight forced reveals visualize the filtering.
Small cases hide mechanisms that large ones expose.
Trust the scaled version, then port the logic back.
Share this: explain the 100-door version to end a debate.

puzzles.title: The Knowing Host
puzzles.question: The 2/3 switching advantage depends on the host knowing where the car is and deliberately avoiding it.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Knowledge plus the rule 'never reveal the car' is what filters probability onto one door. An ignorant host breaks the machine entirely.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The host's knowledge is the engine: deliberate avoidance of the car concentrates the odds. Remove the knowledge and the famous result evaporates — the ritual looks identical but the math differs.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Assumptions about knowledge carry the whole result.
Rituals can look identical while the math differs.
'Knowing' versus 'random' is the load-bearing distinction.
State the host's knowledge before computing anything.
Share this: replay the game with an ignorant host and compare.

puzzles.title: The Random Reveal
puzzles.question: If the host opens a remaining door at random (knowing nothing) and happens to reveal a goat, switching still wins with probability 2/3.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. A random reveal that happens to show a goat leaves two symmetric doors — 1/2 each. Information content, not ceremony, sets the odds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Randomness cannot filter: the surviving doors are symmetric given a lucky random goat, so switching gains nothing. Same stage, same goat, different knowledge — different answer.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Knowledge filters; randomness merely samples.
Condition on the process, not just the outcome.
Lucky random goats carry no information.
Twin scenarios with different knowledge deserve different odds.
Share this: stage both host versions and feel the difference.

puzzles.title: The Forced Goat
puzzles.question: Whenever your first pick is a goat (2/3 of the time), the knowing host is forced to reveal the only other goat, so switching necessarily wins.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. With the car behind one of the two unpicked doors and one revealed as goat, the survivor must hide the car. The host's lack of choice is your gain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Trace the 2/3 branch: first pick wrong, host has exactly one allowable reveal, the remaining door must hold the car. Forced moves transfer certainty — follow the constraint to the win.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Follow forced moves to their certain conclusions.
The 2/3 branch decides the whole game.
Constraints on others are information for you.
'No choice' for the host means a gift for the switcher.
Share this: trace the goat-first branch on paper once.

puzzles.title: The Adversarial Host
puzzles.question: Suppose the host offers the switch only when your first pick already hides the car. Then switching always loses.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. A host who cherry-picks when to offer the deal reverses the advice: the offer itself signals your pick was right. Rules about the offer are part of the game.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Selective offers leak information in reverse — being invited to switch means you already won. Real-world 'deals' work like this: ask why the offer exists before accepting it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Offers are evidence about the offerer.
Ask why this deal exists before taking it.
Selective invitations reverse naive advice.
Game rules include when choices are offered.
Share this: spot one real offer that signals its own trap.

puzzles.title: The Coin Decider
puzzles.question: You pick a door, the knowing host reveals a goat, and then you flip a fair coin to decide whether to switch. This strategy wins with probability 1/2.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Half the time you switch (winning 2/3 of those) and half you stay (winning 1/3) — averaging to 1/2. Randomizing between good and bad advice dilutes to mediocrity.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Compute: 0.5 × 2/3 + 0.5 × 1/3 = 1/2. Coin-flipping between strategies averages their odds — decisiveness for the better branch beats dithering exactly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mixed strategies average their branches' odds.
Randomizing between good and bad dilutes to mediocre.
Commit to the better branch, don't hedge it.
Weighted averages settle strategy debates fast.
Share this: compute one mixed strategy's average aloud.

puzzles.title: The Doubled Chance
puzzles.question: Switching exactly doubles your winning chances compared with staying (from 1/3 to 2/3).
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Staying holds the original 1/3; switching captures the complementary 2/3 — precisely double. Few real decisions offer a free doubling, which is why the result startles.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The arithmetic is exact: 2/3 is twice 1/3. 'Doubling' sounds like hype until the case count confirms it — two winning positions for switching versus one for staying.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Complementary probabilities sum to the whole.
'Exactly double' claims deserve exact verification.
Free doublings are rare — notice this one.
Fractions beat feelings for comparing strategies.
Share this: show someone the 1/3 versus 2/3 split visually.

puzzles.title: The Improved Original
puzzles.question: After the host reveals a goat, your originally picked door becomes more likely to hide the car than it was at first.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Your door never gets touched by the process — it keeps its original 1/3 exactly. All the revealed information concentrates on the other unopened door.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Nothing happened to your door: no reveal, no filter, no new evidence about it. Information flows only where the host acted. Untouched options keep untouched odds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Information lands where actions happened.
Untouched options keep their original odds.
Reveals elsewhere don't bless your pick.
Track the flow, not the furniture.
Share this: point at your door and ask what changed about it.

puzzles.title: The Three Prisoners
puzzles.question: Three prisoners await pardon for one; the warden names one of the other two as doomed. The classic 'three prisoners' puzzle is mathematically the same situation as Monty Hall.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. One winner among three, a knowledgeable revealer naming a loser, and the question of switching — the structure is identical with robes instead of doors. Isomorphic problems share solutions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Map prisoner to door, pardon to car, warden to host: same numbers, same knowledge, same 2/3. Recognizing isomorphisms lets one solution pay rent across many puzzles.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Isomorphic problems share one solution.
Strip stories to structure: choosers, hiders, revealers.
Robes or doors — the math can't tell.
One mastered puzzle can pay across dozens.
Share this: retell Monty Hall as the three prisoners.

puzzles.title: The Final Briefcase
puzzles.question: A TV game with 26 briefcases, no knowledgeable host, and a final swap offer is mathematically identical to Monty Hall, so swapping must be favored.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. With cases eliminated by the player's own random picks and no filtering host, the final two are symmetric — swapping gains nothing. No knowledgeable filter, no advantage.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Deal-style games lack the engine: nobody with knowledge sculpted the survivors. Random elimination preserves symmetry, so the swap is exactly even. Lookalike rituals need engine checks.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Lookalike games need engine checks.
Random elimination preserves symmetry.
No filter, no advantage — demand the mechanism.
Famous fallacies travel under similar costumes.
Share this: explain why the briefcase swap is exactly even.

puzzles.title: The Ten-Door Stretch
puzzles.question: With 10 doors, you pick one and the knowing host opens 8 goats. Switching to the last door wins with probability 9/10.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Your blind pick holds 1/10; eight forced reveals funnel 9/10 onto the survivor. The pattern generalizes: N doors give (N−1)/N to switching.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Generalize the mechanism: initial pick keeps 1/N while the survivor collects (N−1)/N. Ten doors make the funneling vivid — eight deliberate reveals can't be meaningless.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Generalize: N doors give (N−1)/N to the switch.
Patterns across sizes confirm mechanisms.
Funneling scales with every forced reveal.
Test rules at N = 10 before trusting N = 3.
Share this: run the 10-door version with cards.

puzzles.title: The Dependent Choice
puzzles.question: Monty Hall surprises people because the host's choice of which door to open depends on the contestant's first pick.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. When you pick a goat, the host has no freedom; when you pick the car, he chooses between goats. That dependence — his move reacting to yours — is the information channel.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Dependence is the engine: the host's allowable moves change with your pick, so his reveal reports on your pick's quality. Independence would mean no information; dependence means the reveal testifies.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dependence is an information channel.
'His move reacts to mine' is the sentence that dissolves the paradox.
Independence means no news; dependence means testimony.
Find the dependency and the mystery converts to arithmetic.
Share this: state the dependence in one sentence to a friend.

puzzles.title: The Three-Hundred Nights
puzzles.question: A contestant plays the classic game 300 times always switching. She should expect to win roughly 200 cars.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Frequencies make probabilities tangible: 2/3 of 300 is 200. Long-run counts are what single-case odds mean.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Multiply: 300 plays at 2/3 each gives about 200 wins, give or take luck's wobble. Frequency framing ('200 of 300 nights') is the cure for single-case blindness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Frequencies cure single-case blindness.
'200 of 300' persuades where '2/3' puzzles.
Long runs reveal what single nights hide.
Translate odds into imagined repetitions.
Share this: convert one abstract odd into a 300-night story.

puzzles.title: The Staying Harvest
puzzles.question: Playing 300 times and always staying should also yield roughly 200 cars, since persistence pays.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Staying wins 1/3, so 300 loyal nights yield about 100 cars — persistence pays the revealer's tax. Loyalty feels virtuous and costs exactly 100 cars here.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Staying locks in the 1/3 first-guess rate: roughly 100 wins per 300 plays. Persistence is a virtue everywhere except where the math charges it double.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Persistence has a price where odds oppose it.
Virtues don't override arithmetic.
Score loyalty in wins, not in feelings.
100 versus 200 settles the romance of staying.
Share this: price one loyalty of yours in expected wins.

puzzles.title: The Early Reveal
puzzles.question: Picture the ceremony reversed: the host first opens one goat door, and only then do you pick between the two survivors. Your winning chance is 1/2.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. A reveal before the choice filters nothing about your pick — the two survivors are symmetric at decision time. Order of operations decides whether information exists.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Timing is everything: filtering only helps players who chose before it happened. Pick after the reveal and you face a genuinely even pair — no door carries the concentrated 2/3.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Order of operations decides what information exists.
Filtering helps only those who chose before it.
Reversed ceremonies deserve fresh computation.
'Then you pick' resets every asymmetry.
Share this: stage the reversed ceremony with cards once.

puzzles.title: The Informed Door
puzzles.question: After the classic reveal, all the new information belongs to the unpicked unopened door, and none belongs to your original pick.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. The host's actions never touched your door, so its 1/3 is pristine; every bit of filtering evidence landed on the survivor. Information has an address — check where it was delivered.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Your door received zero host attention, so zero updating applies to it. The survivor absorbed the full reveal. Ask of any evidence: which options did the process actually discriminate among?
puzzles.lessonContent:
Evidence has an address — find its delivery.
Undiscriminated options keep prior odds.
Updating applies where filtering happened.
'Who was tested?' beats 'what remains?'.
Share this: trace one reveal to its addressed door.

puzzles.title: The Equal Ceremony
puzzles.question: Because the host always opens exactly one goat door before offering the switch, the ceremony guarantees both final doors are equal.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Fixed ceremony does not mean symmetric information — the rule 'never open the car' loads the procedure. Equal rituals with unequal rules produce unequal odds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Always opens one goat' sounds symmetric but hides the constraint that manufactures asymmetry. Ceremony is theater; rules are mathematics. Read the rules, not the staging.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Ceremony is theater; rules are mathematics.
Fixed rituals can hide loaded constraints.
'Always does X' still needs the why.
Read procedures for asymmetries, not pageantry.
Share this: find one fair-looking ritual with loaded rules.

puzzles.title: The Lucky Guess Boost
puzzles.question: A contestant with a genuine psychic hunch about the car's door should still switch, because hunches cannot beat 2/3.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False — a real edge changes the priors. If the hunch is genuinely better than chance, the first pick exceeds 1/3 and staying can win. The 2/3 result assumes a blind first pick.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Monty Hall's numbers assume random first picks; genuine information (even a calibrated hunch) updates the priors. Assumptions bound every result — change the input blindness and the answer moves.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Results inherit their assumptions' limits.
Blind-pick math needs blind picks.
Genuine edges update priors legitimately.
State inputs before quoting outputs.
Share this: name one assumption behind a famous result.

puzzles.title: The Host Must Choose
puzzles.question: When your first pick hides the car, the knowing host chooses freely which goat door to reveal.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False — that case is reversed. Car-first gives the host two goats to choose between; goat-first leaves him exactly one legal reveal. Freedom lives on the 1/3 branch, force on the 2/3 branch.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Check: pick the car (1/3) and the host selects between two goats; pick a goat (2/3) and only one reveal is legal. The asymmetry of his freedom is precisely what loads the survivor.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Freedom and force swap across branches.
The 1/3 branch grants choice; the 2/3 imposes it.
Host freedom is itself evidence about your pick.
Branch-by-branch analysis beats blanket claims.
Share this: act out both branches with a friend hosting.

puzzles.title: The Revealed Goat News
puzzles.question: The host revealing a goat tells you nothing new, because everyone already knew at least one unpicked door hid a goat.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Everyone knew some goat existed, but which door the host selected — forced or free — reports on your pick. Existence was known; the selection is the news.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'A goat exists somewhere' was indeed old news; 'the host opened this one' is fresh. Selection among knowns carries information — that is the whole paradox in one sentence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Selections report; existences merely sit.
'Which one' is news even when 'some one' isn't.
Old facts plus new choices equal updates.
Separate background knowledge from fresh signals.
Share this: explain the selection-is-news idea in one line.

puzzles.title: The Numbered Survivor
puzzles.question: Suppose you pick door 1 and the host opens door 3. The chance the car is behind door 2 is still 2/3, regardless of which specific door he opened.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. By symmetry between the two unpicked doors, the specific number carries no extra weight — the 2/3 attaches to 'the survivor,' whichever it is. Labels don't leak information here.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Doors 2 and 3 were symmetric before the reveal, so conditioning on 'he opened 3' leaves door 2 at 2/3. Specifics matter only when the rules treat doors differently — here they don't.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Symmetric doors stay symmetric after symmetric rules.
Labels carry no weight without rule differences.
Condition on processes, not on names.
'Whichever survives' inherits the full 2/3.
Share this: swap door numbers mid-game and watch nothing change.

puzzles.title: The Single Loss
puzzles.question: A player switches and loses one game. This single loss is evidence that the 2/3 switching claim is false.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. A 2/3 strategy loses 1/3 of the time by design — single outcomes cannot falsify a rate. Evidence lives in long runs, not anecdotes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Losing once is exactly what 2/3 predicts for a third of games. Probabilistic claims are tested by frequencies across many trials, never by one vivid loss.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rates are tested by runs, never by anecdotes.
One loss is predicted, not disproof, at 2/3.
Vivid singles overweight against dull frequencies.
Demand samples before surrendering strategies.
Share this: defend a good strategy after one bad beat.

puzzles.title: The Giraffe Detour
puzzles.question: A giraffe's voice-box nerve runs from the brain down the neck, loops around the heart, and climbs back up — a 4-meter trip for a 10-centimeter gap. What does this detour reveal about design?
puzzles.correctExplanation: No designer — only inherited history explains a nerve taking the long way because fish ancestors routed it past the heart. Evolution remodels; it never redraws from scratch.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that no designer is involved. A planned layout would wire brain to voice box directly; the 4-meter detour exists because the route was laid in fish ancestors and stretched as necks grew. History constrains every body.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Bodies carry ancestral routing, not optimal wiring.
Long detours expose history better than any fossil.
Remodeling beats redesign in every lineage.
Ask what ancestor laid each strange route.
Share this: trace the giraffe nerve story for a friend.

puzzles.title: The Backward Retina
puzzles.question: Human light sensors sit behind their own wiring, creating a blind spot octopuses avoid. What flaw does our eye's backward wiring prove?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The blind spot — where the optic nerve punches through the retina. Octopus eyes wire sensibly from behind; ours kept the fish layout. Good enough beat perfect.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is the blind spot. Our retina installed sensors behind their cables, so the cable exit leaves a hole in vision. Cephalopods wired it correctly, proving our version is legacy, not logic.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Compare lineages to spot legacy layouts.
'Holes' in senses mark wiring compromises.
Good enough consistently beats perfect in evolution.
Backward installations persist when they work.
Share this: find your blind spot with the finger test.

puzzles.title: The Borrowed Thumb
puzzles.question: Pandas grip bamboo with a 'thumb' that is actually an enlarged wrist bone, not a true digit. What repurposed bone does the panda grip with?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A sesamoid wrist bone, enlarged into a false thumb. Evolution shops from available parts — wrists become thumbs when bamboo is on the menu.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a sesamoid bone from the wrist. Pandas never evolved a sixth digit; they inflated a small wrist bone into a grip. Repurposing beats inventing across evolutionary history.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Available parts beat ideal parts in evolution.
False structures reveal real constraints.
Diets reshape skeletons over deep time.
Ask what each odd tool was before.
Share this: grip a pen panda-style with your wrist edge.

puzzles.title: The Upright Ache
puzzles.question: Our spine stacks like a column yet evolved from a horizontal bridge, leaving most adults with chronic lower pain. What common complaint records our quadruped past?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Back pain — the signature of a horizontal bridge rotated vertical. Discs and curves jury-rigged for upright walking fail under the new load path.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is back pain. Rotating a suspension bridge into a column loads every joint sideways to its design. Our ache is a fossil of posture change, paid monthly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Posture changes leave bills the body keeps paying.
Bridges rotated into columns complain at the joints.
Common aches often have deep-time addresses.
Design debt compounds across posture shifts.
Share this: explain your spine's bridge history to a sufferer.

puzzles.title: The Crowded Jaw
puzzles.question: Human jaws shrank with cooking and farming, but tooth count never caught up — so the last molars often jam. Which teeth does evolution no longer fit?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Wisdom teeth — third molars arriving for jaws that shrank without them. Culture (cooking, farming) outran anatomy in a few thousand years.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is wisdom teeth. Softer diets shrank our jaws fast, but the molar count is ancient — so the last arrivals impact. Extraction clinics are evolution's waiting rooms.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Culture can outrun anatomy in millennia.
Shrinking containers plus fixed contents equals impaction.
Teeth remember diets our jaws forgot.
Mismatch, not decay, fills dental chairs.
Share this: count how many friends kept their third molars.

puzzles.title: The Safe House
puzzles.question: Long dismissed as useless, this gut pouch actually shelters beneficial bacteria to reseed the intestine after illness. Which organ was misjudged?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The appendix — a bacterial safe house, not a mistake. After diarrheal illness flushes the gut, its reserves reseed the microbiome. Useless was a failure of imagination.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the appendix. Dismissed for a century, it keeps a reserve fleet of gut microbes for post-illness recolonization. 'No known function' usually means function not yet found.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Useless' usually means unstudied, not functionless.
Safe houses and reserves hide in small organs.
Microbiome thinking rehabilitated many discards.
Absence of evidence misled generations of textbooks.
Share this: defend one 'useless' body part with new evidence.

puzzles.title: The Furry Leftover
puzzles.question: Tiny muscles still raise our hairs when we're cold or scared — fluffing fur we no longer own. What response betrays our furry ancestry?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Goosebumps — piloerection fluffing a coat we shed. In furry ancestors it trapped heat and bluffed size; on us it merely memorializes both.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is goosebumps. Each bump is a hair muscle firing for fur that isn't there — insulation and intimidation subroutines running on bare skin. Leftovers execute faithfully without their hardware.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Software outlives hardware across evolution.
Muscles fire for fur that vanished millions of years ago.
Fear and cold share one ancient fluffing circuit.
Leftovers run faithfully without their purpose.
Share this: raise your own bumps with cold water and inspect them.

puzzles.title: The Lost Tail
puzzles.question: Humans keep a fused stump of tail vertebrae that anchors pelvic muscles but wags nothing. What tail remnant do we all carry?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The tailbone (coccyx) — a fused souvenir of tails, now a muscle anchor. Deletion left a stump because neighbors found it useful.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the tailbone. Our embryos even grow tails before reabsorbing them. Evolution rarely deletes cleanly; it demotes structures into anchors and brackets.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Deletion usually demotes rather than removes.
Embryos replay structures adults discard.
Stumps persist when neighbors hire them.
Souvenirs carry ancestry in miniature.
Share this: feel your tailbone and greet your inner monkey.

puzzles.title: The Amphibian Echo
puzzles.question: Sudden frights trigger rhythmic diaphragm spasms inherited from tadpole gill-breathing circuits. What reflex echoes our water-breathing past?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Hiccups — the tadpole's gill-ventilation rhythm misfiring in air-breathers. Same nerves, same pattern, three hundred million years later.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is hiccups. Amphibian larvae pump water over gills with this exact rhythm; we kept the circuit and lost the gills. Startles trip ancient wiring that never got the memo about lungs.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rhythms outlive the organs they served.
Startles trip circuits older than lungs.
Tadpole plumbing still runs in your chest.
Ancient wiring misfires under modern triggers.
Share this: explain hiccups as gill-breathing at dinner.

puzzles.title: The Whale's Hips
puzzles.question: Giant whales retain tiny pelvis bones unconnected to any legs. What do these shrunken bones certify about whale ancestry?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Land walking — pelvises certify four-legged ancestors. Whales walked before they swam; the hips stayed as reduced witnesses.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is land walking. Unconnected pelvises make sense only as leftovers of legs. Fossil intermediates (walking whales like Ambulocetus) confirm what the bones allege.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unconnected bones allege deleted limbs.
Leftovers testify louder than adaptations.
Whales are walking mammals returned to sea.
Witness structures outlast their jobs.
Share this: picture a whale with legs, then check the fossil.

puzzles.title: The Python Spurs
puzzles.question: Pythons carry small claw-like spurs near the tail — remnants with no walking job. What lost structures do these spurs memorialize?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Hind legs — spurs are reduced limb remnants, still wired to the pelvis. Snakes are lizards that deleted outward legs but kept the receipts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is hind legs. The spurs anchor to vestigial pelvic bones — a full receipt chain from limb to claw. Leglessness evolved by reduction, and reduction leaves serial numbers.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reduction leaves serial numbers, not clean erasures.
Spurs plus pelvis equals a limb receipt chain.
Leglessness is a deletion story with witnesses.
Receipts outlast the purchases they record.
Share this: look up python spurs and show a skeptic.

puzzles.title: The Distributed Brain
puzzles.question: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live outside its head, letting each arm taste, decide, and act semi-independently. Where do most octopus neurons live?
puzzles.correctExplanation: In its arms — the majority of octopus neurons ring the suckers and arm cords, not the central brain. Cognition distributed to the limbs.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is in its arms. Severed arms still reach, taste, and recoil — the neurons live locally. Brains centralize in vertebrates; octopuses federalized instead.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cognition can federalize out to the limbs.
Local neurons grant arms semi-independent votes.
Central brains are one architecture among many.
Severed-arm behavior reveals where thinking lives.

puzzles.title: The Striped Defense
puzzles.question: Zebra stripes were long called camouflage, but field trials show their main power is confusing landing insects. What attackers do stripes defeat?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Biting flies — polarized-light confusion makes landings fail. Camouflage never survived testing; pest control did. Stripes are flypaper in reverse.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is biting flies. Horse trials with striped blankets confirmed it: flies can't land cleanly on stripes. The camouflage story felt right and tested wrong — mechanism beats narrative.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Felt-right stories must survive field trials.
Patterns can jam senses instead of hiding bodies.
Pest pressure sculpts coats as surely as predators.
Test every 'obvious' function experimentally.

puzzles.title: The Skull Seatbelt
puzzles.question: A woodpecker's brain survives 1,200-G pecks partly because one long organ wraps around the skull as a shock-absorbing sling. What wraps the skull?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Its tongue — anchored at the nostril, looping behind the skull to cushion impact. The eating tool moonlights as a seatbelt.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is its tongue. The hyoid apparatus wraps the cranium like a sling, spreading deceleration. Tools moonlight across jobs in evolved bodies — dinner gear doubles as safety gear.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tools moonlight across jobs in evolved bodies.
Slings and wraps distribute violent forces.
Eating gear doubles as safety gear here.
Ask what each long structure touches en route.

puzzles.title: The Prime Cicadas
puzzles.question: Periodical cicadas emerge every 13 or 17 years — cycle lengths whose mathematical property starves predators that boom on shorter rhythms. What property?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Primality — 13- and 17-year cycles rarely coincide with 2-, 3-, or 4-year predator booms. Number theory becomes a survival strategy.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is primality. Prime cycles minimize synchronization with predator rhythms — a 12-year brood would meet every 2-, 3-, 4-, and 6-year enemy. Arithmetic itself can be selected for.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Arithmetic can be a survival strategy.
Synchronization is death when enemies keep calendars.
Primes minimize coinciding with shorter rhythms.
Math lives inside life cycles, not just textbooks.

puzzles.title: The Devoted Male
puzzles.question: A male anglerfish, tiny and short-lived, bites a giant female and gradually fuses into her body as a permanent appendage. What has he become?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A parasite — fused, shrunken, living off her bloodstream for lifelong sperm delivery. In lightless depths, finding one mate justifies dissolving oneself.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a parasite. He trades body, organs, and independence for guaranteed paternity in an ocean where meetings are miracles. Extremes of scarcity rewrite the definition of male.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scarcity rewrites anatomy and definitions alike.
Meeting once can justify fusing forever.
Parasitism evolves wherever free rides pay.
Depth makes miracles expensive — bodies pay the price.

puzzles.title: The Outsourced Nest
puzzles.question: Cuckoos never build nests; they plant eggs in other species' homes and let strangers raise their chicks. What reproductive strategy is this?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Brood parasitism — outsourcing all parenting to duped hosts. Mimic eggs, evicting chicks, and lightning laying make the con work.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is brood parasitism. The whole parental budget converts into eggs and deception. Hosts evolve egg-spotting; cuckoos evolve better forgeries — a forgery arms race in feathers.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Parenting itself can be outsourced to dupes.
Forgery arms races run in feathers, not banks.
Whole budgets convert from care into deception.
Hosts and cheats coevolve in lockstep.

puzzles.title: The Once Breeders
puzzles.question: Pacific salmon migrate, spawn a single time, then decay and die within days. What life history breeds exactly once before death?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Semelparity — one massive reproductive bet, then death. When migration costs everything, saving nothing for later is optimal.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is semelparity. Salmon spend the entire body budget reaching spawning grounds; survivors with savings would lose to bigger spenders. All-in is optimal when the journey bankrupts everyone.
puzzles.lessonContent:
All-in is optimal when journeys bankrupt everyone.
Single bets beat savings where return is impossible.
Life histories optimize under their own constraints.
'Suicidal' breeding is accounting, not tragedy.

puzzles.title: The Relay Migration
puzzles.question: Monarch butterflies fly thousands of miles south, yet no single butterfly makes the round trip — the journey is split across successive broods. How many generations complete it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Four generations relay the round trip — southern breeders, northbound waves, and the long-lived returners. Migration as a relay, not a voyage.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is four. Great-grandchildren finish what grandparents began, with each brood flying a leg it never learned. Inheritance here is direction, staged across bodies.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Journeys can be relayed across bodies.
No individual needs the whole map.
Broods inherit legs of a trip, not the trip.
Staged inheritance solves impossible voyages.
Share this: map the four monarch generations on paper.

puzzles.title: The Crude Spectrum
puzzles.question: Mantis shrimp eyes carry far more color channels than human three — yet they discriminate hues worse than we do. How many channels do they sample?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Twelve channels sampled crudely — recognition, not discrimination. More sensors don't mean finer vision; brains, not eyes, compare.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is twelve. Mantis shrimp recognize channel patterns instead of comparing signals, so twelve inputs yield coarser color than our three. Hardware counts mislead; processing decides.
puzzles.lessonContent:
More sensors never guarantee finer senses.
Recognition and discrimination are different jobs.
Processing, not hardware, decides perception.
Brains compare; eyes merely sample.
Share this: explain why twelve channels see less than three.

puzzles.title: The Balanced Sickle
puzzles.question: Carrying one copy of the sickle-cell gene distorts red cells yet persists across malaria zones. What killer disease does single-copy carriage fend off?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Malaria — heterozygotes resist severe infection, so the gene survives despite killing double-carriers. Selection balances on a knife's edge.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is malaria. One copy shields against the parasite; two copies cause disease. Genes persist by tradeoffs, not perfection — the ledger, not the symptom, decides.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Genes persist by tradeoffs, never perfection.
Heterozygote advantage balances lethal ledgers.
Disease zones write themselves into genomes.
Read the ledger before judging the symptom.
Share this: explain balanced sickness with coins and dice.

puzzles.title: The Borrowed Altitude
puzzles.question: Tibetans thrive at altitudes that sicken lowlanders, using a gene variant inherited from an extinct cousin species. Which extinct humans donated it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Denisovans — their EPAS1 variant tunes hemoglobin response to thin air. Adaptation can be borrowed, not just built; extinct cousins still breathe in Tibetan blood.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the Denisovans. Tibetans carry a Denisovan EPAS1 version that blunts overproduction of red cells at altitude. Interbreeding stocked humanity's spare-parts shelf.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Adaptation can be borrowed, not only built.
Extinct cousins stock our spare-parts shelf.
Interbreeding was gene shopping, not just history.
Altitude wrote its signature into borrowed DNA.
Share this: tell someone Neanderthals aren't our only exes.

puzzles.title: The Herding Gift
puzzles.question: Most mammals lose milk digestion after weaning, yet herding peoples evolved lifelong tolerance within a few thousand years. What food drove this fast evolution?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Milk — dairying cultures selected for lactase persistence astonishingly fast. Dinner rewrote genomes: culture led, genes followed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is milk. Herding made fresh milk a caloric prize, and persistence mutations swept dairying populations in millennia — evolution you can date by pottery. Food cultures are selection pressures wearing aprons.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Dinner rewrites genomes on historical timescales.
Culture leads; genes follow within millennia.
Selection pressures wear aprons, not just claws.
Recent evolution is visible in your own gut.
Share this: test your own milk tolerance story at dinner.

puzzles.title: The Cool Compromise
puzzles.question: External testicles risk injury and temperature swings, yet persist across mammals. What cooling benefit outweighs this vulnerability?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Sperm cooling — production needs temperatures below body heat, and no internal redesign ever beat hanging the factory outside. Vulnerability is the cooling bill.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is sperm cooling. Spermatogenesis fails at core temperature, so mammals externalized the workshop despite the risks. Tradeoffs, not perfection: cooling purchased with vulnerability.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Workshops move outside when interiors run hot.
Vulnerability is often a cooling bill.
Production constraints beat protection instincts.
Tradeoffs explain anatomy better than ideals.

puzzles.title: The Electric Bill
puzzles.question: A platypus hunts with eyes, ears, and nostrils sealed shut, navigating purely by minute electric fields from prey muscles. What sense does its bill provide?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Electroreception — thousands of bill sensors triangulate prey's muscle currents in muddy dark. A sixth sense, standard equipment on one mammal.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is electroreception. Sealed eyes and ears force the question: what remains? The bill's electric array maps living currents directly. Mammals kept one electrician — the platypus.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sealed senses force the question of what remains.
Muscles broadcast electric signatures constantly.
Sixth senses are standard on some mammals.
Dark water rewards non-visual navigation.

puzzles.title: The Two Sons
puzzles.question: A father says, 'I have two children, and at least one is a boy.' Assuming equal odds, what is the probability both are boys?
choices: 1/2, since the other child is equally either
1/4, since two boys was always unlikely
1/3, because only BB, BG, and GB remain
puzzles.correctAnswer: 1/3, because only BB, BG, and GB remain
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 1/3. 'At least one boy' eliminates only GG, leaving BB, BG, GB equally likely — one of three is BB. Information prunes cases; count survivors.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 1/3, because only BB, BG, and GB remain. 'At least one boy' kills just the GG case, not the mixed ones. List all four original cases, cross out GG, and BB is one of three survivors.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Information prunes cases — recount the survivors.
'At least one' eliminates fewer cases than intuition claims.
List all originals before crossing any out.
Order matters in counting: BG and GB are distinct.
Share this: run the two-sons cases on coins with a friend.

puzzles.title: The Guessing Pass
puzzles.question: A 10-question true-false quiz needs 6 correct to pass. A student guesses blindly on every question. What is the pass chance?
choices: Exactly 1/2, since each answer is fifty-fifty
1/10, since only one score in ten passes
Near zero, since guessing never works
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 386 of 1,024 possible answer keys pass (210+120+45+10+1 for scores 6–10), about 38%. Blind guessing passes far more often than pride admits.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is about 38%, summing the passing combinations. Fifty-fifty per question doesn't mean fifty-fifty overall: 386 of the 1,024 possible keys reach 6+. Count keys, not questions — combinations decide.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Per-trial odds never equal whole-test odds.
Count passing keys among all possible keys.
Combinations, not questions, decide batch outcomes.
Guessing outperforms intuition more often than admitted.
Share this: compute one blind-guessing pass rate by hand.

puzzles.title: The Three Boxes
puzzles.question: Three boxes hold GG, SS, and GS coins. You open a random box, draw a gold coin, and consider the other coin inside. What is the chance it is also gold?
choices: 1/2, since the GS box is now equally likely
Certainty, since silver boxes show silver
2/3, because the draw favors the GG box
puzzles.correctAnswer: 2/3, because the draw favors the GG box
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 2/3. Three gold coins could have been drawn (two in GG, one in GS); two of those three leave gold behind. The draw is evidence for which box you hold.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 2/3, because the draw favors the GG box. Count drawable golds, not boxes: GG offers two paths to this observation, GS only one. Observations update which box you're likely holding.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Count paths to the observation, not containers.
Draws are evidence about which box you hold.
Two-to-one path ratios beat fifty-fifty feelings.
Bertrand's box is Monty Hall's quiet cousin.
Share this: play three boxes with coins and tally thirty draws.

puzzles.title: The Red Streak
puzzles.question: A fair roulette wheel lands red eight times running. A gambler piles onto black, 'due' at last. What is black's chance on the next spin?
choices: Far above half, since balance is overdue
Exactly the wheel's usual black odds, near 18/37
Zero, since red has momentum now
puzzles.correctAnswer: Exactly the wheel's usual black odds, near 18/37
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — wheels have no memory. Eight reds are history, not debt; black pays its usual ~48.6%. Streaks in random data are normal, not corrective.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is exactly the wheel's usual black odds, near 18/37. Independence means history can't load the next spin. Long streaks feel meaningful but occur routinely — casinos price this fallacy into the carpet.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Independent trials carry no memory or debt.
Streaks are routine output of randomness.
'Due' is the costliest word in gambling.
The wheel's odds reset every single spin.
Share this: flip nine heads then ask what comes next.

puzzles.title: The Waiting Pattern
puzzles.question: Flipping a fair coin, which pattern typically appears first: HH (two heads running) or HT (head then tail)?
choices: HT, since it can overlap itself into existence
They tie exactly, both being 1/4 per pair
puzzles.correctAnswer: HT, since it can overlap itself into existence
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — HT wins the race on average (about 4 flips versus about 6). A failed HH attempt (ending in T) restarts from zero, while HT's fragments recycle. Overlap structure sets waiting times.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is HT, since it can overlap itself into existence. Equal per-trial odds don't mean equal waiting times: sequences overlap differently. After a lone H, a T completes HT but merely continues HH's wait — structure, not luck.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Equal odds per trial, unequal waiting times.
Overlap structure governs pattern races.
Failed attempts recycle differently per pattern.
'Feels the same' is not 'arrives the same'.
Share this: race HH versus HT over twenty flips.

puzzles.title: The Dice Duel
puzzles.question: Rolling three dice, a total of 9 beats 10 in folk wisdom. Counting the 216 outcomes shows one total genuinely leads. Which one, and why?
choices: They tie, by symmetry of the dice
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 10 has 27 paths, 9 only 25. Galileo settled a duke's gambling dispute this way: partitions of a total aren't equally numerous. Count compositions, not vibes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 10, with 27 combinations against 9's 25. Folk wisdom counted partitions (ways to split) instead of compositions (ordered outcomes). Ordered dice distinguish 1-2-6 from 6-2-1 — and the totals differ.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Partitions differ from compositions — order counts.
Folk wisdom often counts the wrong units.
216 outcomes is a countable universe; count it.
Dukes and Galileos settled bets by enumeration.
Share this: list the partitions of 9 versus 10.

puzzles.title: The Chevalier's Dice
puzzles.question: A 17th-century gambler preferred betting on at least one six in 4 die rolls, but lost on double-six in 24 rolls of two dice. What explains the reversal?
choices: Dice remember past games and punish greed
The two bets only look equivalent but their odds differ
Double sixes are luckier and rarer by design
puzzles.correctAnswer: The two bets only look equivalent but their odds differ
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. One six in 4 rolls hits ~51.8%; double-six in 24 rolls lands ~49.1% — straddling even. The 'equivalent' scaling (4:6 vs 24:36) is a mirage; compute, don't proportion.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that the two bets only look equivalent but their odds differ. Naive scaling suggests equal chances, but compounding differs: 1−(5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518 versus 1−(35/36)²⁴ ≈ 0.491. Proportional intuition fails compound lotteries.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Naive scaling fails compound lotteries.
Compute both sides; never proportion across bets.
Straddling even by 1% decides professional fates.
de Méré's losses founded probability theory.
Share this: compute 1−(5/6)⁴ with a skeptic.

puzzles.title: The Airport Swab
puzzles.question: A security test catches 99% of threats but false-alarms on 1% of innocents. Threats are 1 in 10,000 travelers. A flagged traveler is most likely…
choices: Equally either, since the test is symmetric
An innocent false alarm, swamped by base rates
puzzles.correctAnswer: An innocent false alarm, swamped by base rates
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Roughly 1 true flag per 100 false ones (1 threat vs ~100 false alarms per 10,000). Accuracy percentages mislead when bases are extreme — always multiply by the base.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is an innocent false alarm, swamped by base rates. 99% accuracy sounds decisive until 9,999 innocents each roll 1% false-alarm dice. Tests screen; base rates judge. Bayes is just this multiplication done honestly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Accuracy percentages mislead at extreme base rates.
Multiply sensitivity by the base before believing flags.
Tests screen populations; bases judge individuals.
Rare targets drown in common false alarms.

puzzles.title: The Sophomore Slump
puzzles.question: Rookies of the year usually play worse the next season. Fans smell curses and pressure. What is the likelier mechanism?
choices: Regression: an extreme season is usually followed by a merely good one
puzzles.correctAnswer: Regression: an extreme season is usually followed by a merely good one
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — regression to the mean. Award seasons select for career-best luck plus skill; the luck component rarely repeats. Extremes are followed by typicals, curses unnecessary.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is regression: an extreme season is usually followed by a merely good one. Best-of-career years bundle peak skill with peak luck, and luck doesn't defend titles. Expect the second year to resemble the career, not the peak.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Extremes bundle skill with unrepeatable luck.
Award filters select peaks, then peaks relax.
Curses are regression wearing a costume.
Predict careers from averages, not trophies.
Share this: name one 'cursed' winner regression explains.

puzzles.title: The Million-to-One Match
puzzles.question: A DNA match with a 1-in-a-million random chance is found by trawling a database of 5 million profiles. What does the match alone establish?
choices: Guilt at a million to one
A lead worth investigating, since trawling multiplies chances
puzzles.correctAnswer: A lead worth investigating, since trawling multiplies chances
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Across 5 million profiles, several random matches are expected — the prosecutor's fallacy confuses P(match|innocent) with P(innocent|match). Database size dilutes single-match meaning.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a lead worth investigating, since trawling multiplies chances. One-in-a-million per comparison times millions of comparisons yields expected hits. Match statistics need the search size attached — without it, they're courtroom confetti.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Search size dilutes every single match.
P(evidence|innocent) is not P(innocent|evidence).
Trawling manufactures expected coincidences.
Attach the database size to every match claim.
Share this: explain why big searches find 'impossible' hits.

puzzles.title: The Green Jellybean
puzzles.question: Scientists test 20 jellybean colors against acne with 5% significance each. Only green 'links' to spots, and headlines erupt. What is the sound conclusion?
choices: Green jellybeans cause acne — publish the warning
Expect about one fluke hit in twenty tests, so replicate first
Ban all jellybeans as a precaution
puzzles.correctAnswer: Expect about one fluke hit in twenty tests, so replicate first
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Twenty tests at 5% error each virtually guarantee a 'finding' by chance. Headlines report the hit; method counts the tries. Replicate before regulating.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to expect about one fluke hit in twenty tests, so replicate first. Multiple testing manufactures significance the way sieves manufacture gravel. The famous cartoon is a methods lesson: count the tries, not just the hit.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Count the tries behind every reported hit.
Twenty tests at 5% guarantee carnival findings.
Headlines harvest; replication verifies.
Pre-register or perish by multiplicity.

puzzles.title: The Missing Holes
puzzles.question: WWII analysts armored bomber zones showing the fewest bullet holes in returning planes. Survivors' pristine zones marked…
choices: Where hits proved fatal, since those planes never returned
puzzles.correctAnswer: Where hits proved fatal, since those planes never returned
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — survivorship bias. Returning planes display survivable hits; missing holes mark where damaged bombers died. Wald armored the absence, and losses fell.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is where hits proved fatal, since those planes never returned. The dataset was pre-filtered by survival — holes cluster where planes can afford them. Armor the silence, not the noise: absence is data.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Surviving datasets pre-filter their own lessons.
Absence is data — armor the silence.
Holes mark survivable zones, not vulnerable ones.
Ask who is missing before patching the present.

puzzles.title: The Heard Head
puzzles.question: Two fair coins flip. You learn at least one landed heads. What is the chance both are heads?
choices: 1/3, since HH, HT, and TH remain
1/2, since the other coin is fifty-fifty
puzzles.correctAnswer: 1/3, since HH, HT, and TH remain
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly 1/3. 'At least one head' removes only TT, leaving three equally likely cases with HH among them. Coins don't consult each other; cases do the work.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 1/3, since HH, HT, and TH remain. The 'other coin' framing smuggles in a specific coin that was never identified. Unspecified information prunes cases, not coins — enumerate, then count.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unspecified news prunes cases, never coins.
'At least one' kills exactly one of four.
The 'other coin' is a mirage without identity.
Enumerate first, intuit second.
Share this: flip two coins and condition aloud ten times.

puzzles.title: The Marble Scoop
puzzles.question: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue marbles. You draw two without looking or replacing. What is the chance both are red?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right: 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. Without replacement, the first draw consumes redness — denominators and numerators both shrink. Replacement status changes everything.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 3/10, since draws multiply and deplete. 9/25 assumes replacement (putting redness back); 3/5 answers a different question. Track what each draw removes, not just what it reveals.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Without replacement, draws consume their own odds.
Shrink numerators and denominators together.
Replacement status is the first question to ask.
Sequential odds multiply; they never merely repeat.
Share this: draw marbles twice and feel the depletion.

puzzles.title: The Blind Pair
puzzles.question: In the dark you grab two socks from 4 black and 6 white. What is the chance they match?
choices: 7/15, counting black pairs plus white pairs
puzzles.correctAnswer: 7/15, counting black pairs plus white pairs
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct: (4/10×3/9) + (6/10×5/9) = 12/90 + 30/90 = 7/15. Matching sums two separate pair-paths — black-black plus white-white.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 7/15, counting black pairs plus white pairs. Matching is a sum over colors: black pairs (12/90) plus white pairs (30/90). Single-color thinking halves the answer; add both roads.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Matching sums over every color's pair-path.
Add both roads; single-color thinking halves answers.
Sequential depletion applies within each path.
Break 'match' into its disjoint cases first.
Share this: compute your own drawer's match odds.

puzzles.title: The Lucky Numbers
puzzles.question: Maya always plays her children's birthdays; her friend plays quick-pick randoms. Both hold one ticket each. Whose jackpot odds are better?
choices: Maya's, since meaningful numbers attract luck
The quick-pick's, since randomness is stronger
Equal — the draw ignores how numbers were chosen
puzzles.correctAnswer: Equal — the draw ignores how numbers were chosen
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly equal. Balls don't read tickets; every combination faces identical odds. (Birthdays do risk sharing jackpots — but winning odds never differ.)
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is equal — the draw ignores how numbers were chosen. Meaning attaches to players, never to balls. One subtlety survives: popular numbers split prizes more often, so randoms keep more when they win.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Draws ignore ticket biographies completely.
Meaning lives with players, never with balls.
Equal odds can still mean unequal payouts (sharing!).
Choose unpopular numbers to keep more if you win.
