puzzles.title: The Doubling System
puzzles.question: A gambler doubles losing roulette bets, certain that one win recovers everything. What flaw sinks this martingale?
choices: Table limits and finite bankrolls meet inevitable long streaks
Casinos ban all mathematics at the door
Doubling is illegal in most jurisdictions
Winning too much gets gamblers arrested
puzzles.correctAnswer: Table limits and finite bankrolls meet inevitable long streaks
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Exponentials outrun wallets: 10 straight losses need 1,024× the base bet, and limits cap recovery. Negative expectation per spin can't be laundered by sizing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is table limits and finite bankrolls meeting inevitable long streaks. The math needs infinite wealth and no ceiling; reality supplies neither. Bet sizing rearranges risk — it never creates edge.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Exponentials outrun every wallet eventually.
Sizing rearranges risk; it never creates edge.
Limits and bankrolls are the system's ceiling.
Negative expectation survives all choreography.
Share this: price ten straight losses at a $5 table.

puzzles.title: The Carnival Eleven
puzzles.question: A carnival charges $5 to roll two dice, paying $20 for totals of 11 or more. What is the player's expected fate per game?
choices: Roughly even money over many plays
A steady loss, since 3 winning faces pay below fair odds
puzzles.correctAnswer: A steady loss, since 3 winning faces pay below fair odds
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Totals 11–12 cover 3 of 36 faces (2/36 + 1/36) — fair pay would be $60, not $20. Expected value: (3/36×$20) − $5 = −$3.33 per roll. Carnivals price hope, not math.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a steady loss, since 6 winning faces pay below fair odds. Count: 11 has two paths, 12 has one — 3 of 36 faces. At $20 for a 1-in-12 shot, the game keeps two-thirds of every dollar long-term.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Count faces before feeling odds.
Fair pay equals the reciprocal of the chance.
Hope is the carnival's highest-margin product.
Expected value settles every game in one line.
Share this: compute one carnival game's true price.

puzzles.title: The Warranty Pitch
puzzles.question: A $400 appliance offers a $90 three-year warranty; breakdowns in that window hit 12% of units at $250 average repair. What says the math?
choices: Buy it — peace of mind is priceless
Decline: expected repair cost ($30) sits far below $90
Buy two warranties for double safety
Repairs always cost exactly the average
puzzles.correctAnswer: Decline: expected repair cost ($30) sits far below $90
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right: 0.12 × $250 = $30 expected cost versus $90 price — a 3× markup funding commissions and profit. Self-insure small risks; reserve insurance for catastrophes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to decline: expected repair cost ($30) sits far below $90. Warranties are profits wrapped in reassurance — retailers push them because margins, not mercy, set the price. Insure catastrophes, not appliances.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Expected cost is probability times price — compute it.
Markups fund commissions, not your safety.
Self-insure the small; insure the catastrophic.
'Peace of mind' has a price — check the tag.
Share this: compute one warranty's expected value aloud.

puzzles.title: The Playlist Cluster
puzzles.question: A music app's true shuffle dealt three same-artist songs in a row, and users cried 'broken!' So the app made shuffles feel fairer. What did engineers sacrifice?
choices: True randomness, since real shuffles cluster naturally
puzzles.correctAnswer: True randomness, since real shuffles cluster naturally
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. Genuine randomness clusters — streaks are its signature — while humans expect unclumpy spread. Spotify-style fixes trade statistical honesty for perceived fairness.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is true randomness, since real shuffles cluster naturally. Random sequences contain runs; 'looks random' means evenly spread, which is non-random. Perceived fairness and statistical fairness are different products.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Real randomness clusters; expectations don't.
Streaks are randomness's signature, not its failure.
'Looks fair' and 'is fair' are different products.
Clustering illusions drive conspiracy thinking everywhere.
Share this: deal cards and admire a natural clump.

puzzles.title: The Jury Majority
puzzles.question: Each juror independently judges correctly 60% of the time. Which verdict is more trustworthy: a unanimous 12–0 or a narrow 7–5?
choices: Equal, since jurors are equally skilled
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — Condorcet's jury logic. Twelve independent 60% signals agreeing is astronomically stronger than a near split. Majorities don't just win; their size testifies.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 12–0, since agreement among fallibles compounds. Independent errors rarely align: unanimity concentrates evidence while 7–5 nearly cancels out. Count the margin, not just the winner.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Margins testify, not just winners.
Independent errors rarely align by chance.
Unanimity concentrates scattered evidence.
Near splits nearly cancel themselves out.
Share this: compare a 12–0 with a 7–5 aloud.

puzzles.title: The Dice Duelists
puzzles.question: Two players race to 6 round-wins at dice, halting at 4–2 when the table collapses. How should the stakes fairly split?
choices: Evenly, since the game never finished
By each player's chance of eventually winning (about 15:1)
puzzles.correctAnswer: By each player's chance of eventually winning (about 15:1)
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — Pascal and Fermat's problem of points. The leader needs 2 more wins, the trailer 4; the trailer must sweep four straight (1/16), so the leader takes ~15/16 of futures. Fairness prices unfinished games by continuation odds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is by each player's chance of eventually winning (about 15:1). Past wins matter only through the remaining paths: the trailer survives only by winning four in a row (1/2)^4 = 1/16. Probability was born settling exactly this bar tab.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unfinished games price by continuation odds.
Remaining paths, not banked wins, set fairness.
The problem of points founded probability itself.
Enumerate finishes before splitting anything.
Share this: settle one interrupted game by counting futures.

puzzles.title: The Exact Streak
puzzles.question: Flipping a fair coin 4 times, which exact sequence is most likely: HHHH, HTHT, or HTTT?
choices: HTHT, since it looks properly mixed
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly equal — every specific 4-flip sequence holds probability (1/2)⁴. 'Looks random' is an aesthetic; the coin writes each script with the same pen.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is all equal at 1/16 each. HHHH feels special and HTHT feels typical, but feelings aren't frequencies: sixteen scripts, one pen, equal ink. Randomness has no favorite handwriting.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Every exact sequence ties at (1/2)^n.
'Looks random' is aesthetics, not arithmetic.
Representativeness fools pattern-hungry minds.
Count scripts before judging handwriting.
Share this: bet a friend HHHH beats HTHT, then collect.

puzzles.title: The Second Picker
puzzles.question: Annemarie calls HHT for three flips; then Bernardo, seeing her call, picks THH. Whose pattern arrives first more often?
choices: Annemarie's, since first picks set the pace
Bernardo's — second pickers hold a systematic edge
puzzles.correctAnswer: Bernardo's — second pickers hold a systematic edge
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — Penney's game. The second chooser can always counter (take the opposite of Annemarie's second symbol, prefixed by her first two): THH beats HHT 2-to-1. Position beats priority in pattern duels.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is Bernardo's — second pickers hold a systematic edge. Penney's game is nontransitive: whatever pattern you name, a counter-pattern wins twice as often. Going second with full information dominates going first.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Second movers with full information dominate.
Nontransitive games have no best first pick.
Counter-patterns exploit overlap structure.
Position can beat priority — check turn order.
Share this: challenge a friend to name a pattern first.

puzzles.title: The Streak Premium
puzzles.question: A bettor wagers that at least one run of 5 heads appears in 100 flips. Should you take the other side?
choices: No: such runs are near-certain across 100 flips
Only if the coin is proven biased
puzzles.correctAnswer: No: such runs are near-certain across 100 flips
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. With ~96 overlapping windows each holding 1/32 odds, the chance of dodging all of them is roughly (31/32)⁹⁶ ≈ 5%. Long sequences make 'rare' runs routine — length manufactures streaks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is no: such runs are near-certain across 100 flips. Five heads feels freakish once, but 96 overlapping chances convert freaks into fixtures. Length is the streak factory; windows multiply chances.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Length manufactures streaks from freaks.
Overlapping windows multiply slim chances.
'Rare once' differs from 'rare somewhere'.
Count windows before pricing run-bets.
Share this: hunt a 5-run inside 100 real flips.

puzzles.title: The Open Lodging
puzzles.question: Rumi compares the mind to a lodging where joy, grief, and shame arrive as unexpected visitors. What building should the self become?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A guest house — every feeling welcomed, entertained, and released. Hospitality toward emotions instead of eviction.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is guest house. Rumi's lodging receives each visitor courteously, even the dark ones, because each was sent as a guide. Welcome replaces resistance.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Feelings arrive as visitors, not residents.
Hospitality beats eviction for every emotion.
Dark arrivals often carry guidance in disguise.
Meet, entertain, and release — then sweep the house.
Share this: welcome one unwelcome feeling as a guest tonight.

puzzles.title: The Lit Wound
puzzles.question: Rumi's most quoted paradox claims the injury itself is the opening. Through what does the light enter?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The wound — breakage as aperture. What hurts opens; what opens admits light. Pain repurposed as entrance.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the wound. The line inverts injury into opportunity: sealed surfaces admit nothing, while breaks let light through. Healing completes the circuit the hurt began.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Breakage can function as aperture.
Sealed surfaces admit nothing new.
Pain repurposed becomes entrance, not just injury.
Inversion turns affliction into instrument.
Share this: name one wound that later let light in.

puzzles.title: The Drop Reversed
puzzles.question: Feeling tiny, you call yourself a drop in a vast sea. Rumi reverses the image entirely. What does he say you wholly contain?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The ocean — the drop contains the sea entire. Smallness inverted: consciousness holds the world it feels lost inside.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the ocean. Rumi flips scale inside out: you are not a fragment adrift but the whole, locally expressed. Containment runs both directions at once.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scale inversions dissolve smallness at a stroke.
Containers and contained trade places in mystic logic.
Feeling lost can signal unrecognized vastness.
Reverse every belittling image once to test it.
Share this: tell someone they hold an ocean today.

puzzles.title: The Reed's Lament
puzzles.question: Cut from its riverbed and hollowed into a flute, the reed sings of one absence above all. What does its music mourn?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Separation — every note mourns the riverbed left behind. Music as homesickness: beauty powered by distance from source.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is separation. The flute's song is the sound of exile — sweetness proportioned to distance from origin. All longing, Rumi suggests, remembers an uncut wholeness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Music can be homesickness made audible.
Sweetness often proportions to distance from source.
Exile narratives explain universal longing.
Trace every lament back to its riverbed.
Share this: listen to one song as pure homesickness.

puzzles.title: The Wise Trade
puzzles.question: Rumi advises selling one prized possession of the mind and buying confusion with the proceeds. What should the seeker purchase?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Bewilderment — trading cleverness for wonder. Certainty closes; confusion opens. The seeker profits by going bankrupt in answers.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is bewilderment. Cleverness defends the known; wonder explores the real. Rumi's economics: sell the fortress, buy the horizon.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Certainty closes doors that wonder opens.
Confusion can be purchased deliberately.
Cleverness defends; bewilderment explores.
Bankruptcy in answers is wealth in questions.
Share this: trade one certainty for a question today.

puzzles.title: The Clever Confession
puzzles.question: 'Yesterday I was clever, so I wanted to change the world. Today I am wise, so I am changing… ' Whom does the wise one work on?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Themselves — ambition matured from world-editing to self-editing. The only renovation project under full jurisdiction.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is themselves. Cleverness assigns homework to billions; wisdom assigns it to one. Jurisdiction decides the project: self is the sole editable territory.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Jurisdiction decides every renovation project.
World-editing is cleverness avoiding homework.
One editable territory exists: the self.
Maturity redirects ambition inward.
Share this: assign yourself one renovation this week.

puzzles.title: The Returning Loss
puzzles.question: Rumi counsels against grieving what vanishes, promising it comes back transformed. What returns in another form?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Anything lost — nothing exits, only re-enters differently. Grief misreads transformation as theft.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is anything lost. Loss is reframed as relocation: forms perish, essences recur. Mourning the shape misses the substance returning.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Forms perish; essences recur in new shapes.
Grief can misread transformation as theft.
Return promises reframe every farewell.
Watch for comebacks wearing strange costumes.
Share this: trace one loss that returned transformed.

puzzles.title: The Burned Barn
puzzles.question: A farmer's barn burns to ash, and that night he finally sees the sky clearly. What becomes visible through the ruin?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The moon — the roof that blocked the sky is gone. Loss as skylight: structures that sheltered also obscured.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the moon. The barn roof had hidden the heavens for years; fire removed the obstruction. Every shelter doubles as a blindfold — ruin occasionally restores the view.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shelters double as blindfolds over time.
Ruin occasionally restores obstructed views.
Roofs block heavens as well as rain.
Ask what each loss unblocks, not just what it burns.
Share this: name one ruin that restored a view.

puzzles.title: The Grief Rhythm
puzzles.question: When grief cracks you open, Rumi prescribes a surprising physical response rather than stillness. What should you do?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Dance — movement metabolizes breakage. Stillness nurses cracks; rhythm weaves them into pattern.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is dance. Rumi's prescription moves grief through muscle instead of marinating in it. Broken-open is a doorway, and doorways are for passing through in motion.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Movement metabolizes what stillness marinates.
Breakage can be danced through, not just endured.
Rhythm weaves cracks into pattern.
Prescriptions beat descriptions for grief.
Share this: move your body through one heaviness today.

puzzles.title: The Divine Language
puzzles.question: Words divide and doctrines quarrel, but Rumi names one wordless medium as the speech of the sacred itself. What is it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Silence — the one tongue no doctrine disputes. Where words fork into sects, quiet stays whole.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is silence. Every claim spoken splits listeners; the unsaid unites them. Rumi's linguistics: truth's native tongue needs no translation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Spoken claims split; the unsaid unites.
Translation needs vanish in wordlessness.
Doctrines quarrel where quiet agrees.
Practice one conversation held mostly in pauses.
Share this: share five minutes of silence with someone.

puzzles.title: The Dark Elephant
puzzles.question: Blindfolded men feel one beast in a dark room — one the trunk, one the leg — then quarrel over its shape. What does each man hold?
puzzles.correctExplanation: One part mistaken for the whole — trunk-men versus leg-men, both right locally, both wrong globally. Perspective + certainty = quarrel.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is one part. Each gripped a genuine piece and universalized it. Rumi's epistemology: touch is honest, extrapolation is the liar. Wholeness needs pooled reports.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Touch is honest; extrapolation lies fluently.
Local rightness plus global certainty equals quarrel.
Wholeness requires pooled, humble reports.
Ask which part of the elephant you are holding.
Share this: pool three views on one dispute today.

puzzles.title: The Complaining Chickpea
puzzles.question: A chickpea protests the boiling pot until the cook explains the heat's purpose. What does the boiling bestow?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Flavor — suffering as seasoning. The pot that tortures raw chickpeas perfects them; heat with purpose is cuisine, not cruelty.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is flavor. The cook's defense reframes torment as preparation: unboiled stays hard and bland. Trials season what comfort leaves raw — maturation needs temperature.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Heat with purpose is cuisine, not cruelty.
Trials season what comfort leaves raw.
Protest measures temperature, not meaning.
Ask the cook before condemning the pot.
Share this: reframe one hardship as seasoning aloud.

puzzles.title: The Parrot's Lesson
puzzles.question: A caged parrot learns that only the apparently dead are carried out past the bars. What must the seeker do before dying?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Die before dying — shed the self while living, and no cage can hold what's left. Freedom through preemptive dissolution.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is die before dying. The parrot's ruse literalizes mystic practice: release identity first, and bars lose their prisoner. Cages confine selves, not the selfless.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cages confine selves, never the selfless.
Release identity and bars lose prisoners.
Ruses can literalize the deepest practices.
Freedom begins before any door opens.
Share this: shed one identity-label for a day.

puzzles.title: The Worn Necklace
puzzles.question: You ransack room after room hunting a diamond necklace, while it has hung around your throat the whole frantic search. Where was the treasure?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The necklace — worn throughout the hunt. Seeking presumes absence; the treasure presumes presence. Stop searching rooms, feel your throat.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the necklace. The frantic rooms dramatize outward seeking; the throat holds the inward answer. Presence overlooked is the oldest treasure plot.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Seeking can presume an absence that isn't.
Outward hunts miss inward holdings.
Feel the throat before ransacking rooms.
Presence overlooked is the oldest plot.
Share this: inventory one treasure already worn.

puzzles.title: The Inward Knowing
puzzles.question: Books can teach one kind of intelligence, but Rumi insists another flows up from inside like a spring. What knowing comes from within?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Inner knowing — spring-water wisdom versus cistern-stored schooling. One is collected, the other erupts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is inner knowing. Acquired intellect stocks cisterns; the soul's intelligence springs. Rumi's hydrology: dig within rather than hauling buckets from libraries.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Springs outlast cisterns in dry seasons.
Collected knowledge differs from erupted wisdom.
Dig within before hauling library buckets.
Two intelligences need two kinds of schooling.
Share this: trust one spring-insight over a stored fact.

puzzles.title: The Sorrow Compost
puzzles.question: Grief feels like waste until Rumi hands you a gardener's task for it. What should sorrow be turned into?
puzzles.correctExplanation: New growth — sorrow composted feeds what comes next. Waste is just fertility awaiting assignment.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is new growth. Gardeners never mourn manure; they assign it. Grief becomes topsoil for futures when worked rather than stored.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Waste is fertility awaiting assignment.
Gardeners assign manure; mourners can assign grief.
Topsoil futures grow from worked sorrow.
Compost, don't warehouse, heavy feelings.
Share this: assign one grief a gardening task.

puzzles.title: The Beyond Field
puzzles.question: 'Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing there is a field.' What lies past all moral quarreling?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A field — meeting ground past right and wrong. Morality's map ends; the meadow begins. Souls rendezvous beyond verdicts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a field. Rumi plants reconciliation outside jurisdiction: no courts, no scorecards, just meeting. Beyond-quarrel space is a place, and arrival is a practice.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reconciliation needs ground outside jurisdiction.
Scorecards end where meadows begin.
Beyond-quarrel is a place, not an idea.
Arrival there is practice, not theory.
Share this: meet someone past one verdict today.

puzzles.title: The Place Soul
puzzles.question: 'Wherever you stand, be the soul of that place.' What should you become of every room you enter?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Its soul — animating presence, not occupying furniture. Rooms have bodies (walls); visitors supply spirit.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is its soul. Standing somewhere is tenancy; ensouling it is stewardship. Rumi converts location into vocation: every place awaits its animating guest.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tenancy differs from stewardship entirely.
Places have bodies; visitors supply spirit.
Location converts to vocation on arrival.
Animate rooms instead of merely occupying them.
Share this: ensoul one room you enter today.

puzzles.title: The Love Bridge
puzzles.question: If love is a bridge, as Rumi says, what two shores does it join?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Self and everything — the span from one to all. Bridges end isolation without erasing either shore.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is self and everything. The bridge image keeps both banks: selfhood stands, and all-ness stands, joined. Union without dissolution is the engineering marvel.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Bridges join without erasing either shore.
Union can preserve what it connects.
Isolation ends where spanning begins.
Span outward without abandoning selfhood.
Share this: bridge yourself to one stranger today.

puzzles.title: The Triple Rescue
puzzles.question: Rumi's triple counsel: be a lamp, a lifeboat, or a ladder. Though different tools, they share one role toward others. What is it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A rescuer — lamp guides, lifeboat carries, ladder lifts. Three metaphors, one vocation: being useful to the stranded.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a rescuer. Lamps guide the lost, lifeboats carry the drowning, ladders lift the stuck — different tools, identical job description. Usefulness is the shared vocation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Different tools can share one vocation.
Guide, carry, lift — usefulness wears many shapes.
Metaphor trios triangulate a single duty.
Ask what unlike images have in common.
Share this: play one rescue role today.

puzzles.title: The Night Moon
puzzles.question: The moon never apologizes for darkness — it shines within it. What must brightness stop avoiding?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Darkness — the moon's canvas, not its enemy. Brightness needs contrast; avoiding night dims the only stage.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is darkness. Moons don't lobby for daylight; they work the night shift gloriously. Contrast is the precondition of radiance, not its obstacle.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Radiance needs contrast to register.
Canvases look like enemies until used.
Night shifts can outshine day jobs.
Stop avoiding the background you need.
Share this: shine deliberately in one dark place.

puzzles.title: The Dark Candle
puzzles.question: 'What hurts you, blesses you. Darkness is your…' What everyday light does Rumi call darkness repurposed?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A candle — darkness converted to illumination. Hurt becomes blessing by the same alchemy: source and gift swap costumes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a candle. The sentence completes by promotion: darkness, renamed, lights the room. Alchemy language turns affliction into equipment.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Affliction converts to equipment by renaming.
Darkness lights rooms once promoted to candle.
Source and gift constantly swap costumes.
Complete bleak sentences with luminous nouns.
Share this: rename one darkness as a candle.

puzzles.title: The Cultivated Ache
puzzles.question: Seekers beg for water — answers, signs, arrivals. Rumi says stop asking for water and request the ache instead. What should you get?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Thirst — the ache that summons water. Answers chase the thirsty; the satisfied are never sought. Wanting is the magnet, not the lack.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is thirst. Begging water skips the engine: thirst draws wells, teachers, and rains toward itself. Cultivate the ache and arrivals volunteer.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Aches summon what satisfactions never attract.
Wanting is the magnet; having is the rest.
Arrivals volunteer toward genuine thirst.
Request engines, not outcomes.
Share this: sharpen one wanting instead of one having.

puzzles.title: The Inner Wall
puzzles.question: 'Your task is not to seek for love, but to seek and find all the barriers within yourself.' What must the seeker locate?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Inner barriers — love already circulates; walls dam it personally. The task is demolition, not acquisition.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is inner barriers. Seeking love outward chases what already flows; the work is removing dams. Find the wall and the river handles the rest.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rivers need un-damming, not chasing.
Walls are personal; currents are universal.
Demolition outperforms acquisition in love.
Locate dams before digging new channels.
Share this: name one inner wall to dismantle.

puzzles.title: The Already Lovers
puzzles.question: Lovers imagine meeting someday, somewhere — but Rumi says the union predates the journey. Where are lovers already?
puzzles.correctExplanation: In each other — union before reunion. The journey doesn't manufacture closeness; it discovers preinstalled belonging.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is in each other. Meeting scenes dramatize what already holds: belonging predates introduction. Travel reveals; it rarely creates.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Belonging can predate introduction entirely.
Journeys discover more often than they manufacture.
Reunion implies a union already installed.
Seek recognition, not construction, in love.
Share this: recognize one preinstalled belonging today.

puzzles.title: The Crowded Schedule
puzzles.question: Parents often hear that the childhood vaccine schedule delivers 'too many too soon' and overwhelms infant immunity. Immunology says the antigen load is trivial beside daily microbial exposure.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False — the claim reverses the scale. Infants meet thousands of antigens daily; the full schedule adds a tiny fraction. 'Too many' mistakes counting shots for counting immune work.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. A baby's immune system confronts thousands of new antigens every day from food, dust, and hands; vaccines contribute a rounding error. The schedule's spacing is logistical, not a concession to overload.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Antigen counts dwarf shot counts by orders of magnitude.
'Overwhelm' needs numbers, not needle counts.
Daily exposure is the denominator critics omit.
Scale intuition before accepting load metaphors.
Share this: compare one playground visit to one vaccine dose.

puzzles.title: The Natural Premium
puzzles.question: Many assume surviving an infection always buys stronger immunity than any vaccine could. In reality, natural infection sometimes protects less (HPV, tetanus) and always charges the disease itself as tuition.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. 'Always stronger' fails twice: some infections (tetanus, HPV) immunize poorly while nearly killing you, and the tuition — the disease — can maim. Vaccines aim for protection without the invoice.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Tetanus survivors gain no immunity at all, and HPV clears without reliably protecting — both while risking death. Natural immunity can be strong (measles), but 'always' plus the disease-price makes the claim collapse.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tuition prices belong in immunity comparisons.
'Always' is the word that breaks most health claims.
Some infections teach nothing while nearly killing.
Compare protection per unit of suffering, not per story.
Share this: name one infection whose tuition exceeds its lesson.

puzzles.title: The Flu Shot Flu
puzzles.question: A coworker feels achy after a flu shot and concludes the injection gave her influenza. Inactivated flu vaccines contain no live virus and cannot cause flu.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Dead-virus shots can't replicate into influenza; aches signal the immune system training, and coincidental seasonal bugs take the blame. Timing plus soreness impersonates infection.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Inactivated vaccines carry no replicating virus, so flu from the shot is mechanistically impossible. Post-shot malaise is boot camp, not battle — plus winter's background sniffles arriving on cue.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mechanistic impossibility beats compelling timing.
Immune training feels like mild illness by design.
Background bugs exploit every coincidence.
Ask what could replicate before blaming the shot.
Share this: explain boot-camp versus battle to a skeptic.

puzzles.title: The Antibiotic Cold
puzzles.question: Colds are viral, so antibiotics — which target bacteria — cannot cure them; rest, fluids, and time do the actual work.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Antibiotics sabotage bacterial machinery that viruses simply lack. Prescribing them for colds buys side effects and resistance while the virus naps through it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Viruses carry none of the cell walls or ribosomes antibiotics attack — the drug finds no target. Demanding antibiotics for colds spends resistance, the shared arsenal, for zero gain.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Drugs need targets; viruses lack these ones.
Mismatched prescriptions spend shared arsenals.
Resistance is the receipt for useless courses.
Match mechanism to microbe before medicating.
Share this: refuse antibiotics for one viral sniffle with confidence.

puzzles.title: The Starved Fever
puzzles.question: Folk wisdom says 'feed a cold, starve a fever,' implying fevers should be denied nutrition. No evidence supports starving fevers; hydration and adequate nourishment aid recovery from both.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The rhyme is mnemonically perfect and medically empty — fevers burn calories and need fuel plus fluids. Rhyming advice deserves the same trials as any other.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. No trial shows starving fevers helps; feverish bodies need water and energy to fund the immune surge. Catchy couplets bypass evidence — audit rhymes like rumors.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rhymes bypass evidence through memorability.
Fevers burn fuel; starving them defunds defense.
Mnemonic perfection is not clinical proof.
Audit couplets exactly like rumors.
Share this: retire one rhyming health myth aloud.

puzzles.title: The Megadose Shield
puzzles.question: Linus Pauling popularized gram-scale vitamin C to prevent colds. Large trials show it does not prevent colds in the general population, though it may slightly shorten them.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False as prevention. Decades of trials: no meaningful drop in cold incidence for ordinary people (marathoners excepted), with at best a small duration trim. Dose size doesn't convert hope into prophylaxis.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The megadose story survived on authority and anecdote against accumulating nulls. Slight shortening is real but tiny; prevention is the claim, and prevention failed. Eminence is not evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Authority plus anecdote loses to accumulating nulls.
Prevention and shortening are different claims — test each.
Dose escalation can't rescue a failed mechanism.
Eminence is not evidence, even Nobel-grade.
Share this: separate shortening from preventing in one remedy.

puzzles.title: The Winter Blame
puzzles.question: Cold air alone cannot conjure a cold — viruses do — though dry winter air helps them spread and survive. Blaming weather skips the actual pathogen.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. No virus, no cold, whatever the thermometer says; winter assists transmission (dry mucosa, indoor crowding, stable virions) without causing infection. Conditions enable; pathogens cause.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Grandmothers confuse accomplices with culprits: chill dries airways and herds people indoors, but rhinoviruses do the infecting. Enable-versus-cause splits most seasonal myths cleanly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Conditions enable; pathogens cause — split them always.
Accomplices (dry air, crowding) aren't culprits.
Seasonality needs a mechanism, not just a correlation.
No virus, no cold, at any temperature.
Share this: defend one hatless outing with virology.

puzzles.title: The Pox Party
puzzles.question: Some parents prefer chickenpox parties over vaccination, judging natural parties gentler. Wild chickenpox hospitalizes and kills at rates the vaccine essentially never approaches.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. 'Natural party' rebrands a virus that caused thousands of yearly hospitalizations; the vaccine's serious-harm rate is orders lower. Gentleness is not a property of nature.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Pre-vaccine chickenpox filled wards yearly with pneumonia and encephalitis cases. Parties guarantee the disease to dodge a far safer needle — risk arithmetic upside down.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Natural' labels no safety level at all.
Party framing hides hospitalization ledgers.
Compare rates, not vibes, across options.
Guaranteed disease versus rare side effect: do the division.
Share this: quote the pre-vaccine ward numbers once.

puzzles.title: The Shielding Herd
puzzles.question: High community vaccination rates protect newborns and immunocompromised people who cannot be vaccinated themselves, by starving outbreaks of pathways.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Herd protection is transmission arithmetic: immunized contacts break chains before they reach the vulnerable. Community coverage functions as a shared shield.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Outbreaks need chains of susceptibles; vaccinated neighbors remove links. The shield is statistical, not moral — fewer pathways, fewer arrivals at fragile doors.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Transmission arithmetic is community armor.
Removing links starves chains aimed at the fragile.
Coverage protects people vaccines can't touch.
Shared shields need shared participation.
Share this: explain herd shielding with a firebreak analogy.

puzzles.title: The Weak Allergy
puzzles.question: Allergy sufferers are sometimes told their immune systems are weak. Allergies actually reflect an overzealous, misdirected response — strength aimed at harmless pollen, not feebleness.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Sneezing at pollen is friendly fire from an aggressive system, the opposite of weak. Misdirected strength, not absent strength, defines allergy.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Weak systems under-react; allergic ones overreact to nothing-dangerous. 'Boosting' an allergic immune system is exactly backwards — treatments calm it down.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Overreaction and underreaction need opposite fixes.
Friendly fire signals strength misaimed, not absent.
'Boost immunity' is meaningless without direction.
Diagnose the direction before prescribing anything.
Share this: correct one 'weak immunity' allergy comment.

puzzles.title: The Civil War
puzzles.question: In autoimmune disease, immune cells mistake the body's own tissues for invaders and attack joints, glands, or nerves accordingly.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Self-tolerance fails and defenses prosecute the homeland — rheumatoid joints, Hashimoto's thyroid, MS myelin. Identity checking is immunity's hardest job.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The same machinery that destroys viruses needs perfect self-recognition, and its failures are autoimmune disease. Friend-or-foe errors at molecular scale cause organ-scale suffering.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-recognition is immunity's hardest exam.
Failed identity checks turn defenses inward.
Same machinery, wrong target, new disease.
Tolerance is an achievement, not a default.
Share this: describe autoimmunity as friendly fire gone chronic.

puzzles.title: The Helpful Heat
puzzles.question: Fever is not merely a symptom to crush — raised temperature directly hampers many pathogens and accelerates immune responses, so routine immediate suppression can be counterproductive.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Heat is a weapon: many microbes replicate worse hot, while immune cells mobilize faster. Treat suffering and danger signs, not the thermometer alone.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Evolution conserved fever across vertebrates because it pays — pathogens slowed, defenders quickened. Suppress for comfort or risky heights, not from thermometer worship.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Symptoms can be weapons, not just warnings.
Conserved responses usually pay their way.
Treat suffering and danger, not numbers alone.
Thermometer worship overtreats useful heat.
Share this: let one mild fever work while you rest.

puzzles.title: The Fading Guard
puzzles.question: Protection from several vaccines declines over years as antibody levels fall, which is why boosters exist — to re-train immunity before exposure tests it.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Waning is normal bookkeeping, not failure — memory cells persist but need refreshing. Boosters are rehearsals scheduled before opening night.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Antibody titers naturally decay; boosters restore readiness without the disease. Needing rehearsal indicts nothing — memory, even immune memory, benefits from review.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Waning is bookkeeping, never betrayal.
Memory of all kinds benefits from review.
Rehearsals precede openings in bodies too.
Boosters refresh readiness without risking disease.
Share this: compare boosters to exam revision aloud.

puzzles.title: The Rewritten Code
puzzles.question: Viral posts claim mRNA vaccines rewrite human DNA. The molecules degrade within days, never enter the nucleus, and lack the machinery to alter genomes.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. mRNA is a temporary work order read in the cytoplasm, then shredded — no nucleus entry, no integration toolkit. Cells process millions of native mRNAs the same way daily.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Genome editing needs nuclear access plus integration enzymes; vaccine mRNA has neither and degrades in days. Familiarity should calm: your cells translate and trash mRNA constantly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mechanistic checklists dissolve scary claims fast.
Ask what machinery each step would require.
Temporary messages can't rewrite permanent archives.
Cells already handle millions of native mRNAs daily.
Share this: explain mRNA as a shredded work order.

puzzles.title: The Invincible Youth
puzzles.question: Healthy young adults sometimes skip vaccines, reasoning strong bodies need no help. Youth lowers personal risk but leaves transmission chains — and rare severe outcomes — fully intact.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. 'Strong' is not 'sterile': the young still catch, carry, and occasionally crash. Skipping trades others' safety plus a personal lottery ticket for zero gain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Low risk is not no risk, and infectiousness doesn't check gym memberships. The young vaccinate partly as couriers' quarantine — protecting grandparents through their own arms.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Low risk never equals no risk or no transmission.
Strength doesn't sterilize; fitness isn't quarantine.
Others' safety rides partly on young arms.
Lottery tickets hide inside 'never happens to me'.
Share this: ask a young skeptic who their shot shields.

puzzles.title: The Trained Tolerance
puzzles.question: The hygiene hypothesis proposes that diverse microbial exposure in childhood calibrates immunity, and its absence may tilt systems toward allergy and autoimmunity.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True — with nuance. Farm-child and microbiome studies support calibration-by-exposure; the hypothesis guides research, not dirt-eating prescriptions. Training data shapes immune judgment.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Systems learn self-from-other partly through early microbial curricula — thin training data, jumpier classifiers. Note the boundary: exposure science, not an excuse to abandon sanitation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Classifiers need training data, immune ones included.
Thin curricula produce jumpier judgments.
Hypotheses guide research, not prescriptions.
Support has limits — sanitation still saves millions.
Share this: explain training-data immunity to a germophobe.

puzzles.title: The Antibacterial Edge
puzzles.question: Antibacterial soaps clean hands better than plain soap for everyday health. Trials find no added benefit, while the additives raise resistance and irritation concerns.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Plain soap's mechanical removal does the work; antibacterial extras add marketing, not medicine — plus resistance selection. Technique beats chemistry at the sink.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Twenty-second scrubbing removes microbes physically; triclosan-style additives show no everyday edge and may breed resistance. Regulators agreed: marketing outran evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mechanical removal does the sink's real work.
Additives need proof, not just prefixes.
Resistance can be selected at bathroom sinks.
Technique (twenty seconds) beats chemistry.
Share this: time one proper handwash tonight.

puzzles.title: The Once Is Enough
puzzles.question: After suffering one cold, people sometimes assume immunity to all future colds. Hundreds of rhinoviruses plus mutating strains make each cold a narrow, temporary shield.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. Immunity covers the culprit strain, not the hundred-plus cousins queuing behind it. One cold is one narrow lesson in a vast curriculum.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Rhinovirus diversity plus constant mutation means last month's shield rarely fits next month's invader. 'A cold' is a hundred diseases sharing a waiting room.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Diversity defeats single-dose experience.
Narrow shields fail against cousin armies.
'A cold' is a hundred diseases in a trench coat.
Temporary, strain-specific: read immunity's fine print.
Share this: blame rhinovirus diversity for your next sniffle.

puzzles.title: The Stressed Shield
puzzles.question: Chronic stress measurably weakens immune defenses — slowing wound healing and dulling vaccine responses — through sustained stress-hormone signaling.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Caregiver and exam-season studies show suppressed immunity under prolonged strain. Acute stress can briefly mobilize; chronic stress taxes and depletes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Cortisol's long simmer redirects resources from defense to endurance — wounds linger, vaccines underperform. Duration flips stress from spur to suppressant.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Duration flips stress from spur to suppressant.
Hormones reallocate defense budgets under strain.
Wounds and vaccines both grade chronic pressure.
Recovery, not endurance, restores the shield.
Share this: prescribe rest as immune medicine once.

puzzles.title: The Endless Training
puzzles.question: If moderate exercise supports immunity, then ever-heavier training must strengthen it further without limit.
puzzles.correctExplanation: False. The curve bends: moderate training boosts, but extreme overtraining opens an infection window (marathon sniffles are classic). Dose makes the medicine — and the poison.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Immunity follows a J-curve with exercise: couch and ultramarathon both raise sick days, moderation minimizes them. More is better until suddenly it isn't.
puzzles.lessonContent:
J-curves hide where straight lines are assumed.
Dose decides medicine versus poison.
Moderation minimizes what extremes maximize.
'U-shaped' thinking beats 'more is better'.
Share this: warn one overtrainer about the open window.

puzzles.title: The Autism Link
puzzles.question: A 1998 paper linked a childhood vaccine to autism; later investigations exposed falsified data, the paper was retracted, and million-child studies found no link.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Fraud, retraction, then massive nulls — the full arc. Timing coincidences (diagnosis age overlaps vaccine schedules) keep the scare shambling without evidence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Wakefield's fabrication collapsed under inquiry, and epidemiology at million-child scale confirmed nothing. Retraction ends the paper; only repetition ends the rumor.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fraud plus timing coincidence outlives retraction.
Million-child nulls outweigh one faked dozen.
Retraction ends papers, not rumors — repeat corrections.
Overlapping schedules manufacture false blame.
Share this: explain schedule-overlap illusion to a worrier.

puzzles.title: The Borrowed Guard
puzzles.question: Newborns arrive with a starter set of maternal antibodies that guard early weeks before fading, which is partly why some vaccines wait for later months.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Placental IgG loans protection that decays over months — a bridge to the infant's own immunity. Schedules time doses for when the loan expires.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Mother's antibodies patrol the newborn temporarily, even blunting some early vaccines — hence the calendar's careful timing. Borrowed guards hold the fort until recruits train.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Borrowed protection bridges to self-sufficiency.
Loans expire on schedule — time doses accordingly.
Maternal gifts can blunt early shots (by design).
Calendars encode decay curves, not bureaucracy.
Share this: explain why some shots wait for month two.

puzzles.title: The Milk Patrol
puzzles.question: Breast milk delivers living immune factors — antibodies, white cells, and prebiotics — that actively protect nursing infants' guts and airways.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Milk is immune logistics: secretory IgA paints mucosa, leukocytes patrol, oligosaccharides feed good microbes. Food plus force in one package.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Beyond nutrition, milk deploys an immune convoy — antibodies coating linings, cells on patrol, prebiotics provisioning allies. Evolution ships defense with dinner.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Food can double as force deployment.
Mucosal painting, patrols, provisioning — layered defense.
Evolution ships defense with dinner.
Logistics thinking reveals milk's second job.
Share this: describe milk as a convoy, not just a meal.

puzzles.title: The Sleeping Virus
puzzles.question: Shingles erupts when the chickenpox virus, dormant in nerve roots for decades, reactivates — which is why only people who had chickenpox (or the live vaccine) risk it.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Varicella never truly leaves; it sleeps in ganglia until immunity wanes with age or stress. Shingles is chickenpox's second act, decades later.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Latency explains the delay: the virus waits out decades in nerve tissue, then encores when surveillance slips. Adult shingles vaccination exists precisely because dormancy ends.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Latency lets viruses outwait decades.
Dormancy ends when surveillance slips.
Second acts follow first infections faithfully.
Nerve tissue harbors history, not just signals.
Share this: explain shingles as chickenpox's encore.

puzzles.title: The Twenty Seconds
puzzles.question: Thorough handwashing measurably cuts respiratory infections, because soap dismantles viral envelopes and scrubbing removes what soap loosens.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Trials show real drops in colds and flu from hand hygiene — chemistry plus mechanics, twenty seconds. The cheapest clinical trial ever keeps replicating.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Enveloped viruses fall apart in surfactants, and friction evicts the rest. No hype, no additives needed — technique and time deliver the effect.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Chemistry plus mechanics beats either alone.
Envelopes dissolve; friction evicts.
Twenty seconds is a dose, not a suggestion.
Cheapest interventions replicate most reliably.
Share this: sing through one full twenty-second wash.

puzzles.title: The Pushed Car
puzzles.question: A man pushes his car up to a hotel door and immediately declares bankruptcy. What is happening?
choices: He crashed into the hotel entrance
His car loan was just denied
He ran out of fuel at the door
puzzles.correctExplanation: He is playing Monopoly — the car token landing on a hotel means bankruptcy. The scene reads as real life until the game frame clicks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is he is playing Monopoly. The car is a token, the hotel sits on Boardwalk, and bankruptcy is the game's verdict. Real-world readings (crashes, loans, fuel) all ignore the word 'pushes,' which is exactly how tokens move.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Verbs betray the frame: tokens get pushed, cars get driven.
Game frames hide inside realistic scenery.
'Bankruptcy' plus 'hotel' is Monopoly vocabulary.
Reframe the nouns before solving the scene.
Share this: narrate one board game as real news.

puzzles.title: The Surgeon's Son
puzzles.question: A father and son are in a crash; the father dies, the boy needs surgery. The surgeon says, 'I cannot operate — he is my son.' How is this possible?
choices: The surgeon is the boy's mother
The surgeon is the boy's grandfather
puzzles.correctAnswer: The surgeon is the boy's mother
puzzles.correctExplanation: The surgeon is his mother. The puzzle works because 'surgeon' primes male-association, making the mother invisible to many solvers.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the surgeon is the boy's mother. The riddle exploits the default assumption that surgeons are men; the grandfather and priest options extend the same bias. Two fathers is possible but not the classic answer.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Stereotypes hide the simplest answers in plain sight.
Gendered role assumptions are the engine of this classic.
When a puzzle feels impossible, check your defaults.
The 'impossible' relation is usually just unassumed.
Share this: pose it to someone and time their pause.

puzzles.title: The Late Pass
puzzles.question: During a race you overtake the next-to-last runner. What position are you now in?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Second to last — you take the passed runner's spot, and they drop to last. Passing near the back works exactly like passing near the front.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is second to last. You swapped with the runner you passed, so you stand where they stood. 'Last place' would require passing the final runner, and 'first place' confuses overtaking with leading.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Overtaking swaps positions at any point in the line.
Back-of-pack passes follow identical logic to front ones.
'Pass X' always means standing where X stood.
Symmetry between race ends defeats the intuition gap.
Share this: ask someone about a late-race pass tonight.

puzzles.title: The Electric Train
puzzles.question: An electric train heads north at 80 km/h; the wind blows south at 20 km/h. Which way does the smoke blow?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Electric trains produce no smoke. The speed and wind details are irrelevant noise designed to trigger a physics calculation on a non-existent phenomenon.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is there is no smoke. Electric locomotives have no combustion, so no smoke exists to blow. The wind and speed are decorative numbers meant to lure you into a vector calculation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Check whether the phenomenon exists before calculating its behavior.
Decorative numbers lure solvers into irrelevant math.
'Electric' is the kill word — it cancels the premise.
Read for contradictions, not just variables.
Share this: verify one phenomenon exists before calculating.

puzzles.title: The Birthday Twice
puzzles.question: A girl was 10 on her last birthday and will be 12 on her next birthday. How is this possible?
choices: She skipped a year in school
She is lying about her age
puzzles.correctExplanation: She was born on February 29, so parties come every four years while age advances yearly. 'Birthday' here counts parties, not years.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is she was born on February 29. A leap-day baby's party count lags her age count, since February 29 returns quadrennially. The puzzle trades on two meanings of 'birthday': annual party versus birth-date anniversary.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Words with multiple meanings are lateral levers.
'Birthday' can mean annual party or birth-date anniversary.
Leap-day edge cases turn calendar logic sideways.
Count what is actually being counted.
Share this: ask a leap-day baby how old they feel.

puzzles.title: The Dark Room
puzzles.question: You have one match and enter a cold room with a kerosene lamp, a wood stove, and a candle. What do you light first?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The match — you must light the match before you can light anything else. The three appliances compete for attention; the prerequisite hides in plain sight.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the match. You cannot light the lamp, stove, or candle without a flame source. The list of three objects is a distractor menu; the true first step is the tool in your hand.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Prerequisites hide inside distractor lists.
Before choosing among options, check what enables them.
The tool in hand often precedes the menu.
Sequence questions: what must happen first?
Share this: strike one match before choosing tools.

puzzles.title: The Two Coins
puzzles.question: Two coins total 30 cents, and one is not a nickel. What are the two coins?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A quarter (25¢) and a nickel (5¢). 'One is not a nickel' refers to the quarter — the other one *is* a nickel. The phrasing excludes exactly one coin from being a nickel.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is quarter and nickel. The statement 'one is not a nickel' is true of the quarter; it does not say 'neither is a nickel.' Scope ambiguity ('one' vs 'both') is the trap.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'One is not X' does not mean 'neither is X'.
Scope quantifiers ('one', 'both', 'neither') are literal.
Check which object the quantifier actually covers.
Precise reading beats pattern guessing.
Share this: parse one tricky sentence aloud today.

puzzles.title: The Months' Code
puzzles.question: What occurs once in a minute, twice in a moment, but never in a thousand years?
puzzles.correctExplanation: The letter M — minute has one M, moment has two Ms, thousand years has zero. Pure orthography, not time.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the letter M. Count the Ms: mInute (1), moment (2), thousand years (0). The riddle masquerades as a temporal puzzle but is a spelling census.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Temporal puzzles often resolve to orthography.
Count letters when time language appears.
'Never in X years' often means zero count in that word.
Shift frames from meaning to spelling.
Share this: count the Ms in your full name.

puzzles.title: The Plane Crash
puzzles.question: A plane crashes on the exact border of the US and Canada. Where do they bury the survivors?
puzzles.correctExplanation: You don't bury survivors — they are alive. The border detail is theater; the verb 'bury' applies only to the dead.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is you do not bury survivors. Survivors, by definition, are living. The border geography is irrelevant theater designed to trigger a jurisdictional debate over a non-existent problem.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Definitions dissolve fake dilemmas.
'Bury' implies dead; 'survivor' implies alive.
Geographic details often mask category errors.
Check the verb against the subject's state.
Share this: catch one fake dilemma this week.

puzzles.title: The Bearded Barber
puzzles.question: A man shaves every single day, yet he always keeps a full beard. How is this possible?
choices: He shaves other people for a living
He only shaves one cheek daily
puzzles.correctAnswer: He shaves other people for a living
puzzles.correctExplanation: He shaves other people for a living — a barber. The verb's object was never stated; solvers supply their own chin.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is he shaves other people for a living. 'Shaves' needs an object the sentence never gives, so readers donate their own face. Occupation splits the actor from the acted-upon.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Transitive verbs need objects the text may withhold.
Readers donate their own face to bare verbs.
Occupation splits actors from the acted-upon.
Ask 'shaves whom?' before answering.
Share this: pose the bearded barber to a friend.

puzzles.title: The Wetter Dryer
puzzles.question: A bath towel soaks up water while making you dry. What common object gets wetter through the very act of drying?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A towel — it absorbs water in the act of drying things. The subject and object of 'dries' are different: it dries you, wetting itself.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a towel. 'Dries' is transitive here: the towel dries you while getting wetter itself. Sponges are close but the classic answer is the towel; deserts and rainbows play no drying role.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Transitive verbs split subject from object.
'It dries' begs the question: dries what?
Absorbers get wetter through their own work.
Find both parties of every action verb.
Share this: ask what gets wetter as it dries.

puzzles.title: The Rooftop Egg
puzzles.question: A rooster lays an egg on a slanted roof. Which side does it roll down?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Roosters don't lay eggs — only hens do. The slanted roof and rolling physics are a complete distractor built on a false premise.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is roosters do not lay eggs. Male chickens cannot lay eggs; the scenario is impossible before the roof angle matters. Impossible premises make all derived questions moot.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Impossible premises nullify all follow-up logic.
Check the subject's capabilities before the scenario.
Biological facts are hard constraints on riddles.
Decorative physics cannot rescue a broken premise.
Share this: check one subject's abilities before its scenario.

puzzles.title: The Hole Dirt
puzzles.question: How much dirt is in a hole 3 feet deep, 6 feet long, and 4 feet wide?
puzzles.correctExplanation: None — a hole, by definition, is the absence of dirt. The dimensions describe the void, not its contents.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is none. A hole is empty space where dirt used to be. Calculating volume answers 'how much dirt was removed,' not 'how much is in it.'
puzzles.lessonContent:
Definitions decide contents: a hole contains absence.
'How much in' vs 'how much removed' are different questions.
Voids hold nothing by definition.
Dimensions of absence are still dimensions of absence.
Share this: describe one void by its dimensions.

puzzles.title: The Pill Schedule
puzzles.question: A doctor gives you three pills and says to take one every half hour. How long will the pills last?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 60 minutes — take the first at 0:00, the second at 0:30, the third at 1:00. The interval is between doses, not after the last one.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 60 minutes. Three doses create two half-hour intervals (0→30, 30→60), not three. Fencepost error: N items make N−1 gaps.
puzzles.lessonContent:
N events create N−1 intervals between them.
Fencepost errors hide in scheduling language.
'Take every X' measures gaps, not total doses.
Count the gaps, not the pills.
Share this: count gaps instead of posts once today.

puzzles.title: The Stamp Dozen
puzzles.question: How many 2-cent stamps are in a dozen?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 12 — a dozen is 12, regardless of the stamp's denomination. The price is irrelevant to the count.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 12. A dozen means twelve. The '2-cent' detail is a distractor trying to redirect you to division or value calculation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A dozen is always twelve — denomination doesn't change count.
Irrelevant attributes (price, color, size) don't alter quantities.
Strip the adjective; the noun carries the number.
Dozen is a count, never a value.
Share this: price a dozen of something silly.

puzzles.title: The Named Fragility
puzzles.question: Name it and you destroy it: what fragile state ends the moment you speak its name?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Silence — speaking ends it. The answer is the phenomenon itself, not an object that can be broken.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is silence. Saying the word produces sound, which ends silence. Glass breaks when dropped and promises break when betrayed — only silence breaks by being named.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Self-referential acts can invert states.
Naming a state can instantiate its opposite.
Fragility here is logical, not material.
Check whether the verb enacts the noun.
Share this: hold a ten-second quiet contest with a friend.

puzzles.title: The River Crossing
puzzles.question: A man must cross a river with a fox, a chicken, and a sack of grain. The boat holds him plus one item. The fox eats the chicken if left alone; the chicken eats the grain if left alone. What is the minimum number of crossings?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 7 crossings. The sequence requires shuttling the chicken back and forth as the 'safe' item: (1) chicken over, (2) return, (3) fox over, (4) chicken back, (5) grain over, (6) return, (7) chicken over. The chicken is the only item that can be left with either other.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 7. The chicken is the shuttle: it must be ferried back to separate the other pairs. Three items with two conflict pairs need 2N+1 = 7 trips. Fewer crossings leave a fatal pairing alone.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Identify the 'safe' item that tolerates both others.
Shuttle the safe item to break conflict pairs.
N conflicting pairs with one safe item needs 2N+1 crossings.
Draw the state graph before counting trips.
Share this: ferry one conflict apart this week.

puzzles.title: The Calendar Puzzle
puzzles.question: Some months have 30 days, some have 31. How many have 28?
choices: None — February has 29 in leap years
puzzles.correctExplanation: All twelve months reach day 28 — February stops near there while the rest continue past it. The question asks 'at least 28,' not 'exactly 28.'
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is twelve — all of them. Every month reaches day 28. The trap is hearing '28 days' and thinking 'February only,' but 30- and 31-day months also contain days 1 through 28.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'How many have X' means 'at least X' unless 'exactly X' is stated.
Threshold questions include all who clear the bar.
February is the minimum, not the only one.
Threshold thinking beats equality thinking.
Share this: ask how many months have 28 days.

puzzles.title: The Penguin Flight
puzzles.question: Penguins are birds. Birds fly. Therefore penguins fly. What is wrong with this argument?
choices: The premise 'birds fly' is false as a universal
The conclusion is true for most birds
Logic does not apply to animals
puzzles.correctAnswer: The premise 'birds fly' is false as a universal
puzzles.correctExplanation: The premise 'birds fly' is a generalization with exceptions (penguins, ostriches, kiwis). Universal premises require zero counterexamples; one breaks the chain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the premise 'birds fly' is false as a universal. Logic is valid (if all birds fly, and penguins are birds, then penguins fly), but soundness fails because the first premise is not universally true. Validity ≠ soundness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Validity needs true premises; soundness needs both.
Generalisations with exceptions are not universal premises.
One counterexample breaks 'all'.
Check premises before trusting the chain.
Share this: test one universal claim for exceptions.

puzzles.title: The Headless Body
puzzles.question: Heads on one face, tails on the other, and no torso anywhere. What pocket object fits this anatomy?
puzzles.correctExplanation: A coin — heads and tails with no body between. Body-part words name coin faces, not anatomy.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a coin. Heads and tails are the two faces; 'body' has no referent at all. Snakes, hammers, and rivers each own real bodies or flows — only the coin fits all three clues.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Body-part words often name faces, not anatomy.
Heads and tails are a small disc's entire vocabulary.
'No body' eliminates every living candidate.
Match all three clues before committing.
Share this: ask what has a head and tail tonight.

puzzles.title: The Family Photo
puzzles.question: A man looks at a photo and says, 'Brothers and sisters I have none, but this man's father is my father's son.' Who is in the photo?
puzzles.correctExplanation: His son. 'My father's son' with no brothers = me. So 'this man's father is me' → the man in the photo is my son.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is his son: with no brothers, 'my father's son' means me, so the photo-man's father is me. Substitute inward and the chain resolves.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Substitute known equals step by step.
'No brothers' collapses 'my father's son' to 'me'.
Chain relations by replacing each link.

puzzles.title: The Lift Button
puzzles.question: A man lives on the 10th floor. Every morning he takes the elevator to the ground floor. Returning, if it's raining or others are in the lift, he goes to 10; otherwise he goes to 7 and walks up three flights. Why?

puzzles.title: The Weighty Feathers
puzzles.question: Which is heavier: a kilogram of lead or a kilogram of feathers?
choices: They are equal — both are one kilogram
puzzles.correctAnswer: They are equal — both are one kilogram
puzzles.correctExplanation: Equal — a kilogram is a kilogram. Density differs, volume differs, mass is identical by definition.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — they are equal. The question fixes the mass (1 kg) for both; density and volume vary, but weight (mass × gravity) is the same. The intuition 'lead feels heavier' confuses density with mass.
puzzles.lessonContent:

Definitions fix the compared quantity; intuition switches it.

puzzles.title: The Sibling Count
puzzles.question: A girl has as many brothers as sisters. Each brother has twice as many sisters as brothers. How many brothers and sisters are in the family?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 4 sisters, 3 brothers: the girl sees 3-and-3 excluding herself, while each boy sees 4 sisters and 2 brothers. Two viewpoints, two equations, one family.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 3 brothers, 4 sisters. Girl sees 3 brothers, 3 sisters (excluding herself) → equal. Boy sees 4 sisters, 2 brothers (excluding himself) → sisters are twice brothers. The two perspectives give two equations.

puzzles.title: The Clock Strike
puzzles.question: A clock strikes 6 times in 5 seconds. How long does it take to strike 12 at the same rate?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 11 seconds. Strikes are points; seconds live in the gaps between them. Six strikes give 5 gaps of one second, so twelve give 11.
puzzles.lessonContent:

puzzles.title: The Cat Correction

Neither alive nor dead in any sense

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is classical ignorance: alive or dead, unknown to us. Decoherence converts would-be superposition into ordinary uncertainty almost instantly at cat scale. Schrödinger's point was the absurdity, and decoherence explains exactly where the quantumness leaks away.

No measurement can ever tell them apart
Brighter light exposes the mixture's impurity

puzzles.title: The Aquarium Buckets
puzzles.question: An aquarium has 15-liter and 11-liter buckets. Two 11-pours into the 15-bucket strand a remainder. How many liters stay in the second bucket?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 7 liters: 11+11=22 against 15 strands 7. Fish-tank subtraction, no third pour needed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 7. Two 11-pours total 22; the big bucket keeps 15 and strands 7. Check the two-pour difference before building chains.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Two-pour differences deserve checking first.
22−15 strands without further choreography.
Short solutions hide behind long habits.
Always test the double-pour before chaining.

puzzles.title: The Ink Wells
puzzles.question: A scribe has 16-dram and 9-dram wells. Two 9-pours into the 16-well strand ink in the second well. How many drams?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 2 drams: 9+9=18 against 16 strands 2. Scribal subtraction in two moves.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 2. Two 9-pours total 18; the big well keeps 16 and strands 2. Ink, water, wine — the arithmetic never changes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Contents never change the arithmetic.
18−16 strands regardless of liquid.
Two moves can distill tiny remainders.
Units change; subtraction doesn't.

puzzles.title: The Orchard Vats
puzzles.question: An orchard has 21-liter and 15-liter vats. Two 15-pours into the 21-vat strand juice. How many liters remain behind?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 9 liters: 15+15=30 against 21 strands 9. Orchard arithmetic, two pours.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 9. Two 15-pours total 30; the vat keeps 21 and strands 9. Big vessels obey the same double-pour rule.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Big vessels obey small-vessel rules.
30−21 strands without further pours.
Scale changes nothing but the numbers.
Double-pour first, choreograph later.

puzzles.title: The Harbor Drums
puzzles.question: A harbor has 22-liter and 16-liter drums. Two 16-pours into the 22-drum strand oil. How many liters stay behind?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 10 liters: 16+16=32 against 22 strands 10. Harbor subtraction, two moves.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 10. Two 16-pours total 32; the big drum keeps 22 and strands 10. Oil obeys water's arithmetic exactly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Liquids share one arithmetic worldwide.
32−22 strands in exactly two pours.
Harbor drums follow garden barrels.
Two-pour checks precede all choreography.

puzzles.title: The Milkmaids' Share
puzzles.question: A full 8-liter pail plus empty 5-liter and 3-liter jugs must yield exactly 4 liters in the 5-jug for a recipe. How many liters end there?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 4 liters: 8→5, 5→3 (2 in 5), 3→8, pour 2→3, 8→5 — the 5-jug holds 4. Three vessels waltz.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 4. The dance: fill 5, park 2 via the 3-jug, return the 3, then refill 5 against the parked 2... precisely landing 4. Three vessels waltz where two march.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Three vessels waltz where two march.
Park remainders in the smallest jug.
Return trips enable final combinations.
Recipes justify the extra choreography.

puzzles.title: The Desert Travelers
puzzles.question: Two travelers share a full 12-liter skin with empty 7-liter and 5-liter skins. After 12→7, 7→5, 5→12, 7→5, 12→7, 7→5, 5→12, 7→5, 12→7, 7→5, and 5→12, what equal share do two skins hold?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 6 liters each: the eleven-pour script parks water in the 5-skin and returns it until the 12-skin and 7-skin both read 6. Fairness by script.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 6. Follow the eleven pours: park 2, return it, park 4, return it, park 6 — ending with 6 in the 12-skin and 6 in the 7-skin. Scripts split fairly; improvisation spills.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fair splits are choreography, not luck.
Park and return across all three vessels.
Equal shares emerge from exact sequences.
Desert fairness runs on pour-count.

puzzles.title: The Chemistry Set
puzzles.question: A set holds a full 6-liter flask with empty 4-liter and 3-liter flasks. After pouring 6→4, 4→3, 3→6, 4→3, and 6→4, how much sits in the 6-flask?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 1 liter: 6→4 leaves 2; 4→3 leaves 1 in 4; 3→6 makes 5; 4→3 empties the 1 over; 6→4 leaves 1 behind. Five scripted pours.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 1. Follow the script: 2 stays, 1 strands in the 4-flask, returns to make 5, vacates, and the final pour leaves a single liter. Scripts beat improvisation.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scripts beat improvisation in long pours.
Follow numbered pours without skipping.
Single liters emerge from five-move dances.
Write the sequence; then pour it.

puzzles.title: The Cider Press
puzzles.question: A press holds a full 15-liter tun with empty 9-liter and 6-liter casks. After 15→9, 9→6, 6→15, 9→6, 15→9, and 9→6, how much sits in the 9-cask?
puzzles.correctExplanation: 6 liters: 15→9, 9→6 (3 in 9), 6→15, 9→6 (the 3 over), 15→9, 9→6 (3 more over) — the 9-cask rests at 6. Scripted cider.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 6. The six-pour script strands 3, returns it, refills, and the final transfer parks 6. Cider obeys the same scripts as water.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scripts transfer across liquids unchanged.
Strand, return, refill, park — the rhythm.
Six pours resolve fifteen liters exactly.
Cider arithmetic is water arithmetic.

puzzles.title: The Barred Measure
puzzles.question: A brewer holds 10-liter and 15-liter vats and needs exactly 7 liters. Can this measure be isolated?
puzzles.correctExplanation: No solution: 10 and 15 share divisor 5, so only multiples of 5 are reachable — 7 never arrives. Fives guard this gate.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is no solution. Every pour combines 10s and 15s, keeping all results in the multiples-of-5 family; 7 is a permanent outsider. Gates first, pours second.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fives admit only multiples of five.
Seven sits outside that family forever.
Divisors gate vats as strictly as jugs.
Test family membership before pouring.

puzzles.title: The Forbidden Four
puzzles.question: With 9-liter and 6-liter cans, a painter needs exactly 4 liters of thinned paint. Can this measure be isolated?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Cannot be done: both vessels are multiples of 3, so every reachable amount is too — and 4 is not. The gate of three bars the painter.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is cannot be done. Multiples of 9 and 6 combine only into multiples of 3; 4 sits outside that family forever. No choreography crosses a divisor gate.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Multiples stay within their divisor family.
Gates of three bar non-members permanently.
Families of amounts never admit outsiders.
Test membership before attempting pours.
Share this: gate one target with threes.

puzzles.title: The Unreachable Five
puzzles.question: An 8-liter and a 12-liter drum stand ready, and the recipe demands exactly 5 liters. Can this measure be isolated?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Not possible: 8 and 12 share divisor 4, so only multiples of 4 are reachable — 5 never arrives. Fours guard this gate.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is not possible. Every pour combines 8s and 12s, keeping all results in the multiples-of-4 family; 5 is a permanent outsider. Gates first, pours second.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Families of four admit no fives.
Every pour preserves the divisor invariant.
Outsiders stay outside regardless of effort.
Gates first, pours second — always.
