puzzles.title: The Blind Ledger
puzzles.question: Escalating decision-makers systematically ignore opportunity costs — what else the committed money and years could accomplish.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Escalation accounting omits roads not taken: visible losses debated, invisible alternatives ignored. Blind ledgers balance falsely.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Opportunity costs stay invisible while sunk costs glare: ledgers record spending, never forgone gains. Blindness to alternatives funds persistence.

Ledgers record spending, never forgone gains.

Roads not taken need pricing too.

puzzles.title: The Overrun Law
puzzles.question: Megaprojects systematically overrun budgets while underdelivering benefits — Flyvbjerg's iron law of doomed big builds.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True. Dams, rails, stadiums: over budget, over time, under benefits — systematically. Iron laws describe, then warn.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Flyvbjerg's databases prove the pattern across continents and decades: strategic misrepresentation plus optimism lock in losers. Bigness guarantees overruns statistically.

puzzles.question: Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider in 1993 despite roughly $2 billion already spent on it.

puzzles.title: The Bygone Rule
puzzles.question: Rational choice treats sunk costs as bygones — relevant to neither future costs nor future benefits.

puzzles.correctExplanation: Are you asleep — yes falsifies itself: sleepers can't testify, liars can only say no. Questions defeating answers.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is are you asleep. Truthful yeses impossible: sleep precludes testifying, waking falsifies content. Self-defeating questions guard paradoxes.
puzzles.hintText:
Yes would falsify itself here.
Sleepers cannot testify truly.
Only no answers honestly.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Yes answers falsify themselves here.
Truth demands negative replies.
Sleepers never testify truly.
Unanswerable yeses guard paradoxes.
Share this: answer no truthfully once.

puzzles.title: The Weightless Load
puzzles.question: I weigh nothing yet crush the bearer; confession lightens what denial doubles. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Guilt — weighing nothing, crushing bearers, lightened by confession. Loads without mass.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is guilt. Weigh-nothing plus crush-bearer plus confess-lightens isolates moral weight: scales miss it, souls feel it. Denial doubles all burdens.
puzzles.hintText:
Scales miss these tons.
Confession lightens crushing loads.
Denial doubles all burdens.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scales miss crushing loads daily.
Confession lightens unweighed tons.
Denial doubles all burdens.
Weightless loads crush bearers.
Share this: lighten one load honestly.

puzzles.title: The Empty Catcher
puzzles.question: I hold everything yet contain nothing; fishermen trust me with their livelihood. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Net — holding everything, containing nothing. Emptiness that catches.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is net. Hold-all plus contain-none isolates mesh: passage constitutes capture. Livelihoods hang on holes.
puzzles.hintText:
Everything passes through my keeping.
Nothing stays within my hold.
Fishermen trust my emptiness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Everything passes through keeping.
Nothing stays within holds ever.
Fishermen trust structured voids.
Holding means letting through.
Share this: cast one empty hold.

puzzles.title: The Monthly Renewer
puzzles.question: I die each month yet never perish; tides obey my phases. What am I?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Moon — monthly dying, never perishing, tide-commanding. Deaths that renew.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is moon. Die-monthly plus never-perish isolates phases: waning funds waxing eternally. Tides keep lunar time.
puzzles.hintText:
Monthly deaths never finish me.
Tides obey all my phases.
Phases renew my whole face.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Monthly deaths never finish cycles.
Tides obey changing faces.
Phases renew wholes nightly.
Dying monthly means living ever.
Share this: howl one phase kindly.

puzzles.title: The Unlived Life
puzzles.question: Socrates declared one kind of life not worth living for a human being. Which life?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Unexamined life — living unquestioned forfeits humanity's signature act: reflection. Examination dignifies existence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is unexamined life. Apology's sentence stands: unscrutinized living wastes humanness. Worth requires wondering first.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Worth requires wondering first always.
Unscrutinized living wastes humanness.
Reflection dignifies bare existence.
Examination is humanity's signature.
Share this: examine one hour today.

puzzles.title: The Wise Ignorance
puzzles.question: Oracle-named wisest, Socrates found only one thing he knew. What was his sole expertise?
puzzles.correctExplanation: His ignorance — knowing the extent of not-knowing: wisdom as measured lack. Experts overflow; Socrates empties.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is his ignorance. Craftsmen knew trades but pretended to wisdom; Socrates knew neither, and knew it. Measured lack beats unmeasured surplus.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Measured lack beats unmeasured surplus.
Knowing limits constitutes wisdom here.
Experts overflow; sages empty usefully.
Ignorance owned outperforms knowledge feigned.
Share this: own one ignorance proudly.

puzzles.title: The Refuting Walk
puzzles.question: Socrates asked definitions, drew out contradictions, and left interlocutors improvedly puzzled. What is this method?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Elenchus — refutation by questioning: premises granted, contradictions derived, conceit purged. Midwifery through embarrassment.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is elenchus. Lectures inform; elenchus transforms by refuting: interlocutors birth truth through aporia. Puzzlement is progress here.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Puzzlement marks progress truly here.
Refutation purges conceit reliably.
Questions birth truths lectures abort.
Midwifery embarrasses productively.
Share this: refute one conceit kindly.

puzzles.title: The Stinging Insect
puzzles.question: Athens dozed like a sluggish horse; Socrates claimed heaven sent something to sting it awake. What was he?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Gadfly — heaven-sent irritant to drowsy democracy: stinging steeds into motion. Annoyance as civic duty.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is gadfly. Horses doze; flies bite awake: Socrates appointed himself Athens' alarm. Civic duty stings sometimes.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Alarms annoy sleepers necessarily.
Stings wake drowsy democracies.
Heaven sends irritants purposefully.
Civic duty buzzes persistently.
Share this: sting one slumber kindly.

puzzles.title: The Tended Soul
puzzles.question: Wealth and reputation mean nothing, Socrates urged, beside caring for one thing above all. What deserves supreme care?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Their souls — care of psyche over property: Apology's economics inverts Athens' ledger. Souls appreciate; fortunes rust.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is their souls. Wealth rusts, reputations fade, souls compound: Socratic portfolio theory. Tend interiors before exteriors.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Interiors compound; exteriors rust fully.
Souls appreciate with tending daily.
Portfolios invert Athenian ledgers.
Care within outlasts wealth without.
Share this: tend one soul today.

puzzles.title: The Knowing Virtue
puzzles.question: Socrates scandalously identified virtue with a cognitive state — vice being mere ignorance. What is virtue?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Knowledge — virtue as understanding the good: knowers act well necessarily. Ethics reduces to epistemology boldly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is knowledge. Habits, commandments, and sentiments miss it: Socratic intellectualism makes wrongdoing a cognitive bug. Teach goodness; behavior follows.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Wrongdoing debugs as ignorance here.
Understanding necessitates right action.
Epistemology grounds ethics boldly.
Teach goodness; watch behavior follow.
Share this: know one good fully.

puzzles.title: The Willing Wrong
puzzles.question: If virtue is knowledge, wrongdoing must be involuntary — error, never malice. Who does evil on purpose?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Nobody willingly — all wrongdoers mistake goods: apparent benefit deceives choosers. Malice dissolves into miscalculation.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is nobody willingly. Volunteers for evil vanish under analysis: everyone aims at seeming good. Mistakes explain monsters fully.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Seeming goods deceive all choosers.
Monsters mistake; none malice purely.
Errors explain evils completely.
Willing wrongs exist nowhere here.
Share this: pity one wrongdoer today.

puzzles.title: The Weak Will
puzzles.question: If virtue is knowledge, why do people act against their better judgment? What threatens intellectualism?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Akrasia — weakness of will: knowing better, doing worse. Appetites veto insights daily.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is akrasia. Judgments lose to appetites nightly: better known gets overruled often. Knowing battles wanting eternally.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Judgments lose to appetites nightly.
Better known gets overruled often.
Weakness challenges intellectualism directly.
Knowing battles wanting eternally.
Share this: strengthen one weak will.

puzzles.title: The Pious Puzzle
puzzles.question: Is conduct pious because gods love it, or loved because pious? What makes piety pious?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Its own nature — gods track goodness; goodness leads. Love follows worth, never founds it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is its own nature. Dependence directions decide: loved-because-pious grounds divinity in goodness. Natures precede divine approval.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Gods track goodness; goodness leads.
Love follows worth, never founds it.
Natures precede divine approval.
Piety stands independent ever.
Share this: love one good for itself.

puzzles.title: The Search Paradox
puzzles.question: Meno asks: how search for unknown things, unrecognizable even if found? What blocks inquiry?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Inquiry paradox — searching puzzles philosophers: unknowns resist seeking logically. Recognition needs prior acquaintance.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is inquiry paradox. Unknowns resist seeking: neither knowledge nor ignorance can start. Paradoxes stall inquiries initially.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Searching puzzles philosophers deeply.
Unknowns resist seeking logically.
Recognition needs prior acquaintance.
Paradoxes stall inquiries initially.
Share this: seek one unknown bravely.

puzzles.title: The Remembered Truth
puzzles.question: Learning, says Meno's Socrates, is really something else entirely — souls retrieving eternal knowledge. What is learning?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Recollection — souls retrieve eternal truths: learning remembers, never acquires. Eternity tutors temporal minds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is recollection. Acquisition models fail: latent knowledge awaits prompting. Remembering replaces stocking up.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Souls retrieve eternal truths slowly.
Learning remembers, never acquires.
Latent knowledge awaits prompting.
Eternity tutors temporal minds.
Share this: recall one eternal truth.

puzzles.title: The Geometry Slave
puzzles.question: An uneducated slave boy solves geometry under questioning alone. Who demonstrates innate knowledge?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Slave boy — untutored minds solve geometry: questioning draws latent proofs. Schooling unnecessary for insight.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is slave boy. Schooling absent, insight present: dialogue extracts what teaching never installed. Geometry sleeps in all minds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Untutored minds solve geometry nightly.
Questioning draws latent proofs.
Schooling unnecessary for insight here.
Geometry sleeps in all minds.
Share this: question one untutored mind.

puzzles.title: The Definition Killer
puzzles.question: Every proposed definition of courage meets cases that break it. What defeats definitions?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Counterexamples surface — cases break neat definitions: courage resists formula. Instances defeat abstractions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is counterexamples surface. Definitions fall to instances: one brave coward or cowardly hero undoes formulas. Neatness yields to cases.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cases break neat definitions daily.
Definitions die by example reliably.
Exceptions emerge from inquiry.
Neatness yields to instances.
Share this: counter one definition kindly.

puzzles.title: The Oracle's Riddle
puzzles.question: Declared wisest for knowing his own ignorance, Socrates outranked experts. What constituted his wisdom?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Knows his ignorance — awareness crowns the ignorant: confessed gaps outrank feigned fullness. Oracles praise measured lacks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is knows his ignorance. Experts overflowed with unexamined certainties; Socrates inventoried emptiness accurately. Wisdom knows its own borders.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Awareness crowns the ignorant truly.
Confessed gaps outrank feigned fullness.
Oracles praise measured lacks.
Wisdom knows its own borders.
Share this: confess one border today.

puzzles.title: The Strange Gods
puzzles.question: Athens charged Socrates with introducing new divinities and corrupting youth. What religious crime was alleged?
puzzles.correctExplanation: New divinities — unlicensed gods threatened civic cults: novelty frightened priesthoods. Charges veil politics.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is new divinities. Asebeia alleged foreign worship: strange gods menaced established rites. Accusations veil political motives.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Charges alleged novel worship falsely.
Strange gods threatened civic cults.
Accusations veil political motives.
Novelty frightens established priesthoods.
Share this: tolerate one strange god.

puzzles.title: The Welcome End
puzzles.question: Death is either dreamless sleep or soul migration — Socrates fears neither outcome. Which should frighten him?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Neither option — sleep rests, migration converses: both outcomes welcome. Fear fits neither alternative.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is neither option. Oblivion rests the weary; migration introduces heroes. Apology disarms death both ways.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sleep rests the weary fully.
Migration converses with heroes.
Fear fits neither outcome ever.
Welcome both alternatives calmly.
Share this: fear neither outcome.

puzzles.title: The Willing Cup
puzzles.question: Socrates drank hemlock conversing cheerfully about immortality. How did he meet death?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Cheerfully drinking — cups emptied conversing: philosophy continued past poison. Willing drinkers teach dying.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is cheerfully drinking. Gloom never entered the cell: dialogue outlasted hemlock. Conversations defeat cups.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Cups emptied conversing calmly.
Cheer accompanies final draughts.
Conversations outlast poison here.
Willing drinkers teach dying.
Share this: drink one cup calmly.

puzzles.title: The Bound Citizen
puzzles.question: Escape arranged, Socrates stayed to drink the cup. What bound him to Athens' verdict?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Laws' authority — verdicts bind consenting citizens: residence implies agreement. Authority legitimized by dwelling.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is laws' authority. Agreements outlive advantages: citizens owe obedience reciprocally. Escape would wrong the laws that raised him.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Verdicts bind consenting citizens fully.
Agreements outlive advantages personally.
Citizens owe obedience reciprocally.
Authority legitimized by residence.
Share this: honor one hard verdict.

puzzles.title: The Better Wound
puzzles.question: Socrates claimed suffering injustice surpasses doing it. Which fate is preferable?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Suffering it — endured wrongs outrank inflicted ones: victims keep cleaner souls. Doing stains; suffering ennobles.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is suffering it. Inflicting corrupts agents; enduring preserves them. Preferable fates favor patients over perpetrators.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Endured wrongs outrank inflicted ones.
Victims keep cleaner souls here.
Doing stains; suffering ennobles.
Preferable fates favor patients.
Share this: suffer one wrong nobly.

puzzles.title: The Stronger Fallacy
puzzles.question: Thrasymachus defined justice as the advantage of the stronger. What does this reduce morality to?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Power worship — strength defines right absurdly: rulers flattered, justice voided. Might makes wrong.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is power worship. Advantage-of-stronger enthrones bullying: morality collapses into flattery. Strong wrongs never make rights.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Strength defines right absurdly here.
Rulers flattered corrupt justice fully.
Might makes wrong, never right.
Advantage worship degrades morals.
Share this: defy one strong wrong.

puzzles.title: The Loving Ladder
puzzles.question: Diotima's ladder climbs from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself. What ascends?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Eros ascending — ladders climb toward Beauty: bodies begin, absolutes complete. Desire educates upward.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is eros ascending. Bodies start what Beauty finishes: love climbs rungs of loveliness. Ascents transform appetites.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Ladders climb toward Beauty steadily.
Bodies begin; Beauty completes.
Desire ascends rungs of loveliness.
Climbing loves reach absolutes.
Share this: climb one rung lovingly.

puzzles.title: The Known Self
puzzles.question: Alcibiades learned that caring for oneself requires first knowing something. What must be known?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Oneself — knowing precedes caring: selves studied yield tended souls. First know, then tend.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is oneself. Care without knowledge misfires: comprehension precedes cultivation. Selves known get tended well.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Knowing precedes caring always.
Selves studied yield tended souls.
Care follows comprehension reliably.
First know, then tend fully.
Share this: know one self better.

puzzles.title: The Dying Art
puzzles.question: Philosophy, says Phaedo's Socrates, is practice for a final separation. What does it rehearse?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Dying practice — rehearsals prepare final separations: souls practice leaving bodies. Philosophy trains farewells.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is dying practice. Separations rehearsed lose terror: practiced farewells free minds. Training outlasts trembling.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rehearsals prepare final separations.
Souls practice leaving bodies.
Philosophy trains farewells daily.
Separation rehearsed loses terror.
Share this: rehearse one farewell.

puzzles.title: The Unharmed Soul
puzzles.question: A better man cannot be harmed by a worse, Socrates claimed at trial. What can't touch him?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Real harm — better souls resist damage: worse men harm themselves only. Virtue armors inwardly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is real harm. Verdicts wound bodies, never souls: goodness insulates essence. Harmlessness crowns the just.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Better souls resist damage fully.
Worse men harm themselves only.
Virtue armors against true injury.
Harmlessness crowns goodness here.
Share this: harm no better soul.

puzzles.title: The Ruling Wisdom
puzzles.question: Plato's Republic crowns lovers of wisdom as rulers of the just city. Who should govern?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Philosopher-kings — wisdom should rule cities: lovers of truth govern best. Knowledge crowns governance.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is philosopher-kings. Warriors fight, producers make, thinkers rule: each part performs its nature. Cities mirror souls hierarchically.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Wisdom should rule cities justly.
Lovers of truth govern best.
Rulers thinking beat warriors fighting.
Knowledge crowns governance ideally.
Share this: elect wisdom once.

puzzles.title: The Soaked Commuter
puzzles.question: If it rains, the plaza gets wet. It is raining right now. What must be true?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The rule fires the moment its condition holds: rain, therefore a wet plaza. Modus ponens is the one move that never misfires.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that the plaza gets wet. The rule says rain always brings a wet plaza, and it is raining, so the conclusion is locked in.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Modus ponens moves from a confirmed condition to its guaranteed result.
It works only when the rule itself is reliable — check the rule before trusting the result.
Real rules hide in contracts, recipes, and warning labels.
Share this: spot one if-then rule in your day and name its condition and result.

puzzles.title: The Silent Alarm
puzzles.question: If the battery were dead, the alarm would not beep. The alarm is beeping loudly. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A dead battery would silence the alarm, yet it beeps — so the battery is alive. Denying the result denies the condition.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the battery is not dead. If it were dead there would be no beep, and the alarm is beeping, so the dead-battery idea is refuted.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Modus tollens kills a hypothesis by disproving its required outcome.
Scientists live on this move: predict an observation, see it fail, drop the theory.
It needs a strict rule — a dead battery must always silence the device.
Share this: catch one failed prediction today and say what it rules out.

puzzles.title: The Blooming Excuse
puzzles.question: If Maya waters the roses, they bloom. The roses are blooming. Maya concludes she must have watered them. Is that valid?
choices: No — the middle term is undistributed
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — blooming roses don't prove who watered them. Rain, a neighbor, or a sprinkler could explain it. The result can't confirm its own condition.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The flaw is affirming the consequent. Blooming follows watering, but other causes bloom roses too, so Maya's watering is unproven.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A result never proves its own cause — many roads lead to the same outcome.
Detectives and doctors both list alternative explanations before concluding.
Ask 'what else could produce this?' before blaming one cause.
Share this: name two causes for one everyday observation tonight.

puzzles.title: The Timely Return
puzzles.question: If you return the book late, you pay a fine. You returned the book on time. So you owe no fine — valid?
choices: Yes — the rule runs both ways
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — returning on time removes one fine, not every possible fine. Denying the condition proves nothing about the result.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the move denies the antecedent. Being on time dodges the late fine only; other fines could still apply, so 'no fine' is unproven.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Removing the trigger doesn't remove every path to the outcome.
Late returns cause fines, but fines have many other causes.
Valid reasoning never treats one cause as the only cause.
Share this: find one 'no trigger, so no trouble' claim and challenge it.

puzzles.title: The Melting Pat
puzzles.question: If the oven is on, the kitchen warms. If the kitchen warms, the butter melts. The oven is on. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — the chain links up: oven on, kitchen warms, butter melts. Linked rules pass certainty down the whole line.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: the butter melts. The oven being on warms the kitchen, and a warm kitchen melts butter, so the end of the chain holds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Chained rules carry certainty from the first link to the last.
One broken link collapses the whole chain — test each connection.
Supply chains, recipes, and travel plans all run on chained rules.
Share this: trace one three-step chain in your routine and check each link.

puzzles.title: The Missing Keys
puzzles.question: The keys are in the coat pocket or the drawer. They are not in the coat pocket. Where are they?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — two options, one eliminated, one remains. Disjunctive reasoning is just careful elimination.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, they are in the drawer. The keys are in exactly one of two places, the coat is empty, so the drawer is the only option left.
puzzles.lessonContent:
With true either-or options, killing one alternative proves the other.
The move demands the list be complete — a hidden third option breaks it.
Troubleshooters narrow fault lists exactly this way.
Share this: solve one lost-item hunt by listing every possible spot first.

puzzles.title: The Driver's Badge
puzzles.question: All tram drivers carry a badge. Lena is a tram driver. What must be true of Lena?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — every tram driver carries one, and Lena is a tram driver, so the badge is certain. What's true of the whole group holds for each member.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — Lena carries a badge. The rule covers all tram drivers with no exceptions, and Lena belongs to that group.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A universal rule plus membership delivers a guaranteed conclusion.
The danger is a rule with hidden exceptions — 'all' must mean all.
Contracts and safety rules work because groups inherit their requirements.
Share this: apply one group rule to a member and state what must hold.

puzzles.title: The Apron Test
puzzles.question: All chefs wear aprons. Sam wears an apron. So Sam must be a chef — valid?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — aprons don't prove chefhood; waiters and artists wear them too. Sharing one trait with a group doesn't make you a member.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is no — aprons don't prove chefhood. Chefs wear aprons, but so do waiters and artists, so Sam's apron proves nothing about being a chef.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sharing a trait with a group never proves membership in it.
Uniforms, jargon, and badges are all shared with outsiders.
Membership needs the defining feature, not a coincidental one.
Share this: catch one 'looks the part, must be one' leap today.

puzzles.title: The Missing Parcel
puzzles.question: If the parcel had arrived, the doorman would have logged it. There is no log entry. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — an arrival would leave a log, and there's no log, so no arrival. Absence of a required trace is evidence of absence.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the parcel has not arrived. The doorman logs every arrival without fail, and nothing is logged, so arrival is ruled out.
puzzles.lessonContent:
A missing mandatory trace disproves the event that must leave it.
Auditors and inspectors reason from absent paperwork daily.
The trace must be truly mandatory, not merely usual.
Share this: name one record whose absence would prove something didn't happen.

puzzles.title: The Open Gate
puzzles.question: If the gate is open, the light is green. The gate is open. What color is the light?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — open gate, green light, no exceptions. Confirm the condition and the result comes free.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the light is green. The rule ties green to open, the gate stands open, so green is guaranteed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reliable mechanisms turn conditions into certainties.
Traffic systems, interlocks, and checklists are built from such rules.
Trust the result exactly as far as you trust the mechanism.
Share this: point out one device whose signal you trust and why.

puzzles.title: The Hiding Dog
puzzles.question: If the dog hears thunder, it hides under the table. The dog is hiding under the table. So it heard thunder — valid?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — hiding has many triggers: fireworks, strangers, a slammed door. The hiding can't name its own cause.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is no — hiding has many triggers. Thunder causes hiding, but fireworks or strangers do too, so thunder is unproven.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One behavior, many possible triggers — behavior alone can't pick the trigger.
Vets rule out causes one by one instead of jumping to one.
List rival causes before settling on your favorite.
Share this: explain one pet behavior with two rival causes.

puzzles.title: The Skipped Revision
puzzles.question: If Amir studied, he passed. Amir did not study. So Amir failed — valid?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — skipping study removes one route to passing, not all of them. Prior knowledge or an easy paper could still carry him through.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is no: passing has other routes. Not studying closes one path to passing, while other paths stay open, so failure is unproven.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Closing one road to success leaves the other roads open.
'No effort, so no chance' ignores luck, talent, and easy tests.
Judge outcomes by all paths, not the one you closed.
Share this: name a goal with two different routes to reach it.

puzzles.title: The Furless Cobra
puzzles.question: No reptiles have fur. A cobra is a reptile. What must be true of the cobra?
choices: The cobra is not a reptile
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — no reptile has fur, and a cobra is fully reptile, so furlessness is certain. Universal denials transfer to every member.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: the cobra has no fur. The 'no reptile' rule covers every reptile, and the cobra is one.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Universal denials apply to each member without exception.
'No' rules are powerful because one counterexample would break them.
Safety bans and allergy rules protect through universal denials.
Share this: apply one 'no' rule to a member and state the result.

puzzles.title: The Rising River
puzzles.question: If the river rises, the ferry stops. If the ferry stops, the market closes. The river is rising. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — rising river stops the ferry, a stopped ferry closes the market, and the river is rising. Three links, one certain end.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the market closes. The chain runs river to ferry to market, and the first link is active, so the last one falls.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Long chains are only as strong as their weakest link.
Flood plans and backup plans exist because chains snap mid-way.
Verify every link before announcing the final outcome.
Share this: map one everyday chain of three events and test it.

puzzles.title: The Tracked Vans
puzzles.question: All delivery vans have GPS. Some vehicles in the depot are delivery vans. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — the vans in the depot inherit the vans' GPS. A universal rule plus a partial membership yields a partial conclusion.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — some depot vehicles have GPS. All delivery vans carry it, and some depot vehicles are delivery vans, so those some carry it.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Some' conclusions need only 'some' membership plus a universal rule.
Never upgrade 'some' to 'all' — the logic won't carry you there.
Surveys and samples trade in careful 'some' claims.
Share this: turn one group fact into a modest 'some' claim.

puzzles.title: The Penguin Leap
puzzles.question: Some birds cannot fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins cannot fly — valid?
choices: No — a 'some' premise proves nothing about penguins
puzzles.correctAnswer: No — a 'some' premise proves nothing about penguins
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 'some birds' might mean sparrows and owls, saying nothing about penguins. A partial premise can't pin a specific member.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! A 'some' premise can't convict a specific member. Some flightless birds exist, but penguins need their own evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Partial premises never settle specific cases.
'Some' tells you a group exists, not who belongs to it.
Stereotypes smuggle 'some' into 'this one' — refuse the upgrade.
Share this: catch one 'some are, so this is' leap in conversation.

puzzles.title: The Correct Password
puzzles.question: If the password is correct, the vault opens. The password is correct. What happens?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — correct password, opening vault, directly. The condition is met, so the mechanism must respond.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the vault opens. The rule promises opening on the correct password, and this password is correct.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Access systems are pure condition-and-result machines.
Right credential in, granted access out — no judgment in between.
Every login you type is a tiny modus ponens.
Share this: explain one login step as a condition and result.

puzzles.title: The Dark Lighthouse
puzzles.question: If the lighthouse lamp were lit, passing ships would see it. The ships report complete darkness. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a lit lamp would be seen for miles, and ships see darkness. The missing glow extinguishes the lit-lamp theory.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the lamp is not lit. Ships would spot a lit lamp easily, yet they report darkness, so the lamp must be out.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Expected sightings that never come are powerful refutations.
Missing ships, missing signals, missing symptoms all argue the same way.
The sighting must be genuinely unavoidable for the logic to bite.
Share this: name one thing whose absence tonight would prove a point.

puzzles.title: The Closed Bakery
puzzles.question: If the bakery is open, its smell fills the street. The bakery is closed today. So the street has no such smell — valid?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — a closed bakery removes one smell-source, while the café next door or a street vendor could still perfume the air.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is no — smells have other sources. The closed bakery kills one source of aroma, but other sources survive, so 'no smell' is unproven.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One closed source never empties a street of smells — or a case of causes.
Markets, kitchens, and arguments all have backup suppliers.
Count the remaining sources before declaring absence.
Share this: list three sources of one everyday smell.

puzzles.title: The Cheering Stand
puzzles.question: If the team won, the fans cheered. The fans are cheering now. So the team won — valid?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — fans cheer goals, but also kickoff, saves, and streakers. The cheering can't identify its own trigger.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is no: cheers have many triggers. Wins cause cheers, yet cheers erupt for many reasons, so a win is unproven.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Crowd reactions have countless triggers — never read one backwards.
Commentators check the scoreboard; they don't infer it from noise.
Celebrations, alarms, and applause all need independent checking.
Share this: hear one crowd noise and verify its cause before guessing.

puzzles.title: The Sweet Citrus
puzzles.question: No lemons are sweet. This fruit in your hand is sweet. What must be true?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — lemons are never sweet, and this fruit is sweet, so lemonhood is impossible. The sweet taste vetoes the category.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, it is not a lemon. The 'no sweet lemons' rule plus real sweetness shuts the lemon door completely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
One clashing property can veto a whole category.
Tasters, sorters, and inspectors wield single decisive tests.
The veto needs a truly exceptionless rule behind it.
Share this: use one decisive test to rule something out today.

puzzles.title: The Vanished Culprit
puzzles.question: The culprit left by taxi, train, or on foot. Taxi records and train cameras both draw a blank. How did the culprit leave?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — three exits, two sealed, one left. Exhaustion of alternatives is a complete proof when the list is complete.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — on foot is the answer. Taxi and train are both ruled out, and those were the only other options, so foot remains.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Ruling out every alternative but one proves the survivor.
Locked-room mysteries run entirely on exhaustive elimination.
The list must be exhaustive or the survivor proves nothing.
Share this: close a small mystery by eliminating every alternative.

puzzles.title: The Overslept Commute
puzzles.question: If Nina oversleeps, she misses the bus. If she misses the bus, she cycles to work. Nina overslept. What does she do?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — oversleeping kills the bus, and a missed bus means the bicycle. Two links carry Nina from bed to bike.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: she cycles. Oversleeping costs her the bus, and losing the bus puts her on the bicycle.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Morning routines are chains of if-then links worth mapping.
Spotting your own chains lets you insert backup links early.
One alarm, one spare key, one backup route each guard a link.
Share this: name the weakest link in your morning chain.

puzzles.title: The Unpaid Deposit
puzzles.question: If the contract were signed, the deposit would be paid. The deposit is unpaid. What follows?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a signed contract would have released the deposit, and the deposit sits unpaid. The missing money unsigns the deal.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The contract is not signed. Signatures release deposits automatically, yet no deposit moved, so no signature happened.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Missing mandatory payments disprove the deals behind them.
Bookkeepers spot unsigned contracts in unpaid invoices.
Automatic consequences make the strongest reverse proofs.
Share this: infer one missing event from one missing payment.

puzzles.title: The Low Tide
puzzles.question: If the tide is out, the causeway is walkable. The tide is out. What must be true?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the tide is out, and an out-tide guarantees a walkable causeway. Condition met, result delivered.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the causeway is walkable. Low tide is the stated condition for walking it, and the tide is out.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tide tables and timetables turn nature into reliable rules.
Conditions you can check beat guesses you can't.
Always confirm the condition before counting on the result.
Share this: check one natural condition before planning around it.

puzzles.title: The Personal Dismissal
puzzles.question: 'We can ignore her budget plan — she's terrible with money.' Which flaw sinks this dismissal?
choices: Ad hominem — it attacks the speaker
False dilemma — it forces two options
puzzles.correctAnswer: Ad hominem — it attacks the speaker
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. The reply attacks the speaker's character instead of touching the claim. Who says it never settles whether it's true.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is ad hominem: it attacks the speaker. A rude expert can still be right, and a kind novice can still be wrong, so character is irrelevant.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Ad hominem swaps the claim for the claimant — always redirect to the evidence.
It appears in debates, reviews, and comment sections everywhere.
Separate the message from the messenger before judging.
Share this: catch one insult-as-argument today and restate the real claim.

puzzles.title: The Crowded Checkout
puzzles.question: 'Everyone is buying this phone, so it must be the best.' What is wrong here?
choices: Appeal to nature — it trusts the natural
Hasty generalization — it leaps from one case
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Popularity is the only evidence offered. Millions of buyers can still be buying a mistake.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is bandwagon: it follows the crowd. Sales figures show popularity, not quality, so the argument needs real evidence.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Bandwagon treats headcounts as proof — crowds are often wrong together.
Fads, bubbles, and viral rumors all ride this fallacy.
Ask what the crowd knows that you don't, and whether they know anything.
Share this: question one popular choice today and demand its evidence.

puzzles.title: The Invented Ban
puzzles.question: 'A small tax on sugary drinks? So you want to ban everything enjoyable!' Which trick is that?
choices: Red herring — it changes the subject
Circular reasoning — it assumes the point
Strawman — it invents an extreme version
Appeal to ignorance — it exploits the unknown
puzzles.correctAnswer: Strawman — it invents an extreme version
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Nobody proposed banning anything; the reply torches an invented extreme. Refute the real proposal or concede nothing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is strawman: it invents an extreme version. The proposal was a small tax, not a ban, so the reply fights a fiction.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Strawmen replace the real position with a flimsy double.
Steel-manning — restating the other side fairly — is the antidote.
In every debate, first check: is this what they actually said?
Share this: restate someone's view so fairly they thank you.

puzzles.title: The Forced Choice
puzzles.question: 'Either you study abroad now or your career is over.' What flaw forces this panic?
choices: Tu quoque — it returns the accusation
Anecdotal — it leans on one story
Composition — it spreads parts to wholes
False dilemma — it hides the middle options
puzzles.correctAnswer: False dilemma — it hides the middle options
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Study abroad and dropping out aren't the only futures. The argument hides every middle path to force a panic.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is false dilemma: it hides the middle options. Between two extremes sit scholarships, part-time work, and gap years unmentioned.
puzzles.lessonContent:
False dilemmas shrink a landscape of options down to two.
'You're with us or against us' is the classic squeeze.
Always ask: what third option was left off the menu?
Share this: add a third option to one either-or ultimatum today.

puzzles.title: The Single Taxi
puzzles.question: 'My taxi driver was rude, so everyone in this city is rude.' Which leap is that?
choices: Hasty generalization — it leaps from one case
Appeal to authority — it borrows a badge
No true Scotsman — it redefines the group
puzzles.correctAnswer: Hasty generalization — it leaps from one case
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. One rude encounter can't convict a whole city. Samples of one prove nothing about millions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is hasty generalization: it leaps from one case. A single taxi ride is no survey of a city's manners.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tiny samples make loud but worthless evidence.
One bad meal doesn't condemn a cuisine; one rude driver doesn't damn a city.
Ask how the sample was picked and how large it is.
Share this: refuse one sweeping judgment based on a single encounter.

puzzles.title: The Borrowed Medal
puzzles.question: 'This vitamin works — a famous sprinter endorses it.' What is borrowed here?
choices: Genetic fallacy — it judges the origin
Division — it splits wholes into parts
Appeal to authority — it borrows an off-topic badge
Middle ground — it splits the difference
puzzles.correctAnswer: Appeal to authority — it borrows an off-topic badge
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A sprinting medal confers no nutrition expertise. Authority transfers only inside its own field.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is appeal to authority: it borrows an off-topic badge. Athletic fame is no license on vitamins, so the claim needs real studies.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Badges impress only inside the field printed on them.
Celebrities sell certainty they never earned — check the credentials.
Ask: expert in what, exactly, and where is the data?
Share this: verify one expert's actual field before trusting the tip.

puzzles.title: The Doomsday Roster
puzzles.question: 'Allow one remote day and soon nobody works, then the company collapses.' Which slide is that?
choices: Equivocation — it shifts a word's meaning
Slippery slope — it slides without evidence
Burden reversal — it flips the homework
puzzles.correctAnswer: Slippery slope — it slides without evidence
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Each slide — remote day to laziness to collapse — is asserted, never shown. Slopes need grip at every step.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is slippery slope: it slides without evidence. Remote work might raise output; every link in the slide is merely assumed.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Slippery slopes assert chains they never demonstrate.
Demand the mechanism at each step: why must this lead to that?
Most predicted avalanches never leave the mountaintop.
Share this: challenge one doomsday chain by asking for step one.

puzzles.title: The Lucky Grandfather
puzzles.question: 'My grandfather smoked and lived to ninety, so smoking is safe.' What promotes the story too far?
choices: Texas sharpshooter — it paints the target late
Anecdotal — it promotes one story to data
Appeal to nature — it trusts the natural
puzzles.correctAnswer: Anecdotal — it promotes one story to data
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Grandfather's smoking proves his luck, not tobacco's safety. Stories illustrate; only samples demonstrate.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is anecdotal: it promotes one story to data. One long-lived smoker cannot outweigh decades of mortality statistics.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Anecdotes are data points with great PR and no statistics.
Survivors tell stories; the silent majority never gets interviewed.
Counter one vivid story with the broader numbers.
Share this: answer one 'my uncle proves it' with the actual statistics.

puzzles.title: The Hiring Loop
puzzles.question: 'We should hire him because he is the right person to hire.' What loop is that?
choices: Circular reasoning — it assumes the conclusion
Red herring — it changes the subject
Moving goalposts — it shifts the target
Division — it splits wholes into parts
puzzles.correctAnswer: Circular reasoning — it assumes the conclusion
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. 'Hire him because he's the best hire' just repeats the hiring decision as its own reason. The premise is the conclusion wearing a disguise.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is circular reasoning: it assumes the conclusion. Restating the hire as its own justification explains nothing.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Circular arguments travel in tight loops: the reason is the claim.
Strip the sentence down — if premise and conclusion match, it's a loop.
Real reasons bring outside evidence, never echoes.
Share this: untangle one 'because I said so' into a real reason.

puzzles.title: The Airport Swerve
puzzles.question: 'Why fund hospitals when airports have delays?' What is dragged in here?
choices: Ad hominem — it attacks the speaker
False dilemma — it forces two options
Red herring — it drags in an irrelevance
puzzles.correctAnswer: Red herring — it drags in an irrelevance
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Airport delays say nothing about hospital budgets. The herring smells strong enough to pull attention off the wards.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is red herring: it drags in an irrelevance. Airports and hospitals share a budget debate but no logical connection.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Red herrings win by changing the subject to something smellier.
Notice the swerve: did the reply address the claim at all?
Drag every debate back to the original question.
Share this: name the original topic when one discussion swerves.

puzzles.title: The Late Retort
puzzles.question: 'I'm late? You're late every day!' What dodge is that?
choices: Tu quoque — it answers a charge with a charge
Hasty generalization — it leaps from one case
puzzles.correctAnswer: Tu quoque — it answers a charge with a charge
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Pointing at others' lateness never defends your own. Two wrongs don't schedule a meeting.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is tu quoque: it answers a charge with a charge. Colleagues' tardiness is a separate trial from yours.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'You too' defends nothing — it just opens a second prosecution.
Answer the charge against you first; file yours separately.
Hypocrisy-spotting feels great and proves nothing.
Share this: answer one criticism on its merits before countering.

puzzles.title: The Shrinking Club
puzzles.question: 'No true food lover dislikes sushi.' When a friend objects, Ken says she was never a true food lover. Which move?
choices: Appeal to ignorance — it exploits the unknown
No true Scotsman — it redefines the group
Composition — it spreads parts to wholes
Equivocation — it shifts a word's meaning
puzzles.correctAnswer: No true Scotsman — it redefines the group
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. The definition of 'food lover' quietly shrank to exclude the counterexample. Real groups survive counterexamples; fake ones redefine them away.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is no true Scotsman: it redefines the group. Disliking one dish can't expel anyone from liking food.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Watch definitions that shrink every time evidence arrives.
Honest categories admit exceptions; rigged ones expel them.
Ask for the definition up front, in writing, before the debate.
Share this: spot one moving definition and pin it down.

puzzles.title: The Natural Baptism
puzzles.question: 'This remedy is safe because it is all-natural.' What baptizes it too fast?
choices: Appeal to nature — it baptizes the natural
Burden reversal — it flips the homework
Middle ground — it splits the difference
puzzles.correctAnswer: Appeal to nature — it baptizes the natural
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly. 'Natural' is doing all the work — hemlock is natural too. Safety needs testing, not adjectives.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is appeal to nature: it baptizes the natural. Nature makes poisons as well as cures, so the label proves nothing.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Natural' is a marketing word, not a safety certificate.
Smallpox is natural; vaccines are not — guess which saves lives.
Demand trials and doses, never vibes and labels.
Share this: question one 'all-natural' claim with a poison counterexample.

puzzles.title: The Due Red
puzzles.question: 'Black came up five times, so red is due.' What does the wheel owe?
choices: Circular reasoning — it assumes the point
Gambler's fallacy — it expects the universe to balance
Texas sharpshooter — it paints the target late
Anecdotal — it leans on one story
puzzles.correctAnswer: Gambler's fallacy — it expects the universe to balance
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The wheel has no memory and owes red nothing. Each spin starts the odds fresh.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is gambler's fallacy: it expects the universe to balance. Five blacks change nothing — the next spin is still nearly fifty-fifty.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Random processes never compensate — they don't remember at all.
Streaks feel meaningful because brains hate coincidence.
Treat each independent event as a fresh coin.
Share this: explain to a friend why the wheel owes them nothing.

puzzles.title: The Painted Bullseye
puzzles.question: 'These lottery numbers predicted the quake — look at the pattern!' What's painted late?
choices: Texas sharpshooter — it draws the target afterward
Red herring — it changes the subject
Ad hominem — it attacks the speaker
False dilemma — it forces two options
puzzles.correctAnswer: Texas sharpshooter — it draws the target afterward
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. The pattern was painted around the hits after the fact. With enough data, bullseyes appear by pure chance.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is Texas sharpshooter: it draws the target afterward. Scanning years of numbers guarantees some 'amazing' cluster somewhere.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Hindsight turns noise into bullseyes by drawing targets late.
Declare the prediction before looking, not after.
Coincidence warehouses stock every 'impossible' pattern.
Share this: ask one pattern-finder what they predicted beforehand.

puzzles.title: The Shifting Target
puzzles.question: 'Ten sources aren't enough — bring twenty.' The demand doubles after delivery. What shifted?
choices: Moving goalposts — it shifts the finish line
Hasty generalization — it leaps from one case
puzzles.correctAnswer: Moving goalposts — it shifts the finish line
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Ten sources were the deal; twenty is a new deal invented after delivery. Shifting targets make winning impossible by design.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is moving goalposts: it shifts the finish line. The requirement changed only after it was met, which is rigging, not rigor.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shifting standards after success is rigging dressed as rigor.
Fix the criteria in writing before the work starts.
Fair judges grade the agreed test, never the invented one.
Share this: lock one goal's success criteria before you begin.

puzzles.title: The Attic Ghost
puzzles.question: 'Prove there is NO ghost in my attic!' Who carries the homework?
choices: Appeal to authority — it borrows a badge
Division — it splits wholes into parts
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. The claimant must prove the ghost exists, not dare others to disprove it. You can't prove a negative about an invisible attic.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is burden reversal: it demands disproof. Claims need evidence from their maker, not refutation from skeptics.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Whoever makes the claim carries the evidence — always.
'Prove me wrong' is homework-dodging, not argument.
Extraordinary claims need ordinary evidence first.
Share this: return one 'prove me wrong' with 'you first'.

puzzles.title: The Untested Powder
puzzles.question: 'No study disproves this powder, so it works.' What crowns the gap?
choices: No true Scotsman — it redefines the group
Appeal to ignorance — it crowns the unknown
Composition — it spreads parts to wholes
Equivocation — it shifts a word's meaning
puzzles.correctAnswer: Appeal to ignorance — it crowns the unknown
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Untested means unknown, not effective. Absence of evidence is not evidence of benefit.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is appeal to ignorance: it crowns the unknown. No trials means no knowledge either way, not secret effectiveness.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The unknown is not a witness for either side.
'No studies' confesses ignorance; it grants no powers.
Suspend judgment until the trials exist.
Share this: greet one untested miracle with 'we don't know yet'.

puzzles.title: The Light Wall
puzzles.question: 'Each brick is light, so the wall is light.' What scales too fast?
choices: Middle ground — it splits the difference
Composition — it gifts parts to the whole
Genetic fallacy — it judges the origin
puzzles.correctAnswer: Composition — it gifts parts to the whole
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Light bricks can still build a heavy wall. Properties of pieces don't automatically scale to the structure.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is composition: it gifts parts to the whole. Each brick's lightness never promised a portable wall.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Wholes surprise their parts — weight, cost, and complexity emerge.
Cheap ingredients still make expensive weddings.
Judge systems at their own level, not their pieces'.
Share this: name one whole greater than its light parts.

puzzles.title: The Profitable Whole
puzzles.question: 'The company is profitable, so every department is profitable.' What scatters wrongly?
choices: Division — it scatters the whole onto parts
Circular reasoning — it assumes the point
puzzles.correctAnswer: Division — it scatters the whole onto parts
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. A profitable company can still harbor a bleeding division. Averages describe the pile, never each grain.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is division: it scatters the whole onto parts. Company profit is an average that can hide a failing unit.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Group averages never describe every member.
Rich nations hold poor citizens; strong teams carry weak links.
Inspect the part before praising or blaming it.
Share this: split one average into its unequal parts today.

puzzles.title: The Double Right
puzzles.question: 'Take the right path — turning right is always right!' What spends a word twice?
choices: Red herring — it changes the subject
Ad hominem — it attacks the speaker
Equivocation — it spends one word twice
False dilemma — it forces two options
puzzles.correctAnswer: Equivocation — it spends one word twice
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. 'Right' slides from moral to directional mid-sentence, and the joke hides a broken inference. One word, two wallets.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is equivocation: it spends one word twice. Moral rightness and right-hand turns share spelling, nothing else.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Watch words that change wallets mid-argument.
'Banks,' 'rights,' and 'free' all moonlight with double meanings.
Pin each key term to one meaning before reasoning.
Share this: catch one pun masquerading as proof today.

puzzles.title: The Cheap Shelf
puzzles.question: 'That water is cheap-store stuff, so it must be bad.' What judges the birthplace?
choices: Tu quoque — it returns the accusation
Genetic fallacy — it judges the idea by its birthplace
puzzles.correctAnswer: Genetic fallacy — it judges the idea by its birthplace
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. A price tag's origin says nothing about water quality. Judge the drink, not the shelf.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is genetic fallacy: it judges the idea by its birthplace. Discount shelves stock fine water and foul water alike.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Origins are biography, not verdicts — test the thing itself.
Cheap, foreign, or new never equals bad; costly never equals good.
Taste the water instead of reading the shelf.
Share this: judge one thing by testing, ignoring its origin.

puzzles.title: The Split Guestlist
puzzles.question: 'You say 100 guests, I say 10 — let's invite 55.' When the count is factual, what baptizes wrongly?
choices: Appeal to nature — it trusts the natural
Burden reversal — it flips the homework
Middle ground — it baptizes the average
puzzles.correctAnswer: Middle ground — it baptizes the average
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right. Splitting the difference between true and false just lands on wrong. Compromise is a virtue in deals, not in facts.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is middle ground: it baptizes the average. Half a myth plus half a fact is still half a myth.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Truth doesn't live at the midpoint of every disagreement.
One side can simply be wrong — averages don't arbitrate facts.
Reserve compromise for interests, never for evidence.
Share this: refuse one false compromise between fact and fiction.

puzzles.title: The Confused Denial
puzzles.question: 'I can't imagine tiny particles acting that way, so they don't.' What mistakes confusion for proof?
choices: Appeal to ignorance — it crowns the unknown
Personal incredulity — it mistakes confusion for refutation
Composition — it spreads parts to wholes
Equivocation — it shifts a word's meaning
puzzles.correctAnswer: Personal incredulity — it mistakes confusion for refutation
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes. Not imagining the mechanism only measures the imagination. Quantum physics survived decades of disbelief.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is personal incredulity: it mistakes confusion for refutation. Inability to picture particles doesn't dent the experiments.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Confusion is a feeling about you, not evidence about the world.
Experts trust instruments over intuition daily.
Say 'I don't get it yet' instead of 'it can't be'. 
Share this: replace one 'impossible!' with 'show me how'.

puzzles.title: The Glossy Brochure
puzzles.question: A fund brochure shows only its five best months of the year. What exhibits too selectively?
choices: Circular reasoning — it assumes the point
Red herring — it changes the subject
Cherry-picking — it exhibits only friendly data
Moving goalposts — it shifts the target
puzzles.correctAnswer: Cherry-picking — it exhibits only friendly data
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct. Five good months were framed; seven bad ones were cropped out. Honest funds show the whole film, not the trailer.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is cherry-picking: it exhibits only friendly data. A full-year record would tell the story the brochure hides.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Curated samples are advertisements wearing lab coats.
Always ask what was cropped out of the frame.
Full records embarrass selective brochures.
Share this: demand the full timeline behind one glowing claim.

puzzles.title: The Classroom Pair
puzzles.question: How many classmates in a room push the odds of a shared birthday past fifty-fifty?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — just 23 classmates push the odds past fifty-fifty. Pairs grow quadratically while birthdays stay fixed at 365.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 23 classmates. Pairs multiply fast (253 pairs among 23), so the tipping point arrives shockingly early.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shared-birthday odds count pairs, not people — and pairs explode quadratically.
That mismatch between linear intuition and quadratic reality is the whole paradox.
Whenever matches matter, count the pairs first.
Share this: ask a room of 23 if any two share a birthday.

puzzles.title: The Office Pool
puzzles.question: In an office of 30 people, what are the odds that some two share a birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — 30 people hold 435 pairs, and 435 chances at 1-in-365 land around 70%. Add seven people past 23 and the odds jump twenty points.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, about 70%. Thirty people make 435 pairs, and that many shots at a 1-in-365 match pile up fast.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Each extra person adds pairs with everyone already present.
That is why the odds climb steeply, not gradually.
Growth problems reward pair-counting over head-counting.
Share this: guess the odds for 30 people before revealing seventy percent.

puzzles.title: The Wedding Collision
puzzles.question: At a wedding with 50 guests, how likely is a shared birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 50 people make 1,225 pairs, nearly certain to collide. At fifty heads the shared birthday is almost guaranteed.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — about 97%. Fifty people generate 1,225 pairs, and that many draws from 365 days almost always repeat.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Twelve hundred pairs drawn from 365 days cannot plausibly all differ.
Certainty arrives long before intuition expects it.
Big groups make coincidences routine, not remarkable.
Share this: test a fifty-person wedding party for a match.

puzzles.title: The Lecture Hall
puzzles.question: In a lecture hall of 70 students, what are the odds of a shared birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — 70 people make 2,415 pairs against 365 days. A miss would be the real miracle.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! About 99.9%. Seventy people hold 2,415 pairs, so dodging every collision is a one-in-a-thousand fluke.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Past a point, the surprise flips: no match becomes the miracle.
Knowing where certainty lives stops you betting against it.
Rare events stay rare only while the trials stay few.
Share this: name the group size where you'd bet the house.

puzzles.title: The Birthday Trap
puzzles.question: How many party guests give even odds that someone shares YOUR birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — matching YOUR birthday needs about 253 guests for even odds. Any-pair needs 23; a specified date needs ten times more.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, 253 party guests. Your date is one fixed target, so each guest is a single 1-in-365 shot — a far slower climb than any-pair.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Any-match and my-match are wildly different questions.
Specified targets climb linearly; free pairs climb quadratically.
Always check which game is actually being played.
Share this: challenge friends to match your birthday specifically.

puzzles.title: The Iron Guarantee
puzzles.question: How many strangers guarantee that two share a birthday (ignoring leap day)?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 366 people and 365 birthdays force a repeat. That iron guarantee is the pigeonhole principle wearing a party hat.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — 366 people. With one more person than birthdays, some date must double up no matter the arrangement.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Guarantees come from pigeonholes: more items than boxes forces sharing.
Odds describe likelihood; pigeonholes describe certainty.
Spot the boxes-and-items structure to find free guarantees.
Share this: explain why 366 strangers guarantee a pair.

puzzles.title: The Squad List
puzzles.question: A World Cup squad has 23 players. What are the odds two share a birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — a 23-player squad sits just past the tipping point. Real squads really do collide this often.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Over fifty-fifty. Twenty-three players cross the classic threshold, so shared birthdays in squads are the norm, not news.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The paradox predicts real dressing rooms, not just textbooks.
Sports squads, casts, and crews of 23-plus collide constantly.
Theory earns trust when it calls real outcomes.
Share this: check any 23-player squad list for a pair.

puzzles.title: The Crowded Count
puzzles.question: In a crowd of 100, how many shared-birthday pairs should you expect on average?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — 100 people hold 4,950 pairs, averaging about 14 collisions. Big rooms don't just match once; they match repeatedly.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, about 14 pairs. Divide 4,950 pairs by 365 days and the average lands near fourteen shared dates.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Averages reveal what single-match odds hide: collisions pile up.
Expected counts come from pairs divided by possibilities.
Ask 'how many' after asking 'how likely'. 
Share this: guess how many pairs a hundred minds hold.

puzzles.title: The Quiet Average
puzzles.question: Among 23 people there are 253 pairs. How many collisions happen on average?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — 253 pairs across 365 days average under one collision. Fifty-fifty odds with under one expected pair is the paradox inside the paradox.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — under one pair. Spread 253 pairs over 365 dates and the average stays below one, yet the odds still top half.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Averages and odds tell different stories — learn to hear both.
Below-average expectations can still carry above-half chances.
Distributions matter more than their centers.
Share this: explain how half the time beats the average.

puzzles.title: The Clean Room
puzzles.question: With 23 people, what are the odds that NO two share a birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — the no-match chance at 23 is just under half, mirroring the match chance just over it. The threshold sits exactly there.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! About 49%. Multiply the shrinking no-collision fractions for 23 people and just under half the scenarios stay clean.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Complementary odds always sum to one — compute whichever is easier.
No-match chains multiply cleanly; match events tangle.
Flip to the complement whenever counting gets messy.
Share this: solve one probability by counting its opposite.

puzzles.title: The Month Match
puzzles.question: Among five friends, what are the odds two share a birth month?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — five friends across twelve months collide over 60% of the time. Fewer boxes mean faster collisions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, over 60%. Five people make ten pairs against twelve months, so a shared month is the likely outcome.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Shrink the boxes and collisions arrive sooner.
Twelve months behave like a miniature 365-day year.
Box-count sets the whole tempo of matching.
Share this: test five friends for a shared birth month.

puzzles.title: The Four Friends
puzzles.question: Drop four friends' birthdays into twelve month-boxes. How often does one box end up holding two?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — four friends across twelve months land near 43%. One fewer person nearly halves the action.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — about 43%. Four people hold six pairs against twelve months, landing well short of even odds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Removing one person removes pairs with everyone else.
Small groups swing wildly with each arrival or exit.
Feel the sensitivity: every head counts double.
Share this: compare four friends against five and feel the jump.

puzzles.title: The Weekday Clash
puzzles.question: Four colleagues were born on various weekdays. What are the odds two share one?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — four people across seven weekdays collide about 65% of the time. Tiny boxes fill astonishingly fast.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! About 65%. Four people make six pairs against seven weekdays, so a shared weekday is favored.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Seven boxes are so few that four people nearly fill them doubly.
Weekday collisions explain déjà vu rotas everywhere.
Small universes make repeats the default.
Share this: check four colleagues for a shared weekday birthday.

puzzles.title: The Three Siblings
puzzles.question: Three siblings' weekday birthdays land in seven day-slots. How often does some slot collect two?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — three people across seven weekdays land under 40%. Three heads make only three pairs.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — under 40%. Three people hold three pairs against seven days, so distinct weekdays stay likely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Few pairs mean the boxes usually survive unshared.
Three is the quiet zone before collisions take over.
Thresholds hide between small numbers — map them.
Share this: find the smallest group where you'd bet on a clash.

puzzles.title: The Team Rota
puzzles.question: Deal five teammates' birthdays across the seven weekdays like cards. How often does a weekday pair up?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — five people across seven weekdays reach about 85%. Ten pairs against seven boxes barely miss.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, about 85%. Five people make ten pairs, overwhelming seven weekdays, so a clash is highly likely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Ten pairs versus seven boxes is a rout, not a contest.
Watch certainty assemble as pairs outnumber boxes.
Count pairs against boxes to forecast any collision.
Share this: predict a five-person weekday clash before checking.

puzzles.title: The Season Twins
puzzles.question: Three strangers meet. What are the odds two were born in the same season?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — three people across four seasons collide nearly two-thirds of the time. Four boxes are almost no boxes at all.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Nearly two in three. Three people make three pairs against four seasons, favoring a shared one.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Four seasons behave like a toy calendar for collisions.
Season-mates are everywhere once you start looking.
Tiny category counts turn strangers into sharers.
Share this: find two season-mates in your next trio.

puzzles.title: The Trail Quartet
puzzles.question: Four hikers each name a birth season — four names drawn from four seasons. How often do two names coincide?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — four people across four seasons hit about 91%. Six pairs against four boxes rarely all spread out.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — about 91%. Four people make six pairs, and squeezing six pairs into four seasons almost always doubles one.
puzzles.lessonContent:
More pairs than boxes makes spreading out the real long shot.
Full houses of distinct seasons are the rare outcome.
Expect stacking whenever pairs exceed boxes.
Share this: bet on a season clash in any foursome.

puzzles.title: The Date Digits
puzzles.question: Six friends compare day-of-month birthdays (1–30). What are the odds two match?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — six people across thirty day-numbers land near 40%. Fifteen pairs against thirty slots stay under even odds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, roughly 40%. Six people hold fifteen pairs against thirty possible day-numbers, keeping a clash the underdog.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Day-of-month is a thirty-box calendar with its own tempo.
Fifteen pairs versus thirty boxes lands below half.
Every calendar size writes its own collision schedule.
Share this: test six friends for a shared day-number.

puzzles.title: The Leap Wait
puzzles.question: About how many people give even odds of including a leap-day (Feb 29) birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — a 1-in-1461 shot needs about 1,013 people for even odds. Rare birthdays obey the same pair logic, just stretched thin.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! 1,013 people. Leap-day odds climb far slower than ordinary birthdays, but the same math governs the wait.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Rare categories just stretch the same curve longer.
Leap babies wait a thousand heads for even odds.
Scale the groups with the rarity, not against it.
Share this: estimate the wait for any one-in-a-thousand trait.

puzzles.title: The Star Share
puzzles.question: In a crowd of 365, what are the odds someone shares a chosen celebrity's birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 365 strangers each take one 1-in-365 shot at the star's date, landing near 63%. One fixed target, hundreds of arrows.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — about 63%. Each of 365 strangers independently risks the star's exact date, and the hits accumulate.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Fixed-target problems accumulate single shots, not pairs.
Three hundred sixty-five arrows at one date hit most years.
Crowds make even exact-date matches routine.
Share this: check a crowd for your idol's birthday.

puzzles.title: The Close Call
puzzles.question: Fourteen people gather. What are the odds two birthdays fall within a day of each other?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — fourteen people give birthdays within a day of each other roughly even odds. Widen the window and collisions come sooner.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Roughly even odds. A three-day window triples every pair's chances, so fourteen people suffice.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Wider windows multiply every pair's collision chance.
Near-matches arrive far sooner than exact ones.
Adjust the window deliberately before estimating.
Share this: hunt near-birthdays, not exact ones, in a group.

puzzles.title: The Quiet Dinner
puzzles.question: At a dinner of ten, what are the odds of any shared birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — ten people hold just 45 pairs, worth about 12%. Below the threshold, collisions stay genuinely surprising.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — about 12%. Ten people make only 45 pairs, far too few to threaten 365 dates.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Below-threshold groups keep coincidences honestly rare.
Ten heads feel social but compute nearly silent.
Respect the quiet zone under the tipping point.
Share this: enjoy a ten-person dinner with no clash expected.

puzzles.title: The Conference Clash
puzzles.question: A conference room holds 40 people. What are the odds of a shared birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — forty people hold 780 pairs, good for about 88%. The seventies-to-eighties climb is steep and fast.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, about 88%. Seven hundred eighty pairs against 365 dates miss only about one time in eight.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Mid-size groups live on the steepest part of the curve.
Each added guest shifts the odds several points.
Steep zones are where small changes matter most.
Share this: watch odds jump as a guest list grows past thirty.

puzzles.title: The Full Hall
puzzles.question: Sixty strangers enter a hall. What are the odds two share a birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — sixty people hold 1,770 pairs, clearing 99%. Past sixty, doubters pay up.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Over 99%. One thousand seven hundred seventy pairs leave almost nowhere for birthdays to hide.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Sixty heads turn a party trick into a bankable bet.
Know the number where skepticism becomes foolishness.
Certainty has an address — memorize it.
Share this: offer even money on sixty strangers and collect.

puzzles.title: The Host's Date
puzzles.question: At the host's party of 30, what are the odds someone shares the HOST's birthday?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the host's date is one fixed target, and thirty guests take thirty single shots: under 8%. Compare the 70% any-pair odds for the same thirty.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — under 8%. Thirty independent 1-in-365 shots at the host's date rarely connect, unlike any-pair's 435 chances.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Side-by-side numbers teach the any-versus-mine lesson forever.
Same room, same count, tenfold different odds.
Framing chooses the game; the game chooses the odds.
Share this: stage both bets at one party and watch jaws drop.

puzzles.title: The Classic Switch
puzzles.question: Three doors, one car. You pick door 1; the host, who knows all, opens door 3 showing a goat. Switch or stay?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — your first pick holds the car one-third of the time, so the other closed door carries two-thirds. Switching doubles your odds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — switch: it wins two-thirds. Your door keeps its original one-third; the host's reveal concentrates the rest onto the other door.
puzzles.lessonContent:
The host's forced reveal moves probability — it never splits it evenly.
Your first pick freezes at one-third the moment you choose.
Information with rules behind it is worth real money.
Share this: run ten penny-cup trials and watch switchers win.

puzzles.title: The Ninety-Eight Goats
puzzles.question: One hundred doors, one car. You pick one; the host opens 98 goat doors. Switch to the survivor?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — your door keeps its 1% while the host's 98 reveals pile 99% onto the survivor. Scale makes the logic undeniable.
