puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: 99% wins. Your first pick is almost surely wrong, and the host just eliminated every alternative but one.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Scaling a puzzle to a hundred doors exposes the mechanism.
Your pick stays 1-in-100 no matter what opens elsewhere.
When intuition rebels, scale the numbers until it surrenders.
Share this: explain the hundred-door version to a skeptic.

puzzles.title: The Ten Chests
puzzles.question: Ten chests, one treasure. You choose one; the host opens 8 empty chests. Switch to the last closed chest?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — ten doors mean your pick is 10% and the nine others share 90%, all landing on the survivor. Switching wins nine times in ten.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Switch: 90% wins. Your door's 10% never grew; the host funneled the other 90% onto a single door.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Reveals concentrate probability the way lenses focus light.
Count what your door held at the start — that never changes.
Forecasting who gains from news is a tradeable skill.
Share this: deal ten cards and play host for a friend.

puzzles.title: The Fourth Door
puzzles.question: Four doors, one car. You pick one; the host opens one goat door. Two others remain. Your best move?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — staying holds 25% while the 75% remainder splits across two doors at 37.5% each. Switching to either still beats staying.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — switch: 37.5% beats 25%. One reveal can't carry the whole remainder onto one door when two remain.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Leftover probability splits among ALL survivors, not your favorite.
Count the survivors before crowning a winner.
Partial reveals give partial edges — take them anyway.
Share this: split a remainder fairly across survivors once today.

puzzles.title: The Forgetful Host
puzzles.question: The host forgot where the car is, opened a random door, and luckily showed a goat. Switch or stay?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — a clueless host reveals nothing, so the two doors stand truly equal. Knowledge, not ceremony, moves the odds.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — no gain: genuinely fifty-fifty. The host stumbled onto a goat blindly, so no information entered the game.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Only informed reveals move probability; accidents move nothing.
Ask what the revealer knew before updating your odds.
Luck that looks like news is still just luck.
Share this: separate one informed signal from one lucky accident.

puzzles.title: The Premature Peek
puzzles.question: The host opens a goat door BEFORE you choose. Does any door now beat the others?
choices: No advantage — one in three anywhere
puzzles.correctAnswer: No advantage — one in three anywhere
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a reveal before your pick informs nobody. All three doors still hold one-third each, including the opened... the two closed ones.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, no advantage: one in three anywhere. Information must arrive after your commitment to favor anyone.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Timing decides whether news is useful or decoration.
Early reveals help everyone equally, which means no one.
Commit first, then let information work for you.
Share this: notice one decision where order decided everything.

puzzles.title: The Empty Offer
puzzles.question: You pick a door; the host opens nothing but offers a swap. Should you?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — with no reveal, switching just trades one one-third door for another. Ceremony without information changes nothing.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Indifferent: still one in three. Nobody learned anything, so the swap is pure theater.
puzzles.lessonContent:
No news means no edge — demand the reveal before moving.
Rituals feel strategic while changing zero odds.
Patience beats motion when information is missing.
Share this: skip one purposeless switch today and smile.

puzzles.title: The Rigged Stage
puzzles.question: The host watches your pick, then slides the car behind a door to defeat switchers. Now what?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — an adversary who places the prize to punish switchers flips the math. Assumptions about the host ARE the math.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — stay: the game is rigged. If placement reacts to your strategy, the classic numbers no longer apply.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Every probability answer sits on assumptions — audit them first.
'Random placement' is a load-bearing claim, not décor.
Rigged games punish textbook play on purpose.
Share this: name one hidden assumption behind a famous answer.

puzzles.title: The Late Arrival
puzzles.question: After the classic reveal, a newcomer who saw nothing picks between the two closed doors. Their odds?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — the newcomer shares no history with either door. Information is personal: yours moved your odds, not theirs.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — fifty-fifty for the newcomer. They never made a first pick, so the reveal concentrated nothing for them.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Probability follows the observer, not the furniture.
Two people can rationally hold different odds about one door.
Ask whose history a number belongs to before borrowing it.
Share this: explain why latecomers face fresh odds.

puzzles.title: The Watching Friend
puzzles.question: Your friend watched your pick and the host's reveal, then takes over your choice. What should they do?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — having watched your pick and the reveal, the friend inherits the full situation. Knowledge transfers by watching, not by touching.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: the watcher knows. They saw the original pick and the forced reveal, so the two-thirds sits on the same door for them.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Watching a random process can grant the player's edge.
Information travels with attention, not participation.
Spectators with full history bet like insiders.
Share this: learn one game fully by watching before playing.

puzzles.title: The Warden's Whisper
puzzles.question: Prisoners A, B, C await fate; one is pardoned. The warden tells A that B will die. What are A's vs C's chances now?
choices: A stays one-third; C rises to two-thirds
puzzles.correctAnswer: A stays one-third; C rises to two-thirds
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — naming B sacrifices B's third to C, never to A. A's pardon chance never moved; C inherits the freed probability.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! A stays one-third while C rises to two-thirds. The warden's news spends B's share entirely on C.
puzzles.lessonContent:
News about others reallocates their share, never yours.
Prisoners, doors, and envelopes all obey this conservation.
Track whose slice the news spends before celebrating.
Share this: retell the three-prisoners twist at dinner.

puzzles.title: The Golden Drawer
puzzles.question: Boxes hold gold-gold, silver-silver, gold-silver. A drawn drawer shows gold. How likely is the other drawer gold?
choices: Two-thirds — the other drawer is gold
puzzles.correctAnswer: Two-thirds — the other drawer is gold
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — three gold drawers against three silver mean a gold draw points to the double-gold box two-thirds of the time. Draws sample drawers, not boxes.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — two-thirds: the other drawer is gold. Gold drawers cluster in the double-gold box, weighting the odds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Samples come from drawers, and rich boxes hold more of them.
Counting containers instead of contents is the classic slip.
Weight every hypothesis by how many draws it supplies.
Share this: demo the three-box paradox with coins.

puzzles.title: The Five Doors
puzzles.question: Five sealed envelopes hold one prize ticket. Yours is marked; the host tears open two losing envelopes. Move your claim to a survivor?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — staying keeps 20% while the 80% remainder splits over two survivors at 40% each. Either switch doubles your fate.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: 40% beats 20%. Two reveals leave two doors sharing the 80% your pick never held.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Multiple reveals still obey one conservation law.
Your pick's share never grows; survivors divide the rest.
Bigger casts shrink individual shares but keep the rule.
Share this: compute one five-door split by hand.

puzzles.title: The Double Reveal
puzzles.question: Four caskets hide one gem. After your claim, the host lifts two empty lids, leaving a single rival casket. Take it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — one pick holds 25% and two reveals pile the other 75% onto the last door. Two reveals, one jackpot door.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Switch: 75% wins. Your quarter never budged while the host swept three-quarters onto a single door.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Each reveal sweeps more of the field onto the survivor.
Late survivors carry the weight of every opened door.
Let the host's labor work for you — then take it.
Share this: feel 75% land on one door and grin.

puzzles.title: The Lucky Number
puzzles.question: Does always picking door 1 beat picking randomly each show?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — every door starts equal, so door 1 and a dice-picked door both hold one-third. Rituals can't bend symmetry.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — no difference: symmetry protects you. No door outranks another before the reveal, however chosen.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Symmetric choices are interchangeable — pick fast and move on.
Superstition taxes the indecisive with wasted rituals.
Save deliberation for asymmetric decisions.
Share this: pick one trivial choice by dice today.

puzzles.title: The Strange Host
puzzles.question: This host opens a door ONLY when you first picked the car. A door opens. Now what?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — a host who opens only for winners just announced your victory. The reveal itself is the message; read it.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — stay: opening confesses your win. This host's policy turns every reveal into a winner's certificate.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Policies leak through actions — decode the policy, not the move.
A reveal conditioned on your success announces it.
Ask why THIS move happened now before reacting.
Share this: read one policy hidden inside one action.

puzzles.title: The Cruel Host
puzzles.question: At this table the curtain rises only to mock a losing first pick. Tonight it rises. Where is the car?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — a host who opens only for losers just announced your defeat. Flee the losing door while flight is offered.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: opening confesses your loss. The policy guarantees your pick is wrong whenever a reveal occurs.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Conditioned reveals are confessions wearing stage makeup.
Losers get curtains; winners get silence — learn the grammar.
Meta-rules about behavior outrank the behavior itself.
Share this: spot one rule that flips the obvious move.

puzzles.title: The Fifty Fallacy
puzzles.question: 'Two doors remain, so it must be fifty-fifty.' What is wrong with that?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — 'two doors left' ignores HOW one left. The forced reveal funneled two-thirds onto the survivor; counting doors erases that history.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Wrong: history concentrates the odds. Two survivors are not two equals when one inherited the opened door's share.
puzzles.lessonContent:
'Two options' never implies 'fifty-fifty' — ask about their pasts.
Equal counts with unequal histories deceive everywhere.
Resumes matter more than headcounts in odds and hiring.
Share this: kill one fifty-fifty myth with its backstory.

puzzles.title: The Thousand Shows
puzzles.question: A computer simulates 1,000 classic shows with always-switch. About how many wins?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — simulation sides with switching about two times in three. Frequencies confirm the fractions; run it yourself.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — about 667 switcher wins. A thousand simulated shows let the two-thirds emerge from noise.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Simulations settle bar bets that algebra cannot.
Code ten lines and watch theory become frequency.
Empiricism is the friend logic deserves.
Share this: simulate one paradox and show a skeptic.

puzzles.title: The Sting Study
puzzles.question: Losing after switching feels worse than losing after staying. What does that predict?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly — switch-losses sting more, so players cling to their doors. Anticipated regret, not math, picks the strategy.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Players stay too often. The extra sting of a failed switch scares contestants into the worse strategy.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Feelings tax rationality — regret aversion costs real money.
Design choices that forgive the better strategy.
Notice when comfort, not calculation, steers you.
Share this: take one right-but-scary switch this week.

puzzles.title: The Loaded Stage
puzzles.question: The car sits behind door 1 twice as often as elsewhere. You pick door 2; the host opens door 3 (goat). Switch to door 1?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — with door 1 doubly likely, a reveal elsewhere concentrates even harder: switching to door 1 wins four times in five. Priors amplify the edge.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: now 80%. The loaded prior plus the reveal stack together, pushing the survivor past the classic two-thirds.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Unequal priors stack with reveals instead of canceling.
Update in order: prior first, evidence second.
Loaded dice and loaded doors obey one update rule.
Share this: update one belief twice — prior, then news.

puzzles.title: The Cash Temptation
puzzles.question: Car worth $10,000. After the reveal, the host offers $4,000 cash to walk away. Take it?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — switching wins a $10,000 car two-thirds of the time: about $6,667 of expectation against $4,000 cash. The math declines politely.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Close! Refuse: switching beats the cash. Two-thirds of ten thousand outweighs four thousand certain — take the odds, not the bribe.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Price every offer against expectation, not excitement.
Certainty seduces; arithmetic decides.
Game shows monetize your fear of variance.
Share this: compute one expectation before accepting one offer.

puzzles.title: The Great Shuffle
puzzles.question: After the classic reveal, the host shuffles the car randomly behind the two closed doors. Now what?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — shuffling re-randomizes the car between the two doors. Information destroyed is probability reset.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — fifty-fifty: shuffling erases history. The car now sits randomly behind either door, and the reveal's work is undone.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Randomization destroys information as surely as fire destroys paper.
Shuffles, redraws, and resets return odds to flat.
Guard information — it evaporates on disturbance.
Share this: name one shuffle that reset somebody's edge.

puzzles.title: The Return Ticket
puzzles.question: You switched to the survivor. The host offers to switch you BACK for $100. Accept?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — switch then switch-back equals never moving: one-third. The extra ceremony can't launder the odds.

puzzles.title: The Boring Film

puzzles.title: The Sour Vacation

Deposits are designed to feel like chains — they aren't.

puzzles.title: The Corked Bottle

Trial end-dates deserve calendar alarms.

puzzles.title: The Bleeding Shop
puzzles.question: A shop bleeds monthly despite a signed lease. Logic says the lease alone shouldn't keep it open.

Leases feel like destinies — they're just expensive options.

puzzles.title: The Streak Trap

Streaks gamify persistence past usefulness.

puzzles.title: The Thirsty Car

puzzles.title: The Dead Talk

puzzles.title: The Dull Badge
puzzles.question: A conference proves dull on day one. Logic says the fee shouldn't chain them to day two.
puzzles.correctExplanation: True — the conference fee is gone; only today's sessions' value matters. A dull hall taxes two days for one fee's sake.

Conferences sell FOMO by the badge.

puzzles.title: The Dusty Shelf

Inventory is frozen optimism paying rent.

Clearance beats delusion at any margin.

puzzles.title: The Joyless Dinner
puzzles.question: Reason says decades of friendship alone shouldn't force joyless monthly dinners.

Audit circles yearly for energy, not tenure.

puzzles.title: The Two-Thirds Rule
puzzles.question: In the classic three-door game with a knowing host, switching wins two times in three.

puzzles.title: The Loyal Half
puzzles.question: After the classic reveal, staying with your first pick wins half the time.

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Staying keeps the original one-third; the survivor holds two-thirds.

Two survivors with unequal histories deceive counters.
'One of two' is not 'fifty-fifty' without equal pasts.
Histories weight doors; counts merely list them.

puzzles.title: The Ninety-Nine Percent

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's true. One pick in a hundred is almost surely wrong, and 98 reveals leave one heir to 99%.

puzzles.title: The Lucky Stumble

puzzles.title: The Premature Curtain

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's true. News before commitment spreads evenly across all doors, favoring none.

puzzles.title: The Blind Swap

puzzles.title: The Lazy Half
puzzles.question: Two closed doors remaining always means a fifty-fifty chance each.

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's false. One door carries its original third plus the revealed share; the other carries only its third.

Equal counts never guarantee equal chances.

Fifty-fifty needs symmetric pasts, not pairs.

puzzles.title: The Fresh Eyes
puzzles.question: A newcomer who saw nothing and picks between the two closed doors faces fifty-fifty.

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's true. They made no first pick, so no reveal ever worked in their favor.

Latecomers inherit furniture, never fortunes.

puzzles.title: The Keen Spectator

puzzles.title: The Winner's Curtain

puzzles.title: The Mocking Curtain

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Equal denominators turn totals into honest averages that follow their parts.

Equal mixes keep totals truthful.
Balance denominators before trusting blends.

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Women applied to tougher departments; within departments rates matched.

Disparity in totals never alone proves discrimination.
Selection patterns mimic bias with precision.

Disaggregation is the universal solvent of reversals.

Tables with subgroups tell truth; totals tell tales.

puzzles.title: The Broken Math
puzzles.question: Simpson reversals violate the laws of arithmetic.

Paradoxes of aggregation obey arithmetic perfectly.

puzzles.title: The Enrolled Illusion

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Identical rates with different mixes still reverse; mixes alone suffice.

Weights write outcomes rates merely propose.

Denominators decide more than numerators.

puzzles.title: The Fair Control
puzzles.question: Equal-mix control comparisons confirm honest rankings.

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is composition. Light parts build heavy totals routinely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Wholes surprise their lightest parts.
Cheap bricks raise dear houses.

puzzles.title: The Speedy Squad
puzzles.question: 'Fast team, so every runner is fast!' Name the scatter.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — team speed describes averages, never every runner. Piles hide their grains.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is division. Fast teams shelter slow legs comfortably.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Group speed never sprints every leg.
Averages cloak their weakest members.
Inspect parts before praising them.

puzzles.title: The Slippery Word
puzzles.question: 'Light bags, light colors — all light!' Name the slide.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — 'light' slides from weight to color mid-pitch. One word, two wallets.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is equivocation. Weight-light and color-light share spelling only.

Puns prove nothing, however pretty.

puzzles.title: The Garage Guitar
puzzles.question: 'Garage-made guitar — must sound awful!' Name the judgment.

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is genetic fallacy. Garages birth legends and junk alike.

Birthplaces never tune guitars or ideas.
Play the thing before judging the shed.
Origins narrate; tests decide.

puzzles.title: The Split Clock
puzzles.question: 'You say 8, I say 10 — meet at 9!' The clock says 8:40. Name the split.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct — splitting arrival times equally serves nobody's facts. Compromise arbitrates interests, never clocks.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is middle ground. Halfway between claims lands on nobody's truth.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Midpoints mediate deals, never facts.
Clocks don't compromise with wishes.
Reserve splits for interests alone.

puzzles.title: The Ancient Doubt
puzzles.question: 'Mountains can't be THAT old — impossible!' Name the limit.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Yes — bafflement measures the mind, never the mountain. Peaks ignore disbelief.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is personal incredulity. Inability to picture vast time dents nothing.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Disbelief reports on believers, not mountains.
Deep time dwarfs every imagination.
Trade 'impossible' for 'show me'.

puzzles.title: The Glowing Ad
puzzles.question: A ad shows three glowing reviews, hiding two hundred angry ones. Name the frame.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Right — three five-star quotes frame; two hundred complaints crop out. Brochures curate, never confess.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is cherry-picking. Friendly quotes exhibit; full records decide.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Curated quotes advertise; they never audit.
Demand denominators behind glowing excerpts.
Full records embarrass selective frames.

puzzles.title: The Thousand-Time Prophet
puzzles.question: A being that predicted you correctly a thousand times offers an opaque million box and a transparent thousand. Take one box or both?
puzzles.correctAnswer: One box — the predictor foresaw it
acceptedAnswers: One box — the predictor foresaw it
puzzles.correctExplanation: One box wins — a near-perfect predictor fills it exactly for one-boxers. Expected value, not dominance, decides under prediction.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is one box — the predictor foresaw it. Two-boxers find emptiness; one-boxers find millions, by the predictor's design.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Prediction couples your choice to the world before you choose.
Expected value counts what foresight arranges.
Dominance assumes independence prediction destroys.

puzzles.title: The Visible Million
puzzles.question: Now the million box is transparent — you SEE the cash, placed for predicted one-boxers. Still one box, or grab both?
puzzles.correctExplanation: One box still wins — the visible million was placed for predicted one-boxers. Seeing the stake doesn't untie the prediction.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is one box — seeing changes nothing. The million sits there because the prophet foresaw restraint.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Visible stakes tempt violations of invisible logic.
Seeing the prize changes feelings, never forecasts.
Hold strategy against spectacle always.

puzzles.title: The Bare Edge
puzzles.question: The prophet is right only 51% of the time. Million versus thousand boxes — one or both?
puzzles.correctExplanation: One box wins at 51%: 510,000 beats 491,000. Bare edges above chance still crown restraint.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is one box — even 51% suffices. The arithmetic favors restraint down to a hair above coin-flip accuracy.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Tiny predictive edges compound into commanding strategies.
Compute thresholds instead of trusting round numbers.
Fifty-one percent can rule like ninety-nine.

puzzles.title: The Open Pair
puzzles.question: Both boxes stand open — you see exactly what each holds. Take one or both?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Both boxes win — with contents visible, prediction is spent and dominance rules. No paradox survives full transparency.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is both boxes — transparency decides. Seeing everything dissolves the forecast's grip entirely.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Full transparency dissolves prediction paradoxes instantly.
Secrets power prophets; daylight disarms them.
Demand visibility before surrendering dominance.

puzzles.title: The Inverted Prophet
puzzles.question: This prophet is wrong every single time. Million-or-thousand boxes await. One or both?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Two boxes win — an always-wrong prophet fills the million for predicted two-boxers. Invert the prophet, invert the play.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is two boxes — perversity pays. Wrongness is information too; ride it backwards.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Perfectly wrong predictors inform as surely as right ones.
Invert every signal from an inverted source.
Perversity is reliability wearing a mask.

puzzles.title: The Binding Contract
puzzles.question: Before the prophet predicts, you may sign an unbreakable one-box contract. Sign or stay free?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Sign first — a binding one-box contract, signed before prediction, compels the prophet to fill the box. Freedom surrendered early buys millions.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sign first — precommitment pays. Chains chosen beforehand become fortunes afterward.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Binding your future self reshapes others' predictions now.
Contracts with yourself pay in others' behavior.
Freedom kept can cost more than freedom spent.

puzzles.title: The Desert Promise
puzzles.question: Stranded, you promise a driver a fortune for rescue. Rescued, must you pay?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Pay — drivers rescue known payers; your paying disposition is the ticket. Evidential agents keep profitable habits.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is pay — dispositions rescue. Rescuers predict payers, so payers get rescued.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Habits that predict rescue earn rescue.
Dispositions travel ahead of you into others' forecasts.
Cultivate the traits rescuers select.

puzzles.title: The Fatal Urge
puzzles.question: A gene causes both smoking urge and fatal lesions; smoking itself is harmless. Light up?
puzzles.correctExplanation: Abstain — smoking evidences the lesion that kills, whatever causation says. Evidence, not arrows, guides evidential agents.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is abstain — smoke evidences lesions. Lighting up certifies the fatal condition statistically.
puzzles.lessonContent:
Symptoms of doom deserve refusal even when harmless.
Evidence guides where causation shrugs.
Correlations command the cautious correctly.

puzzles.title: The Hidden Coin
puzzles.question: You may flip a hidden coin the prophet cannot predict to choose. Then one box or both?

puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is two boxes — blind chance blinds it. Sealed randomness severs prediction's grip.

Unseen randomness dissolves prediction games entirely.
Opacity is armor against prophets.

puzzles.title: The Counterfactual Wager

Priors price every pitch before details do.
Vastness of prize never substitutes proof.

puzzles.title: The Yielding Principle
puzzles.question: Dominance says two boxes; expected value says one. Which principle yields?
puzzles.correctExplanation: One box wins — dominance assumes causal independence that prediction annihilates. Principles bow to forecasts here.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The answer is one box — evidence beats dominance. The sure-thing principle misfires under perfect foresight.

Dominance reigns where independence holds.
Forecasts suspend textbook rules legitimately.

puzzles.title: The Character Pill

Air banks daytime heat for nighttime spending.

puzzles.title: Truth Tellers
puzzles.question: You meet two people at a fork in the road. One always tells the truth, one always lies. One path leads to treasure, the other to danger. You can ask ONE question to ONE person. What do you ask to find the treasure?
choices: What would the other person say leads to treasure?
Is this the path to treasure?
puzzles.correctAnswer: What would the other person say leads to treasure?
puzzles.lessonContent:
The 'knights and knaves' puzzle was popularized by logician Raymond Smullyan.
The trick: a truth-teller and a liar will give the SAME wrong answer about what the other would say.
This is because: truth-teller reports the liar's lie (false), liar lies about what truth-teller would say (also false).
You then take the OPPOSITE path to what they say.

Share this: this puzzle is famous for a reason â€” ask someone 'What one question would you ask?' and watch their brain short-circuit.
puzzles.correctExplanation: Correct! Both will point to the wrong path. The truth-teller will honestly say what the liar would say (wrong path), and the liar will lie about what the truth-teller would say (also wrong path). Take the opposite.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The clever trick: ask 'What would the other say?' Both will point to the WRONG path. The truth-teller reports the liar's lie (wrong), the liar lies about the truth-teller's answer (also wrong). Take the opposite path.

puzzles.title: The Missing Dollar
puzzles.question: Three friends pay $30 for a hotel room ($10 each). Later the clerk realizes the room is only $25, so gives $5 to the bellboy to return. The bellboy keeps $2 and gives $1 back to each friend. Now each friend paid $9 ($27 total) plus the bellboy's $2 = $29. Where is the missing dollar?
choices: There is no missing dollar â€” the logic is flawed
puzzles.correctAnswer: There is no missing dollar â€” the logic is flawed
puzzles.lessonContent:
This puzzle tricks you with irrelevant arithmetic.
The correct math: $25 (hotel) + $2 (bellboy) + $3 (refund) = $30.
The error: adding $27 (what friends paid) + $2 (bellboy's portion) is double-counting.
The $2 is already INCLUDED in the $27 ($25 hotel + $2 bellboy).
puzzles.correctExplanation: Exactly! The puzzle misdirects you. The $27 already includes the bellboy's $2. The proper accounting is $25 (hotel) + $2 (bellboy) + $3 (refund) = $30. There's no missing dollar.
puzzles.incorrectExplanation: The trick is in how the numbers are added. The friends paid $27 ($25 for the room + $2 to the bellboy). Adding the bellboy's $2 again is wrong. Correct: $25 (room) + $2 (bellboy) + $3 (refund) = $30.
